docs.title: Bulwark
docs.text:
One scan, one deduplicated list of findings. Bulwark runs five open-source security scanners against a repository, merges what they agree on, and shows you a single list you can actually work through.

Every scanner covers a different slice, so you run several, and then drown. A single SQL injection shows up as a Bandit finding, a Semgrep finding and a CWE entry; one vulnerable npm package appears in Trivy and OSV-Scanner, each with its own severity. Bulwark treats the pile as one problem:

  1. Run Bandit, Semgrep CE, Gitleaks, Trivy and OSV-Scanner, each in a locked-down container.
  2. Normalize every result into one Finding schema.
  3. Correlate: merge duplicates across tools, keep every tool's evidence, take the highest severity.
  4. Map each finding to its CWE and OWASP Top 10:2021 category.
  5. Rank by risk: severity combined with EPSS and CISA's known-exploited list.
  6. Show and export it: web UI, API, CLI, and downloadable SARIF, HTML and PDF reports.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Quickstart

    Get a scan running against your own code in a few minutes, either the full hosted stack (Docker Compose) or the standalone CLI.

  • Concepts

    How a scan actually works: the pipeline, the risk score, the vulnerability taxonomy, and what "reachable" means.

  • Writing a plugin

    Add a scanner Bulwark doesn't ship, as an ordinary installable Python package -- no fork required.

  • Policy cookbook

    Write a Rego policy for rules severity thresholds can't express ("no secrets, ever", "an accepted risk expires after 90 days").

  • API reference

    Every endpoint, generated straight from the running app's own OpenAPI document -- never hand-maintained, never out of sync with it.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
1.0.0. All 26 weeks of the original plan are done -- scanners, correlation, risk ranking, LLM-backed fix suggestions, reachability, a VS Code extension and GitHub Action, SBOMs and signed attestations -- and a second, larger plan (multi-tenancy, a plugin SDK, DAST, attack-path modeling, and more) is in progress on top of it. Not ready for untrusted multi-user hosting yet: see Limits in the project README.

Source: https://github.com/rago12bit/cybernatics. License: Apache-2.0.

docs.title: OWASP ASVS 4.0.3 self-assessment (Level 1 + 2)
docs.text:
Bulwark scanning other projects for security issues without holding itself to the same bar would be a strange place to stop, so this is a real self-audit against OWASP ASVS 4.0.3, Level 2. Every row cites real code or docs, verified by reading the file, not assumed from a description. Where something is genuinely absent, it says so plainly rather than being left off the table.

Status key: Met (verified in the code), Partial (some real mitigation, a real gap remains), Not met (no mitigation found), N/A (the feature this control applies to doesn't exist in Bulwark's architecture, explained inline). Where a control area applies to something Bulwark doesn't have (native mobile apps, biometric auth, server-rendered HTML forms with CSRF tokens for a stateless API), whole sub-areas are marked N/A once rather than enumerated line by line.

Last reviewed: 2026-10-01 (Week 48 task 3, plan §22.3). Three real gaps found during this review were fixed as part of it, not just written down: see the "Fixed during this review" note under V8/V9/V10/V12.

docs.title: V1 — Architecture, Design and Threat Modeling
docs.text: Control Status Evidence A documented, current threat model exists Met docs/THREAT-MODEL.md — STRIDE-based, per-threat status, last reviewed 2026-09-25 Security decisions are recorded with rationale, not just implemented silently Met 33 ADRs in docs/adr/, each with a Status line; e.g. ADR-002 (Docker isolation), ADR-0013 (tenancy/RLS), ADR-0019 (audit log), ADR-0032/0033 (encryption, mTLS) High-value components (auth, tenancy, sandboxing) are componentized, not scattered Met core/tokens.py (auth), core/tenancy.py (isolation), core/sandbox/ (sandboxing) are each single-purpose modules other code depends on, not reimplemented per call site Known limitations are disclosed, not silently assumed away Met SECURITY.md's "Known limits" section; core/tenancy.py:29-35's own docstring on the shared-token org-claiming limitation

docs.title: V2 — Authentication
docs.text:
Bulwark has no password-based authentication anywhere in the codebase (confirmed: no password hashing, no login form, no "forgot password" flow exist). Authentication is bearer-token only. Controls about password policy, account lockout, biometrics, and OTP hardware tokens are N/A — there is no password to have a policy about.

Control Status Evidence Credentials are compared in constant time, not with == Met api/deps.py:49-50 — hmac.compare_digest for the shared token Tokens are not stored or logged in recoverable form Met core/tokens.py:58-59 — SHA-256 hash stored, never the raw token; raw token is shown to the operator exactly once at creation (cli/main.py's token create command) Tokens can be scoped to least privilege Met core/tokens.py:23 — SCOPES (scans:read/scans:write, fixes:read/fixes:write, ingest:read/ingest:write); api/deps.py:116-125's require_scope Tokens can expire and be revoked Met api/deps.py:83-93 (expiry check on every request); cli/main.py's token revoke command Rate limiting on authentication attempts (brute-force resistance) Not met No rate limiting found on the auth path itself in api/deps.py. The only rate limiting in the codebase (core/llm/limits.py's UsageLimiter) gates LLM-feature cost, not authentication attempts. A high-entropy 40-hex-char token (core/tokens.py:14-23) makes brute-forcing impractical regardless, but there is no explicit lockout/backoff mechanism Multi-factor authentication N/A No user-identity concept exists yet (real per-user auth is plan §19.2, not built — this is a known, disclosed future item, not an oversight)

docs.title: V3 — Session Management
docs.text:
Bulwark's API is fully stateless: no server-side session store, no session cookies. Every request re-authenticates via its bearer token. Session-fixation, session-timeout, and CSRF-token controls are N/A in the traditional sense — there is no session to fix, time out, or forge a request against via a stolen cookie.

Control Status Evidence No session identifier is transmitted that could be fixed or hijacked Met (N/A by design) api/deps.py:100-113 — auth is per-request from the Authorization header, nothing session-based exists to attack A revoked credential takes effect immediately, not at next login Met Scoped-token revocation is checked on every request (api/deps.py:83-93), not cached

docs.title: V4 — Access Control
docs.text: Control Status Evidence Tenant data is isolated by a mechanism the database itself enforces, not application code alone Met migrations/versions/0005_tenancy_rls.py:132-154 — Postgres ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY + FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY + CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation on assets/scans/tool_runs/findings/issues, extended to every later table (llm_usage, verified_fix_runs, hypotheses, code_chunks, data_retention_policies, scan_data_keys, ...) The application connects as a role RLS actually restricts, not a superuser Met migrations/versions/0005_tenancy_rls.py:80-97 creates the non-superuser bulwark_app role — the docstring is explicit that FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is a no-op against a superuser regardless of policies Least-privilege database identity per service, not one shared credential Met migrations/versions/0020_per_service_db_roles.py — bulwark_api/bulwark_worker/bulwark_fixagent, each a distinct mTLS-authenticated identity; bulwark_app itself set NOLOGIN API scopes are enforced server-side on every relevant endpoint Met require_scope(...) dependency (api/deps.py:116-125), applied per-endpoint in api/main.py Cross-tenant access is proven impossible, not just assumed from code review Met tests/integration/test_tenancy_rls_docker.py, test_data_protection_rls_docker.py — live tests against real Postgres RLS, run in CI on every push (.github/workflows/ci.yml's tenancy-rls job) A caller cannot claim access to organizations it doesn't belong to Partial Disclosed, known limitation: core/tenancy.py:29-35 — the legacy shared bearer token can specify any X-Bulwark-Org header value and RLS will isolate that org's data correctly, but nothing yet verifies the caller is entitled to act as that org (real per-organization identity is plan §19.2, not yet built). Scoped tokens (core/tokens.py) close this for themselves — an org is fixed on the token row and the header is ignored (api/deps.py:128-139)

docs.title: V5 — Validation, Sanitization and Encoding
docs.text: Control Status Evidence Output is escaped by default, not manually per call site Met React's default JSX escaping; no dangerouslySetInnerHTML found rendering scan-derived content Attacker-controlled content (a scanned repo's own code) cannot execute as script in the browser Met web/tests/xss.test.tsx — a Finding with <script>, onerror=, javascript:/data: URLs injected into every field; asserts no live script/event-handler survives and only https:// reference links pass an explicit allowlist A per-request CSP with no unsafe-inline for scripts backs the escaping Met web/proxy.ts:11-25 — nonce-based CSP, strict-dynamic, no unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval in production API request bodies are structurally validated before use Met api/schemas.py — Pydantic models throughout (464 lines), e.g. Literal type discriminators, max_length constraints SQL queries are parameterized, never string-concatenated Met No f-string/%/.format()-built SQL passed to execute() found in core/persistence/repo.py; the ORM (SQLAlchemy) is used throughout. The two places raw SQL text appears (migrations/versions/0005_tenancy_rls.py, 0020_per_service_db_roles.py) bind org id as a parameter (core/tenancy.py:51-54, explicit comment: "always a bound parameter, never concatenated into SQL text") and embed a password literal only inside a DO $$ $$ block (which can't take driver placeholders), sourced only from scripts/init-env.sh's random hex generator, never user input — documented and justified in the code, not an unexamined oversight Archive extraction rejects path traversal, symlinks, and decompression bombs Met core/ingest.py:28-46 — _safe_dest rejects absolute paths and traversal; symlinks/special files rejected for both zip and tar; size/count/ratio limits checked against both metadata and actual bytes written

docs.title: V6 — Stored Cryptography
docs.text: Control Status Evidence Data at rest is encrypted with a modern, authenticated cipher Met core/secrets/envelope.py:17-39 — AES-256-GCM via cryptography.hazmat, random 12-byte nonce per call, nonce \|\| ciphertext+tag format Encryption keys are managed by a dedicated system, not embedded in application config Met core/secrets/openbao.py — OpenBao Transit engine mints/unwraps per-organization data keys; plaintext keys are never persisted, only OpenBao's own wrapped ciphertext A ciphertext cannot be swapped onto a different record and still decrypt Met core/secrets/envelope.py:33-34 — the storage key is bound as AEAD associated data; core/persistence/storage.py:79,85 passes it through; a live test proves a swapped ciphertext fails closed (DecryptionError), not a wrong-but-plausible plaintext Cryptographic failures fail closed, not open Met core/secrets/envelope.py:42-55 — InvalidTag is mapped to a hard DecryptionError, never a silently-accepted fallback Password hashing (bcrypt/argon2/scrypt) N/A No password authentication exists anywhere in the codebase (see V2) High-entropy token identifiers are hashed before storage Met core/tokens.py:58-59 — SHA-256 (a reasonable, standard choice for a 40-hex-char random token, which is not a low-entropy secret bcrypt-class slow hashing exists to protect)

docs.title: V7 — Error Handling and Logging
docs.text: Control Status Evidence Logs are structured and machine-parseable, not free-text string concatenation Met core/observability/logs.py:24-27 — JSON-line logs carrying scan_id/trace_id/span_id via contextvars Log injection (newline forgery) is structurally prevented Met JSON-line format means a value containing a newline is encoded, not interpreted as a new log line (core/observability/logs.py's own docstring) Secrets are scrubbed from logs, not just from user-facing output Met core/observability/logs.py:20 imports the same core.llm.scrub.scrub_secrets detector the LLM layer uses Security-relevant events are recorded in a tamper-evident audit trail Met core/audit.py — hash-chained entries (entry_hash = SHA256(seq \|\| prev_hash \|\| timestamp \|\| actor \|\| action \|\| target \|\| payload_digest)), genesis hash fixed, payload stored as a digest so deleting the underlying record (a revoked token, a removed installation) never breaks the chain The audit chain's integrity can be independently verified Met bulwark audit verify (cli/main.py) walks the whole chain and recomputes every hash; core/audit_rekor.py can publish checkpoints to Sigstore Rekor's public transparency log (opt-in per publish, not automatic — a real, permanent public write is deliberately not silent) Error responses do not leak stack traces or internal details to the client Met No debug=True passed to FastAPI(...) (api/main.py:248), so FastAPI's safe default (no traceback in the response body) applies; HTTPException call sites raise clean, specific messages, not interpolated exception internals

docs.title: V8 — Data Protection
docs.text:
Fixed during this review: none needed — this area was already solid going in (see below).

Control Status Evidence Sensitive data is encrypted at rest with per-tenant, per-record keys Met See V6 — core/secrets/envelope.py + core/secrets/openbao.py, wired into core/persistence/storage.py's EncryptingObjectStore Data can be made permanently unrecoverable on request/expiry, including against backups Met core/retention.py:38-73 — crypto-shredding: destroying a scan's wrapped data key (not the ciphertext object itself, and never the Scan/Issue/Finding rows) makes it permanently unreadable, backups included, without needing to locate and erase every copy Retention is configurable per tenant, not a single global policy Met core/persistence/repo.get_retention_days — per-org, default 7 days, configurable via GET/PUT /settings/retention Secrets are redacted from data that reaches a person or a model, not just from the primary output Met core/redact.py:21,36-37 (findings), core/llm/scrub.py/core/llm/pii.py (LLM prompts), Gitleaks output redacted at the source tool (core/pipeline.py:348) Sensitive data does not appear in URLs or query strings Met Scoped tokens are sent as Authorization: Bearer, never a query parameter; no grep hits for tokens/secrets in URL construction in web/lib/api.ts

docs.title: V9 — Communications
docs.text: Control Status Evidence Internal service-to-service connections are mutually authenticated Met docker/postgres/pg_hba.conf — cert clientcert=verify-full required for every network connection to Postgres; migrations/versions/0020_per_service_db_roles.py ties each service's certificate CN to its own database role A third-party dependency that can't meet the internal standard is an explicit, scoped exception, not a silent gap Met docker/postgres/pg_hba.conf's own comment: Temporal's auto-setup image (temporal_svc) is carved out by role name for password auth, since it cannot present a client certificate — every role Bulwark's own code uses keeps the certificate requirement unconditionally HTTP Strict Transport Security is sent wherever the deployment is actually served over HTTPS Fixed during this review Previously: web/proxy.ts set HSTS only when NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO_ONLY=1, meaning any other production deployment — including one that does terminate real TLS — never got it. Fixed: HSTS now also fires when an operator explicitly sets BULWARK_FORCE_HTTPS=1 (web/proxy.ts, this review). Forcing it on by default for every NODE_ENV=production build was deliberately rejected: Bulwark's documented self-hosted path may run over plain HTTP with no TLS termination at all, and HSTS would make browsers refuse to reconnect entirely in that case — opt-in is the honest fix, not a default that could break a real, documented deployment path Cross-origin isolation headers are set on real pages Met web/proxy.ts — Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp, -Opener-Policy: same-origin, -Resource-Policy: same-origin, all added and live-verified (real browser load, zero console errors, ZAP re-scan) as part of Week 48 task 2's own ZAP baseline findings CORS is an explicit allowlist, never a wildcard Met core/config.py:25 (default origin list), api/main.py:255-260 — explicit CORSMiddleware origins, comment "never '*'", methods and headers both restricted

docs.title: V10 — Malicious Code
docs.text: Control Status Evidence Untrusted code (a scanned repository) never executes on the host outside a sandbox Met core/sandbox/docker_runtime.py:27-62 — one ephemeral container per tool: --network=none, --read-only rootfs, --cap-drop=ALL, non-root uid, --security-opt=no-new-privileges, memory/CPU/pids limits, target mounted read-only; ADR-002 A deeper isolation layer exists for the case a container escape isn't enough Partial ADR-0031's own status line: SandboxRuntime/gVisor backend is written and argv-tested, but has never actually executed (no Linux dev host, no macOS runsc build) — a real, disclosed gap, not a claim of completion Bulwark's own dependencies are scanned for known vulnerabilities, not just the dependencies it scans for others Fixed during this review Previously: no evidence of this at all — Bulwark ships OSV-Scanner/Grype as products for other people's code (ADR-0024) but had no equivalent check on its own pyproject.toml/package.json. Fixed: .github/workflows/ci.yml's new dependency-audit job runs pip-audit and npm audit on every push and pull request; .github/dependabot.yml (new) proposes weekly update PRs for pip, both npm projects, and GitHub Actions versions Third-party licenses are checked, not just vulnerabilities Met scripts/gen-licenses.py — a real policy (deny AGPL/SSPL/BUSL-class licenses, flag weak-copyleft for review), enforced in CI's licenses job

docs.title: V11 — Business Logic
docs.text: Control Status Evidence Expensive, cost-bearing operations (LLM calls) are rate-limited per tenant Met core/llm/limits.py's UsageLimiter, wired at api/deps.py:36; 429 responses on every LLM-backed endpoint Concurrent long-running workflows are capped Met api/main.py's verified-fix/scan endpoints return 429 on a per-organization concurrency cap General-purpose API rate limiting / abuse prevention on ordinary read/write endpoints Not met No general request-rate-limiting middleware found in api/main.py/api/deps.py. The only rate limiting that exists is cost-driven (LLM usage), not abuse-prevention-driven. A single-operator, bearer-token-gated deployment (this project's current documented trust model, SECURITY.md's "Known limits") makes this lower-severity than it would be for a multi-tenant public service, but it is a real, disclosed gap for anyone exposing the API more broadly

docs.title: V12 — Files and Resources
docs.text:
Fixed during this review: see below.

Control Status Evidence Uploaded archives are protected against zip-slip / path traversal Met core/ingest.py:28-35 — _safe_dest rejects absolute paths, null bytes, and traversal via .resolve() + parent-containment check Uploaded archives are protected against decompression bombs Met core/ingest.py:38-46 — compressed size, uncompressed size, file count, and compression-ratio limits, checked against both metadata and actual streamed bytes Symlinks and special files inside an archive are rejected Met core/ingest.py:73-74 (zip), 93-94 (tar) Pathologically deep directory structures inside an archive are rejected Fixed during this review Previously: SECURITY.md claimed "depth limits" but no such check existed in core/ingest.py — an inaccurate claim, found and corrected by actually checking the code rather than trusting the doc. Fixed: Limits.max_depth (default 64 path components), enforced in _safe_dest, tested (tests/unit/test_ingest.py's new depth-limit tests). SECURITY.md's claim is now accurate rather than aspirational

docs.title: V13 — API and Web Service
docs.text: Control Status Evidence The API is documented from its actual implementation, not a hand-maintained spec that can drift Met scripts/gen-api-docs.py generates docs/openapi.json/docs/api.md from the live FastAPI app CORS is scoped, not permissive Met See V9 Every endpoint but the health check requires authentication Met SECURITY.md's own stated control, api/deps.py's require_auth/require_scope dependencies applied per-route in api/main.py Interactive API documentation exposure is a considered choice, not a default left unexamined Partial FastAPI's /docs//openapi.json are live by default (FastAPI(...) at api/main.py:248 passes no docs_url=None). This exposes the API's schema to anyone who can reach it — not a vulnerability on its own (every real call still requires a bearer token), but worth an explicit decision for any deployment that shouldn't advertise its API surface publicly; not disabled or made configurable in this review

docs.title: V14 — Configuration
docs.text: Control Status Evidence The application refuses to start with an insecure configuration, rather than starting insecurely Met api/main.py:244-247 — refuses to start if BULWARK_API_TOKEN is unset or below the minimum length Debug/verbose error modes cannot be accidentally enabled in production Met No debug flag exists in core/config.py at all; no debug=True passed to FastAPI(...) — there is no configuration knob to leak, rather than one that defaults safely Secrets prefer a dedicated secrets store over plain environment variables Met core/secrets/resolve.py — GitHub App credentials, the API token, and the LLM API key all prefer OpenBao's KV store when configured, with an unconditional environment-variable fallback (bulwark secrets migrate-env moves existing values over) Security-relevant HTTP response headers are set comprehensively Met web/proxy.ts — CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Embedder/Opener/Resource-Policy, conditional HSTS (see V9) Default credentials are never shipped Met Every secret (scripts/init-env.sh) is generated fresh via openssl rand -hex 24; nothing ships with a fixed default password or token

docs.title: Summary of gaps found and their disposition
docs.text: Gap Severity Disposition No rate limiting / brute-force protection on authentication attempts (V2) Low (high-entropy tokens mitigate) Disclosed, not fixed this pass A caller can claim any org via the legacy shared token's header (V4) Already disclosed pre-existing limitation Unchanged; real per-org identity is plan §19.2 No general API rate limiting / abuse prevention (V11) Medium for a multi-tenant deployment, low for the current single-operator model Disclosed, not fixed this pass HSTS not set for most production deployments (V9) Medium Fixed: opt-in via BULWARK_FORCE_HTTPS=1 No CVE scanning of Bulwark's own dependencies (V10) Medium Fixed: dependency-audit CI job + Dependabot No archive path-depth limit despite SECURITY.md claiming one (V12) Low, and a documentation-accuracy issue Fixed: Limits.max_depth, tested gVisor/Firecracker isolation layer never actually executed (V10) Already disclosed (ADR-0031) Firecracker built for the fix agent's test runs (2026-10-12) and its guest side booted under QEMU; neither runtime has run on a KVM/runsc host yet Interactive API docs live by default (V13) Low Disclosed, left as a deployment-time decision

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
Bulwark downloads or accepts untrusted code and runs third-party tools over it, then renders what those tools say. That is an attack surface. This document lists what we defend against, what actually exists in the code today, and what does not. Status is stated per threat so it can be checked, not assumed.

Status key: Done (implemented and tested), Partial (some of the mitigation exists), Open (not implemented), N/A yet (the feature that creates the threat is not built).

Last reviewed: 2026-10-07 (Week 75: sign-in, sessions and access, T11 and T18). Review again before any deployment that accepts scans from people you do not trust.

docs.title: Assets and trust boundaries
docs.text:
Asset Why it matters The host running the worker and Docker The worst outcome is code from a scanned repo running on it Source code and secrets inside scanned repos Users upload private code; findings can echo secrets The API tokens and sign-in sessions Tokens act as their organization or person; a session is a signed-in person (T11, T18) Report consumers (browsers, GitHub, PDF readers) They render text that came from an attacker-controlled repo

Boundaries: (1) the scanned repository is untrusted input to everything; (2) scanner containers are untrusted processes; (3) the worker, API and database are trusted; (4) the browser is trusted only to render text, never to run scan-derived markup.

docs.title: STRIDE summary
docs.text: # Threat Category Status T1 Container escape / RCE via a scanner parser bug Elevation of privilege Partial T2 Code execution during dependency install Elevation of privilege Done T3 Decompression bomb Denial of service Done T4 Zip-slip / path traversal Tampering Done T5 SSRF via Git URL Information disclosure Done T6 Resource exhaustion Denial of service Partial T7 Secret leakage via findings Information disclosure Partial T8 Prompt injection into remediation LLM Tampering Partial T9 Stored XSS in the report UI and exports Tampering / Elevation Done T10 Malicious or compromised scanner image Tampering Open T11 Unauthorized API access Spoofing Partial T12 Worker's Docker access abused Elevation of privilege Partial T13 Poisoned or unavailable exploit-data feeds Tampering Partial T15 Forged or tampered scan results, reports or SBOM in transit Tampering / Repudiation Partial T14 Parser bug or resource exhaustion while analysing scanned source for reachability Denial of service / Elevation Partial T16 A wrong VEX claim tells customers they are not affected Repudiation / Information integrity Partial T17 An evidence pack discloses another organization's activity, or is forged Information disclosure / Tampering Partial T18 Sign-in, sessions and access Spoofing / Elevation of privilege Partial T19 Untrusted text steering an agent through MCP; /fix run by the wrong person or on a fork Tampering / Elevation of privilege Partial

docs.title: T1 Container escape / RCE (Partial)
docs.text: A crafted repo exploits a bug in Bandit, Semgrep, Trivy, OSV-Scanner or Gitleaks. - Done: every scanner runs with --network=none --read-only --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges, non-root UID 10001, --memory=2g --cpus=1.0 --pids-limit=256, a noexec 64 MB tmpfs, and the target mounted read-only (core/runner.py, ADR-002). Docker's default seccomp profile applies. Integration tests run the real containers. - Open: rootless Docker or gVisor. The default runtime shares the host kernel, so a kernel or runtime exploit is not contained. Required before hosting for strangers.

docs.title: T2 Code execution during dependency install (Done)
docs.text: Dependencies are never installed. Trivy and OSV-Scanner read lockfiles offline; vulnerability databases are baked into the images at build time.

docs.title: T3 Decompression bomb (Done)
docs.text: Before extraction: maximum compressed size (100 MB), uncompressed size (500 MB), file count (20,000) and compression ratio (100:1) (core/ingest.py). Git clones are size-watched and killed past the limit.

docs.title: T4 Zip-slip / path traversal (Done)
docs.text: Every archive entry is resolved against the extraction root; escaping entries, absolute paths, dot-segments and symlinks are rejected. Covered by unit tests.

docs.title: T5 SSRF via Git URL (Done)
docs.text: Strict URL grammar, https only, host allowlist (github.com, gitlab.com, bitbucket.org), DNS resolved and every address required to be public, the resolved IP pinned for the clone, no redirects, no submodules, hooks disabled (core/gitfetch.py). The API never scans server-side paths: only Git URLs and uploads.

docs.title: T6 Resource exhaustion (Partial)
docs.text:
• Done: per-container memory, CPU, PID and wall-clock limits; upload size cap; scans stuck past 30 minutes are reaped; orphaned containers and scratch directories are cleaned every 5 minutes.
  • Open: no disk quota on the scan workspace beyond the ingestion size limits, and no limit on how many scans one caller may queue. With a single shared token this is an availability risk to whoever holds it.

docs.title: T7 Secret leakage (Partial)
docs.text:
• Done: Gitleaks runs with --redact; snippets become [secret redacted] and the finding id is a hash of rule, path and line, never of the secret. Bandit's hard-coded-password messages are scrubbed. A cross-tool pass redacts snippets and quoted literals near a detected secret (correlation runs first so distinct defects are not merged). Raw scanner output is not stored when secrets were found. Exports (SARIF, HTML, PDF, JSON) are built from the already-redacted findings.
  • Open: findings are not encrypted at rest (Postgres and the object store hold plaintext, minus the redactions above). Rely on disk or volume encryption for now.
  • Note: redaction before any LLM call applies when the LLM features exist (see T8).

docs.title: T8 Prompt injection (Partial)
docs.text: The remediation layer (Week 12, docs/llm-remediation.md, ADR-010) is off by default and, once enabled, runs only when a user clicks "Generate AI suggestion" on a finding (POST /scans/{id}/suggestion); reading guidance never contacts a model. Model calls are capped per minute and per day, and results are cached by rule and snippet. - Done and tested: instructions only in the system message; repository text in random-nonce fenced data blocks with the task reminder after them; strict schema validation of the reply (extra keys, dismissal language, control/bidi characters and patches outside the finding's file are rejected whole); the model has no way to change severity, triage or taxonomy and the Finding object is never modified; any failure degrades to static CWE/cheat-sheet text; secrets findings send no code, other code is scrubbed first; the retrieval query never uses the code snippet; injection-like text in a repository is reported to the user. Tested with 20 hostile payloads across four placements and with simulated hijacked models (135 tests). - Open: no real model has been run against these defences, so real-world resistance is unmeasured (Week 14). A well-formed reply can still be a wrong or misleading fix; patches are labelled and never applied. The secret scrubber is pattern-based and can miss unusual formats. The dismissal filter is phrase-based. - Privacy: enabling the feature sends finding text and the scanner's code snippet to the configured provider (the CLI can add +/-20 lines). Cache entries are shared across scans on a server. - Cost abuse: the per-process spend limit bounds a shared-token holder's spend but resets on restart and is not per user (there are no users yet).

docs.title: T9 Stored XSS (Done)
docs.text: Scanner-derived text is rendered as React text nodes, never HTML; the UI runs under a per-request-nonce Content-Security-Policy with no inline styles or scripts; links are only built from validated ids and https URLs. One exception, contained: the threat-model diagram is drawn by Mermaid, whose SVG needs inline styles, in a same-origin frame (/diagram-frame) whose policy allows inline styles but scripts only from this origin (Mermaid's build and the frame's own script), with no network access, framable only by the app. It takes the diagram source by postMessage from its parent only, and Mermaid sanitizes its own output (securityLevel: "strict"). The HTML export escapes every value and carries its own CSP that forbids scripts and network access; the API serves downloads with nosniff and a sandbox CSP; PDF text is escaped before layout. Regression tests inject hostile titles, paths, snippets and descriptions into each of them (web/tests/xss.test.tsx, tests/unit/test_export.py).

docs.title: T10 Malicious scanner image (Open)
docs.text: Images are pinned by tag, not SHA-256 digest (bulwark/*:1.7.10 etc., zricethezav/gitleaks:v8.21.0), and the compose file uses :latest for the object store and the Docker socket proxy. Signatures are not verified. A compromised upstream tag would be pulled and run (still inside the sandbox flags). Fix: pin digests in production, verify signatures where publishers provide them.

docs.title: T11 Unauthorized API access (Partial)
docs.text:
• Done: every endpoint except /healthz needs a bearer token; comparison is constant-time; the API refuses to start with a weak token (under 16 characters); CORS is an explicit allowlist; the WebSocket authenticates in its first message so the token is never in a URL.
  • Done since (Weeks 29 and 75): scoped, expiring, revocable tokens per organization (ADR-0018); user accounts that sign in through the organization's identity provider, with roles per organization, business unit and project, and tokens that act as their person and die with them (T18, ADR-0058).
  • Open: the shared BULWARK_API_TOKEN still exists for the operator and has every scope; there is no rate limiting, so a token can be guessed at online (they are 160 random bits). Keep the shared token for automation you control, and do not expose the API to the internet without a reverse proxy that limits rates.

docs.title: T12 Worker's Docker access (Partial)
docs.text: The worker starts scanner containers through docker-socket-proxy, which allows only container create/start/kill, image inspect and volumes, not the raw socket. Residual risk (also in ADR-002): a compromised worker can still ask for containers with arbitrary host bind mounts. Production should use a dedicated runner on an isolated host, or rootless Docker or gVisor, with the worker holding no Docker access.

docs.title: T13 Poisoned or unavailable exploit-data feeds (Partial)
docs.text:
EPSS and CISA KEV are fetched from two fixed https URLs by the API/worker side only (scanners still have no network). Downloads are size-capped, structurally validated with minimum-size sanity floors, and replace the cache atomically; a bad file leaves the previous one in place; a missing feed degrades scores to "unknown" rather than failing scans. Open: the files are trusted on TLS alone; there is no signature to verify. A compromised feed could distort ranking, not execute code.

Since Week 68 (ADR-0052) the advisory engine also fetches OSV's per-ecosystem data, CISA KEV and NVD's CVE API, on the worker, from three fixed HTTPS hosts only (any other URL is refused), certificates verified against certifi's bundle. Sizes are capped (1 GiB per dump, 2 MiB per record), records are parsed as data, a KEV file with fewer than 100 entries never replaces the catalog, and an advisory's reference links are kept only if they are http(s) addresses; its text is shown as text, never rendered. Open: as above, a compromised source could add or hide advisories (false alarms or missed ones); it cannot run code. Fetching sends nothing about an organization: the requests are plain GETs of public files, unlike osv-scanner's online mode, which posts package lists to api.osv.dev.

docs.title: T14: reachability analysis parses untrusted source outside the sandbox
docs.text: Unlike the scanners, core/reachability runs in the API/worker process. It never executes scanned code: Python is parsed with the standard ast module and JavaScript/TypeScript with tree-sitter (native code). Mitigations: symlinks are not followed and dependency/build directories are skipped, at most 20,000 files and 1 MB per file are read, parse errors (including RecursionError/MemoryError) mark the file unparsed instead of failing the scan, and any failure of the whole analysis leaves findings without reachability rather than failing the scan. Residual: a memory-safety bug in tree-sitter or CPython's parser triggered by a hostile file would run in the worker, which is the one component with (proxied) Docker access. Moving the analysis into a sandboxed container is the fix and is not done. Status: Partial.

docs.title: T15: scan results can be altered after the fact
docs.text: bulwark attest sign and bulwark attest provenance sign a report, SARIF or SBOM with a cosign key pair and record which Bulwark and which scanner images (by content hash) produced it, with the result counts. cosign runs in a container with no network and a read-only root filesystem; the key is mounted read-only and its password is passed by environment-variable name, never on a command line. Residual: signatures are key-based with no transparency log, so they prove who held the key but not when the signature was made; a stolen key forges results; keyless (OIDC) signing is not implemented; nothing yet stops an attacker with the key from attesting a scan they did not run, and the attestation says nothing about whether the findings are correct. Status: Partial.

docs.title: T16: a wrong VEX claim (Week 69, ADR-0053)
docs.text: A not_affected statement published to customers that is not true hides a real exposure from them. Done: Bulwark only proposes; a person confirms each statement with a personal token (the shared token is refused), and the confirmation, the evidence and its limits are in the statement and the audit log. Evidence errs towards "used" (names matched loosely, an unknown import name means "can't tell"); nothing is proposed for malicious packages, uncertain versions or unscanned projects. A confirmed statement a later scan contradicts is exported as under_investigation, and reopening its Issue withdraws it. Residual: the evidence does not see calls made inside other dependencies, by reflection or through function values; a reviewer who confirms without reading can still publish a wrong claim; the proposals' precision has not been measured. Status: Partial.

docs.title: T17: evidence packs (Week 69, ADR-0053)
docs.text: A pack holds an organization's SLA history, risk acceptances, issue counts and audit-log extract. Done: packs are stored under forced RLS and served only to their organization; the audit extract shows other organizations' entries as hashes only, which still lets every link be recomputed (version-2 entries put the organization inside the hash); payloads are never in the log, only their digests. verify.py checks the files and the chain without Bulwark; the manifest is signed with cosign when a key is configured, and a pack is never produced unsigned after signing failed. Checkpoints can be verified against Rekor offline. Residual: the number and timing of other organizations' audit entries are visible in an extract; entries from before migration 0041 can be checked by link only; whoever holds the signing key can sign a fabricated pack (the chain and Rekor checkpoints still have to agree); a pack is only as current as its last checkpoint. Status: Partial.

docs.title: T18: sign-in, sessions and access (Week 75, plan threat T30, ADR-0058)
docs.text: Done: OIDC with PKCE and strict checks of the ID token: asymmetric signatures only (never none or an HMAC "signed" with the public key), exact issuer, our audience (and azp when there are several), expiry, and the nonce of this sign-in; one-time state; HTTPS to the provider. SAML only through pysaml2 with xmlsec1, assertions required to be signed, no unsolicited responses, audience and destination checked; tests forge an unsigned assertion, another key's signature, a tampered one, three kinds of signature wrapping, a comment inside the NameID, another service's response, an expired one, a replayed one and an unsolicited one, and each is refused for its own reason. A person is bound to the provider's stable subject, so a second account with the same email cannot take theirs. Sessions are HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure cookies holding a secret whose SHA-256 alone is stored, at most 12 hours and 2 idle; every change made with one needs its CSRF token. SCIM deprovisioning (and turning someone off by hand) ends their sessions and revokes their tokens in the same request. A person limited to some projects runs as the bulwark_guest database role, whose restrictive RLS policies hide every other project's rows in every table that names one; the two-project test proves it on Postgres. Evidence files are served with Content-Security-Policy: sandbox, so a file that runs script cannot use the session. Residual: Google, Entra ID and Okta are covered by standard OIDC but were exercised only through a local Keycloak; the shared token and pre-account tokens are nobody in particular and keep their scopes; a provider administrator can sign in as anyone the provider vouches for. Status: Partial.

docs.title: T19: agents and pull request comments (Week 76, plan threat T29, ADR-0059)
docs.text:
MCP server. bulwark mcp calls the API with the person's own token, so scopes, roles, project limits and RLS apply unchanged; the shared token is refused; ids are checked before a request; redirects are not followed and a remote API must be https. Read-only by default (run_scan needs --allow-scans and a token that may write scans); no tool changes a status. Every value Bulwark does not set itself is wrapped as {"untrusted_text": ...}, default-deny: a trusted key must also hold a value that looks like one. Hidden and reordering characters are shown as <U+XXXX>; long text is cut. Tested with a Hypothesis property (no unwrapped string escapes) and live: a planted injection in a scanned file came back wrapped, with its bidi override shown as a code, to the SDK's own stdio client. Residual: a label informs an agent, it cannot stop one from following the text; the agent's own permissions are the real limit.

/fix. Only from a GitHub owner, member or collaborator (author_association) whose login an admin linked to an active person with the Member role or higher on that project; never for a pull request from a fork (its code must not run with the base repository's credentials, the pull_request_target lesson); only a new comment's first line is a command, never an edit; a bot is ignored; the organization comes from the App installation, and a comment never creates one. A preview shows the findings and the token cap and spends nothing; the confirm repeats every check and is refused when the pull request has new commits since the preview, the code has expired (24 h) or been used, the monthly budget cannot cover the cap, or the organization is at its concurrency limit. The agent stops at the cap (checked before each model call) and every token is charged to the organization's budget. Results are posted as comments; Bulwark never pushes to the branch. Tested on SQLite, on Postgres (RLS, a project-limited guest), and live with the real worker on Temporal. Residual: not exercised with a real GitHub App or a real model; a scan of the head commit is matched by the commit the webhook named, so a push in the seconds between the webhook and the clone could make the scan describe a newer commit. Status: Partial.

docs.title: Observability endpoints
docs.text: The worker's /metrics (port 9101) has no authentication and is not published to the host; only the compose network reaches it. Grafana's default admin password (admin) and anonymous viewer access are for localhost use only (the port is bound to 127.0.0.1); change the password and remove anonymous access before exposing it anywhere. Logs are scrubbed of credentials by pattern, which is best effort, and traces carry tool names, statuses and counts but never code or findings.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: DAST (ADR-003); the security of the upstream scanners themselves; multi-tenant isolation is covered by RLS (ADR-0013) and, between projects, by T18; physical and cloud-account security of wherever it runs.

docs.title: Before a public deployment
docs.text:
1. Resolve the Semgrep rules licence (ADR-006).
  2. Run scanners under gVisor or rootless Docker on a host that holds nothing else (T1, T12).
  3. Per-user authentication, rate limiting and a scan queue cap (T6, T11).
  4. Pin image digests (T10); encrypt storage at rest (T7).

docs.title: Adding a scanner (and what Week 22 measured)
docs.text: The design plan claims a new scanner is about 40 lines of adapter. Week 22 added four (Grype, Checkov, gosec, Dockle) to test that, and the honest result is: true only after a refactor, and only for tools that fit the assumptions.

docs.title: The measurement
docs.text:
Code lines = non-blank, non-comment, non-docstring lines in the adapter file, imports included, formatted by black (100 columns).

Adapter First, in the style of the existing ones After core/adapters/helpers.py gosec 47 in the class + ~17 of imports and constants 45 Checkov 48 + ~17 48 Dockle 47 + ~17 42 Grype 60 + ~17 45 Bandit (existing, migrated as a check) 75 33
  • The first versions were 76 to 89 lines of file each, about twice the claim. The repeated part was parsing safety, the canonical Finding shape, snippet hashing and severity normalisation.
  • JsonAdapter (safe parsing, one bad record never loses the rest) and make_finding (the canonical shape) now hold that. Adapters are 42 to 48 lines for the four new ones: close to the claim, not under it. Grype and Checkov are dense because their output has more to map. Bandit shrank from 75 to 33 and its golden test passes unchanged.
  • A test (test_a_new_scanner_stays_small) fails any tier-2 adapter over 50 code lines.

Time to add each scanner was not measured; do not read anything into it.

docs.title: What happened on a real repository
docs.text:
Scanning terragoat (a deliberately vulnerable Terraform project) through the API and worker with Trivy, Checkov and Grype, all ok:

  • SCA: Grype reported 468 findings, 365 of them (78%) also reported by Trivy; Trivy reported 561 dependency findings, 365 (65%) also found by Grype. The tools genuinely disagree, which is the point of running two.
  • IaC: no cross-tool merging. Trivy reported 243 misconfigurations, Checkov 477, and 0 were merged. They use different rule ids and IaC findings carry no CWE or advisory id to correlate on, so overlapping findings show up twice. Correlation only understands dependencies (shared advisory) and code (file, CWE, nearby lines). Adding an IaC identity (for example resource address plus a mapped control) is open work.

docs.title: What did NOT need to change
docs.text: Correlation and deduplication (a Grype finding for lodash merged with Trivy's and OSV-Scanner's on the shared advisory id, verified against the real tools), scoring, taxonomy, redaction, storage, the API, all exports and the UI's rendering. That is the part of the abstraction that held.

docs.title: What did not fit, found by doing it
docs.text:
1. Output file names. Checkov chooses its own file name inside --output-file-path. The runner assumed result.json. Now ToolSpec.output_name.
  2. Sandbox resources silently change results. gosec's taint rules (G701, G702, G705) vanished when /tmp was 64 MB: the Go build cache did not fit, and gosec still exited normally with fewer findings. Now ToolSpec.tmp_size (512 MB for gosec), and an integration test asserts the taint rules appear. Any tool needing a toolchain deserves that test.
  3. Offline analysis is partial. gosec type-checks code and cannot download modules. Non-vendored third-party imports are not analysed, so results on a typical Go project are a subset. The fixture has no dependencies.
  4. Scope differences. Grype cannot include dev dependencies, unlike Trivy and OSV-Scanner here, so agreement counts on dev-only packages will not include it. Open-source Checkov reports no severity, so every check is MEDIUM (a judgment call in the severity matrix, not Checkov's opinion).
  5. The target is not always a source tree. Dockle lints a built image, which is not in a repository. The abstraction assumed a directory. It now supports one archive named bulwark-image.tar (RepoContext. has_image_archive) and the bulwark scan-image REF command saves a local image with docker save and scans it. This is a workaround, not a redesign: a scanner whose input is a registry image or a running system still does not fit.
  6. Image cost. The Grype image is 3.7 GB because the vulnerability database is baked in (the sandbox has no network); Checkov is 550 MB. This is why tier 2 is opt-in.
  7. Default safety. Adding tools to the registry must not change what an existing scan runs. DEFAULT_TOOLS (the original five) is what the CLI, API, UI, extension and action run unless told otherwise.

docs.title: Steps to add one
docs.text:
1. docker/<tool>/Dockerfile: pin the version (by digest where the base allows), bake in any data, run as uid 10001, set env so it never calls home. Add it to docker-compose.yml (scanners profile) and CI.
  2. core/adapters/<tool>.py: a JsonAdapter with spec, build_command, records, to_finding. Override applies_to if the tool is not language-based.
  3. Register it in core/scan.py (ADAPTERS; not DEFAULT_TOOLS unless it earns it), add its row to core/scoring/severity.py, its name to core/observability/metrics.py TOOLS, and an entry in scripts/gen-licenses.py (a test fails if you forget).
  4. Run it for real in the sandbox on a fixture, save the raw output as tests/golden/<tool>/raw.json, read the parsed result against the raw output, then save expected.json. Add an integration test that asserts something the tool must find.
  5. If it has scope or resource quirks, write them down in this file.

docs.text: GET /scans/{scan_id}/ws (not part of OpenAPI).

docs.title: Attack paths
docs.text: A ranked chain from an entry point through this project's own open issues to real impact, computed from the current scan -- never a hypothetical scenario. Design reasoning in ADR-0030; the honest verification record is in v2-week45-verification.md.

docs.title: How a path is built
docs.text:
core/attackpath/rules.py has three deterministic chaining rules, each versioned by its own rule_id so a path's provenance is always traceable:

Rule Verified or heuristic What it connects ssrf-metadata-v1 Verified -- walks the real call graph An SSRF issue reachable from a public route -> the cloud metadata service secret-grants-resource-v1 Heuristic -- co-location only A cloud-flavored secret + an IAC issue in the same asset ci-secret-workflow-v1 Heuristic -- path-based proxy A secret + an IAC issue under .github/workflows/

The heuristic rules are disclosed as such in their own docstrings: neither Checkov nor gitleaks output in this codebase records which specific credential grants access to which specific resource, so co-location is the only real signal available. likelihood reflects this -- high only for the call-graph-verified rule, medium for the heuristics -- rather than presenting all three as equally certain.

docs.title: Ranking and the cheapest link
docs.text: Paths are ranked by likelihood x impact (impact from the highest severity issue in the chain). cheapest_link names the one node whose remediation would disconnect the chain -- no fix-effort estimate exists in this codebase, so it's a disclosed, deterministic proxy: a SECRET node (rotating a credential is a cheap, always-correct first move) is preferred over an ordinary ISSUE node.

docs.title: The narrative
docs.text: A model-written description of the path, generated per path, never gating the endpoint: the graph itself is always real and returned even with no model configured. The narrative's own contract (core/attackpath/contract.py) requires it to mention every node's label it was given -- "the graph is the source of truth; the narrative only describes it" -- rejected and retried once otherwise.

docs.title: Turning the narrative on
docs.text:
export BULWARK_LLM_ENABLED=1
export BULWARK_LLM_API_KEY=...
export BULWARK_LLM_ROUTE_ATTACK_PATH=hosted   # optional: this task's own route

Without it, GET /assets/{id}/attack-paths still returns every path with narrative: null.

docs.title: Bulwark 1.0.0: what a scanner correlation pipeline actually gets you
docs.text: I spent 26 weeks building Bulwark, a security scanner that runs five open-source tools in locked-down containers, merges what they find into one deduplicated list, and ranks it by a risk score instead of raw severity. This week I tagged v1.0.0. Here's what it does, what I measured, and where it falls short — with numbers, not adjectives.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Run Bandit, Semgrep, Gitleaks, Trivy and OSV-Scanner against a repository and you get five separate reports. A SQL injection shows up as a Bandit finding, a Semgrep finding and a CWE entry; a vulnerable npm package shows up in both Trivy and OSV-Scanner. Nobody reads five overlapping lists, so most people read one and ignore the rest, which throws away whatever the other four saw.

Bulwark's job is narrow: normalize every tool's output into one schema, correlate what's the same vulnerability, and score what's left by how likely it is to matter (severity, EPSS exploitation probability, CISA KEV, and whether the code path is reachable), not just by the tool's own severity label. Everything runs in a container with no network access, a read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities and a non-root user, because the whole point is to point untrusted third-party scanners at code you don't fully trust either.

docs.title: What shipped
docs.text:
• Five scanners by default (Bandit, Semgrep, Gitleaks, Trivy, OSV-Scanner), four more opt-in (Grype, Checkov, gosec, Dockle).
  • Correlation and a risk score — EPSS, CISA KEV, and static reachability analysis, not just severity.
  • LLM-backed fix suggestions, retrieval-grounded in CWE and OWASP cheat-sheet text, labelled as AI-generated and never presented as a verdict.
  • A CLI, a REST + WebSocket API, a web UI, a VS Code extension and a GitHub Action — one pipeline, four surfaces.
  • SBOMs (CycloneDX 1.6) and signed attestations (in-toto provenance, cosign).
  • Observability: structured logs, OpenTelemetry tracing, Prometheus metrics.

All of it is in the CHANGELOG; the architecture is in docs/adr.

docs.title: What I actually measured
docs.text:
I didn't want to ship a scanner and just assert it works, so weeks 23–25 were entirely about evaluation: a public benchmark with labelled ground truth, a synthetic per-CWE suite, and a corpus of real repositories. Full method and limits: docs/evaluation.md.

Measure Result OWASP Benchmark: recall / false-positive rate / F1 88.2% (CI 86.4–89.8) / 43.7% / 77.0% Juliet (per-CWE, Java): recall / false-alarm rate 23.8% / 19.6% Corpus (25 repos, 94 tool runs): crash rate 0 Corpus: dedup, vulnerable apps / ordinary repos 19.9% / 1.3% Corpus: wall time per repository, median / p90 6 s / 42 s Top-20 precision: risk score / severity-only / random 63.3% / 52.4% / 48.2%

A few things worth saying plainly, because a benchmark table with no caveats is just marketing:

  • All of this is Semgrep's number, not an ensemble's. Only one of the five default scanners analyses Java, so neither Java benchmark says anything about whether combining scanners improves detection. That question needs a language with more than one analyser in the default set, which I don't have yet.
  • Detection is strong where the flaw is a syntactic pattern and weak where it needs data-flow analysis. 88% recall on OWASP Benchmark sounds good until you see the false-positive rate on injection categories: 65–88%. On Juliet, a synthetic suite built to isolate individual weaknesses, recall drops to 24%, and where Semgrep does flag an injection CWE it flags the safe variant about as often as the vulnerable one. That finding carries almost no signal.
  • The risk score is not shown to beat severity-only ranking. It's ahead at every top-K I measured, but the 95% confidence interval on the difference includes zero every time. With one scanner and only two severity levels in play, there isn't much for the score to separate findings with. I'm reporting the honest result of that limitation, not the flattering headline.
  • Zero crashes in 94 tool runs is one run on one laptop, not a reliability guarantee. By the rule of three, that only bounds the true crash rate at roughly 3% with 95% confidence.
  • Correlation's dedup rate depends entirely on what you scan. Deliberately vulnerable test apps have the same bug reported by two tools about a fifth of the time; ordinary open-source repositories, about 1%. A single pooled "dedup rate" number without that split is close to meaningless.

Performance got a real pass too: I found Semgrep was spending ~26 seconds of every scan just loading 337 small rule files, merged them into one file per language at image build time, and that plus giving Semgrep and Trivy more CPU quota took the corpus's median per-repository wall time from 47 seconds to 6. Chasing that down also surfaced a real correctness bug — Semgrep silently drops a rule/file pair after a 5-second timeout and still exits 0, so a CPU-starved run can lose most of its findings with no error. Bulwark now surfaces that as a warnings field instead of staying quiet about it.

docs.title: What's not measured, and what's not done
docs.text:
• SCA prioritization (does the risk score help for vulnerable dependencies specifically) has no dataset with exploitation ground truth, so it's unevaluated. I say so rather than guess.
  • The VS Code extension and GitHub Action are built and unit-tested but have not run in a real VS Code install or on GitHub's runners. That's the next real-world test, not a benchmark.
  • AI fix suggestion quality is unmeasured — I have no rubric or human evaluation for it yet.
  • Auth is one shared bearer token. This isn't multi-user software yet; don't point it at the public internet.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/rago12bit/cybernatics
cd cyberimp && ./scripts/init-env.sh
docker compose --profile scanners build && docker compose up -d
# http://localhost:3000 — the first page is a real sample report, no sign-in needed

Source, docs and the full evaluation writeups: https://github.com/rago12bit/cybernatics.

docs.title: Bulwark 2.0.0: from a scanner pipeline to a platform
docs.text: v1.0.0 answered one question: given five scanners' worth of overlapping noise, what's the deduplicated, risk-ranked list of things actually worth fixing? That shipped 26 weeks ago. v2.0.0 is another 26 weeks on top of it, and it answers a different question: once you have that list, what actually closes it out — and can the thing producing the list survive being used by more than one person, on more than one machine, for more than a week? Here's what changed, what I measured, and what I'm still not claiming.

docs.title: From findings to fixes
docs.text:
The single biggest gap in v1.0.0 was that it stopped at the list. v2.0.0's flagship feature is the verified-fix agent: it proposes a patch, then actually checks its own work — reruns the rule that triggered, reruns every scanner, runs the project's own test suite — and only then opens a real GitHub PR for a human to approve. An LLM suggesting a diff is cheap and has been possible for a while; an LLM suggesting a diff that's been mechanically proven not to break anything else is a different, much smaller claim, and it's the one v2.0.0 actually makes.

Two more LLM-backed features sit next to it, both scoped narrower than they could be, on purpose: a triage assistant that gives a "likely false positive" verdict a human can override, never a silent suppression; and a hypotheses lane that finds exactly one pattern deterministic scanning can't — a route missing the authorization check its siblings have — then asks a model to confirm it against real code before showing it to anyone. Both are narrow because a false "this is fine" from a security tool is worse than a missed finding, and I'd rather ship a feature that does one thing honestly than five things that half-work.

docs.title: Correlation didn't stop being the point — it got deeper
docs.text:
v1.0.0's correlation merged duplicate findings. v2.0.0 adds a layer underneath that: taint analysis that confirms whether a SAST finding is actually reachable from a real HTTP entrypoint, not just present somewhere in the code. The distinction matters in practice, not just in theory — on a real scan of OWASP Juice Shop, Semgrep's plain pattern rule flags any eval() call it sees; the taint engine additionally confirms that in three specific cases, the argument demonstrably comes from the request body. That's a materially stronger claim than "this function exists," and it's the kind of signal the risk score now folds in alongside EPSS and CISA KEV.

Ranking is still a scoring question, and I still don't have a result I'm willing to oversell: the risk score beats severity-only ordering at every top-K I've measured, but the confidence interval on that difference includes zero. I'm reporting that plainly in docs/evaluation-v2.md rather than quietly dropping the caveat because it's two years old now.

docs.title: The part that isn't about features at all
docs.text: Multi-tenancy with Postgres Row-Level Security, a stable Issue/Occurrence data model (so "fixed" and "returned" are real states instead of a guess from diffing two reports), a hash-chained audit log, mTLS between every internal service, envelope-encrypted scan data with crypto-shredding on deletion, a gVisor sandbox option, and authorized DAST (ownership verification before a URL can be scanned, a scope-enforcing egress proxy actually wired into campaign execution, not just configured and left unused — a gap I found and closed in the same week I found it). None of this is a "feature" a user clicks on. All of it is the difference between a weekend project and something you'd trust with a second organization's data.

docs.title: What I actually measured
docs.text:
Full method and every caveat: docs/evaluation-v2.md.

Measure Result Taint engine: hand-verified precision on a real spot-check (NodeGoat) 3/3, zero false confirmations Ranking: top-20 precision, risk score / severity-only / random 63.3% / 52.4% / 48.2% (CI includes 0) Scale: p95 latency (scan submission / results browsing) 675ms / 1.84s Platform security: ASVS 4.0.3 Level 2 self-audit complete, 3 findings fixed Red-team: structural-defense pass rate 60/60 adversarial payload x contract combinations rejected Incremental scanning: warm vs. cold PR scan (1 repo) 3.6x faster

The honest gaps, stated the same way v1.0.0's were:

  • No human-measured usability improvement. The UX overhaul (new design system, new screens, a verdict-first project overview) is real and shipped. The before/after SUS study that would prove it's actually better, not just different, needs real participants and hasn't been run. I'm not fabricating that data to round out a launch post.
  • Five evaluation rows need a live model and aren't measured: the verified-fix agent's acceptance rate and blind human review, the triage assistant's and hypotheses lane's precision/recall against labelled ground truth, Copilot's citation accuracy, and a real attack-success-rate for the red-team suite (its structural-defense pass rate is measured; a live model actually trying to be persuaded is a different, harder thing I haven't funded yet).
  • The taint-engine number above is a spot-check, N=3, one repository — real and hand-verified, not a corpus-scale study.
  • Still one shared bearer token for most API auth. Multi-user identity is explicitly a v3 item.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/rago12bit/cybernatics
cd cyberimp && ./scripts/init-env.sh
docker compose --profile scanners build && docker compose up -d
# http://localhost:3000 -- the first screen is now a replay of a real scan of OWASP Juice Shop

Source, docs, and the full evaluation writeups: https://github.com/rago12bit/cybernatics. A technical report on correlation, taint-based ranking, and verified fixes, written for people who want the method rather than the pitch, is at docs/technical-report-v2.md.

docs.title: Bulwark 3.0: three things a security platform has to get right
docs.text:
Week 78 (plan §59). Bulwark 3.0.0 was tagged on 2026-10-08 without the third usability study (M16), which needs five real people and has not run. Every number links to the record of how it was measured. Nothing here is a claim the evaluation (evaluation-v3.md) does not back.

Version 2 found vulnerabilities and helped fix them. Version 3 manages them: imports from tools Bulwark doesn't run, SLAs, risk acceptance with a second person, a rules engine, an SBOM inventory, advisory matching, VEX, compliance, dashboards, reports, single sign-on, an MCP server and /fix on pull requests. Most of that is plumbing every platform has. Three parts are where a platform can quietly be wrong in a way that costs someone, so they get the space here.

docs.title: 1. Reimport must never close what it didn't look at
docs.text:
Importing a report is easy. Reimporting it -- the same tool, a week later -- is where platforms hurt people: the Issues the new file no longer lists get closed. If the file was cut off, or came from a different scope, or another tool still sees the problem, that closure is false, and a real vulnerability leaves the queue looking fixed.

Bulwark treats reimport as the default (import is reimport with an empty history) and makes closing the thing that has to earn its way in:

  • A file that can't be read completely closes nothing. Every parser streams and reports whether it reached a real end. A Hypothesis property test cuts every vendored report at random points and requires each cut to be either refused or unable to close (Week 54). That test kept finding things: in Week 76 a Nessus CSV cut right after a quoted field read as a whole row, and the follow-up found the same for a cut after an empty field. Since then every cut of every vendored Nessus and OpenVAS CSV has been checked -- 199,038 of them -- and none can close an Issue; before, 29 dropped or garbled a finding and could still close it. A CSV whose last row has no line break is read but closes nothing, because a real Tenable export ending that way can't be told from a cut one.
  • Another source keeps an Issue open. A finding no longer in this Test's file but still reported by a scan or another Test is detached, not closed, and the preview says how many.
  • You see the four numbers before anything is saved -- new, unchanged, reopened, closed -- with the reopened ones listed by id. The same file twice is a no-op; the latest import can be undone.
  • Checked against ground truth, not examples. Random import sequences into two Tests are compared, count by count, with an independent set-arithmetic oracle; every deliberate regression tried -- ignoring other sources, ignoring "don't close", widening the close scope, swallowing truncation errors, letting an SBOM close Issues, removing the row lock, and six more -- makes the tests fail.

What this doesn't show: the sequences are generated, not a corpus of real reimport histories.

docs.title: 2. Advisory matching must not miss
docs.text:
"Which of our projects use this library at an affected version?" is only useful if the answer has no false negatives. Version ranges are where that goes wrong: every ecosystem orders versions its own way, and OSV records mix ranges with explicit version lists.

Bulwark matches with OSV's semantics, per ecosystem, and was checked against osv-scanner on the same data: OSV's dumps for PyPI, npm, Go and Maven, and SBOMs built from the hardest versions to get right -- every range boundary for up to 1,000 packages per ecosystem (evaluation-advisory-matching.md).

21,619 of 21,721 package versions agree (99.5%), and osv-scanner never reports an advisory Bulwark misses. In all 102 differences Bulwark reports more, and each is explained: 80 are Go modules with capital letters, which osv-scanner lowercases and then cannot find. The check runs Bulwark twice -- the function, and the stored answer after a real inventory import -- so the database is checked, not only the code.

What this doesn't show: boundary versions are adversarial on purpose, not a sample of real SBOMs.

docs.title: 3. "Not affected" needs evidence
docs.text:
A VEX statement that says not_affected tells customers they can ignore a CVE. If it's wrong, it's worse than no statement. So Bulwark never writes one on its own:

  • For Go, it proposes vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path only when the advisory names the vulnerable functions and the project's code does not call them, and it attaches where it looked. For Python and JavaScript, the weaker claim: the package isn't imported by application code.
  • A person confirms each proposal with their own token; confirming dismisses the matching Issue with the justification, and reopening withdraws it.
  • The screen never says "unreachable": the call graph is unsound in known places, so it says "no call path found".
  • Exports are OpenVEX v0.2.0 and CycloneDX 1.6, validated against their schemas; OpenVEX's own vexctl merged a Bulwark document and filtered a SARIF file with it, dropping the not_affected CVE and keeping the affected one (Week 69).

What this doesn't show: the plan's measure -- a blind review of 100 proposals by someone who didn't build it -- has not been done. The review kit is ready (scripts/vex-review-kit.py); until it's used, the share of correct not_affected claims is unknown.

docs.title: What else was measured, and what wasn't
docs.text:
From evaluation-v3.md, with the method next to every number:

  • 10 parsers ported from DefectDojo agree with its own expected results on 156 sample files, except 12 recorded differences and 2 deliberate refusals.
  • Ingest: 2,400 Nessus findings a second end to end on a 95 MB file; SARIF 3,700 a second.
  • Parser safety: 669,000 fuzzing runs, no crash or hang; XXE, entity expansion and depth bombs refused.
  • Dashboards: every widget under 300 ms at p95 over a million Occurrences, on Postgres under RLS.
  • SSO: 13 of 13 SAML attack cases refused, each for its own reason.
  • Rules: one OPA evaluation at p95 15 ms -- but the plan's load test was not run.

Not measured: deduplication accuracy (it needs hand-labelled duplicate pairs), the VEX blind review, and the third usability study's SUS and time on task (it needs five security leads or pen testers). Each is "not measured" in the table, with the reason, rather than left out.

cd cyberimp && ./scripts/init-env.sh
