docs.title: Compliance mappings, the ASVS checklist and evidence packs
docs.text: Bulwark shows where the evidence it holds supports a framework's controls. It is not a certification, an audit opinion or a statement of compliance, and no screen or file says it is. The design is ADR-0053.

docs.title: Mappings
docs.text:
One versioned file per framework in core/compliance/frameworks/, each citing its source, version and terms, and mapping each control to the kinds of evidence Bulwark holds:

Framework Controls Source and terms OWASP Top 10:2021 10 categories, each with OWASP's own CWE list OWASP, CC BY-SA 4.0 OWASP ASVS 4.0.3 278 requirements with level and CWE OWASP, CC BY-SA 4.0, not reworded PCI DSS v4.0, Requirement 6 6.1.1 to 6.5.1 PCI SSC; numbers and Bulwark's paraphrases only ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A 8.8 "Management of technical vulnerabilities" ISO/IEC; the control's name only SOC 2 TSC (2017, rev. 2022), CC7.1 Detection and monitoring of vulnerabilities AICPA; Bulwark's paraphrase only

The kinds of evidence: scan coverage, web (DAST) scans, SLA adherence, risk acceptances, open Issues, open Issues of a control's CWEs, the audit-log extract, the component inventory, advisory monitoring, VEX statements, assessments, and the policies in force. Some controls have none (developer training, a web application firewall, payment-page scripts) and say so.

GET /v2/compliance/frameworks
GET /v2/compliance/frameworks/{id}

docs.title: The ASVS checklist of a project
docs.text:
Project → ASVS: every ASVS 4.0.3 requirement up to level 1, 2 or 3, with a status:

Status Set by Means Met / Not met / Not applicable A person, with a note (required for met and not applicable) and links What the person decided Not met An assessment that failed the requirement A tester's result Issues open Open Issues of the requirement's CWE Evidence against it Passed a test An assessment that passed it Evidence for it, not "met" Not assessed Nothing No evidence either way

Bulwark never marks a requirement met: no findings is not evidence that a control works. A person's "met" that open Issues or a failed test contradict is flagged.

GET /v2/projects/{id}/asvs?level=2
PUT /v2/projects/{id}/asvs/{requirement}   {"status": "met", "note": "...", "links": [...]}

docs.title: Evidence packs
docs.text:
Evidence in the top bar: pick a period (up to 400 days) and frameworks, see what will be included, generate. The pack is a zip:

File What evidence.pdf The pack to read evidence.json The same, machine-readable audit-extract.json The audit log for the period: your entries in full, others' as hashes checkpoints/ Each Rekor checkpoint's Sigstore bundle verify.py Checks it all without trusting Bulwark (Python 3, standard library only) manifest.json, manifest.json.sig Every file's SHA-256, and cosign's signature over it audit.pub, trusted-root.json When the deployment provides them: the checkpoint key and a private Rekor's trust root

What it reports, and how:

  • SLA adherence: Issues whose deadline fell in the period, under the SLA policy in force at its end. Met: fixed by the deadline. Missed: fixed after. Open past deadline: not fixed by the period's end. Exempt: marked not a risk or accepted (as triaged now). Adherence = met / (met + missed + open past deadline).
  • Risk acceptances requested, decided or in force in the period, with requester, approver and expiry, and whether a second person approved.
  • Scan coverage per project: full and pull-request scans, web scans and imported reports in the period, the tools, the last scan.
  • Open Issues by priority, as of generation (not as of the period's end).
  • Components, advisories, VEX, assessments and SLA/priority policies.
  • For each framework, each control with the evidence in the pack for it.

docs.title: Checking a pack
docs.text:
unzip evidence-pack.zip -d pack && cd pack && python3 verify.py

verify.py checks every file against manifest.json, recomputes the audit chain (every entry's hash, every link), and checks that each checkpoint names a hash that is in the extract at that position. It then prints the two cosign commands it cannot run itself: the signature on the manifest (with the organization's public key, obtained from the organization, not only from the pack) and each checkpoint's signature and Rekor entry.

docs.title: Signing and Rekor
docs.text:
• BULWARK_EVIDENCE_SIGNING_KEY (a cosign private key; its password in COSIGN_PASSWORD) signs packs. Without it, packs are generated and marked unsigned; with it, a signing failure produces no pack.
  • bulwark audit checkpoint --key cosign.key [--rekor-url URL] publishes the chain's head to Rekor: Sigstore's public instance (permanent and public) by default, or a private one.
  • bulwark audit verify --pub cosign.pub [--trusted-root trusted-root.json] checks the whole chain and every checkpoint's signature and Rekor entry; with a trusted root (cosign trusted-root create for a private Rekor) it needs no network.
  • BULWARK_AUDIT_CHECKPOINT_PUB and BULWARK_REKOR_TRUSTED_ROOT add the checkpoint key and trust root to packs.

docs.title: Why another organization's entries are hashes
docs.text: The audit log is one chain for the whole deployment. Since migration 0041 each entry's organization is inside its hash, through a digest of the entry's body, so a pack can show its organization's entries in full and every other entry as (seq, prev_hash, body_digest, entry_hash): every hash still recomputes, and nothing about the other entry is revealed except that it exists. Entries from before 0041 have no organization; they are shown as hashes and checked by link only.

docs.title: Security copilot
docs.text: Tool-grounded chat about one project: issues, code, routes, and scan history. Every answer cites real issue IDs or file:line -- checked against what actually exists before you ever see it. Design reasoning in ADR-0029; the honest verification record is in v2-week44-verification.md.

docs.title: What it can answer
docs.text:
The model calls tools that read real, already-scanned data:

Tool What it reads query_issues The project's currently-open issues, filterable by severity/category/CWE/path. fetch_code_range A range of lines from a file, with line numbers. get_call_path The known callers of the function enclosing a given file:line. list_routes Every HTTP route code intelligence found, optionally filtered by method. compare_scans New/fixed/reintroduced/unchanged issues between two scans of this project.

Before the model does anything else, the most relevant already-indexed code (function-level chunks, Week 44 task 1) is found by similarity search and handed to it as extra context -- not a tool it calls itself, just grounding for the question you actually asked.

docs.title: Citations
docs.text: Every answer names which issues or file:line it's based on. A citation is checked against real data (a real issue id for this project, a real file this checkout actually contains) before the answer is shown; if a citation doesn't check out, the model is told which one and asked to try again. An answer with nothing to cite (the tools genuinely found nothing relevant) still gets shown -- it just says so, instead of citing something invented to look complete.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Hosted-only, same posture as the triage assistant and Hypotheses lane:

export BULWARK_LLM_ENABLED=1
export BULWARK_LLM_API_KEY=...
export BULWARK_LLM_ROUTE_COPILOT=hosted   # optional: this task's own route

A local/Ollama backend routed to this task is rejected with a clear 409, not a crash: tool-calling needs the provider's native tool-use protocol, which only the hosted backend implements (ADR-0027).

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Endpoint What it does POST /assets/{asset_id}/copilot/conversations Start a conversation. Optional context_kind/context_id ("issue"/ or "scan"/) records which page it was opened from. 409 if the copilot isn't enabled, there's no completed scan, or the asset isn't git-sourced. POST .../conversations/{id}/messages Ask one question. Clones the project's latest scan's source on the conversation's first message, reuses that checkout for later messages in the same conversation. GET .../conversations/{id}/messages The conversation's history so far.

All three need scans:read (the GET) or scans:write (the rest) -- the same scopes every other LLM feature in this codebase already uses.

docs.title: What leaves your machine
docs.text: Per question: the question itself, the top few similarity-matched code chunks, and whatever a tool call reads (an issue's title/severity/path, a range of code, a route list) -- secret-scrubbed and PII-redacted first, the same as every other model call this codebase makes. Never the whole repository at once.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove
docs.text: No live run against a real hosted model in this environment (no API key here) -- the tool-calling loop is unit-tested against a fake client covering the real control-flow paths, the same disclosed gap Weeks 41-43 already carry for their own LLM call sites. No measurement against the plan's own 100-question reference set (needs a live model). The panel's code citations render as plain text, not a link: this frontend has no view that jumps to an arbitrary file:line yet. The panel isn't wired into the scan-comparison page's "this scan" context yet. Full account in v2-week44-verification.md.

docs.title: Data protection
docs.text: How scan data is encrypted at rest and deleted, how internal services authenticate to Postgres, and where secrets live. Design reasoning is in ADR-0032 (envelope encryption, crypto-shredding) and ADR-0033 (mTLS, secrets); the honest verification record is in v2-week47-verification.md.

docs.title: Envelope encryption
docs.text:
Each organization has a key-encryption key (KEK) held in OpenBao's Transit engine. Each scan gets its own data key, wrapped by its organization's KEK, encrypting that scan's raw tool output before it's written to object storage. Turning it on:

export BULWARK_OPENBAO_ADDR=http://openbao:8200
export BULWARK_OPENBAO_TOKEN=...

Without both set, scans store raw tool output exactly as they always have -- unencrypted, the original behavior, not a degraded mode.

docs.title: Crypto-shredding and retention
docs.text: An hourly sweep (core.tasks.crypto_shred_task) destroys a scan's data key once its organization's retention window has passed -- default 7 days, configurable per organization at Settings → Retention (GET/PUT /settings/retention). Destroying the key, not deleting the encrypted object itself, is the entire mechanism: it makes that scan's raw tool output permanently unreadable, including in any backup, without needing to locate and erase every copy of the ciphertext. Issues and findings are never affected by this -- only the raw artifact.

docs.title: mTLS between services and Postgres
docs.text:
Every network connection to Postgres requires a client certificate whose CN matches the role connecting: api connects as bulwark_api, worker as bulwark_worker, fixagent-worker as bulwark_fixagent, and migrate as bulwark itself -- four distinct, individually revocable identities instead of one shared credential. Generate a local dev CA and per-service certificates once:

./scripts/gen-mtls-certs.sh

This writes a certs/ directory (gitignored, never committed) that docker-compose.yml mounts into Postgres and every service that talks to it. A real deployment needs its own CA and certificate issuance process (cert-manager or equivalent) -- this script is dev/self-signed only.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
BULWARK_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY, BULWARK_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET, BULWARK_API_TOKEN, and BULWARK_LLM_API_KEY all prefer a value stored in OpenBao's KV store when one exists there, falling back to the plain environment variable otherwise -- unconditionally, so a deployment that has never touched OpenBao for secrets keeps working exactly as before. Move existing plaintext secrets into OpenBao once BULWARK_OPENBAO_ADDR/BULWARK_OPENBAO_TOKEN are set:

bulwark secrets migrate-env

This reports which secrets it moved and which were left alone (not set in the environment). It is the only thing that writes to OpenBao's secret store; nothing does this automatically.

docs.title: Attachments and their origin
docs.text:
Evidence on manual findings, proof on risk acceptances and files on notes share one store: the bytes are sniffed (the uploader's claimed type is kept only for display), encrypted with a fresh data key wrapped by the organization's OpenBao key, and never rendered in the app. They download only through a link signed for one file and one organization, valid for five minutes, served as application/octet-stream with Content-Disposition: attachment, nosniff and a sandboxing CSP.

Set BULWARK_ATTACHMENTS_ORIGIN to a separate host routed to the API (Helm: api.attachmentsOrigin) so that a captured HTML or SVG file, if someone opens it anyway, lands on a host with no cookies, no token and no API behind it (threat T24, ADR-0048):

  • that host serves signed downloads and nothing else (every other path answers 404), and never sets a cookie;
  • the API's own host then refuses those downloads.

For local use, http://attachments.localhost:8000 works without DNS: browsers resolve any *.localhost name to this machine. Without the setting, files download from the API's own host, which sets no cookies either.

docs.title: Advisories and project owners
docs.text: Since Week 68 (ADR-0052) a project may name an owner: a reference to one of the organization's people (assets.owner, the same token:<prefix> an Issue's assignee is), shown on advisory impact views and audit-logged when it changes. The advisory data itself (OSV, CISA KEV, NVD) is public and shared by every organization; what it means for one organization (advisory_impacts, advisory_states) is under forced RLS. Fetching advisories sends nothing about an organization's packages anywhere: matching happens inside Bulwark.

docs.title: VEX, compliance statuses and evidence packs
docs.text: Since Week 69 (ADR-0053) Bulwark keeps, per organization and under forced RLS: what each project's Go code imports and calls (code_usage: package paths, function and method names with a file and line, never source text), VEX statements with their evidence and who decided them, a person's status for ASVS requirements with a note and links, and generated evidence packs (the zip, including the PDF and an audit-log extract). Evidence packs are kept until deleted with the organization; they hold the actors (token references) of the organization's own audit entries in the period, and no payloads. Audit entries now record their organization (audit_entries.org_id) inside their hash.

docs.title: Email addresses and notifications
docs.text:
Since Week 66 (ADR-0050) Bulwark stores one piece of personal contact data: the email address a person gives in their notification settings, in notification_prefs under the same forced RLS as every per-organization table. Only that person sets or clears it; the audit log records that it changed, never the address. Notifications themselves (notifications) hold the one-line title and a short excerpt of what happened -- a note's first 600 characters, for example -- and are kept with the organization's other data.

Mail goes only to the operator's own SMTP server (BULWARK_SMTP_*), as plain text. Nothing is emailed when no server is configured, and items waiting for a digest are then marked skipped rather than kept.

docs.title: v2.0.0 demo video: script and shot list
docs.text:
Recording needs a person (screen capture and voiceover) -- this is the plan, not the video (plan §33, Week 52 task 3; the video itself is explicitly left to you). Record at 1440x900, dark system theme, browser zoom 100%, notifications off. Have the full stack running (docker compose up -d), the API token on the clipboard, and a GitHub App or test repo ready if you show the verified-fix agent.

Time Screen Say 0:00-0:15 The new homepage (/), let the replay run "This is a real scan of OWASP Juice Shop -- five scanners, watched as they finish, not a stats block." 0:15-0:30 Scroll to "271 unique, 287 raw", severity bars "287 raw findings became 271 after merging duplicates across scanners -- the same correlation v1.0 shipped, still doing the work." 0:30-0:50 Open a finding with a taint path attached "This isn't just 'Semgrep found an eval() call' -- the taint engine confirmed the argument actually flows from this HTTP request. That's new in v2." 0:50-1:10 /app, open a project, click into Hypotheses or the Copilot panel "An LLM layer sits on top now: a triage assistant that flags likely false positives, a hypotheses lane for authorization flaws pattern matching can't see, and a project-scoped copilot you can ask questions." 1:10-1:35 The verified-fix agent: propose a patch, show it rerun the rule + scanners + tests "The flagship feature: it doesn't just suggest a fix. It applies it, reruns the triggering rule, reruns every scanner, runs your own tests, and only then opens a real PR for a human to approve." 1:35-1:50 Asset verification -> a DAST campaign view "And now it isn't just static analysis -- authorized DAST, behind ownership verification and a scope-enforcing proxy, confirms some of this is exploitable at runtime, not just present in the code." 1:50-2:05 bulwark precommit install, a terminal, a blocked commit "Catch a secret before it's even committed -- native, no Docker, fast enough for every commit." 2:05-2:15 docs/ site homepage (mkdocs serve) "And it's documented like a real project now, not just a README." 2:15-2:25 Close on the GitHub repo / release page "Open source, Apache-2.0. v2.0.0, and the evaluation numbers -- including what we don't claim yet -- are public too."

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Juice Shop's own scan (homepage replay) is pre-captured, honestly labelled "replaying" on-screen -- say "a real scan, replayed" in the voiceover too, not "scanning live right now."
  • The verified-fix agent segment needs docker compose --profile fixagent up -d and a real ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -- rehearse this one once before recording; it's the slowest, most moving-parts part of the stack.
  • Never show a real API token, webhook secret, or .env file on screen.
  • Export as MP4. A 15-second GIF of the taint-path finding (0:30-0:50) is a good README/launch-post asset, the same way the Week 8 filter GIF was for v1.

docs.title: 90-second demo video: script and shot list
docs.text:
Recording needs a person (screen capture and voiceover), so this is the plan, not the video. Record at 1440x900, dark system theme, browser zoom 100%, notifications off. Have the stack running (docker compose up -d) and the API token on the clipboard before starting.

Time Screen Say 0:00-0:10 http://localhost:3000, the sample report "Security scanners each find a slice, and running four or five leaves you with duplicates and noise. Bulwark merges them into one list." 0:10-0:25 Scroll the numbers under the header "This is a real scan: five scanners, raw findings on one side, unique findings after merging on the other." 0:25-0:45 Filter to High, click a finding, show the panel "Open a finding: which scanners flagged it, each one's own severity, the code, the fix, and its CWE and OWASP category." 0:45-1:00 j / k through findings, then Export JSON "Keyboard-friendly, and you can export exactly what you filtered." 1:00-1:20 /app, paste token, submit https://github.com/OWASP/NodeGoat "Now a real repo. Each scanner runs sandboxed: no network, read-only." Cards fill in live. 1:20-1:30 Finished report, "771 raw to 463 unique" "771 raw findings became 463. Open source, runs on your machine."

Notes: NodeGoat takes about 80 seconds, so cut the wait in editing. Never show the token on screen. Export as MP4; a GIF of the 0:25-0:45 section is the Week 8 README asset.

docs.title: Deploying the public sample site
docs.text: The public site is the web app only, built in sample mode: it serves the sample report and the About page. It has no API, no database, no scanners, no sign-in and no secrets, so nothing untrusted ever runs on it. This is deliberate: hosting real scanning needs the fixes listed in THREAT-MODEL.md and a decision on ADR-006.

docs.title: What "sample mode" changes
docs.text:
Build with NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO_ONLY=1 (a build argument in web/Dockerfile):

Normal build Sample build / home, /sample yes yes /app, /scans/* scanning UI redirect (307) to /self-host /self-host n/a how to run Bulwark locally, and why there is no hosted scanner Header / hero buttons "Open the app" "Run it yourself" API reference link the API's /docs /self-host (no API exists) CSP connect-src 'self' + the API 'self' only Extra headers Strict-Transport-Security

Tests for this live in web/tests/demo-only.test.tsx. The flag is inlined at build time, so a sample build contains no reference to an API address.

docs.title: Verified locally
docs.text:
The sample image was built and run: /, /sample, /self-host return 200; /app and /scans/x redirect to /self-host; /about redirects to / and /demo to /sample; the container runs as a non-root user (uid 1000) and passes its health check; the browser page contacts only its own origin, with a clean console; and no built file contains localhost:8000. It has not been deployed to a real host from this repository.

docker build -t bulwark/web:demo --build-arg NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO_ONLY=1 --build-arg NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL= web
docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:3100:3000 bulwark/web:demo     # http://localhost:3100

docs.title: Fly.io
docs.text:
web/fly.toml is ready. You need a Fly account and flyctl.

cd web
fly launch --no-deploy --copy-config    # pick a free app name when asked (edit `app` in fly.toml)
fly deploy

It runs one always-on 256 MB shared-CPU machine, so there is no cold start for the first visitor. That is a small recurring cost (Fly has no free tier for new accounts; check their current pricing). To pay nothing when idle instead, set auto_stop_machines = "stop" and min_machines_running = 0 and accept a few seconds on the first visit after idle. Fly terminates TLS and redirects http to https.

App name: app in fly.toml must be unique across Fly. It is set to bulwark-scan-demo; if that is taken, fly launch says so and you pick another. I could not check availability from here (no flyctl, no account).

Footer links: the site shows a "Source code" and a "Contact" link only if you set them. Both are already set in web/fly.toml under [build.args] (repository: github.com/rago12bit/cybernatics). To change them, edit (NEXT_PUBLIC_REPO_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_CONTACT_URL), or pass them as --build-arg to docker build. Other schemes are ignored. They are baked in at build time and visible to everyone, so use an address you are happy to publish.

docs.title: Railway, Render, a VPS
docs.text:
Any host that runs a Dockerfile works: point it at web/, set the build argument NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO_ONLY=1 (build-time, not a runtime variable), expose port 3000. On a VPS:

docker run -d --restart unless-stopped -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 bulwark/web:demo

and put a TLS-terminating proxy (Caddy or nginx) in front. Do not publish port 3000 directly to the internet without TLS: the app sets HSTS assuming it is served over https.

docs.title: Checklist before you share the link
docs.text:
• [ ] Open the URL: the sample report loads and /app lands on "Scanning happens on your machine".
  • [ ] curl -sI https://YOUR-URL/ | grep -i content-security-policy shows connect-src 'self'.
  • [ ] The repository link and contact you set (if any) appear in the footer and are ones you want public.
  • [ ] Consider a custom domain; the default *.fly.dev name is fine for a CV.

docs.title: Dogfooding: Bulwark scanning Bulwark
docs.text: The Bulwark self-scan workflow (.github/workflows/bulwark.yml) runs the action on this repository. On pull requests it fails on new findings of severity HIGH or critical; findings already on main do not count. On pushes it reports and uploads SARIF only. It has not yet run on GitHub; everything below is from running the same CLI locally.

docs.title: First scan of this repository (2026 Week 19, all five scanners completed)
docs.text:
Findings First scan, no ignore file 1,191 unique (4 critical, 81 high, 52 medium, 1,054 low) After .bulwarkignore (183 hidden, counted) 1,010 (0 critical, 31 high, 27 medium, 952 low)

The 183 hidden findings are the deliberately vulnerable scanner test fixtures, saved raw scanner outputs, one old lockfile kept to seed the OSV database, the OWASP/CWE corpus text, and three test files that need realistic-looking fake secrets. Each entry in .bulwarkignore says why.

docs.title: What it found and what was done
docs.text:
• Real bug in Bulwark itself: scanning an ordinary working directory that contains node_modules or a virtualenv failed with "target exceeds max total size". The workspace copy now skips installed dependencies, tool caches and virtualenvs (lockfiles are still scanned). This affected the VS Code extension too.
  • Real dependency advisories: the extension's dev tooling (vitest 2.1.9 with vite 5.4 and esbuild 0.21) carried 1 critical, 1 high and 5 medium advisories. Upgrading to vitest 4 leaves the extension's lockfile with none.
  • Literal bidirectional-control characters in source (core/ci/report.py, core/llm/contract.py, two tests): the sanitising regexes contained the raw characters, which Bandit flags as a Trojan Source pattern. They are now written as \uXXXX escapes, so the source is clean and behaviour is unchanged.
  • SHA-1 used for a sampling id (core/llm/evaluation.py): not a security use; marked usedforsecurity=False.
  • Missing feature: there was no way to say "these paths are test inputs", which the self-scan needed, so .bulwarkignore was added (with the rule that pull requests cannot ignore their own findings).

docs.title: What remains (31 HIGH), and why it is not "fixed"
docs.text:
Most of what is left is scanner noise, which is exactly what a triage layer should be for:

  • 23 findings only Semgrep reports: for example "function defined inside a function but never used" on FastAPI route handlers registered by decorators, time.sleep in retry code, innerHTML in web tests, and "use defusedxml" on XML written by our own PDF code.
  • 4 that Bandit and Semgrep both report: subprocess calls with argument lists (no shell) and SQL text assembled from fixed fragments with bound parameters. Bandit alone rates none of them HIGH; the merged finding takes the higher severity.
  • 3 Gitleaks findings on a local, git-ignored .env (not present in a CI checkout).
  • 1 Trivy finding: the Postgres image's build stage runs as root (the final image is the upstream one).

None was judged a vulnerability, but that is a manual judgment with no ground truth. They stay visible and will not block anyone: the gate only counts findings a pull request adds. A reviewer should still look at the SQL built with text() in core/rag/store.py and the migration string concatenation: both use only fixed fragments and bound parameters today, which is why they were not changed, but a scanner cannot tell that.

docs.title: Limits of this exercise
docs.text:
• One repository, one run, no comparison with what a human reviewer would flag.
  • Counting findings measures noise as much as risk. The number that matters is whether a pull request introducing a real HIGH issue would be caught; that was shown on a small synthetic repository, not on this one.

docs.title: Advisory matching, checked against osv-scanner (Week 68, plan §46.2, §60)
docs.text: Plan §46.2: "Getting range matching right is the hard part; test it against osv-scanner on the same SBOMs." This is that test: what was run, what agreed, and every case that did not.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
scripts/osv-crosscheck.py, seed 68:

  1. The same data for both. OSV's per-ecosystem dumps for PyPI, npm, Go and Maven, downloaded once on 6 October 2026 (the all.zip files, 276 MB). osv-scanner reads them as its offline database (hard links in its cache layout, --offline --offline-vulnerabilities, so it downloads nothing); Bulwark ingests the same files through feeds.update_osv.
  2. The hard versions. For up to 1,000 packages per ecosystem that advisories name, every version at a range boundary (each introduced, fixed and last_affected) and up to three listed affected versions: where range matching goes wrong. One CycloneDX SBOM per ecosystem.
  3. Both matchers, both paths in Bulwark. osv-scanner 2.6.0 (Google's release binary, SHA-256-verified) on each SBOM. Bulwark twice: affects() directly, and the real path -- the SBOM recorded as a project's inventory, matching run by the inventory, impacts read back from the database -- so the stored answer is checked too, not only the function.
  4. Compared per package and version: the set of advisory ids each says apply.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Ecosystem Advisories in the dump Package versions Agree Differ Matches, Bulwark Matches, osv-scanner PyPI 26,080 4,903 4,888 15 83,769 83,717 npm 229,998 1,584 1,583 1 2,031 1,720 Go 9,491 4,960 4,879 81 131,902 131,412 Maven 7,168 10,274 10,269 5 166,976 166,908 All 21,721 21,619 (99.5%) 102 384,678 383,757

osv-scanner never reports an advisory Bulwark misses. In all 102 differences Bulwark reports more. Bulwark's stored matches equal its direct evaluation everywhere except one Go package (below). The full report, every difference listed, is benchmarks/advisories/osv-crosscheck-2026-10-06.json.

docs.title: Every difference
docs.text:
• Go, 80: module paths with capitals (github.com/QuantumNous/new-api). osv-scanner lowercases a Go package URL, as the purl specification suggests, and then finds nothing, because OSV records Go modules in their real case and Go module paths are case-sensitive. Bulwark keeps the case and matches. Probed directly: osv-scanner reports no vulnerability for that module at any version.
  • Go, 1: a record whose package name is a URL (https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser). Bad data in the source; no package URL can name it, so it is in neither tool's results through an SBOM (Bulwark's direct evaluation matched it; its stored path, like osv-scanner, could not).
  • Maven, 5: Maven's own order. 9.0.0-M1 and 9.0.0M1 against a range starting at 9.0.0.M1, and Liferay's 7.3.1-1 against one starting at 7.3.1-ga2. Maven 3.9.16's ComparableVersion, asked directly, says 9.0.0-M1 == 9.0.0.M1 and 7.3.1-1 > 7.3.1-ga2: the versions are inside the ranges. osv-scanner's Maven ordering differs from Maven's here; Bulwark follows Maven.
  • PyPI, 15: versions PEP 440 calls equal. Each is an affected entry with a GIT range, which both tools match by its explicit list of versions only; the list has 6.0 and the SBOM has 6.0.0 (or 2.0/2, 2.8.0rc0/2.8.0-rc0). osv-scanner compares the list as text (after dropping a leading v), Bulwark as versions; PEP 440, and PyPI, say they are the same release. All 52 advisory matches behind these 15 were checked to be exactly this case.
  • npm, 1: a capitalised name (OpenClaw, 311 advisories). Bulwark compares npm names in lower case (npm's own rule for new names, and the purl specification's); osv-scanner compares exactly.

docs.title: What the comparison changed in Bulwark
docs.text:
The first runs disagreed far more, and each cause was fixed rather than explained away:

  1. Timestamps. OSV writes up to nine fractional digits; Python 3.10 reads three or six. Every record with another number was silently dropped (most of PyPI's). Now parsed with any number.
  2. Lenient semver for npm and Go, as osv-scanner reads it: 19.03.0, 2.62, 9.6.0b1 are in OSV's own Go data.
  3. GIT ranges: an entry with one is matched by its version list alone (probed: osv-scanner flagged 0 of 40 versions inside such an entry's ECOSYSTEM range but missing from its list, 39 of 40 for entries without a GIT range).
  4. PyPI legacy versions (not PEP 440, such as Debian's 0.8.3ubuntu7.5): ordered before every PEP 440 version, as setuptools did, instead of "could not compare".
  5. The version list compared as versions, so v1.6.5 is found in a list holding 1.6.5.
  6. The stored path: a verdict cache keyed by advisory instead of by package entry reused one range's "no" for the package's other ranges (OSV lists a package once per range); found by the unit tests, and the database comparison above was added so this class of bug is caught here too.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Four ecosystems; the plan says every one.
  • The sample is boundary versions of advisory-named packages: harder than real SBOMs, not representative of them. Real projects' SBOMs were not available to compare.
  • osv-scanner was run on CycloneDX SBOMs, not lockfiles; its lockfile readers were not compared.
  • One snapshot of OSV's data, one osv-scanner version (2.6.0).

docs.title: Evaluation: Juliet, a real-repository corpus, and prioritization
docs.text: Three measurements, produced by the scripts in benchmarks/ and taken from a single run each on 2026-09-26. Raw results are committed in benchmarks/results/. The OWASP Benchmark result is in evaluation-owasp.md.

docs.title: 1. Juliet Test Suite for Java 1.3 (detection rate per CWE)
docs.text:
Juliet (NIST SARD; 15,848 files staged from 24 security CWE directories) has a bad method with the flaw and matching good methods without it. Ground truth is method-level, from the naming convention (benchmarks/juliet/regions.py): a finding counts for the bad side if it starts inside a bad* method (or a _bad.java file) and for the good side if it starts inside a good* method. That gives 15,192 real cases and 15,330 safe cases. A real case is detected if the scanner names the CWE (exact), a CWE in the same family (related, see benchmarks/juliet/score.py), or anything (any).

Only Semgrep analyses Java, so this is Semgrep's result, not an ensemble's. The scan took 937 s in 11 chunks. A single scan of everything exceeds the tool's 900 s limit; my first attempt timed out and produced no findings, so the runner now scans in chunks of 1,500 files.

Matcher Recall (95% CI) False-alarm rate Precision F1 TPR − FPR exact 21.7% (21.0%–22.3%) 19.5% 52.4% 30.6% +0.022 related 23.8% (23.1%–24.5%) 19.6% 54.6% 33.1% +0.042 any 41.7% (40.9%–42.4%) 35.9% 53.5% 46.8% +0.057

Per CWE (related matcher):

CWE Real Safe Detection rate (recall) False-alarm rate Score CWE-113 2088 2124 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-134 1044 1062 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-15 696 696 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-209 34 34 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-23 696 696 9% 2% +0.08 CWE-256 58 59 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-259 174 174 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-315 58 59 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-319 580 590 45% 44% +0.01 CWE-321 58 58 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-327 34 34 100% 100% +0.00 CWE-328 51 51 67% 0% +0.67 CWE-338 34 34 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-36 696 696 9% 2% +0.08 CWE-470 696 696 61% 57% +0.04 CWE-601 522 522 10% 10% +0.00 CWE-614 17 17 100% 0% +1.00 CWE-643 696 708 8% 8% +0.00 CWE-78 696 696 9% 2% +0.08 CWE-80 1044 1044 10% 0% +0.10 CWE-81 522 522 0% 0% +0.00 CWE-83 522 522 10% 0% +0.10 CWE-89 3480 3540 56% 50% +0.06 CWE-90 696 696 64% 59% +0.05

What this shows, and what it does not:

  • Detection is low overall (24%) and very uneven. Semgrep's open-source rules do well on pattern-shaped weaknesses (CWE-328 weak hash, CWE-614 cookie without Secure, CWE-327) and poorly on the taint-style ones that make up most of Juliet. My explanation, not verified rule by rule: most Juliet variants route the value through helper methods, fields or other classes, which Semgrep's single-function matching does not follow, and some CWEs (113, 134, 259, 321, 338) probably have no matching rule at all.
  • Where it does fire on injection-type CWEs (89, 90, 319, 470) it fires about as often on the safe good methods as on the flawed ones, so a finding there carries almost no signal. The TPR − FPR score of +0.04 says the same.
  • The 24 CWEs are the security ones that map to a scanner. The other 89 Juliet directories (arithmetic, null pointer, resource handling) were left out as out of scope, so this is not a score over all of Juliet.
  • Juliet is synthetic: small self-contained programs written to be analysable. It says little about real repositories.

docs.title: 2. Real-repository corpus (25 projects)
docs.text:
benchmarks/corpus/corpus.json pins 25 public repositories by commit: 12 deliberately vulnerable (VAmPI, NodeGoat, WebGoat, terragoat, ...) and 13 ordinary (flask, requests, express, gin, gson, ...). Each was scanned with the five default scanners through the real sandbox, one repository at a time, with nothing else running. The plan asked for 20 to 30; this is 25. Per-repository numbers: benchmarks/results/corpus-2026-09-26-v2-optimized.json (the numbers below; see the correction and performance notes after the table).

Measure Result Repositories scanned 25 of 25 Tool runs (skipped tools not counted) 94 Crash rate (error or timeout) 0.0% (0 failures) Raw findings, before correlation 11,319 Unique findings, after correlation 10,313 Dedup rate, pooled 8.9% Dedup rate, median repository 2.0% Dedup rate, vulnerable apps / ordinary repos 19.9% / 1.3% Wall time per repository: median / p90 / max 6 s / 42 s / 75 s Wall time, whole corpus 338 s

Reading it:

  • Dedup depends on what you scan. Vulnerable apps have the same flaw reported by several tools (Semgrep and Bandit, Trivy and OSV-Scanner on the same lockfile) so about a fifth of findings merge. Ordinary repositories produce mostly single-tool findings and merge about 1%. The pooled 8.9% is between the two and is not a general figure. Do not quote it without the split.
  • Crash rate 0% is one run. It is not a reliability guarantee: zero failures in 94 runs bounds the true rate at roughly 3% (rule of three, 95%).
  • Wall time includes sandbox start-up for each tool and the correlation step; the machine is one laptop running Docker Desktop. terragoat is the slowest (75 s), and that is Trivy's IaC scan (measured in Week 25).
  • Correction to the first run (corpus-2026-09-26-v1.json, kept for the "before" timings). dvpwa reported 65 unique findings there and 224 in the rerun. Semgrep gives up on a rule/file pair after 5 s and still exits successfully, so under CPU pressure it silently returned 5 findings instead of 169. Bulwark now reports this (warnings in the tool status, and on stderr in the CLI). I checked whether my other headline numbers were affected by rerunning the OWASP and Juliet scans: predictions were identical and no timeouts were reported. Only the first corpus run's dvpwa figure was wrong.
  • The wall times above are after the Week 25 optimizations (evaluation.md). The first run's were 47 s median and 214 s max; dvpwa and NodeGoat are still slow because of vendored JavaScript.
  • No claim of accuracy comes from this table. The corpus has no ground truth; it measures behaviour and cost.
  • Small oddities: cfngoat yields 2 findings and terragoat's languages show "-" because IaC is not a language. Checkov, which would cover them better, is tier 2 and not in the default five.

docs.title: 3. Prioritization quality (risk score vs severity only)
docs.text:
Question: when a user reads only the top K findings, does ordering by Bulwark's risk score put more real vulnerabilities there than ordering by severity alone? Method (benchmarks/prioritize.py): scan the OWASP Benchmark with Semgrep through the full pipeline, label each finding true (the test is a real vulnerability and the finding names its weakness) or false, rank three ways, and report top-K precision. Ties are scored by expected value, not input order. The bootstrap interval resamples findings 500 times with a fixed seed.

2894 findings, 1395 true positives (48.2% base rate); 7 distinct risk scores, 2 distinct severities.

Top-K Risk score Severity only Random Risk − severity (95% CI) 10 69.2% 52.4% 48.2% +16.8% (-10.7% to +40.3%) 20 63.3% 52.4% 48.2% +10.9% (-6.4% to +28.3%) 50 56.8% 52.4% 48.2% +4.4% (-2.0% to +10.8%) 100 54.6% 52.4% 48.2% +2.2% (-0.6% to +5.3%)

Reading it:

  • The risk score is ahead at every K, and the lead is largest at the top, but every interval includes zero, so this run does not show the risk score beating severity. It is weak evidence in that direction, not a result.
  • Both rankings sit close to random (48.2%). With one scanner there are only 2 severities and 7 distinct risk scores (rule-level severity and confidence), so the score has almost nothing to separate findings with. That is a property of this setup, not a general ceiling.
  • What is not evaluated: the parts of the score built for dependencies (EPSS, CISA KEV, reachability) have no exploitation ground truth in any dataset I have, so their effect on ordering is unmeasured here. Their contribution is argued in risk-score.md, not measured. Multi-scanner agreement, which raises confidence in the score, is also absent because only one scanner analyses Java.
  • Only OWASP Benchmark findings were used; Juliet predictions store CWEs, not scores.

docs.title: Reproducing
docs.text:
python -m benchmarks.juliet.run fetch && python -m benchmarks.juliet.run scan --label v1
python -m benchmarks.juliet.run score benchmarks/results/juliet-java-1.3-<date>-v1.predictions.json.gz
python -m benchmarks.corpus.run scan --label v1        # fetches 25 repos at pinned commits
python -m benchmarks.prioritize collect --label v1 && python -m benchmarks.prioritize score <records.json>

Juliet is downloaded at run time (77 MB, sha256 pinned in the script) and not redistributed. Run each on an otherwise idle machine if you want comparable wall times.

docs.title: Evaluation: OWASP Benchmark v1.2beta
docs.text:
How well do Bulwark's scanners find real vulnerabilities in a labelled corpus, and how often do they cry wolf? This is the first measurement of correctness (the deduplication benchmark measures only duplicate reduction).

Headline (Semgrep, the only scanner here that analyses Java): it finds 88% of the real vulnerabilities and also flags 44% of the safe look-alikes, so precision is 68%, F1 77%, and the Benchmark's own score (recall minus false-positive rate) is +0.445 on a scale where 0 is a coin flip. It is excellent on pattern-shaped weaknesses and weak on data-flow ones (below).

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Corpus: OWASP Benchmark tag 1.2beta, commit 2734ae4: 2,740 small Java servlets in 11 weakness categories. 1,415 are really vulnerable, 1,325 are "fake": they look vulnerable but are not (input replaced by a constant, sanitised, or never reaching the sink). The answer for each is in the corpus's own CSV (its SHA-256 is recorded in the result file). GPL-2.0; downloaded at run time by python -m benchmarks.owasp.run fetch (about 150 MB), never committed here.
  • What was scanned: only the 2,740 .java test files and pom.xml (the repository also ships other tools' reference results, which must not be seen by the scanners).
  • How each tool was run: through Bulwark's own runner, in its sandbox, one tool at a time (so findings are not merged across tools), with each finding's CWE enriched by Bulwark's taxonomy. Findings outside the test files are counted but not scored.
  • Scoring per test case: predicted positive means the tool reported that weakness in that file. TP, FP, TN, FN follow. Recall = TP / real; false-positive rate = FP / fake; precision = TP / flagged; F1; and the Benchmark's score TPR − FPR. 95% Wilson intervals are in the result file. Precision and F1 are shown as n/a when a tool flagged nothing, never as 0.
  • What counts as "reported that weakness" is a judgment call, so three matchers are scored and published together (benchmarks/owasp/score.py):
  • exact: a finding with the case's own CWE id.
  • related: exact, plus CWE ids that describe the same weakness for that category. Deliberately narrow: crypto {327, 326, 780}, hash {328, 327, 916}, weak randomness {330, 338, 331, 335}. A cookie missing HttpOnly (CWE-1004) earns no credit for a missing Secure flag (CWE-614). related is the headline.
  • any: any finding in the file. An upper bound with no credit for being right; it shows how much the matcher matters.

docs.title: Results (Semgrep, community Java rules pinned at build, semgrep 1.90.0)
docs.text:
Wall time 200 s for all 2,740 files. Result files: benchmarks/results/owasp-1.2beta-2026-09-26-v1.*.json.

Matcher Recall (95% CI) False-positive rate Precision F1 Score (TPR − FPR) TP / FP / TN / FN exact 79.0% (76.8–81.1) 41.7% 66.9% 72.5% +0.374 1118 / 552 / 773 / 297 related 88.2% (86.4–89.8) 43.7% 68.3% 77.0% +0.445 1248 / 579 / 746 / 167 any 90.0% (88.3–91.4) 67.4% 58.8% 71.1% +0.226 1273 / 893 / 432 / 142

docs.title: By category (related)
docs.text: Category Real Fake Recall False-positive rate Score weakrand (insecure randomness) 218 275 100% 0% +1.00 securecookie (no Secure flag) 36 31 100% 0% +1.00 crypto (weak cipher) 130 116 100% 23% +0.77 hash (weak hash) 129 107 69% 0% +0.69 xss 246 209 82% 52% +0.30 xpathi 15 20 93% 65% +0.28 sqli 272 232 93% 73% +0.20 pathtraver 133 135 90% 79% +0.12 ldapi 27 32 96% 88% +0.09 trustbound 83 43 52% 42% +0.10 cmdi (command injection) 126 125 93% 87% +0.06

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text:
• Two very different regimes. Categories decided by what is called (a weak random generator, an unsafe hash, a cookie without Secure) are solved: near-perfect recall and almost no false positives. Categories decided by where the data came from (SQL, command, LDAP, XPath injection and path traversal) have 65–88% false-positive rates: the score sits just above a coin flip (+0.06 to +0.28).
  • A likely cause, checked on one example, not proven. The rules match the dangerous call (string concatenated into a query) but Semgrep's community rules do little data-flow tracking. In a sampled false positive (BenchmarkTest00104) the "tainted" value is replaced by a constant behind an always-true condition, and Semgrep flags the query anyway. 170 safe sqli cases were flagged. Other causes were not ruled out.
  • The matcher matters. Crediting any finding in a file (any) drops the score from +0.445 to +0.226 because it also counts 314 more false alarms: reporting something is not the same as reporting the right thing.

docs.title: What this does not tell you
docs.text:
• Only one scanner analyses Java here. Bandit, gosec and the others do not apply; Gitleaks found nothing in the corpus (0% recall, scored as such); Trivy and OSV-Scanner cover dependencies, not these servlets. So there is no ensemble result: with one analysing tool an ensemble equals it, and the harness says so instead of printing a duplicate row. Showing what multiple tools add needs a corpus several of them cover (Week 24's Juliet suite, or the Python and JavaScript repositories).
  • It is a synthetic corpus. The Benchmark is small, uniform servlets written to be scored; real code differs, and tools can be tuned to it. Treat the numbers as a comparison instrument, not a promise about your code.
  • No comparison with other tools was made. No published scorecard was reproduced or cited.
  • One run, one rule-pack version, one tag. The Benchmark is known to have quirks; 1.2beta is the tag the design targets, not the final 1.2 release.
  • related is my mapping, chosen before seeing scores and kept narrow, but it is a choice: see exact if you disagree.

docs.title: Found while doing it
docs.text:
• Maven projects never triggered the dependency scanners: pom.xml was not in the list of files that mark a repository as having dependencies, so Trivy and OSV-Scanner were skipped on it. Fixed (with a test). Scanning the corpus's pom.xml for dependencies was not part of the scoring.
  • The dedup benchmark script had started running every registered scanner after tier 2 landed; it is pinned back to the original five so its published numbers stay reproducible.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
python -m benchmarks.owasp.run fetch                       # about 150 MB, needs git and network
python -m benchmarks.owasp.run scan --label v1             # needs Docker and the scanner images; about 4 minutes
python -m benchmarks.owasp.run score benchmarks/results/owasp-1.2beta-<date>-v1.predictions.json

Scoring reads the saved per-test predictions, so it re-runs without any scanner.

docs.title: Evaluating AI fix quality
docs.text:
Status: not yet run. Everything below is built and tested, but the evaluation itself needs two things this project does not have inside the repository: a model API key, and a person to score the answers. No result from this evaluation is reported anywhere until it has been run and scored. The README says the same.

Goal (plan, Week 14): sample 50 generated fixes, hand-score their correctness, and record the result honestly.

docs.title: What is ready
docs.text: Piece Where State A fixed sample of 50 real findings benchmarks/remediation/sample.jsonl Committed, deterministic (seed 1) Runner (uses the product's own prompt, contract and patch check) benchmarks/remediation/run.py generate Tested with fake models; not run with a real one Blinded offline scoring page run.py scorer Tested in a simulated browser Report with confidence intervals and a README table run.py report Tested on synthetic scores; refuses unscored data Automatic patch check (does it apply to the code?) core/llm/patchcheck.py Tested against the real patch tool

docs.title: The sample
docs.text:
50 findings from real scans of four public vulnerable projects (NodeGoat, nodejs-goof, Vulnerable-Flask-App, VAmPI): 35 code findings (each a different rule, so the sample is not dominated by the one noisy Semgrep rule that produced 111 of NodeGoat's findings) and 15 dependency findings (each a different CVE). Secrets are excluded (no code is sent for them) and so is anything without a usable code snippet. Code findings can carry a patch; dependency findings are scored on the fix advice only.

Known limits of the sample: only JavaScript and Python code, no infrastructure-as-code findings, and the projects are deliberately vulnerable teaching apps, so their flaws are more textbook than real-world code. Rebuild or enlarge it with run.py sample EXPORT.json ... -n 50 --seed 1 (exports come from GET /scans/{id}/export?format=json).

docs.title: How to run it
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[llm]"

# 1. See what would be sent and how many tokens (no key, nothing leaves the machine)
python benchmarks/remediation/run.py generate --dry-run
#    50 calls, about 87,000 input tokens in total, output capped at 1,500 tokens per call

# 2. Generate answers. This SENDS finding text and code snippets to your model provider.
export BULWARK_LLM_ENABLED=1 BULWARK_LLM_API_KEY=...   # never commit or paste a key into a chat
python benchmarks/remediation/run.py generate

# 3. Score them: open the page, judge each item, click "Download scores.json"
python benchmarks/remediation/run.py scorer --results benchmarks/remediation/runs/<run>/results.jsonl

# 4. Turn scores into numbers and a README table
python benchmarks/remediation/run.py report --results benchmarks/remediation/runs/<run>/results.jsonl --scores scores.json

The report is written to benchmarks/results/remediation-<date>.json. It records the model, the prompt version and the date, so a later run with a different model is a separate, comparable result.

docs.title: The rubric (what "correct" means)
docs.text:
Score each item from the code and the answer, not from how confident or fluent the answer sounds. The page hides the model's own confidence and the automatic patch check so they cannot sway you.

Question 0 1 2 Explanation accurate? Wrong or misleading Partly right Accurate for this code Fix correct? Wrong, would not fix it, or harmful Generic or incomplete Correct and specific to this code Patch correct? (only if a patch is shown) Wrong or breaks the code Helps but needs edits Correct as written

Two yes/no flags: unsafe (following it would introduce a new vulnerability or a bad practice) and hallucination (it refers to code, APIs or files that are not in the snippet). The baseline question (optional) applies the fix rubric to the non-AI reference text shown beside it, so the report can say whether the model adds anything over plain CWE and OWASP guidance.

Guidance for hard cases: a fix that is right in principle but names a function the snippet does not show is a 1 and a hallucination. A patch that applies cleanly but changes behaviour is a 0. If the model's answer was rejected and reference text was shown instead, score the fix on that text and say so in the notes.

docs.title: What is reported, and how to read it
docs.text:
For the items the model answered: the share whose fix is correct (score 2) and acceptable (score 1 or 2), the share with an accurate explanation, the unsafe and hallucination rates, and, for answers with a patch, the share the automatic check found to match the code and the share you scored correct. Also: results by category, whether the model's stated confidence predicts your score (calibration), how many answers fell back to reference text and why, and, if you scored the baseline, how often the AI beat, tied or lost to it.

Every rate comes with a 95% Wilson interval and its sample size. With about 50 items the intervals are wide (a measured 70% is consistent with roughly 56% to 81%), so small differences are noise.

docs.title: Limits of this design
docs.text:
• One scorer. Correctness is a judgement; a single person's scores are not the ground truth. Getting a second person to score the same page and comparing would be better, and is not built.
  • The patch check is necessary, not sufficient. "Applies to the code shown" says nothing about whether the fix is right. It also cannot check patches that reach beyond the stored snippet (they are marked unverified).
  • A fix is not run. Nothing here compiles the patched code or reruns the scanner to see the finding vanish. That would be a stronger test and is future work.
  • Small, single-model, single-prompt. It says nothing about other models or prompt versions until they are run.
  • The scorer knows which model is being tested; a blind comparison of two models is not built.

This document's job is to put all eleven rows in one place, not to re-litigate or soften what they already said.

docs.title: Taint engine: what was actually measured
docs.text:
The taint engine (core/taint/) doesn't detect vulnerabilities on its own -- it confirms whether a SAST finding some other scanner already reported is reachable from a real HTTP entrypoint (core/taint/reachability.py's own documented design). So "precision and recall on labelled cases" means: of the SAST findings it could confirm, were the confirmations correct, and of the ones it could have confirmed, how many did it?

Method. Ran the real scan pipeline (bulwark scan --tools bandit,semgrep, no mocks) against 8 already-cached, real, deliberately-vulnerable repositories from this project's own 25-repo corpus -- every Python/JavaScript one it has (NodeGoat, nodejs-goof from Week 52; VAmPI, Vulnerable-Flask-App, pygoat, dvpwa, vulpy, dvna added afterward) -- then read the flagged source by hand to check each confirmation against the real code. Full method, two real bugs found and fixed along the way (a resolver name-collision that could silently erase real taint, and a missing subprocess.Popen catalog entry), and three freshly-confirmed real scope limits: docs/v2-gap-closure-taint-corpus.md.

Result: 9 confirmed reachable findings across 5 of 8 repositories, 9/9 hand-verified genuine true positives, 0 false confirmations -- up from the original 3/3 on NodeGoat alone: - NodeGoat (unchanged): 3 findings, app/routes/contributions.js:32-34, eval(req.body.preTax) et al. -- NodeGoat's own documented "A1 SSJS Injection" tutorial vulnerability, the file's own comment reads // Insecure use of eval() to parse inputs. - pygoat: 4 SAST findings confirmed reachable (cmd_lab's and mitre_lab_17_api's subprocess.Popen command injections, cmd_lab2's and mitre_lab_25_api's direct eval injections -- one of the four only found after this week's bug fixes, see the linked doc), plus a 5th genuine reachable sink (ImageMath.eval) with no SAST finding at that exact line to attach to. - Vulnerable-Flask-App: 1 (request.json-sourced SQL injection via db.engine.execute). - dvna: 1 (req.body.login-sourced SQL injection via db.sequelize.query). - VAmPI, dvpwa, vulpy: 0 confirmed each, for three different, real, documented reasons (an OpenAPI-path-parameter source the catalog doesn't recognize; an ambiguous same-named function across the repo's own parallel bad/good implementations; an aiohttp app, a framework core.codeintel's entrypoint detector doesn't cover) -- not silent gaps, each confirmed and named in the linked document. - Every confirmed finding's originating SAST rule fires on the pattern alone (eval(), subprocess.Popen(..., shell=True), a raw .execute()/.query() call), tainted or not -- the taint engine's actual contribution is narrowing each one down to "and this argument provably comes from this HTTP request," which the pattern rule alone cannot say.

What this is not: a corpus-scale precision/recall study, and not a comparison against Semgrep's own taint mode specifically (its bundled community rules use pattern mode here; a taint-mode comparison would need hand-authored Semgrep taint rules for the same source/sink pairs, which wasn't built). This is a real, hand-verified spot-check, larger than before -- 9 confirmed cases across 8 repositories, 0 false confirmations -- not the full "labelled Python and JavaScript corpus" the plan describes, and no Go-language vulnerable repository exists in the corpus at all.

docs.title: Ranking detail
docs.text:
Already measured and published in docs/evaluation-juliet-corpus.md; reproduced here because it's one of §34's own named rows, not because anything changed:

Top-K Risk score Severity only Random Risk − severity (95% CI) 10 69.2% 52.4% 48.2% +16.8% (-10.7% to +40.3%) 20 63.3% 52.4% 48.2% +10.9% (-6.4% to +28.3%) 50 56.8% 52.4% 48.2% +4.4% (-2.0% to +10.8%) 100 54.6% 52.4% 48.2% +2.2% (-0.6% to +5.3%)

The risk score leads at every K, but every confidence interval includes zero -- this is weak evidence in its favor, not a demonstrated result. "Severity only" here is a fair stand-in for v1's own pre-EPSS/KEV ranking, since that's literally what v1.0 sorted by before Week 9 added EPSS and KEV. The parts of the score that matter most for dependency findings (EPSS, KEV, reachability) have no exploitation ground truth in this dataset, so their effect on ordering is argued in risk-score.md, not measured here -- unchanged since the original measurement.

docs.title: LLM security detail
docs.text: tests/redteam/ (see docs/redteam.md) runs 20 adversarial payloads against every contract that parses raw model text (core.llm, core.triage_assistant, core.attackpath) -- 60 payload x contract combinations, all 60 correctly rejected, plus four more targeted suites (patch confinement, severity immutability under injection, Copilot tool-scope enforcement, a real secret-forwarding bug this suite itself caught and fixed). This is a structural defense pass rate: it proves the contracts can't be tricked into producing a harmful result regardless of what a model says. It is not the plan's "attack success rate per release," which needs garak actually attacking a live model and tracking how often persuasion succeeds -- deliberately deferred, same reasoning docs/redteam.md already gives: that needs a real API key, ongoing spend per run, and a probe-budget decision, not something to fake with a hardcoded number.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• Five of eleven rows need a live model and were not measured: verified-fix acceptance/blind review, triage assistant precision/recall, hypotheses lane precision, Copilot citation/correctness, and the LLM security attack success rate specifically (its structural-defense pass rate is measured, above). Every one of these gaps was already disclosed in that feature's own week (41/42/43/44) -- this document doesn't newly discover them, just collects them.
  • The UX row has no "before" or "after." The baseline usability study (Week 31) was never run with real participants; there is nothing to compare a redesign against yet.
  • The taint engine measurement is a spot-check (N=9 confirmed cases across 5 of 8 repositories), not a corpus-scale study, and makes no claim about recall against vulnerability classes outside its declared sink categories, or against the 4 corpus repositories whose own language (Java, CloudFormation, Terraform) has no taint catalog at all. The Go catalog specifically has never been run against a real vulnerable repository -- the corpus has none.
  • Scale and platform-security numbers are a single developer laptop's, not a provisioned server's -- see each one's own week for the full caveat.
  • Incremental scanning is 7 repositories with a 3-file edit each, not the plan's "last 20 merged PRs of each repository in the 30-repository corpus" -- benchmarks/incremental/run.py supports more repos; running it across the full corpus, and against real historical PRs rather than a synthetic edit, was not done. One repository (Vulnerable-Flask-App) showed a much smaller speedup (1.2x) than the rest, plausibly but not confirmed-as-root-caused to a Semgrep per-rule timeout on that repository: docs/v2-gap-closure-incremental-corpus.md.

docs.title: What the Phase 14 numbers do not show
docs.text:
• Agreement with DefectDojo is agreement with DefectDojo's tests, not with ground truth. Where Bulwark differs on purpose (a finding per place, licence findings not imported, an empty Nuclei file closing nothing) the difference is in the test file with its reason.
  • The ingest numbers are throughput on a laptop for files built by repeating real records; the whole import peaks at 1.5 GB for 117,000 SARIF findings, and nothing was run at the plan's other scale (one million Occurrences) here.
  • Fuzzing found one real bug (memory, not a crash) in minutes of running; that is evidence the harness works, not that the parsers are clean.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Covers scanning, correlation and ranking only. For the rest of v2 (taint engine, verified fixes, triage assistant, Copilot, scale, platform security, and an honest list of what still needs a live model to measure), see evaluation-v2.md (plan §34, Week 52).

What was measured, how, and what it does and does not show. Every figure is produced by a script in benchmarks/ from a result file committed in benchmarks/results/, from one run on one machine (a laptop running Docker Desktop with 10 CPUs) in September 2026. Run-to-run variation was not measured; the OWASP and Juliet scans were repeated once after the Week 25 changes and gave identical predictions.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Measure Result OWASP: recall / false-positive rate / F1 (related matcher, Semgrep) 88.2% (CI 86.4–89.8) / 43.7% / 77.0% OWASP: Benchmark score (TPR − FPR) +0.445 (exact matcher +0.374, any +0.226) Juliet: recall / false-alarm rate / score 23.8% / 19.6% / +0.042 Corpus: tool-run failures 0 of 94 Corpus: dedup, vulnerable apps / ordinary repos / pooled 19.9% / 1.3% / 8.9% Corpus: wall time per repository, median / p90 / max 6 s / 42 s / 75 s Top-20 precision: risk score / severity only / random 63.3% / 52.4% / 48.2% (difference not significant)

docs.title: How to read them
docs.text:
• Only Semgrep analyses Java. The OWASP and Juliet numbers are Semgrep's, not an ensemble's, so they say nothing about whether combining scanners helps. That question needs a language with several analysers, which neither suite provides.
  • Detection is strong where the flaw is a pattern and weak where it needs data flow. OWASP recall is 88%, but the false-positive rate on injection categories is 65–88%. On Juliet the detection rate is 24% and where injection CWEs are detected the safe variants are flagged about as often.
  • Dedup depends on the target. Roughly a fifth of findings merge on deliberately vulnerable apps, about 1% on ordinary repositories. Do not quote the pooled figure alone.
  • Zero crashes in 94 runs bounds the true crash rate at about 3% (rule of three, 95%). It is not a reliability guarantee.
  • Prioritization is not shown to help. The risk score is ahead of severity-only at every K, but every confidence interval includes zero, and with one scanner there are only 7 distinct scores. The parts of the score built for dependencies (EPSS, KEV, reachability) cannot be evaluated: no dataset has exploitation ground truth for them.
  • Not measured at all: AI fix quality, the VS Code extension and GitHub Action in their real hosts, secret detection recall (Gitleaks has no benchmark here), SCA accuracy against ground truth.
  • Synthetic vs real. OWASP and Juliet are synthetic. The corpus is real code but has no ground truth, so it measures behaviour and cost, not accuracy.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Week 25 profiled the corpus scan. Tools already run in parallel, so a scan takes as long as its slowest tool, and that was Semgrep in 21 of 25 repositories (median 52 s), Trivy in 3 (IaC repositories).

Finding Change Measured effect Semgrep spent ~26 s of every scan loading 337 small rule files (config time 25.9 s of 26.2 s on an empty repo) Rules are merged into one file per language at image build time, ids preserved (docker/semgrep/merge-rules.py) config time 26 s → 1 s. Rule ids and findings identical on 6 repositories, then across the whole corpus (except dvpwa, below) Semgrep was limited to 1 CPU cpus=4 and --jobs=4 for Semgrep 20–40% faster on larger repos; no effect on rule loading Trivy IaC scan of terragoat took 133 s at 1 CPU cpus=4 for Trivy 68 s Semgrep silently skips a rule/file after 5 s and exits 0 Bulwark now reports warnings on the tool status and on stderr dvpwa returned 5 findings under load instead of 169

Result on the corpus (corpus-2026-09-26-v1.json before, ...-v2-optimized.json after):

Before After Median wall time per repository 46.9 s 6.2 s 90th percentile 74.2 s 41.5 s Slowest 214 s (terragoat) 75 s (terragoat) Whole corpus 1,235 s 338 s OWASP Benchmark Semgrep scan 202 s 30 s Juliet Semgrep scan (11 chunks) 937 s 313 s

Unique findings were identical for 24 of 25 repositories. dvpwa went from 65 to 224 because the first run lost Semgrep findings to timeouts under CPU pressure (see above); the optimized run and repeated direct runs agree on 169 Semgrep findings. The OWASP and Juliet reruns gave identical predictions, so those headline results were not affected.

What was not fixed:

  • Trivy misconfiguration scanning is slow when more than one IaC scanner is enabled. On terragoat, Terraform alone takes 1.6 s and any second scanner (Dockerfile, Kubernetes, CloudFormation) brings it to about 130 s, though each alone is fast. This looks like Trivy 0.55.2 behaviour. The obvious workaround (one invocation per scanner) needs a wrapper the sandbox runner does not have, so it is left as is; 4 CPUs halve it.
  • Vendored JavaScript. dvpwa and NodeGoat spend ~40 s matching rules against bundled libraries such as materialize.js. Skipping vendored files would be faster and would also hide findings, so it is not done by default.
  • Capacity trade-off. Semgrep and Trivy now take up to 4 CPUs each per scan. On a busy worker that raises the CPU a single scan can consume; the sandbox still caps it. The values are in the adapters' ToolSpec.
  • Wall times here are from an otherwise idle laptop. A shared or smaller host will be slower, and Semgrep's timeout behaviour above is the main way that shows up as missing findings, now flagged.

docs.title: Reproducing
docs.text: See evaluation-juliet-corpus.md and evaluation-owasp.md. Public suites are downloaded at run time and not redistributed. Run each on an otherwise idle machine to compare wall times.

docs.title: /fix on pull requests
docs.text: A member comments /fix on a pull request. Bulwark replies with what the verified-fix agent would try and the most it may spend. Nothing runs until someone allowed to replies /fix confirm <code>. Each verified patch is then posted as a comment for a person to apply; Bulwark never pushes to the branch. Design: ADR-0059. The agent itself: verified-fix-agent.md.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. The GitHub App is installed, with the Issue comment event subscribed (in addition to Pull request and Installation). Its "Pull requests: Read & write" permission covers reading the pull request and commenting.
  2. The verified-fix agent runs: a Temporal server and python -m core.fixagent.worker, with a hosted model configured (BULWARK_LLM_ENABLED=1 and a key). The worker needs the App's id and key too, to post results.
  3. An admin links each person's GitHub username under Settings → People and access → GitHub account. Only an admin can: a person naming their own could name someone else's.

Limits you can set:

Setting Default What it does BULWARK_FIX_TOKENS_PER_FINDING 60000 The cap per finding; the preview's total is this times the findings. BULWARK_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_PER_ORG_MONTH 2000000 The organization's monthly budget; every fix-agent token counts. BULWARK_LLM_COST_PER_1K_TOKENS_USD unset When set, the preview shows a price. BULWARK_FIXAGENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_PER_ORG 3 Runs at once per organization; a confirm that would pass it is refused.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The command must be the whole first line of a new comment (an edited comment never counts).

Comment What happens /fix A preview: up to 5 findings this pull request introduced (code, secrets, configuration), most severe first, and the token cap. A new preview replaces the last one. /fix confirm K7M2PQ9X Starts one run per finding, if everything below still holds. A code works once, for 24 hours. /fix cancel K7M2PQ9X Withdraws the preview.

docs.title: Who may, and when
docs.text:
Checked on the preview and again on the confirm:

  • the commenter is an owner, member or collaborator of the repository on GitHub, and an admin linked their GitHub account to an active person whose role on this project is Member or higher;
  • the pull request is open and not from a fork -- the agent runs the pull request's code, which must never happen with the base repository's credentials;
  • Bulwark has a finished scan of the commit the pull request is at;
  • on confirm: the pull request has no new commits since the preview, the organization's budget left covers the cap, and it is under its concurrency limit.

Anything else gets a one-line reply saying why. A comment on a pull request Bulwark never scanned gets no reply.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• Push, merge or approve anything. A patch is a comment.
  • Fix dependency findings (a version bump is not a code patch) or findings already on the base branch.
  • Spend past the cap. The cap is checked before each model call, so the last call can pass it by that one call's size.

docs.title: GitHub Action
docs.text:
Runs Bulwark on every push and pull request. It uploads SARIF to Code Scanning, comments the findings a pull request introduces, and fails the check at a severity you choose.

name: Bulwark
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write   # upload SARIF to Code Scanning
  pull-requests: write    # the PR comment

jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: rago12bit/cybernatics@main   # pin a release tag or commit SHA once one is published
        with:
          fail-on: high

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Input Default path . Directory to scan. tools all five Comma-separated scanners. fail-on high none, low, medium, high or critical. On a pull request only new findings count. upload-sarif true Needs security-events: write. comment true Needs pull-requests: write. sbom false Also write a CycloneDX 1.6 SBOM (output sbom-file); upload it with actions/upload-artifact if you want to keep it. compare-base true On pull requests, also scan the base commit so only new findings are reported and gated. github-token github.token Used only for the comment. python-version 3.12

Outputs: new-findings, total-findings, sarif-file, sbom-file (empty unless sbom is true).

docs.title: How "new" is decided
docs.text:
The action scans the pull request and the base commit (a second checkout of the base SHA) and compares the two by Bulwark's fingerprint, the stable defect identity from correlation. A finding that only moved lines or was reported by a different set of scanners is not new. The comment also says how many findings already existed and how many the change fixed.

If the base cannot be scanned, or a scanner failed on the base (which would make its findings look new), Bulwark does not guess: it lists and gates on all findings and says so in the comment.

On a push there is no baseline; the threshold applies to every finding.

docs.title: What happens on failure
docs.text: Upload and comment run before the check fails, so a red run still shows the findings. The upload step is allowed to fail (forks, missing permissions) without hiding the gate result; the comment is skipped with a warning when the token cannot write. The run summary always contains the same table.

docs.title: Ignoring paths: .bulwarkignore
docs.text:
Put a .bulwarkignore at the scan root (see this repository's own for an example): one glob per line, # for comments. tests/fixtures/ (anchored at the root), fixtures/ (any directory of that name), *.lock, docs/**/*.md. Ignored findings are dropped from the report but counted, and the count appears in the comment and JSON (stats.ignored_findings), so ignoring is never silent.

A change cannot hide its own findings. On pull requests the action reads the ignore file from the base commit and passes it to both scans; a .bulwarkignore added or edited by the pull request has no effect until it is merged (checked by running the action's scan step against a real repository whose head tried to ignore its own new file). If the base commit cannot be fetched, nothing is ignored. On pushes the file in the checkout applies.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Use the pull_request trigger. Do not use pull_request_target with a checkout of the PR head: that runs untrusted code with a write token.
  • Fork pull requests get a read-only token: the scan and the gate work, the comment and SARIF upload are skipped.
  • Inputs reach shell steps only through env:, never interpolated into the script, so a branch name or input value cannot become code (checked by a test). Third-party actions are pinned to commit SHAs.
  • Only the one comment authored by github-actions[bot] that carries the Bulwark marker is ever updated; a user quoting the marker cannot redirect the update. Every scan-derived string in the comment is escaped: no links, images, HTML or @mentions.
  • The scanners run in sandboxed containers (see the threat model). The action builds their images on the runner (about 2 to 4 minutes on a cold runner) and pulls Gitleaks from Docker Hub.
  • It uses actions/cache v6 and github/codeql-action v4, which run on Node 24: a self-hosted runner needs version 2.327.1 or later. GitHub-hosted runners already are.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• It has not been run on GitHub. Its logic was checked by running the exact step scripts locally against a real git repository with a base and a head commit (the base worktree was scanned, only the new finding was reported, the gate failed), by unit tests, and by static checks of action.yml. Expect first-run surprises around runner permissions and Docker.
  • No image caching, so every run rebuilds the scanner images.
  • Marketplace listing is a manual step: see releasing.md.

docs.title: GitHub App integration
docs.text:
Installs once on an org or repository and scans every pull request automatically — no workflow file to write or maintain (that's the GitHub Action, a separate, complementary integration: use the Action if you already have CI and want Bulwark as a step in it; use the App if you want PRs scanned without touching your CI config at all).

Status: implemented, not yet live-verified against a real App (ADR-0017, docs/v2-week30-verification.md) — the steps below are what's needed to close that gap; nothing here has been exercised against a real GitHub App yet.

docs.title: Register the App
docs.text:
1. GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App.
  2. Webhook URL: https://<your-bulwark-host>/integrations/github/webhook (needs to be reachable from GitHub — a public host, or a tunnel such as ngrok/smee.io for local testing).
  3. Webhook secret: generate one (openssl rand -hex 24) and set it both here and as BULWARK_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET below — this is what proves a webhook actually came from GitHub.
  4. Permissions: Repository → Contents: Read-only, Pull requests: Read & write (for the result comment), Metadata: Read-only (mandatory).
  5. Subscribe to events: Pull request, Installation, and Issue comment (for /fix, docs/fix-on-pull-requests.md).
  6. Create the App, then generate a private key (downloads a .pem file) and note the App ID shown on its settings page.
  7. Install the App on the account/repos you want scanned.

docs.title: Configure Bulwark
docs.text:
Three environment variables, all optional (unset = the integration is simply off and the webhook endpoint 404s):

BULWARK_GITHUB_APP_ID=123456
# The PEM's newlines, escaped as literal \n (most secret stores flatten multi-line values this way).
BULWARK_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY="-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\nMIIEvQ...\n-----END PRIVATE KEY-----\n"
BULWARK_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=<the secret from step 3>

docker-compose.yml already wires these through to both api (receives webhooks) and worker (posts the result comment once a scan finishes) — set them in .env and docker compose up -d api worker.

docs.title: What happens
docs.text: Opening or updating a pull request on an installed repo: Bulwark clones exactly that PR's head commit (refs/pull/<n>/head, not the default branch), scans it with the default tool set, and posts a summary comment on the PR once it finishes — reusing the same comment format the GitHub Action uses. The first webhook for a new installation creates a Bulwark organization for it (there's no separate org management yet, ADR-0013); every PR scanned through that installation shares it.

docs.title: Known limitations (Week 30)
docs.text:
• No UI for connected repositories or installations — API/webhook only.
  • No diff against the base branch (the GitHub Action's compare step does that separately); the PR comment is a plain summary of that PR's own findings.
  • No Check Runs annotation — a PR comment only.
  • PR-triggered scans don't affect the "new/fixed/reintroduced" issue tracking (ADR-0012) shown for the repository's regular scans — a PR previews code that might never merge, so its findings aren't folded into that history.

docs.title: Hypotheses lane
docs.text: A separate, off-by-default tab for flaws pattern-based scanning can't express. v1 detects one type: a route with no recognized authorization check, in a file where a sibling route has one. IDOR and mass assignment are named in the plan but not implemented yet -- a disclosed scope decision, not an oversight. Design reasoning in ADR-0028; the honest verification record is in v2-week43-verification.md.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
re-check out the asset's latest scan's source
    │
    ▼
find every route with no auth-looking decorator/middleware, in a file where a sibling route
has one -- entirely deterministic, no model involved (core.hypotheses.facts)
    │
    ▼
for each candidate: show the model the structured facts + that route's own code
    │
