Repository Packages true false unknown NodeGoat 83 6 1 76 (75 transitive, 1 named in scripts) nodejs-goof 100 15 2 83 (80 transitive, 3 named in code or scripts) Vulnerable-Flask-App 21 10 11 0 VAmPI 3 3 0 0

Not an accuracy figure. There is no ground truth. What was checked by hand: NodeGoat's one false (async) is imported only from test/, as reported; nodejs-goof's mongodb and npmconf are indeed never imported by the app, but mongodb is used through mongoose, which is exactly the indirection limit above. In Vulnerable-Flask-App most of the 11 false results are packages from a fully pinned requirements file (Jinja2, click, certifi and similar) that Flask and other packages use themselves: the "frozen requirements" limit in practice. The main practical effect is that most dependency findings in real projects are transitive, and v1 cannot say anything about those.

docs.title: Red-team suite
docs.text: Plan §21.9. Tests whether this project's own LLM-consuming features (core.llm fix suggestions, core.triage_assistant, core.hypotheses, core.copilot) hold up against adversarial content planted in scanned code, and whether their output contracts reject a malformed or manipulative model reply. Lives at tests/redteam/, discovered automatically by the existing test CI job (pyproject.toml's testpaths = ["tests"] already covers it) -- it runs on every push and pull request, not only nightly.

docs.title: The corpus
docs.text: tests/fixtures/injection_payloads.json: 20 named payloads (prompt-injection variants, format breakers, path-traversal bait, a fake credential, resource-exhaustion strings) curated in an earlier week but never wired into a test suite until this one.

docs.title: What's tested, against real code (not mocks of it)
docs.text:
• test_contract_hardening.py -- every one of the 20 payloads, fed as a raw model reply directly to every contract that parses raw text (core.llm.contract.parse_response, core.triage_assistant.contract.parse_response, core.attackpath.contract.validate_narrative): none of them are valid replies under any schema, so all 60 combinations must be rejected.
  • test_patch_confined_to_finding_file.py -- schema-valid replies (so the broad net above isn't doing the work for the wrong reason) that try, one adversarial detail at a time: redirecting a suggested patch outside the finding's file (absolute path, .. traversal, a different real file), and arguing in otherwise-valid prose that the finding isn't real, or smuggling an extra "severity" field. Maps to the plan's "writes outside the patch" and "downgrades severity."
  • test_severity_immutable_under_injection.py -- a worst-case fully compliant fake model that reads a suppression-style payload planted in scanned code and returns a legitimate "likely_false_positive" verdict (which core.triage_assistant is allowed to say -- that's the feature's purpose). Confirms the real Finding object's severity, taxonomy and triage state are byte-identical before and after, regardless of what the model said.
  • test_copilot_tool_scope_and_unknown_tools.py -- an injected instruction naming a tool outside the copilot's five real schemas comes back as an ordinary error string, never executes or crashes; and query_issues never sees another asset's data even when the model's own tool-call arguments try to redirect it, because asset/org scope comes only from CopilotContext (fixed at conversation start), never from anything the model supplies. Maps to "calls disallowed tools" and "reaches another tenant's data."
  • test_secrets_never_forwarded.py -- a real-looking AWS key planted in a finding's own title (not just its code). This test caught a real bug: core/llm/prompt.py and core/triage_assistant/prompt.py scrubbed secrets from the code block but never from finding.title/.description, so a secret-shaped string sitting in the title text would have reached the model untouched. Fixed in the same change that added this test (both files now scrub title/description the same way code already was) -- kept here as a permanent regression test, not removed once green.

docs.title: Disclosed gap: no live-model probing
docs.text:
The plan also calls for garak and a tracked attack success rate. Both assume a real model call: garak's probes are meant to test whether the model itself resists persuasion, which a deterministic test cannot measure, and "success rate" only means something for a run that can fail differently each time. Wiring this up needs a real ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in CI, ongoing spend for every scheduled run, and a decision about probe count/budget -- deliberately deferred rather than faked with a hardcoded number. If it's picked up later, garak needs a custom generator plugin routing its probes through core.llm.client.AnthropicClient, gated on the secret being present (skipped otherwise, the same pattern this project already uses for every other optional live-model feature).

One related scenario this suite does not claim to structurally prevent: a fully-compliant model choosing to recite its own system prompt back in free-text output (a rationale/explanation field has no filter against echoing prompt text). The mitigating factor is that none of this project's system prompts contain secrets or credentials -- only instructions -- so the impact of a leak is low, not that leaking is architecturally blocked. That is a live-model behavioral question, not one a contract validator can answer.

docs.title: Bulwark v2.0.0
docs.text: Weeks 27-52 of the plan, Milestone M11: "v2.0 public launch." v1.0.0 was a sandboxed multi-scanner pipeline that found, correlated and ranked vulnerabilities. v2.0.0 turns that into a platform: stable issue identity across scans, multi-tenancy, an LLM-backed analysis layer that proposes and verifies real fixes, hardened-by-default infrastructure, authorized DAST, and a plugin/integrations ecosystem around it. Full detail for every line below is in CHANGELOG.md; the honest numbers are in docs/evaluation-v2.md.

docs.title: Platform foundations (Phase 7, weeks 27-30 -> v1.1.0)
docs.text:
• Stable issue identity. A finding used to be a new row every scan; an Issue/Occurrence split (ADR-0012) now tracks one real vulnerability across scans with a location-independent fallback fingerprint, so "new", "fixed" and "returned" are real states, not a guess from diffing reports.
  • Multi-tenancy, for real. Organizations, projects, roles, and Postgres Row-Level Security with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on every tenant table (ADR-0013) -- not an application-level WHERE org_id = ... a future query could forget. An automated two-tenant leak test runs on every endpoint, on every pull request.
  • A GitHub App replaces the OAuth app; scoped, hashed, prefixed API tokens; a hash-chained, tamper-evident audit log with signed checkpoints published to Sigstore's Rekor.

docs.title: UX overhaul (Phase 8, weeks 31-35)
docs.text:
• A heuristic evaluation and journey maps against the real v1 UI (the actual baseline usability study with real participants is still pending real participant recruitment -- disclosed, not faked).
  • A real design system: tokens, severity shapes, Radix primitives, Storybook.
  • The app shell, project overview (opens with a verdict sentence, not a stats block), a virtualized issues table with keyboard triage, onboarding, empty/error states, and an accessibility pass.

docs.title: Advanced analysis engine (Phase 9, weeks 36-40 -> v1.3.0)
docs.text:
• Incremental scanning: a content-addressed result cache turns an unchanged-file rescan into a cache hit -- 3.6x faster on a real warm PR scan (measured).
  • Code intelligence and taint analysis: a real call graph (Python/JS/Go, tree-sitter-based) and a taint engine that confirms whether a SAST finding is actually reachable from a real HTTP entrypoint -- attached to Issues and fed into risk scoring and the UI as a step-by-step path.
  • Policy-as-code: Open Policy Agent evaluates a Rego policy's deny rules alongside the severity threshold -- "no secrets, ever" and "an accepted risk expires after 90 days" are rules a threshold alone can't express.
  • Supply-chain risk: malicious-package detection (OSSF MAL- ids via OSV), typosquat detection, and OpenSSF Scorecard for direct dependencies.

docs.title: LLM intelligence (Phase 10, weeks 41-45)
docs.text:
• A model gateway (ADR-0026): a real local backend option, caching, and budgets -- not locked to one hosted provider.
  • The verified-fix agent -- "the flagship v2 feature": proposes a patch, reruns the triggering rule, reruns every scanner, runs the project's own tests, and only then offers it for human approval, as a real GitHub PR.
  • Triage assistant and Hypotheses lane: an LLM verdict on "likely false positive", and a deterministic-candidate-generation + LLM-verdict lane for authorization flaws pattern matching can't express on its own.
  • Security copilot: tool-grounded chat scoped to one project, never another tenant's data.
  • Attack paths, a threat model draft, and an LLM red-team suite: 20 adversarial payloads against every contract that parses raw model text, run in CI on every push.

docs.title: Platform security and DAST (Phase 11, weeks 46-49b -> v1.5.0)
docs.text:
• A pluggable SandboxRuntime interface with a gVisor backend and egress denial for fix verification; envelope encryption via OpenBao with per-scan data keys and crypto-shredding; mTLS between every internal service.
  • Nightly fuzzing of every parser, a full OWASP ASVS 4.0.3 Level 2 self-assessment, SLSA Level 3 provenance and signed images.
  • Authorized DAST: ownership verification before a URL can ever be scanned, a scope-enforcing egress proxy wired into real campaign execution (not just configured), ZAP/Nuclei behind rate limits and time windows, and SAST/DAST correlation ("confirmed at runtime").

docs.title: Scale, ecosystem, and launch (Phase 12, weeks 50-52 -> v2.0.0)
docs.text:
• Scale: a Helm chart with KEDA autoscaling on real Celery queue depth (1 to 5 replicas on a real 3,000-task backlog, drained in under 30s on a real kind cluster), k6 load tests that found and drove the fix for two genuine capacity bugs, and a cost-per-scan dashboard.
  • Ecosystem: a Plugin SDK (entry-point discovery, a shared conformance kit, keyless Sigstore signing re-verified on every use); Slack/Discord/GitHub Issues/Jira integrations with asymmetric two-way sync; a native, no-Docker pre-commit hook; a real MkDocs Material documentation site.
  • Launch: docs/evaluation-v2.md (the honest numbers, including what still needs a live model to measure), this landing page you're reading about -- its first screen is now a replay of a real scan of OWASP Juice Shop, not a stats block -- and this release.

docs.title: What v2.0.0 is honest about not having yet
docs.text:
• No real, human-measured usability improvement. The UX overhaul shipped real screens on a real design system; the before/after SUS study that would prove it's actually more usable needs real participants, not fabricated data, and hasn't been run.
  • Five evaluation areas need a live LLM to measure: verified-fix acceptance rate and blind human review, triage assistant and hypotheses-lane precision/recall, Copilot's citation accuracy, and a real attack-success-rate (as opposed to the structural-defense pass rate that is measured) for the red-team suite. Every one of these is disclosed in its own week's verification doc.
  • Still a single shared bearer token for API auth outside the GitHub App flow -- no per-user identity yet; that's v3's Part 6 ("Identity, AI v3, Launch").
  • Taint analysis, risk ranking, and the LLM layer are all still disclosed-scope-cut, judgment-call systems, not formally verified ones -- see each feature's own ADR for exactly where the lines are drawn.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: No breaking API changes from v1.x to v2.0.0's /v1 surface; the /v2 endpoints added since Week 28 are additive. Database migrations run automatically (alembic upgrade head in the migrate job for Helm, or on worker start for Compose). See helm/bulwark/README.md or the Quickstart for either deployment path.

docs.title: Bulwark 3.0.0 — release notes
docs.text:
Released 2026-10-08, with 2.5.0 the same day.

Released without the third usability study. The plan tags v3.0.0 after milestone M16, whose study needs five security leads or pen testers; it has not run (ux-study.md), and both tags were cut at the owner's decision without it. The tag also starts the release workflow, which publishes signed images; no run of it has been observed from here. Every change since 2.4.0 is in CHANGELOG.md, under 2.5.0 and 3.0.0.

Version 2 found vulnerabilities, ranked them and helped fix them. Version 3 (Weeks 53–78) manages them, alongside the tools a team already uses. The write-up is blog-v3.0.0.md; the numbers, including the ones that don't flatter, are evaluation-v3.md.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
Bring in what you don't scan yourself. One import endpoint for SARIF, CycloneDX, SPDX, OSV and ten formats ported from DefectDojo (ZAP, Nuclei, Burp, Nessus, OpenVAS, Grype, Trivy, Snyk, GitLab, Checkov), plus a universal mapper for anything else. Every report is parsed in a sandbox, previewed as new, unchanged, reopened and closed before anything is saved, and reimported without closing what it didn't look at. Connectors pull from DefectDojo and other tools on a schedule; deduplication can be set per source, with a dry run. (2.1.0–2.2.0)

Run the program. Portfolios, projects, engagements and tests. SLAs from first detection; risk acceptance that needs a second person and expires; a priority engine you can weight; pen-test engagements with manual findings (CVSS 4.0), checklists, retests and a report at close. (2.3.0)

Automate the routine. A rules engine (Rego, with a dry run over the last seven days), notifications, two-way tickets with Jira and GitHub Issues, and a calendar. (2.4.0)

Know what you run. An SBOM inventory per project, advisory matching with OSV's semantics (checked against osv-scanner: 99.5% agreement, never missing one it finds), and VEX drafted from call-graph evidence that a person confirms. Compliance mappings and signed evidence packs an auditor can check. (2.4.0)

See it. A metrics layer, dashboards with a keyboard alternative to drag-and-drop, role homes, a report builder with signed PDFs and schedules, and filters, saved views and bulk changes that work across every project. (2.5.0)

Who and how. OIDC and SAML sign-in, SCIM, organization roles with per-portfolio and per-project overrides enforced by Postgres row-level security, personal API tokens. An MCP server so your own agent can ask Bulwark as you, read-only by default, with scanned text labelled as untrusted; /fix on pull requests, previewed with its cost and never run for a fork. A public website with a recorded scan of OWASP Juice Shop and a generated integrations catalogue. (3.0.0)

docs.title: Upgrading from 2.x
docs.text:
• Migrations run in order to 0050; run alembic upgrade head as the table-owning role, as before.
  • New settings are optional and listed in the docs they belong to: single sign-on (identity.md), connectors, the advisory feeds, /fix (fix-on-pull-requests.md), the MCP server (mcp.md).
  • The GitHub App needs the Issue comment event for /fix (github-app.md).
  • Tokens made before accounts keep working with their scopes.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Not measured: deduplication accuracy, the blind review of VEX proposals, and the usability study (SUS and time on task for J6–J10). Each is in evaluation-v3.md with the reason.
  • No real model has run the verified-fix agent or /fix: patch quality is unmeasured.
  • /fix has not been exercised with a real GitHub App delivering real comments.
  • The rules engine's p95 is for one evaluation, not the plan's load test.
  • The release workflow's signing and provenance have not been observed on a real run.

The full list of what is proven and what isn't, week by week, is in docs/v2-week*-verification.md.

docs.title: Releasing: tags, the VS Code Marketplace and the GitHub Marketplace
docs.text:
Tagging is done from here (see below); the Marketplace steps need your own accounts and tokens, so those are yours to run. As of v1.0.0, neither Marketplace listing has been created.

v0.1.0 and v0.2.0 were tagged in git directly, without bumping pyproject.toml/package.json or giving v0.2.0 its own CHANGELOG entry (see the note at the top of the v1.0.0 entry in CHANGELOG.md). v1.0.0 is the first release where the tag, the CHANGELOG and the package versions agree; keep them in sync from here on.

docs.title: 0. Before tagging
docs.text:
• CI is green on main, including the Bulwark self-scan workflow.
  • CHANGELOG.md: move "Unreleased" under the new version, and bump pyproject.toml, web/package.json and extensions/vscode/package.json to match.
  • Decide the names: the action's name in action.yml ("Bulwark security scan") and the extension's publisher (bulwark-scan in extensions/vscode/package.json is a placeholder). Marketplace names must be unique; neither has been checked.
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "v1.0.0: all 26 weeks of the plan"
git push --tags

docs.title: 1. VS Code Marketplace
docs.text:
1. Create a publisher at https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/manage and set "publisher" in extensions/vscode/package.json to its id.
  2. Create an Azure DevOps personal access token with Marketplace > Manage scope (keep it out of the repo and out of chat).
  3. Build, test, package and inspect:
cd extensions/vscode
npm ci && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build
npm run package            # writes bulwark-vscode.vsix (about 21 KB, 15 files)
npx vsce ls --no-dependencies   # review exactly what ships
  1. Try it before publishing: in VS Code, Extensions: Install from VSIX..., open a folder, run Bulwark: Scan Workspace. This is the first time it runs in a real VS Code: check the Problems panel, the hover, the Quick Fix and the status bar by eye.
  2. Publish: npx vsce login <publisher> then npx vsce publish --no-dependencies.

The extension needs the bulwark CLI and Docker on the user's machine; say so on the listing page (the README does).

docs.title: 2. GitHub Marketplace (the Action)
docs.text:
The repository root already holds action.yml, which is what the Marketplace requires.

  1. Repository Settings > General: accept the GitHub Marketplace Developer Agreement (first time only) and enable two-factor authentication.
  2. Releases > Draft a new release, choose the tag you want to publish (v1.0.0 or later), tick Publish this Action to the GitHub Marketplace, pick a category (Security) and publish.
  3. Also move a floating major tag so uses: rago12bit/cybernatics@v0 works:
git tag -f v0 v1.0.0 && git push -f origin v0
  1. Users then write uses: rago12bit/cybernatics@v0 (or pin the commit SHA, which is safer).

Known limitations to state in the listing: the action has not been run on GitHub before its first release; it rebuilds the scanner images on every run (2 to 4 minutes); fork pull requests cannot receive comments or SARIF.

docs.title: 3. After publishing
docs.text:
• Watch the first real pull request's run: expect surprises around Docker and permissions, and fix them in a patch release.
  • Turn on branch protection requiring the Bulwark self-scan check, so "blocks on new HIGH findings" is enforced and not just displayed.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: Build a report from blocks, generate a signed PDF, share it by a link that expires, or have it sent on a schedule (plan §48.3, ADR-0055).

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
Block What it shows Cover Title and subtitle; the organization, the period and when it was generated are added. Executive summary A person's text, or a model's draft that a person has reviewed (below). Metric Any dashboard metric, with the same filters: portfolios, projects, a tag, the last N days. Issue table Open Issues, Issues past their SLA, or Issues first seen or fixed in the period; by priority; up to 200 rows. One issue in detail Its project, location, severity, priority, state, dates, CWE and description. Risk acceptances In force, awaiting a decision, or expiring within 30 days. Compliance mapping One framework's controls with the evidence Bulwark holds for each, as in evidence packs. Engagement scope A pen test or audit's targets, routes, out-of-scope note, people and dates. Appendix The definition of every metric used, and how to check the PDF's signature.

Three templates start you off: a weekly program summary for leads, a penetration test report, and a compliance summary. Each report covers "the last N days" (1 to 366), so a schedule always reports on the latest period.

docs.title: The executive summary
docs.text:
Write it yourself, or choose Draft with AI (when a model is set up for the report task: see BULWARK_LLM_ROUTE_REPORT and the model gateway). The model sees the report's numbers and at most five Issue titles per table. Those come from scanned code, so they are scrubbed of anything that looks like a secret and marked as untrusted data, never instructions. Drafting counts against the organization's AI budget.

A draft is labelled as AI-written. Nothing is generated or sent until a person confirms it, edited or not. The PDF then says, above the summary, "Drafted by AI (model) from this report's data; reviewed by (name) on (date)." Drafting and confirming need a personal token, because the reviewer's name is printed.

docs.title: Generating, signing and sharing
docs.text:
Generate PDF queues the report, and the worker renders it with headless Chromium. Chromium runs in a container with no network, a read-only file system, every capability dropped and a non-root user. The page itself allows nothing but its own styles, so nothing in an Issue's title can load or run. The image is Microsoft's Playwright image, pinned by digest; set BULWARK_PDF_IMAGE to use a mirror with the same layout.

Each PDF is kept as it was, with its SHA-256. When BULWARK_EVIDENCE_SIGNING_KEY is set (the same cosign key as evidence packs), it is signed too. To check a copy:

cosign verify-blob --key cosign.pub --bundle report.pdf.sig --insecure-ignore-tlog report.pdf

Create a link makes a link that opens the PDF without signing in, for 1 to 90 days. It is shown once; only its hash is stored. Every link can be revoked, each opening is counted and audit-logged, and the signature is at the link plus /signature.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
A report can be generated weekly (a weekday) or monthly (a day from 1 to 28), at an hour in UTC, and each recipient (up to 20) is emailed a link to it, never the PDF itself. The worker checks every five minutes. Scheduled emails need BULWARK_SMTP_* and BULWARK_API_PUBLIC_URL, the API's public address; without them the report is still generated, and the run says why nothing was sent. A report whose AI summary nobody has confirmed is not sent.

Every change, generation, link and send is in the audit log.

docs.title: Risk score and "Fix these first"
docs.text: Every finding gets scoring.risk_score (0-100) and scoring.risk_factors, a list of the reasons in plain words. The UI's Fix these first panel is the ten highest scores; the API equivalent is GET /scans/{id}/findings?sort=risk&limit=10.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Signal Source Used for CVSS v3.1 base score, else normalized severity Trivy, OSV-Scanner / severity matrix impact EPSS: probability a CVE is exploited in the next 30 days FIRST.org, daily file likelihood KEV: CVE is known to be exploited in the wild CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog likelihood, and a floor Scanner agreement (merged confidence) correlation likelihood, for findings with no CVE

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
impact     = CVSS / 10                       if known
           = {CRITICAL .95, HIGH .75, MEDIUM .5, LOW .25, INFO .05}   otherwise
likelihood = 1.0                             CVE is in KEV
           = min(1, sqrt(EPSS / 0.5))        EPSS known (full weight at 50%)
           = 0.3                             dependency finding, exploit data unknown
           = merged confidence               code, secrets and IaC findings (no CVE exists)
risk       = round(100 * impact * (0.5 + 0.5 * likelihood))
risk       = max(risk, 90)                   if in KEV
risk       = round(risk * 0.85)              if reachability says the application does not import it
                                             (KEV floor becomes 80 instead of 90)

Impact sets the ceiling; exploit evidence decides where between 50% and 100% of it a score lands. EPSS values are heavily skewed (most CVEs sit below 1%), which is why the square-root curve is used instead of a linear one. A finding can list several CVE ids; the highest EPSS and any KEV hit count.

docs.title: Priority: the score as a policy per project (Week 63)
docs.text:
The issues table ranks by each Issue's priority (ADR-0047). With no saved policy it is exactly the score above. On a project's Priority page you can weight each factor (multiplier ** weight: 1 as designed, 0 off, 2 doubles its pull) and describe the project:

Factor Effect at weight 1 Severity, EPSS, tool agreement, not reachable, triage assistant as above Known exploited (KEV) a floor of 90 × weight (80 × weight if not reachable) Taint path confirmed × 1.1 Confirmed at runtime (DAST) × 1.25 Path context: test, example, docs or vendored code × 0.6 Internal only × 0.8 Data sensitivity: confidential / internal / public × 0.9 / 0.8 / 0.65 Business criticality: high / medium / low × 0.9 / 0.8 / 0.65

Context left unset is the worst case (internet-facing, restricted data, critical), so describing a project can only lower its scores. Bands: P1 80 and up, P2 60, P3 30, P4 below. An SLA can set deadlines by band instead of severity. Saving shows the top 50 before and after first, then re-ranks every Issue in the background; the page refuses another change until that finishes. Every Issue's "Why it's ranked here" lists each factor with its weight and the multiplier it applied.

docs.title: Behaviour you can rely on
docs.text:
• Feeds missing or stale never fail a scan. Scores fall back to "unknown exploit data" and the factor list says so (Exploit feeds not loaded).
  • Scoring is a pure function of the finding and the two files; no network at scoring time.
  • Downloads are validated before they replace the cache: https only, size-capped, header and minimum-row checks; a bad file leaves the previous good copy in place.
  • Secrets and code findings are scored from severity and confidence only; nothing in EPSS or KEV applies to them.

docs.title: Feeds
docs.text:
bulwark update-feeds downloads both files into <workdir>/feeds (about 4 MB). The worker also refreshes them daily (Celery beat) and before a scan when the cache is missing or over 48 hours old. GET /risk/feeds (authenticated) reports the dates, sizes and last errors. Only the API/worker side needs the network; scanner containers still have none.

Sources: https://www.first.org/epss/ (score files) and https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A heuristic for ordering work, not a probability and not validated against real outcomes. The weights and the KEV floor are judgment calls, kept in one place (core/risk/score.py) for review.
  • Reachability is coarse. It tells whether the application's own code imports a package, not whether the vulnerable function is called (see reachability.md).
  • A dependency advisory without a CVE id (GitHub-only advisories) cannot be looked up, so it scores as "unknown".
  • EPSS and KEV describe the whole internet, not your environment.

docs.title: Sandbox runtimes
docs.text: Which kernel enforces a scanner container's isolation, and what network a fix-verification test run can reach, are both now a matter of configuration rather than a code change. Design reasoning is in ADR-0031; the honest verification record, including two real bugs this caught before shipping, is in v2-week46-verification.md.

docs.title: The SandboxRuntime interface
docs.text:
core/sandbox/runtime.py defines one small interface every backend implements: given a tool adapter and a target, produce the argv to run it. core/runner.py's run_tool takes an optional instance of it and defaults to DockerRuntime -- the boundary Bulwark has always run on, and the only one available on macOS.

Backend Where it runs Status DockerRuntime (default) Anywhere Docker runs In production since v1 GvisorRuntime Linux only, needs runsc installed Written and argv-tested; never actually executed (no Linux dev host) Firecracker (core.sandbox.firecracker) Linux only, needs KVM The fix agent's test runs only (BULWARK_TEST_SANDBOX=firecracker). Built 2026-10-12; its guest side booted under QEMU, Firecracker itself never run (no KVM here)

GvisorRuntime reuses the exact same argv DockerRuntime produces and adds one flag (--runtime=runsc): it can only add a deeper enforcement layer, never loosen the existing contract. A seccomp-profile hook is wired into it but currently always returns None -- see ADR-0031 for why shipping a hand-written profile now would be a regression, not hardening.

docs.title: Egress denial for fix verification
docs.text:
core/fixagent/sandbox.py's test-execution sandbox denies egress to the cloud metadata range (169.254.0.0/16 -- the same SSRF target core.attackpath already flags for scanned code) and to RFC1918 networks, by default. DNS and HTTP(S) to the rest of the internet stay open, so pip install/npm install keep working. A purpose-built sidecar (docker/egress-sidecar, built as bulwark/egress-sidecar:1) loads the policy into the target's network namespace from the outside, so it works no matter what's inside the target's own (arbitrary, caller-supplied) image.

from core.fixagent.sandbox import TestRunSpec, run_tests

# Default posture: metadata and internal networks blocked.
run_tests(checkout, TestRunSpec(image="python:3.12-slim", command="pytest -q"))

# Opt out for a case that genuinely needs the old, fully-open network (e.g. a private
# registry on a non-standard port). Reproduces the exact original behavior.
run_tests(checkout, TestRunSpec(image="python:3.12-slim", command="pytest -q",
                                 deny_internal_egress=False))

This part is real, live-verified, and running today -- unlike gvisor and Firecracker below.

docs.title: Running gvisor for real (not yet done -- a runbook for when it is)
docs.text:
Nothing in this repository has ever executed under runsc. This is what closing that gap needs, so it's an explicit plan rather than an implied "someday":

  1. A Linux host with KVM/nested virtualization, not a container -- runsc needs to run alongside the real Docker daemon, not inside another container. A cloud VM (any provider) with nested virtualization enabled works; Docker Desktop's own Linux VM on macOS does not expose this to an inner runsc install.
  2. Install Docker + gVisor's runsc on that host, then register it as a Docker runtime (gVisor's own install docs cover the /etc/docker/daemon.json runtimes entry -- docker run --runtime=runsc hello-world should print gVisor's own banner, not just Docker's).
  3. Smoke-test one real scanner through GvisorRuntime end to end: run_tool(BanditAdapter(), target, runtime=GvisorRuntime()) against a real checkout, confirming the scan still produces the same findings a DockerRuntime run would -- gVisor's syscall emulation is not 100% coverage of every syscall every tool might use, so this has to be checked per scanner, not assumed.
  4. Only then does authoring a real seccomp profile become possible: either vendor Docker's actual default seccomp profile and trim entries a scanner family provably never uses, or strace a real run of each scanner image and derive a true minimal allowlist. Neither is guessable from a Mac.
  5. Wire the host into CI (a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on that box, or an equivalent) so a future change to GvisorRuntime gets checked automatically instead of silently regressing.

docs.title: Firecracker for the fix agent's test runs
docs.text:
core/sandbox/firecracker.py runs the fix agent's "run this project's own tests" step in a microVM when BULWARK_TEST_SANDBOX=firecracker: the project's code runs under its own guest kernel, behind KVM, instead of sharing the host's. Scanners do not use it (they stay on Docker or gVisor).

How a run works -- every step without root on the host:

  1. The root filesystem is the same image the Docker sandbox would use (TestRunSpec.image), exported with Docker, unpacked without device nodes, ownership or setuid bits, plus an init script and the command, then made into an ext4 image with mkfs.ext4 -d.
  2. The checkout becomes a second, writable ext4 disk, thrown away afterwards.
  3. No network interface at all, so a command that installs dependencies fails: use an image that already has them.
  4. The guest's init runs the command in /work, kills every other process, prints the exit code on the serial console and reboots, which ends the VM.

A host that cannot run a microVM is an error, never a silent fall-back to Docker.

Setting up a host (Linux, x86_64 or arm64, with KVM):

  1. Check /dev/kvm exists and your user can read and write it (sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER, then log in again).
  2. Install Docker, e2fsprogs (for mkfs.ext4) and the firecracker binary from a Firecracker release on GitHub, on your PATH.
  3. Get an uncompressed guest kernel (vmlinux) -- Firecracker's getting-started guide points at the ones its own CI uses -- and set BULWARK_FIRECRACKER_KERNEL to it.
  4. Run pytest tests/integration/test_firecracker_live.py: it boots real microVMs (a passing and a failing command, and one that tries to reach the network) and skips, saying what is missing, anywhere it cannot.

What has been checked, and what has not. The unit tests cover the VM document, the init script, reading the result, the image unpacking (nothing written outside its directory through a link, .. or a hard link; setuid bits dropped) and the orchestration. The guest side was booted for real on 2026-10-12: disks built by this module's own code from a real python:3.12-slim, under QEMU's software emulation in a container (a stock Alpine kernel; no KVM on the Mac). The image's Python ran, the checkout was at /work, a command that printed a fake success marker and exited 3 read as 3, and a leftover background process did not keep the VM up. Firecracker itself has not run: that needs the host above. For production, launch it through Firecracker's jailer (chroot, cgroups, a dedicated uid), as Firecracker recommends; this module runs firecracker directly, which still applies its built-in seccomp filters.

docs.title: Severity normalization matrix
docs.text:
Generated from core/scoring/severity.py by scripts/gen-api-docs.py; do not edit.

Tool severity vocabularies are not comparable. This table is a judgment call, not a derived truth: it maps each tool's native label to one shared scale.

Tool CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW INFO semgrep — ERROR WARNING INFO — opengrep — ERROR WARNING INFO — bandit — HIGH MEDIUM LOW — trivy CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW UNKNOWN grype CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW NEGLIGIBLE, UNKNOWN gosec — HIGH MEDIUM LOW — checkov CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW — dockle — FATAL WARN INFO — gitleaks — (any) — — — precommit-secrets — (any) — — — precommit-sast — HIGH MEDIUM LOW — osv-scanner CRITICAL HIGH MODERATE, MEDIUM LOW — syft — — — — — sarif — ERROR WARNING INFO — zap — HIGH MEDIUM LOW INFORMATIONAL nuclei CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW INFO, UNKNOWN snyk CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW — gitlab CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW INFO, UNKNOWN, UNDEFINED burp — HIGH MEDIUM LOW INFORMATION, INFO nessus CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW NONE, INFO, INFORMATIONAL openvas CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW LOG, INFO, DEBUG, FALSE POSITIVE cyclonedx CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW INFO, NONE, UNKNOWN OSV via CVSS v3.1 ≥ 9.0 7.0–8.9 4.0–6.9 0.1–3.9 0 / none

docs.title: SBOM
docs.text:
bulwark sbom ./my-project -o sbom.cdx.json

Writes a CycloneDX 1.6 JSON SBOM generated by Syft (image pinned by digest, run in the same sandbox as every scanner: no network, read-only root, non-root). It lists what the project contains; it does not judge it, and it is separate from the findings.

  • Built from Bulwark's sanitized workspace, so installed dependency directories (node_modules, virtualenvs) are not included; lockfiles and manifests are. Dev dependencies are included, matching the scope Trivy and OSV-Scanner scan.
  • Verified against the official CycloneDX 1.6 JSON schema on a real project (tests/integration).
  • CycloneDX 1.6 rather than Syft's newer default (1.7), for the widest tool support.
  • In the GitHub Action: sbom: true writes it and exposes sbom-file.

docs.title: Signing a report
docs.text:
You need a cosign key pair, which you create and keep:

cosign generate-key-pair          # or run cosign's container; writes cosign.key and cosign.pub
export COSIGN_PASSWORD=...        # the key's password; never put it on a command line
bulwark scan ./my-project --format json -o scan.json
bulwark attest sign scan.json --key cosign.key          # writes scan.json.sig.bundle

cosign runs in a container with no network and a read-only filesystem; the key is mounted read-only and the password is passed by name. No transparency-log entry is made: the signature proves the holder of the key signed exactly these bytes, not when. Keyless (OIDC) signing is not implemented.

docs.title: Provenance attestation
docs.text:
bulwark attest provenance scan.json --scan scan.json --key cosign.key \
  --artifact sbom=sbom.cdx.json --source-label owner/repo --commit "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"

Produces scan.json.provenance.bundle: a signed in-toto statement (cosign emits Statement v0.1) whose subject is the file and whose predicate (https://github.com/Rag2102/cyberimp/attestations/scan/v1 -- the project's first repository name, kept as is: it identifies the predicate format, and changing it would make every attestation made so far stop matching) records:

  • the Bulwark version and, per scanner, its image reference, local image id (content hash) and status;
  • the source label and commit you gave;
  • result counts (unique, raw, ignored, by severity), never the findings;
  • the SHA-256 and size of the report and every --artifact;
  • the time the attestation was made, and a plain statement of what it does not claim.

docs.title: Verifying
docs.text:
bulwark attest verify scan.json --pub cosign.pub

Checks whichever bundles sit next to the file. Exit 0 only if every check passes; a modified file, another key, an attestation for a different file, or a different predicate type is rejected (all exercised in the integration tests). It prints the verified predicate summary.

docs.title: What this does and does not give you
docs.text:
• Gives: evidence that a specific file is the one a holder of your key signed, and a record of which scanner builds produced it. Useful for handing a report to an auditor or gating a release on a specific scan.
  • Does not give: any statement that the findings are correct or complete; protection if the key is stolen; a timestamp you can trust (no transparency log); attestation of the scanner databases (vulnerability data and EPSS/KEV feeds are not recorded); identity beyond "holds this key". Local image ids are only as trustworthy as the machine that reported them.
  • Not automated in the action: signing needs your private key, so it is a step you add yourself with your own secret handling.

docs.title: Talk outline: "Bulwark: what I learned building a security scanner correlation platform"
docs.text: For a college tech club or a local OWASP chapter meeting (plan §33, Week 52 task 4). ~20-25 minutes plus Q&A. Giving the talk is yours; this is the outline and speaker notes, in the same honest voice as blog-v2.0.0.md and the technical report it's drawn from.

docs.title: 1. Hook (1 min)
docs.text: Open with the live homepage (localhost:3000), let the Juice Shop replay run while you talk: "This is a real scan of a real, deliberately vulnerable app, happening live on screen. By the end of this talk you'll know exactly how the three interesting parts of it work, and — just as importantly — what I still can't honestly claim about it."

docs.title: 2. The problem (2 min)
docs.text:
• Five open-source scanners, five formats, five severity vocabularies, massive overlap.
  • Show a raw finding from two different tools side by side for the same bug. Nobody reads five reports; most people read one and silently lose whatever the other four caught.
  • One sentence on scope: "I'm not building a better detector. Bandit, Semgrep, Trivy already exist and are good at this. I'm building the layer on top: merge, rank, and eventually fix."

docs.title: 3. Correlation (4 min)
docs.text:
• The core idea: two identity rules, not one magic fingerprint. Dependency findings merge on a shared advisory id (CVE/GHSA); code findings merge on file + line window + shared CWE or snippet overlap.
  • Why rule-id matching doesn't work: no two tools name a SQL-injection rule the same thing.
  • Real number: 19.9% of findings merge on deliberately vulnerable test apps, about 1.3% on ordinary open-source repos. Make the point explicit: report both numbers, never the pooled one alone — it's an easy place to accidentally mislead an audience.

docs.title: 4. Taint-confirmed reachability (6 min) — the centerpiece
docs.text:
• The gap: a SAST tool says "this function could be dangerous." It usually can't say "and here's proof user input actually reaches it."
  • Live demo moment: open the taint-confirmed eval() finding from the Juice Shop/NodeGoat demo. Show the taint path UI. Say out loud: "Semgrep's rule just pattern-matches eval(...). My taint engine additionally proves the argument comes from req.body. That's the whole contribution, visualized."
  • Be honest about the measurement here on stage, don't skip it: "I hand-verified 3 real cases on one real app. That's a spot-check, not a published precision/recall number. I'll show you exactly why that distinction matters" — segue into:
  • The ranking result that didn't work: show the top-20 precision table. Risk score beats severity-only at every K... but every confidence interval includes zero. "I could have cut this slide. I kept it because reporting a result you don't like is the actual point of doing evaluation at all, not a footnote you bury."

docs.title: 5. Verified fixes (5 min)
docs.text:
• The loop: propose a patch → re-run the rule → re-run every scanner → run the project's own tests → only then offer it to a human. Draw this as a simple diagram live if you have a whiteboard.
  • The key framing line: "An LLM suggesting a diff is cheap. An LLM suggesting a diff that's been mechanically proven not to break your test suite is a much smaller, much more defensible claim — and it's the one I'm actually making."
  • Disclose the gap on stage, don't wait for Q&A to be asked: "The acceptance rate — how often a verified fix actually gets approved by a real reviewer — needs a live model running continuously, which costs real money I haven't spent yet. I'm not going to make up a number for this talk."

docs.title: 6. What I'd tell past-me (3 min)
docs.text:
• Pick 2-3 real "found and fixed" stories from the CHANGELOG with specific numbers — these land better live than architecture slides. Good candidates: the reap_stale_scans RLS bug (silently a no-op in any real deployment, found this project's own Week 50), the pre-commit hook's one-git-show-per-file perf bug (1.93s → 0.45s from one batching fix), or Semgrep's silent 5-second rule/file timeout (found while chasing a performance regression, now surfaced as a warning instead of quietly dropped findings).
  • The theme across all three: "The bug wasn't in the hard, interesting code. It was in the boring path nobody was watching. Evaluation and honest verification found more real bugs for me than clever architecture ever did."

docs.title: 7. Close (2 min)
docs.text:
• Apache-2.0, link to the repo, link to the evaluation docs specifically ("read the numbers, not just the pitch").
  • One line on what's next if you want to invite follow-up questions: v3 is explicitly modeled on DefectDojo's ingest/engagement model, not a clone of it — portfolio hierarchy, SLAs, risk acceptance, a universal import endpoint.

docs.title: Q&A prep: likely questions
docs.text:
• "Why not just use CodeQL / Snyk / [commercial tool]?" — This is about correlation and prioritization across open-source tools specifically; licensing is also a real constraint (see ADR-006: Semgrep's community rules are self-host-only, which is why there's no hosted scanning service today — a hosted multi-tenant mode is a planned v3 item that would need to switch to Opengrep with project-authored rules instead).
  • "Does the LLM ever hallucinate a finding?" — No: the model never originates findings, only explains/suggests fixes for or triages findings deterministic tools already produced. Detection stays delegated to the scanners.
  • "What stops the fix-verification loop from being gamed by a prompt injection in the scanned code?" — This is exactly what tests/redteam/ checks: 60 adversarial payload x contract combinations, all rejected regardless of what a (simulated) model returns, because severity/taxonomy mutation and patch-file-scope are enforced in code, not trusted from model output.
  • "What's the actual precision/recall of [feature]?" — If it's one of the five LLM-gated rows, say so directly: "Not measured yet — needs a live model and a cost budget I haven't allocated. Here's what I'm confident about instead: [structural guarantee]." This is a stronger answer than a vague deflection.

docs.title: CWE and OWASP Top 10 mapping
docs.text: Every finding carries taxonomy.cwe (weakness ids) and taxonomy.owasp_top_10_2021 (categories such as A03:2021). Scanners fill these unevenly, so Bulwark completes them from one table after correlation (core/taxonomy, applied in core/scan.py).

docs.title: Source and licence
docs.text: core/taxonomy/owasp_top10_2021.json is transcribed by script from the OWASP Top 10:2021 project (https://github.com/OWASP/Top10, 2021/docs/en), which is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. It holds, per category, the CWE ids OWASP lists for it and their names. Categories with count: A01 34, A02 30, A03 33, A04 40, A05 20, A06 3, A07 22, A08 10, A09 4, A10 1. A unit test pins these counts so a truncated file fails CI. Some CWEs belong to two categories (for example CWE-259 is in A02 and A07); both are kept.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Normalize. 79, "cwe_79" and CWE-79 all become CWE-79; unparseable values are dropped (scanner output is untrusted).
  2. Map. Each CWE adds the OWASP categories the table lists for it.
  3. Keep the scanner's own tags. An OWASP tag a scanner reported (Semgrep does this) is normalized and kept, never overwritten.
  4. Defaults for CWE-less findings (the only inference in the system): a vulnerable dependency (sca) is A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components; an infrastructure misconfiguration (iac) is A05 Security Misconfiguration. Code (sast) and container findings with no CWE stay unmapped rather than guessed.

Secrets map through CWE-798 (hard-coded credentials) to A07.

docs.title: Measured on the sample scan
docs.text: Of 38 merged findings, 3 had an OWASP category before; 35 have one now. The 3 still unmapped are container findings that carry no CWE.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The table covers only CWEs OWASP lists. A CWE outside the Top 10 mapping gets no category and no name.
  • OWASP's own mapping is many-to-many and coarse; treat the category as a grouping aid, not a verdict.
  • Refreshing for a new Top 10 edition means a new JSON file and a new field; the 2021 field name is deliberate.

docs.title: Cross-Tool Correlation, Taint-Confirmed Reachability Ranking, and Mechanically Verified Fixes in an Open-Source Security Scanning Pipeline
docs.text: Bulwark v2.0.0 technical report. Source and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/rago12bit/cybernatics. An informal, plain-language companion post is at blog-v2.0.0.md.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Running several open-source static analysis tools against one codebase produces a union of findings with substantial redundancy and no shared notion of severity. We describe three mechanisms in Bulwark, an open-source scanning platform, that address this: (1) cross-tool correlation, which merges findings describing the same underlying defect using a composite fingerprint rather than relying on any single tool's own identifiers; (2) taint-confirmed reachability ranking, which augments a severity-and-exploitability risk score with a binary signal derived from static data-flow analysis — whether a reported sink is demonstrably reached from an HTTP entrypoint — rather than treating every static-analysis finding as equally actionable; and (3) a verified-fix pipeline in which a model-proposed patch is accepted only after it is shown, mechanically, not to regress the finding, the originating tool, the full scanner suite, or the project's own test suite. We report measurements against the OWASP Benchmark, the Juliet Test Suite, a 25-repository corpus, and a hand-verified spot-check against real deliberately-vulnerable applications, and we are explicit about which claims remain unmeasured because they require a live, costly model call this evaluation environment does not have provisioned.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
A developer running Bandit, Semgrep, Gitleaks, Trivy and OSV-Scanner against one repository receives five reports in five formats with five severity vocabularies. The same SQL injection may appear as a Bandit finding and a Semgrep finding; the same vulnerable dependency may appear in both Trivy and OSV-Scanner's output. The engineering problem we address is not detection — that is delegated to mature, independently maintained tools — but normalization, correlation, and prioritization over their combined output.

Two further problems compound this. First, a reported weakness (e.g., "this function may be callable with attacker-controlled input") is not the same claim as "this function is callable with attacker-controlled input from a concrete, traceable entrypoint" — the former is what most SAST tools report; the latter requires data-flow analysis most of them do not perform. Second, once a true positive is identified and prioritized, nothing in a conventional pipeline closes the loop: a suggested fix, if offered at all, is typically unverified prose or an unapplied diff.

This report describes how Bulwark v2.0.0 addresses all three.

docs.title: 2. System Overview
docs.text: Each configured scanner executes in an isolated container (--network=none --read-only --cap-drop=ALL, non-root, resource-limited) against a read-only mount of the target. Raw tool output is parsed into a canonical Finding record (location, taxonomy, native and normalized severity, evidence). This canonical representation is the substrate correlation, ranking, and the fix pipeline all operate on.

docs.title: 3.1 Method
docs.text:
Two findings are considered the same underlying defect if they satisfy one of two identity rules: (a) dependency identity — same package name/ecosystem and a shared vulnerability advisory identifier (CVE/GHSA/etc.), independent of which SCA tool reported it; or (b) code identity — same file, a configurable line-proximity window, and either a shared CWE or sufficient snippet token overlap, independent of each tool's own internal rule identifier. Rule (b) exists because no two SAST tools share a rule-naming scheme; relying on rule-id equality would merge nothing across tools.

Every contributing tool's evidence is retained on the merged record; the highest normalized severity among contributors is kept, never averaged or discarded.

docs.title: 3.2 Results
docs.text:
Measured on a 25-repository corpus (12 deliberately vulnerable applications, 13 ordinary open-source projects), all five default scanners, one run per repository on an otherwise-idle machine:

Deliberately vulnerable apps Ordinary repositories Pooled Dedup rate 19.9% 1.3% 8.9% Tool-run failures 0 / 94

The pooled figure is not independently meaningful: deliberately vulnerable test applications concentrate the kind of dependency overlap (two SCA tools reporting the same advisory) that drives most of the merging; ordinary repositories' findings rarely overlap at all. We report both strata rather than the pooled number alone for this reason.

docs.title: 4.1 Method
docs.text:
The taint engine performs intraprocedural and limited interprocedural data-flow analysis (tree-sitter parse trees; language-specific source/sink/sanitizer catalogs for Python, JavaScript and Go) to determine whether a declared sink (e.g., eval, a raw SQL query call, child_process.exec) is reached by data originating at a declared source (an HTTP framework's request object). Deliberately, the engine does not emit new findings: it only annotates an existing SAST finding from another tool, at the same file and line, with a confirmed reachability signal. A finding with no corresponding taint-sink match is left annotated reachable: null — "unknown," never a fabricated "not reachable" — the same discipline this platform's existing package-level dependency-reachability analysis already applies.

A confirmed reachable finding's scoring.confidence is set to a fixed high value (0.9), which this platform's existing risk-scoring formula already treats as the dominant likelihood term for any finding category without CVE/EPSS/KEV data (SAST, secrets, IaC). This reuses an existing, already-reviewed scoring path rather than introducing a second, parallel rule that would need to be kept consistent with it.

docs.title: 4.2 Results
docs.text:
Reachability confirmation (spot-check). We ran the full pipeline (Bandit, Semgrep) against two real, deliberately vulnerable JavaScript applications (NodeGoat, nodejs-goof) already present in our corpus, then manually inspected every confirmed-reachable finding against the underlying source. All three confirmations (NodeGoat, app/routes/contributions.js:32-34, data from an Express request body flowing to eval) were verified true positives by inspection — the target file's own source comment reads "Insecure use of eval() to parse inputs," with a safe alternative commented out directly below it. Notably, the originating report (Semgrep's eval-detected rule) is a syntactic pattern match with no data-flow component; the taint engine's contribution is specifically the flows-from-request claim, which the pattern rule alone cannot make. This is a small, hand-verified sample (N=3) and does not constitute a corpus-scale precision/recall study; we report it as such rather than extrapolating.

Ranking. We evaluate whether ordering findings by the full risk score (severity combined with EPSS, CISA KEV status, and reachability) yields better top-K precision than ordering by severity alone, using the OWASP Benchmark (2,894 Semgrep findings, 1,395 true positives by the Benchmark's own ground truth) with expected-value tie-breaking:

Top-K Risk score Severity only Random Difference (95% CI) 10 69.2% 52.4% 48.2% +16.8 pp (−10.7, +40.3) 20 63.3% 52.4% 48.2% +10.9 pp (−6.4, +28.3) 50 56.8% 52.4% 48.2% +4.4 pp (−2.0, +10.8) 100 54.6% 52.4% 48.2% +2.2 pp (−0.6, +5.3)

The risk score leads at every K, with the largest margin at the smallest K, but every confidence interval includes zero: this dataset does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement over severity-only ranking. We attribute this in part to the dataset's low score cardinality (only one Java-capable scanner contributes, yielding 7 distinct risk scores and 2 distinct severities across the whole corpus) and to the complete absence of exploitation ground truth for the dependency-specific signals (EPSS, KEV) in any benchmark available to us — the OWASP Benchmark contains no dependency findings at all. We report this as a negative result rather than omit it.

docs.title: 5.1 Method
docs.text: Given a finding, a model proposes a patch. Rather than presenting this patch directly, the system executes a four-stage verification loop before any human sees it as "ready for review": (1) apply the patch in an isolated, network-denied sandbox; (2) re-run the specific rule that produced the original finding, confirming it no longer fires; (3) re-run the full configured scanner suite over the patched code, confirming no new finding is introduced; (4) run the project's own test suite, confirming no regression. Only a patch that survives all four stages is offered for human approval as a pull request; a patch that fails any stage is discarded, not shown with a caveat. The system deliberately does not attempt to automatically merge a verified patch — human approval remains mandatory.

docs.title: 5.2 Results and a disclosed limitation
docs.text: The contract, prompt construction, verification-loop control flow, and PR-creation mechanics are implemented and unit-tested against the real control-flow paths (valid model reply, a malformed reply repaired once, exhausted retries) using fake model clients covering each path. The acceptance rate of verified fixes, and blind human review of proposed patches, require a live model and ongoing per-run cost; this evaluation environment is not provisioned with one, and we report this gap explicitly rather than substitute a smaller, unrepresentative number. The mechanism's correctness under adversarial input (a planted prompt-injection payload attempting to redirect the patch outside the finding's own file, or to claim a real finding is a false positive) is separately verified: 60 payload x contract combinations across the full LLM-consuming surface (this fix pipeline, the triage assistant, the attack-path narrator) were tested, and all 60 were correctly rejected by the parsing contract regardless of what the (simulated) model returned.

docs.title: 6. Limitations and Threats to Validity
docs.text:
• Single-analyzer coverage for Java. Both the OWASP Benchmark and Juliet results are Semgrep's alone; no claim here generalizes to an ensemble of Java analyzers, which we do not have.
  • The taint-engine result is a spot-check, not a corpus study, and does not evaluate recall against vulnerability classes outside the three sink categories exercised (JavaScript eval/exec/query).
  • Scale measurements (p95 latency, autoscaling behavior) were taken on a single developer machine and a local kind cluster, not a provisioned production environment; relative findings (a bottleneck exists, a fix resolves it) are more robust than the absolute millisecond figures.
  • No independent replication. All measurements in this report were produced by the same team that built the system under test, on infrastructure that team controls. We mitigate this only by publishing method, raw result files, and reproduction commands alongside every number.

docs.title: 7. Related Work
docs.text: Cross-tool SAST aggregation is the explicit design goal of DefectDojo (OWASP), which this project's third development phase (not covered in this report) is explicitly modeled on for ingest and vulnerability-management workflow, while deliberately not reusing its name or branding. Taint analysis for web application vulnerability detection is long-studied (e.g., Livshits and Lam, 2005, for Java); our contribution is narrower and more modest — using taint analysis purely as a confirmation signal over findings other tools already produced, rather than as an independent detector, to keep the analysis tractable within a multi-language, multi-tool pipeline. LLM-assisted vulnerability remediation has seen substantial recent interest; our verified-fix design's distinguishing property is that acceptance is gated on reproducible, mechanical verification (rule re-check, full scanner re-run, test suite) rather than on the model's own confidence or a single rerun of the triggering check alone.

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text: Correlation, taint-confirmed reachability, and mechanically verified fixes are three independent mechanisms addressing three distinct failure modes of a naive multi-scanner pipeline: redundant reports, undifferentiated severity, and unverified remediation. We report real measurements for all three, including a negative result (ranking improvement not statistically demonstrated on available data) and an explicit, unfilled gap (verified-fix acceptance rate, which needs a live model this evaluation was not provisioned with). We consider the explicit reporting of what is not yet measured to be as much a contribution of this work as the mechanisms themselves.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: All result files referenced are committed at benchmarks/results/ in the source repository. Commands to reproduce every number in this report are in evaluation-v2.md, evaluation-owasp.md, evaluation-juliet-corpus.md, and benchmarks/README.md.

docs.title: Threat model draft
docs.text:
A Mermaid data-flow diagram plus a STRIDE table, generated from code intelligence already computed for this project -- explicitly a starting point for a person's own review, never an assessment. Design reasoning in ADR-0030; the honest verification record is in v2-week45-verification.md.

Not to be confused with docs/THREAT-MODEL.md, Bulwark's own security threat model for itself as a tool running untrusted code -- a naming coincidence, unrelated infrastructure.

docs.title: How it's built -- no model call
docs.text: core/threatmodel/generate.py makes no LLM call at all. Every core.codeintel entrypoint becomes a diagram process; a sql_injection-category sink (core.taint.catalog, the same patterns the taint engine already uses for vulnerability detection) reachable from that route via the real call graph implies a Database node, and a command_injection-category sink implies an OS-process node. The STRIDE table is a fixed set of starter questions per element kind (spoofing/tampering/repudiation/ information-disclosure/denial-of-service/elevation-of-privilege where each applies), not a model's per-project judgment.

docs.title: Editable, and never silently overwritten
docs.text:
GET /assets/{id}/threat-model auto-generates a draft on first access (free, deterministic, so there's no cost gate to ask for first) and persists it. A person can edit the Mermaid source or the STRIDE table directly (PUT); their edit stays current until an explicit POST .../regenerate, which discards it and rebuilds from the latest scan. source ("generated" | "edited") and version (a plain incrementing counter, not full history) tell a client which state it's looking at.

The web app draws the diagram in its own frame (web/app/diagram-frame): Mermaid's SVG needs inline styles, which the app's Content-Security-Policy forbids, and without them the diagram rendered as black boxes with invisible arrows. See T9 in THREAT-MODEL.md.

One current row per asset, RLS via assets -- verified live against a real disposable Postgres container that org-a and org-b are isolated on threat_models, connected as bulwark_app (not a superuser), the same standard held for every other RLS table in this project.

docs.title: Triage assistant
docs.text: For one Issue, a model reads its taint path and surrounding code and returns an advisory verdict: likely_real, likely_false_positive, or unsure, with a rationale and the specific lines it based that on. It never changes the issue's status, severity, or visibility. Design reasoning in ADR-0028; the honest verification record is in v2-week43-verification.md.

docs.title: What it does, and doesn't, affect
docs.text: The verdict is stored on the Issue and shown in the issue detail screen immediately. It also feeds core.risk.score as one ranking input -- a bounded nudge (never suppressing the finding, never overriding a CISA KEV floor) -- but only starting with the asset's next scan, not retroactively. It is a separate signal from the human triage_status (not-a-risk/accepted/reopen): nothing here can ever set that; only a person can, through the existing triage action.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Hosted-only, same posture as remediation and the verified-fix agent:

export BULWARK_LLM_ENABLED=1
export BULWARK_LLM_API_KEY=...
# optional: route this task to a different backend/model than the default
export BULWARK_LLM_ROUTE_TRIAGE=hosted

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Endpoint What it does POST /assets/{asset_id}/issues/{issue_id}/triage-assistant Generate a fresh verdict. Sends the finding's taint path and code to the model provider. 409 if the assistant isn't enabled, or if the asset has no completed scan or the issue has no occurrence in it. GET /assets/{asset_id}/issues/{issue_id}/triage-assistant The stored verdict. 404 if none has been generated yet.

Both need scans:read (the GET) or scans:write (the POST) -- the same scopes the issue list and human triage endpoints already use; no dedicated scope was carved out for a feature this closely related to them.

docs.title: What leaves your machine
docs.text: The same category of data Week 41/42's LLM features already send: the finding's title, description, CWE id, file path, its taint path, and the surrounding code -- secret-scrubbed and PII-redacted first, exactly like remediation's own prompt.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove
docs.text: No live run against a real hosted model, and no measurement against the OWASP Benchmark's ground-truth labels (the plan's own stated evaluation) -- both need a live model this environment doesn't have. Full account in v2-week43-verification.md.

docs.title: Heuristic evaluation of the current UI (Week 31, plan §32)
docs.text: Evaluated 2026-09-28 against Nielsen's ten usability heuristics, by walking the actual running app (localhost:3010, the sample scan and the real findings table/detail panel) rather than reading the design intent alone. This is an expert evaluation, not a substitute for the baseline usability study with five real participants (plan §32) — that study is still pending; see docs/ux-study-protocol.md for the ready-to-run script. Where a heuristic issue is really a gap against a plan-defined target journey rather than a heuristics violation per se, it's cross-referenced to docs/ux-journey-maps.md instead of duplicated here.

docs.title: 1. Visibility of system status
docs.text:
• Good: scan progress shows each tool (bandit/semgrep/gitleaks/trivy/osv-scanner) with a live status chip (OK/skipped), a duration, and a findings count as it completes — this is real, specific status, not a generic spinner.
  • Issue found (real, observed): the "Top 10 by risk" widget's own list does not highlight which row is currently open in the detail panel when you navigate with j/k — only the main findings table's list does. Confirmed directly: pressing j inside the Top 10 widget correctly advanced the panel to finding 2 of 10, but the left-hand list kept finding 1 highlighted. A user keyboard-triaging from the Top 10 widget loses track of which item is selected.

docs.title: 2. Match between system and the real world
docs.text:
• Good: severity labels (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/INFO), plain risk descriptions ("An ingress security group rule allows traffic from 0.0.0.0/0"), and the "Fix these first" framing all use the user's own vocabulary, matching Principle 7 (§25) directly — no "Adapters," no "Suppress."
  • Issue found (real, observed, not hypothetical): the static "How to fix" reference guidance shown for the AWS ingress-rule finding above is generic content about service meshes, mTLS and Istio — completely unrelated to fixing a security group rule. This is a real content-quality bug in the remediation knowledge base (core/rag), not a UI bug, but it directly violates this heuristic: the guidance doesn't match the real-world fix a developer needs for this finding. Worth a follow-up ticket against the KB corpus, independent of the UX redesign.

docs.title: 3. User control and freedom
docs.text:
• Good: Esc closes the finding detail panel cleanly; filters (severity/category/scanner/path) are all independently clearable.
  • Gap against the target, not a heuristic violation today: J3's "mark as not a risk with a reason, or accept risk with an expiry" has no UI at all yet — there is nothing to give freedom over, since risk acceptance itself doesn't exist as a feature (ADR-0012 defers it to Week 62). Not a redesign problem to solve now.

docs.title: 4. Consistency and standards
docs.text:
• The finding detail panel's layout (severity/risk box → location → rule ids → code → guidance) is identical whether opened from the Top 10 widget or the main table — good internal consistency.
  • Severity color coding is consistent across the scan-list page, the Top 10 widget, and the full findings table.

docs.title: 5. Error prevention
docs.text:
• The sign-in screen's help text ("It stays in this browser tab only and is never put in a URL") proactively prevents a real mistake (pasting a token into a URL/query string) before it happens — a strong example of this heuristic done well.
  • File-path filtering and severity/category filters are dropdowns/checkboxes, not free text prone to typos, except the path filter (a deliberate, reasonable exception — substring search needs it).

docs.title: 6. Recognition rather than recall
docs.text:
• Every finding's location, rule id, and CVSS/EPSS numbers are shown inline in the detail panel — a user never has to remember a rule id to look it up elsewhere.
  • Issue found: there is no visible on-screen hint that j/k (or the up/down arrow buttons) navigate between findings until a user either discovers the arrow buttons or already knows the convention from another keyboard-first tool (email clients, Vim). Principle 5 (§25) commits to "keyboard-first triage," but nothing teaches a novice the keys exist. A brief, dismissible hint or a ? shortcuts-help overlay (the plan's own §30.1 "command palette, keyboard map, shortcut help," scheduled for Week 33) would close this.

docs.title: 7. Flexibility and efficiency of use
docs.text:
• Sorting by severity, path, or risk score, plus scanner/category filters, gives a security engineer (per §26.1's persona table) real flexibility for triage.
  • j/k navigation on the full findings table works well for the "triage 100 issues" persona goal once discovered (see #6 above).

docs.title: 8. Aesthetic and minimalist design
docs.text: • The severity bars, dedup summary ("62 raw findings became 38 after merging duplicates, 39% fewer") and the plain-language top line are calm and information-dense without clutter — matches Principle 2, "calm by default," directly.

docs.title: 9. Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
docs.text: • Not exercised in this pass without real error states (a failed scan, a timed-out tool) — the sample scan is a clean "completed" run. Deferred to the actual usability study, which should include a task that hits a partial/failed scan if one can be arranged.

docs.title: 10. Help and documentation
docs.text:
• The "About Bulwark" page and inline explanatory copy ("Ranked by severity and how likely each one is to be exploited... a heuristic for ordering work, not a guarantee") reduce the need for separate docs for the core flows.
  • No in-app shortcuts/keyboard-map documentation yet (ties back to #6) — scheduled work, not a new finding.

docs.title: Summary: prioritized list of UX problems (plan §31's own deliverable)
docs.text:
1. Top 10 widget's list doesn't track keyboard navigation (visibility of system status) — small, concrete fix.
  2. No shortcut discoverability for j/k (recognition vs. recall) — addressed by the plan's own Week 33 command-palette/shortcut-help work; flagged here so it isn't lost.
  3. KB remediation guidance can be topically wrong (match between system and real world) — a content-quality bug, not a UX-redesign item; worth its own ticket against core/rag.
  4. J1's "sign in with GitHub" doesn't match reality (still API-token paste) and J3's risk- acceptance actions don't exist yet — both are journey-target gaps, detailed in docs/ux-journey-maps.md, not heuristic violations of the current design.

docs.title: Journey maps J1–J5 (Week 31, plan §26.2/§31)
docs.text: Current-state walkthroughs of the plan's five acceptance-test journeys, against what's actually built as of Week 30 — not the plan's aspirational v2 end state. Each entry says what happens today, what target the plan sets (§26.2), and the concrete gap. These become Playwright end-to-end tests once the redesign closes them (plan §31/§35), and are the task list for the baseline usability study (docs/ux-study-protocol.md) — trimmed to what's actually walkable today.

docs.title: J1 — First scan
docs.text:
Target: land on the site, sign in with GitHub, install the GitHub App on one repository, scan starts automatically, verdict appears. Under 2 minutes, no documentation needed.

Today: landing page → "Open app" → a screen asking to paste an API token from the server's .env file (confirmed live: /app shows "SIGN IN / Connect to your Bulwark server / Paste the API token..."), not GitHub sign-in. Once past that, submitting a scan (URL or archive upload) does work and does produce a verdict-style report (severity summary, dedup rate, top-10-by-risk).

The GitHub App (Week 30) does now exist and does create an organization automatically the first time it's installed — but it only scans on a pull_request event, not automatically on installation. Installing it does not, by itself, produce a first verdict the way J1 describes.

Gap: no GitHub sign-in exists (the plan's identity work, §19.2, is explicitly deferred — see ADR-0018's "what was actually built"). An install-triggered baseline scan doesn't exist either. J1 is walkable today only via the API-token path, which is a materially different first-run experience than the one the target describes.

docs.title: J2 — Fix the first issue
docs.text:
Target: overview → top issue → explanation → review a verified fix → open a pull request. Under 5 minutes.

Today: the overview/top-10-by-risk → finding detail → explanation chain all work (confirmed live) and are genuinely fast. The explanation is static reference guidance from the CWE/OWASP corpus (AI suggestions are available but off by default, per docs/llm-remediation.md). There is no verified-fix step — no agent proposes, applies, or tests a patch — and nothing opens a pull request on the user's behalf.

Gap: the last two steps of J2 (verified fix, auto-opened PR) are the plan's own Phase 9+ deliverable (the verified-fix agent, not yet built — see ADR-0015's scope). J2 today ends at "read the explanation."

docs.title: J3 — Triage
docs.text:
Target: filter, move through issues with j/k, mark as not a risk with a reason or accept risk with an expiry. 100 issues in 30 minutes.

Today: filtering (severity/category/scanner/path) and j/k navigation both work, confirmed live on the real 38-finding sample scan — j correctly advanced from finding 5 of 38 to 6 of 38, with the list's own highlight following it correctly (see docs/ux-heuristic-evaluation.md for the one place this breaks: the Top 10 widget, not the main table). There is no "mark as not a risk" or "accept risk" action anywhere in the UI.

Gap: risk-acceptance states don't exist as a feature yet (ADR-0012 defers them to Week 62, matching the plan's own sequencing). J3's filter-and-navigate half is genuinely close to the target today; its triage-decision half doesn't exist to test.

docs.title: J4 — Gate pull requests
docs.text:
Target: choose a policy template, test it against the last scan, enable it. Under 3 minutes.

Today: the GitHub Action supports one blunt severity gate (fail-on: high, a single CLI flag in the workflow file) — no policy templates, no "test against the last scan" preview, no enable/disable UI of any kind. This lives in a YAML file the repo owner edits directly, not a product screen.

Gap: essentially the entire journey. Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego, ADR-011 in the plan's own numbering) is a later-phase deliverable this project hasn't reached.

docs.title: J5 — Report upward
docs.text:
Target: generate an executive summary, share a link that expires. Under 1 minute.

Today: per-scan export exists (JSON/SARIF/HTML/PDF), but that's a technical report for the person who ran the scan, not an executive summary, and there is no link-sharing mechanism — expiring or otherwise. Sharing today means sending the exported file itself.

Gap: the entire journey is unbuilt. Nothing to test yet.

docs.title: What this means for the baseline study
docs.text: Only J1 (partially, via the token path instead of GitHub sign-in) and J3 (its filter-and-navigate half) are realistically testable against today's product. §32 specifies the baseline study covers J1–J3 — J3's testable portion should be reframed for participants as "find and filter down to a specific finding" rather than the full target journey including risk acceptance, and J1 as "get from the landing page to a scan result," not literally "sign in with GitHub," since that flow doesn't exist. This is noted directly in docs/ux-study-protocol.md's task list, not glossed over.

docs.title: Two overview layout options (Week 31, plan §31)
docs.text: Sketched at claude.ai/artifact/KuunrLeog2Pa3omV5tfJat (private; share it from the page's Share menu if others need to see it). Both use the plan's own §28.1 sample data (acme/payments-api, the SQL injection / leaked key / lodash CVE trio) so they're directly comparable to the plan's own wireframe, not an invented example.

docs.title: Layout A — two column (the plan's own §28.1 direction)
docs.text: Verdict full-width at top; below it, a wide "Fix first" column (primary) beside a narrower, persistent sidebar: trend since last week, PR-gate status, and what was/wasn't scanned.

docs.title: Layout B — vertical stack (the alternative)
docs.text: Same verdict. Below it, the trend/PR-gate/coverage info condenses into one slim horizontal stat strip, then the "Fix first" list runs the full width underneath. Trades a persistent sidebar for giving 100% of the width to the actionable list.

docs.title: Chosen: A, with B as a narrow-viewport fallback
docs.text:
Evaluated against the plan's own seven principles (§25):

Principle A (two column) B (vertical stack) 1. Verdict, not a list Both: verdict is full-width, first, unboxed. Tied. 2. Calm by default A's persistent sidebar risks feeling like "another panel to scan." Slightly favors B. 3. Every number has a reason Both show the same numbers with the same context. Tied. 4. Progressive disclosure A wins clearly: the sidebar is a natural place to collapse/hide for novice mode (§30.4) without touching the fix-first list at all. B's stat strip has nowhere to go except off-screen entirely. 5. Keyboard-first triage A wins: the fix-first list's own column never changes width or position regardless of sidebar content length. In B, a longer "what was scanned" line could wrap the stat strip taller and shift the list down between renders. 6. Honest about uncertainty Both carry "Found by 2 scanners · Verified fix ready" identically. Tied. 7. User's words Layout-independent. Tied.

A wins on progressive disclosure and layout stability for keyboard triage — two principles this project has stated it cares about explicitly (§25.4, §25.5) — and it's also what the security engineer and team-lead personas (§26.1) most directly benefit from: persistent PR-gate and trend visibility without scrolling.
