Two new regression tests (test_code_fingerprint_distinguishes_different_rules_with_no_snippet, test_code_fingerprint_distinguishes_different_rules_sharing_one_quoted_block) reproduce both real cases directly. tests/unit/test_issues.py's fallback_key tests were rewritten for the new, intentionally different behavior (it no longer gives up and returns None for a placeholder/empty snippet — it anchors on the rule id instead, which is more useful: a redacted-secret finding can now be tracked across a file move too, not just abandoned).
  • Found live: while testing the new /assets/{id}/issues endpoint against real Postgres data, marking VAmPI's "root user" Dockerfile finding as not-a-risk silently also hid its unrelated "no HEALTHCHECK" finding. Confirmed via direct API inspection (fingerprint and issue.id identical for two differently-titled findings), root-caused, fixed, and the exploration-triaged issue was reopened afterward to leave the demo data clean. Both the API and worker Docker images were rebuilt and the migration re-run against the live Postgres so the fix is live in the running deployment, not just the source tree.

docs.title: Backend — new endpoints, all reusing existing data paths
docs.text:
• GET /assets/{id}/issues — the asset's latest scan's findings, filtered to the active triage queue by default (untouched issues, plus any accepted issue whose expiry has passed — "reappears automatically," per §28.3) or to an explicit triage= list. Same query_findings-style severity/category/sort/pagination as the existing scan-scoped endpoint; the only new work is the triage join (core/persistence/repo.py's list_asset_issues).
  • GET /assets/{id}/issues/{issue_id} and .../history — one issue's full Finding for its detail screen, and a real event timeline built from IssueRow.first_seen_at/fixed_at plus the tamper-evident audit log (AuditEntry.target == issue_id) — nothing synthesized.
  • POST /assets/{id}/issues/{issue_id}/triage and .../bulk-triage — not_a_risk (reason required), accepted (expiry required), reopen. Every action writes a real audit entry (core/persistence/repo.py's triage_issue, reusing the Week 29/30 backfill's append_audit_entry) — exactly §28.3's "Both write to the audit log." Bulk triage reports partial failure per issue rather than aborting the whole batch.
  • New issues table columns (migration 0009_issue_triage.py): triage_status, triage_reason, triage_expires_at, triaged_at, triaged_by — deliberately separate from the existing ADR-0012 state column (lifecycle vs. human decision are orthogonal). No RLS changes needed: issues already carries the tenant-isolation policy from migration 0005, and it covers new columns automatically. Migrated against the real live Postgres deployment, not just SQLite — confirmed via \d issues that the columns, index, and existing RLS policy are all present and correct.
  • 13 new backend tests (tests/unit/test_issue_triage_api.py, test_project_overview.py's existing suite unaffected) plus the 2 correlation regression tests above — all against real SQLite through the actual FastAPI TestClient, not by calling repo functions directly. Full suite: 869 passed, 2 skipped; ruff, black --check, and mypy clean on every changed file.

docs.title: Frontend — built, then clicked through end to end
docs.text:
components/IssuesTable.tsx (plan §31: real @tanstack/react-table for the column model — selection, severity, title/location, triage status, rule id — combined with @tanstack/react-virtual for windowed row rendering, not a hand-rolled scroller), severity and triage-status filter chips, sort, bulk-select with a triage action bar, and saved views (named filter presets in localStorage per project — no per-user backend exists yet, same honest simplification as the API token itself; see "what this doesn't claim" below).

components/IssueDetail.tsx: the why-ranked panel (reused from Week 33's design-system/why-ranked.tsx, carrying the real risk_factors text), a taint-path stepper (design-system/taint-stepper.tsx — "static until Phase 9 supplies real paths," per Week 34's own line item: the one real step shown is the finding's own location, never an invented intermediate hop), a Shiki code view (design-system/code-view.tsx, real syntax highlighting, theme-synced to the design system's light/dark via a MutationObserver on data-theme rather than fighting Shiki's own dual-theme CSS-variable convention), a real event history, and the triage actions themselves.

design-system/mode.tsx (novice/expert, plan §30.4): a localStorage-persisted per-viewer toggle controlling exactly what this session's own instructions asked for concretely — row density on the issues table, the plain-language explanation's default open/closed state, and whether rule ids are shown or one click away. It does not change the landing page after sign-in (no per-user sign-in flow exists yet to hang that on).

docs.title: Verified live, not just built
docs.text:
A disposable local FastAPI+SQLite server (a freshly secrets.token_hex-generated test token, never the user's real one) seeded with 6 findings across two projects, driven by hand in the built-in browser:

  • Issues table: severity/triage filter chips, sort, real data rendering with the correct severity shapes.
  • Bulk triage → "Mark as not a risk": reason dialog required and enforced (Confirm stays disabled without one), the issue disappeared from the active queue immediately after confirming, and reappeared correctly under the triage=not_a_risk filter with its status tag.
  • Issue detail: the why-ranked panel showed the real risk score and factors; the taint stepper showed the one real step, correctly labeled "Where this happens" (not "How the input gets there") since there's only one; the Shiki code view rendered real syntax-highlighted Python.
  • Expert mode toggle: "What this means" auto-collapsed and a real "Rule IDs" section appeared — confirmed live, not just that the code compiles.
  • Reopen: banner cleared, both triage actions re-enabled, and — the strongest single piece of evidence that the whole audit-backed history mechanism works — the History panel showed all three real events in order: "First seen," "Marked as not a risk," "Reopened." Accept risk: date input filled via a form-level set (native <input type=date> doesn't take raw keystrokes reliably in this automation harness — a tooling limitation, not a product one; the expires_at-required validation was independently confirmed by the disabled Confirm button before that, and by the backend's own passing test), confirmed "Risk accepted — until 31/12/2026," and a fourth real history entry appeared.
  • Caught and fixed live: IssuesTable's "N findings" text was unconditionally plural even for a count of 1; fixed and re-verified in the same session (distinct from, but same class of bug as, Week 33's).

All CI-equivalent checks (npm run typecheck, npm test, npm run build, npm run build-storybook) were re-run from a clean npm ci, matching what the web CI job actually runs, not just what worked with a locally-mutated node_modules. Throwaway server state (SQLite db, work directories, the two dev processes) was torn down after verification.

docs.title: What Week 34 does not claim
docs.text:
• Saved views are per-browser, not per-user: same limitation as the API token (sessionStorage) and Week 33's project switcher — no real per-user identity/settings backend exists yet. A real "shared team view" needs that first.
  • The taint-path stepper shows one real step, never a fabricated multi-hop path. A richer, illustrative multi-step example exists only in Storybook, explicitly labeled as such. Phase 9 (Weeks 36-40) is where a real taint engine makes multi-step paths a real, per-finding thing.
  • j/k and the rest of the issues-table keyboard shortcuts are still not wired here. The Week 33 shortcuts dialog already marks them "reserved"; that stays true this week too. The existing scan report's FindingsTable.tsx has its own separate j/k handling (with the Week 31-documented desync bug against the old "Top 10 by risk" widget) — unifying keyboard navigation properly across both the new issues table and the old scan report is real, separate work this week didn't attempt, rather than a partial, bug-prone version of it.
  • Novice/expert mode does not change the landing page after sign-in (§30.4's table also lists this) — there is no per-user sign-in flow yet for that setting to route.

docs.title: Week 35 verification — onboarding, states, accessibility, validation (plan §28.2, §30.3, §31)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and clicked through — for Week 35: the live scan screen, every empty/partial/error/loading state's copy, an accessibility pass, and Playwright end-to-end tests with visual regression for journeys J1 and J3.

docs.title: Live scan screen (§28.2)
docs.text:
• A real elapsed-time header (components/ElapsedTime.tsx) while a scan is queued or running, hydration-safe like LocalTime.
  • A real, honestly-scoped "progress so far" line: N of M scanners reported in, R raw findings so far, using the live tool_status[tool].findings counts that already stream over the WebSocket/polling path.
  • What this deliberately does not claim: the plan's own wireframe shows "2 critical issues found so far. You can start reviewing now. [Review]" while a scan is still running. Checked against the real backend and confirmed this isn't honestly buildable in one week without a much larger, riskier change: core/pipeline.py correlates and persists every Finding/Issue row in one atomic step after every tool finishes (_run_scan_job's correlate() → finalize() → add_findings()), because cross-tool deduplication needs to see every tool's output at once to decide what's a duplicate — exactly the class of correctness problem Week 34's correlation-identity fix was about. Persisting per-tool findings incrementally and re-correlating live is real, valuable future work, not something to rush right after that fix. The progress line is explicit that its count is "raw" and not yet deduplicated, so it doesn't overclaim what's live.
  • Named, actionable failure copy: a failed/timed-out scanner is now named directly ("trivy timed out, so its results may be incomplete") with a link to start a new scan — replacing a generic "some scanners failed or timed out" message. "Retry" in the wireframe is deliberately not a single-tool re-run: the backend has no such endpoint, and ScanView doesn't expose a reusable source URL/reference for uploads. "Start a new scan" is the same action stated honestly, not a fabricated one-click retry.
  • "No findings" now names how many scanners actually ran ("5 scanners found no issues"), instead of a bare "No findings." — still not the wireframe's coverage-gap sentence ("Terraform files weren't scanned…"), which needs real gap detection this codebase doesn't have yet (Week 33's own verification doc already noted this honestly).

docs.title: State copy audit (§30.3)
docs.text:
• Loading states are real skeletons now, not spinners on a blank page: ProjectsList, ProjectOverview, IssueDetail, and ScanPage all showed bare "Loading…" text before this week; all four now render skeleton rows shaped like their final layout, reusing the existing .sk shimmer primitives from app/globals.css (already used elsewhere — FindingGuidance, RecentScans, TokenGate, app/loading.tsx).
  • "No projects yet" copy tightened toward the plan's own wording ("Run your first scan to see it here. It takes about two minutes.") — not the literal "Connect a repository… [Connect GitHub]" text, since there's no GitHub-App-connect UI to link to yet (no per-user GitHub sign-in exists; same honest gap earlier weeks' verification docs already recorded).
  • Git-clone errors now lead with a plain-word summary, not a raw git stderr string (core/gitfetch.py's new _friendly_clone_error()): "Couldn't find this repository. Check the URL is correct." / "Couldn't clone this repository. Bulwark can only scan public repositories right now — make sure this one is public." The raw detail stays attached in parentheses, so nothing is hidden, just led with what happened and what to do next (§30.3's own stated principle). Two new backend tests reproduce both cases directly.
  • AI-unavailable copy: already real before this week (FindingGuidance.tsx) — off entirely ("AI suggestions are off on this server…"), a degraded/failed call shown with its reason, and a rate-limit hit shown with "Reference guidance above still applies." The plan's example is a monthly budget; this codebase has a real per-minute/per-day rate limiter (core/llm/limits.py) instead of billing/budget tracking, so that's the honest equivalent actually implemented, not a gap this week introduced or fixed.

docs.title: Accessibility pass
docs.text:
axe-core was already wired into npm test (tests/a11y.test.tsx, axe-core in package.json) from an earlier week — already effectively "in CI" via the web job's existing npm test step, not a new thing this week added. What Week 35 did add: axe coverage for every screen built in Weeks 33-34 that had none — AppShell's screens weren't a gap (Week 33 verified those live), but ProjectsList, ProjectOverview, IssuesTable, IssueDetail (including its triage dialogs, opened, not just the closed state), and ScanReport's new running/partial states had zero automated a11y coverage before this week. That coverage found two real bugs, both fixed:

  1. The triage reason/expiry inputs had only placeholder text, no <label> — a real WCAG failure (placeholder text is not a reliable accessible name), only caught because the new test opens the dialog rather than checking the closed state. Fixed in both IssueDetail.tsx and IssuesTable.tsx's (bulk) triage dialogs.
  2. The new virtualized Issues table had zero table/grid ARIA semantics — a <div>-based virtualized grid (real @tanstack/react-virtual, can't use a native <table> with absolute-positioned rows) with no role="table"/"row"/"cell"/"columnheader" at all, invisible to a screen reader as tabular data. Fixed with the standard ARIA grid pattern.

A real, manual keyboard-only walkthrough (not just automated checks) against a disposable local server, driven by hand in the built-in browser — sign-in, submitting a scan, opening a finding, and closing it — found and fixed two more real issues:

  1. Checkboxes had no visible focus indicator at all. app/globals.css's input:focus-visible, select:focus-visible { outline: none; border-color: var(--teal); } is a fine treatment for a bordered text input (the border-color change is the focus indicator) but a native checkbox has no CSS border box for that to repaint — removing its native outline left nothing in its place. Confirmed via getComputedStyle before (outlineStyle: "none") and after (outlineStyle: "solid", matches(':focus-visible')). This affects every checkbox in the app: the old scan report's scanner-selection checkboxes and the new Issues table's row-select checkboxes both share this one global rule.
  2. The issue detail page had no heading at all — the title was a <span>, not an <h1>, so a screen-reader user navigating by headings (a standard pattern) had nothing to land on. Fixed by making it a real <h1> (CSS specificity meant no visual change was needed).

What this doesn't claim: no VoiceOver (or any real screen reader) testing — no such tool is available in this environment, and simulating one honestly isn't possible; axe-core plus a real keyboard walkthrough catches a meaningful, real subset of the same issue class (as items 1-4 above show), but isn't the same thing. Flagged here explicitly rather than silently skipped, the same pattern used for this project's other real capability gaps.

docs.title: Playwright end-to-end tests + visual regression (§31)
docs.text:
No Playwright setup existed before this week. Built from scratch:

  • scripts/e2e_server.py (new): a disposable, self-seeding Bulwark API server for CI, since the web/e2e jobs have no Docker, Postgres, or Redis. Runs the real api.main.create_app and real core.persistence.repo functions against a real file-backed SQLite database (WAL mode — see below for why not in-memory), so every HTTP request Playwright makes runs real application code. Only two things a scanner-less, worker-less job genuinely can't do are faked, both marked in the module's own docstring: running actual scanner containers (a fake "worker" thread marks the scan running, then completed, writing real Finding rows through the same sync_issues_for_scan/add_findings/finish_scan calls the real pipeline uses — the frontend cannot tell the difference), and Redis pub/sub for live WebSocket updates (an empty subscriber, so the frontend correctly falls back to its own real polling path).
  • A real bug found building this fixture, not a hypothetical: the first version used sqlite:// in-memory with StaticPool (matching tests/conftest.py's pattern) — fine for pytest's single-threaded-per-test usage, but this server genuinely serves concurrent requests (uvicorn's thread pool plus the fake worker's own background threads), and StaticPool's one shared raw connection can't safely interleave transactions from more than one of them. Surfaced as sqlite3.OperationalError: cannot commit transaction - SQL statements in progress — but only under real parallelism (multiple Playwright workers in a Linux container; serial runs on this Mac never hit it). Fixed by switching to a real file-backed database with WAL mode and a busy timeout, SQLite's own documented answer to concurrent access.
  • playwright.config.ts: two webServer entries (the Python API on port 8811, next dev on 3911 — both deliberately far from any port the real dev stack uses), NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL wired to the fake API.
  • web/next.config.mjs: added allowedDevOrigins: ["127.0.0.1", "localhost"] — Next 16 blocks cross-origin dev-server requests by default, and Playwright drives the app via 127.0.0.1.
  • tests-e2e/journeys.spec.ts: J1 (sign in → submit a scan → live status transitions → a real verdict) and J3 (filter, open an issue, mark not-a-risk with a reason, j/k between issues, accept risk with an expiry, reopen) — all against real HTTP, real SQLite persistence, real triage/audit-log writes. J2 is not covered: its literal target ("review the verified fix, open a pull request") depends on a verified-fix/PR-creation feature that doesn't exist anywhere in this codebase yet (confirmed by searching for it) — Phase 9/10 territory, not something to fake a test for. Plan §26.2's time targets (J1 under 2 minutes, J3 100 issues in 30 minutes) describe a person's pace, which a scripted test can't assert; these tests assert the flow completes with no unnecessary step and no dead end instead.
  • A real test-isolation bug found and fixed: the first version of these tests reused one fixed repo URL across every test. sync_issues_for_scan's fallback-key matching (Week 34's correlation work) correctly recognized the same finding recurring across scans of the same asset and reused its existing Issue — triage state included — which is exactly what it's supposed to do. The bug was the test's assumption that each test got an independent, untouched issue queue. Fixed with a distinct fake repo path per test (journeys.spec.ts's uniqueRepoUrl()), giving each test its own asset for real, not a coincidence of run order.
  • tests-e2e/visual.spec.ts: full-page screenshots of the project overview, issues table, and issue detail screens. Linux baselines, not the ones this Mac's browser would generate: Playwright encodes the OS into the snapshot filename on purpose (font rendering differs), and CI runs ubuntu-latest, so macOS-generated baselines would fail on the very first real CI run. Generated and — critically — independently re-verified against, not just written by, the official mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.63.0-jammy Docker image (matching the installed Playwright version exactly), run fully self-contained (its own npm ci and pip install, so nothing from this Mac's compiled native modules leaks in). Two more real flakiness sources found by actually re-running the comparison after generating a baseline, not assumed stable:
  • The per-test unique repo URL (needed for isolation, see above) is rendered on screen as the project's label, so different Date.now()-based text between the baseline run and any later run guaranteed a diff. Fixed for the visual spec specifically with fixed, deterministic labels (one literal per test — test isolation doesn't need to survive re-running the whole suite the way journey-test isolation does).
  • Three dates (triage_expires_at, first_seen_at, and each history entry's timestamp in IssueDetail.tsx) were rendered as plain text, not <time> elements, so they weren't covered by the existing mask: [page.locator("time")]. Fixed by making them real <time dateTime=...> elements — a genuine semantic/accessibility improvement on its own, and it means the existing mask now covers them for free. (The finding id in the topline — a real, freshly generated UUID every scan — is masked directly by selector instead, since it's supposed to differ every run.)
  • Confirmed stable across three independent full re-runs against the committed baselines, including one exactly matching how CI actually invokes it (CI=true, default parallel workers).
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml: new e2e job (Python + Node, no scanner images) running npm run e2e; uploads the Playwright HTML report as an artifact on failure.

docs.title: Follow-up usability study — deferred
docs.text: Plan §32's Week 35 line item is a follow-up study with five new participants on the redesign, publishing before-and-after SUS results against Week 31's baseline. Week 31's baseline study itself was never run (still deferred pending real participant recruitment, as that week's own verification doc already recorded) — there is no "before" to compare a "after" against yet, so a before-and-after publication is doubly not possible right now, not just deferred once. Recruiting and running a real study with real people isn't something to fabricate or simulate; both studies remain a real, separate task for when participant recruitment is actually in scope.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Backend: ruff check ., black --check ., mypy clean. Full suite: 871 passed, 2 skipped (869 + 2 new core/gitfetch.py regression tests for the friendlier clone-error copy).
  • Web: npm run typecheck, npm test (145 passed, up from 137 — the new ElapsedTime/ ScanReport tests and 14 new/extended a11y tests), npm run build, npm run build-storybook — all clean from the actual CI commands.
  • npm run e2e: 7 passed (4 journeys + 3 visual regression), verified independently in the official Linux Playwright Docker image, including a run shaped exactly like the new CI job (CI=true, parallel workers).
  • A real, manual keyboard-only walkthrough in the built-in browser (not just automated checks), documented above under Accessibility, found and fixed two real bugs beyond what axe-core alone caught.

docs.title: Week 36 verification — incremental scanning (plan §20.1, §36, §28.6)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured — for Week 36: the content-addressed result cache, pull-request-mode issue classification, the scan comparison screen, and a real measurement of PR scan time against a full scan.

docs.title: Content-addressed result cache (§20.1)
docs.text:
core/cache.py's ResultCache is disk-backed, keyed on (tool, tool_version, ruleset_hash, content_hash). File-local tools (Bandit, Semgrep, Gitleaks) are cached per file — a cache-miss subset directory is built by copying (not symlinking: the sandbox mounts a directory the real scanned tree isn't inside, so a symlink back out to it would dangle inside the container) only the changed files, and the real tool runs against just that subset. Repo-wide tools (Trivy, OSV-Scanner) are cached as a whole, keyed on the files that actually drive their output — Trivy's key correctly includes Dockerfile/IaC files alongside lockfiles, since its applies_to() covers all three; keying it on lockfiles alone would have served a stale result after an unrelated Dockerfile edit.

Opt-in via bulwark scan --cache-dir PATH; unset, every existing test and CLI invocation behaves exactly as before (verified: the full 894-test backend suite passed both before and after this change with no cache-dir set anywhere in it). Tier-2 tools (Grype, Checkov, gosec, Dockle) are not cached this week — a documented cut, not an oversight: they're opt-in, not part of any default scan, and not on the pull-request-speed critical path this week measures.

Wired into the GitHub Action (action.yml): actions/cache restores/saves ~/.bulwark-result-cache across runs (keyed by run id, with an OS-scoped restore-keys prefix so any prior run's cache is found), and both the head and the base-commit scans pass --cache-dir. This is what turns compare-base's extra base-commit scan — previously a second full scan on every single run — into something that's usually almost entirely cache hits after the first run on a repository.

Not done: wiring the cache into the hosted (DB-backed) worker pipeline (core/pipeline.py/Celery). The plan's speed target is specifically about the standalone CLI/Action path; the hosted product's own speed characteristics weren't part of this week's deliverables, and extending caching there is real, separable future work.

docs.title: Pull-request mode and "new in this PR" (§36)
docs.text:
core/issues.py's classify_for_pr() is a read-only counterpart to sync() for PR-triggered scans: it matches a scan's findings against the asset's currently-live issues without deciding anything is fixed. This matters because sync()'s fixed_issue_ids logic is wrong for a PR diff — a pull request necessarily touches only some of a repository's files, so every issue elsewhere would look "fixed" simply for not appearing in a scan that never looked at it. A fixed issue reappearing in a PR classifies as new, not "open" — the base branch has no such problem, so a PR bringing it back must still trip the gate, even though the same event is called "reintroduced" on the real branch.

A real bug this surfaced and fixed: a PR-triggered scan's Asset was keyed on its own "owner/repo#42" display label, not the repository's URL, so it never actually shared the repository's real Issue history — every PR silently got its own throwaway asset, and "new in this PR" would have compared against nothing every time. core/persistence/repo.py's create_scan() now takes an explicit asset_label distinct from the scan's own display label; the GitHub webhook handler passes the clone URL, the same identity an ordinary scan of that repository already uses. Verified end to end (tests/unit/test_github_webhook.py): two different PRs of the same repository, and an ordinary scan of it, now all resolve to one Asset row.

Where it shows up: - API: ScanView.issue_counts and each finding's issue.state needed no code changes to pick this up — they already read from FindingRow.issue_state, which classify_for_pr's output now populates for PR scans the same way sync() already did for ordinary ones. - Action: already existed (bulwark ci compare --base, new-findings output, the PR comment) — verified still working, now made fast by the cache above. - VS Code extension: new "Bulwark: Scan (new since base branch)" command (extensions/vscode/src/git.ts, diff.ts). Resolves the merge-base with the real system git, scans a throwaway worktree of it alongside the workspace, and tags (not hides — every finding is still shown) the ones that don't match by fingerprint, the same comparison core/ci/compare.py runs in CI.

docs.title: Scan comparison screen (§28.6)
docs.text:
GET /scans/{id}/compare?against={id} (core/persistence/repo.py's compare_scans()) categorizes an asset's issues between any two of its own scans as new/fixed/reintroduced/unchanged, ordered by created_at rather than trusting which id the caller passed first. Web UI at /app/projects/[id]/compare, picking from the project overview's existing recent-scans data (no new listing endpoint needed).

Reduced scope, stated honestly: the plan describes this screen "with the commit range between them." core/persistence/repo.py's Scan doesn't capture a resolved commit SHA today — only a git ref for PR scans (refs/pull/<n>/head), never a specific commit. Capturing one would mean threading a new return value through core/gitfetch.py::clone_repo and core/source.py::materialize into every one of their ten call sites (the CLI, the worker pipeline, and eight benchmark/test call sites) — real, bounded work, but a wider, more invasive change than this specific display detail justified this week. The screen instead shows each scan's source label, finish time, and PR number when there is one, which is genuinely what's available; the gap is noted in web/components/ScanComparison.tsx's own docstring rather than faked with placeholder data.

docs.title: Measured: PR scan time against a full scan (§20.1's target, §34's methodology)
docs.text:
benchmarks/incremental/run.py, real Docker, real clone, no mocking:

Repository Tools Cold full scan Warm PR scan (median of 3, 3 files changed) Speedup NodeGoat bandit, semgrep, gitleaks, trivy, osv-scanner 71.2s 19.6s 3.6x

Target met (under 60s) on this repository. Full numbers, methodology, and an honest explanation of why the speedup is 3.6x and not closer to instant (the warm run's remaining ~17-20s is almost entirely core.correlation.correlate() — cross-tool dedup over every finding, unrelated to this week's cache and not sped up by it) are in benchmarks/README.md's "Incremental scanning" section. This is one repository with a 3-file simulated diff, not the plan §34 evaluation methodology ("replay the last 20 merged PRs of each repository in the 30-repository corpus") — that is a separate, larger evaluation task for a later phase.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 904 backend tests passing before the scan-comparison work, 910 after, plus the VS Code extension's 91 and the web app's 150 — all passing; ruff/black/mypy clean throughout.
  • The cache's per-file and repo-wide behavior verified directly (cache hit/miss counts, which files actually got rescanned) via tests/unit/test_cache.py and test_cache_scan.py, not just "the scan still produces the same findings."
  • classify_for_pr's non-mutation guarantee verified directly (existing == snapshot after calling it), not just its output.
  • action.yml's existing static checks (SHA-pinning, no shell-injection via unescaped ${{ }}) needed no changes to keep passing with the new steps; two new checks added for the cache wiring specifically. The actions/cache/restore/save SHA was verified against the real tag on github.com/actions/cache, not guessed.
  • The web comparison screen's populated view was not exercised in a live browser against a real backend (would need a seeded Postgres + multiple real scans) — covered instead by mocked unit and axe accessibility tests; the route itself was confirmed to render (sign-in gate, then the API-unreachable state) via next build and a real browser.

docs.title: Week 37 verification — code intelligence: symbols, call graph, entrypoints (plan §20.2)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured — for Week 37: core/codeintel/, a multi-language symbol table, call graph, and framework entrypoint detector, built as foundation for Week 38's taint analysis. See docs/adr/0020-code-intelligence-call-graph.md for the design decisions and their reasoning.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
Four pieces, one package:

  • models.py: Symbol, CallEdge, Entrypoint, and CodeGraph (with callers_of()/ calls_from() one-hop queries).
  • Per-language extractors — python_lang.py (stdlib ast), js_lang.py/ts (tree-sitter), go_lang.py (tree-sitter) — each turning one file into raw symbols, (caller, callee_name, line) call sites, and any entrypoints its own decorators/exports/route registrations reveal.
  • resolve.py: intra-file-first, then repo-wide-if-unique name resolution into a CodeGraph, leaving ambiguous or absent matches unresolved rather than guessing.
  • __init__.py: analyze(root)/analyze_or_none(root), the same never-raises directory-walk contract core/reachability already established.

Entrypoint detection covers six framework conventions: FastAPI and Flask decorators, Django urlpatterns, Express route registration, Next.js App Router and Pages Router (by file location, not decorator shape — Next.js has no decorator to inspect), and Go's net/http.HandleFunc/ Handle.

docs.title: Python uses ast, not tree-sitter-python
docs.text: Deliberate, matching the precedent core/reachability/imports.py already set: Python ships a real, maintained parser in the standard library, so tree-sitter would add a dependency for no benefit. JavaScript/TypeScript and Go have no such built-in, so they use tree-sitter (tree-sitter-go added this week; JS/TS grammars were already a dependency).

docs.title: Real-world validation, not just synthetic snippets
docs.text:
Hand-written test snippets alone would have missed two real gaps. Both were found by running the freshly-built analyzer against NodeGoat (a real, intentionally-vulnerable Node.js application, already cloned in ~/.cache/bulwark-benchmarks/ from Week 36's own benchmark), not by inspection:

  1. Express routes registered with an object-method reference (app.get('/login', sessionHandler.displayLoginPage) — a member_expression, not a bare identifier or inline function) were silently skipped entirely. This is NodeGoat's actual routing style throughout, so only 2 of its ~19 real routes were detected before the fix.
  2. The pre-ES6 "constructor function" idiom (this.method = (req, res) => {...} inside function Foo(db) {...}) had no matching case in the extractor's dispatch at all, so these handler methods — NodeGoat's entire route-handler layer — were never registered as Symbols, making every call to them permanently unresolvable regardless of the resolver's own logic.

Fixing gap 1 took entrypoint detection from 2 to 19 routes (matching NodeGoat's real route surface: /, /login, /signup, /logout, /dashboard, /profile, /contributions, /benefits, /allocations/:userId, /memos, /learn, /research). Fixing gap 2 took the resolved-edge rate from 15/417 (3.6%) to 54/417 (12.9%) — verified end to end, not just by count: /login GET's entrypoint symbol now resolves its one call all the way to SessionHandler.displayLoginPage's own body.

Chasing gap 2 down also surfaced a third, pre-existing bug, unrelated to this week's new code: value.type in ("arrow_function", "function") (used in three places — the inline Express handler case, the const x = () => {} case, and the new constructor-function case) never matched a plain function () {} expression, because tree-sitter's JS grammar names that node type function_expression, not function. Every one of those checks silently missed the non-arrow, function-keyword form of an inline or assigned function — a real, common pattern, not a hypothetical. Fixed in all three places; two new regression tests (test_const_function_expression_becomes_a_named_symbol, test_express_route_with_inline_function_keyword_handler_gets_its_own_symbol) cover it going forward. NodeGoat's own edge/resolution numbers were unaffected by this particular fix (it doesn't happen to use the function-keyword form where it matters for resolution), which is itself a useful data point: the fix is real and necessary for other codebases, even though this one benchmark didn't exercise it.

The remaining ~87% of NodeGoat's call edges stay unresolved for reasons the design accepts as honest limits, not bugs: calls into framework/library code with no local definition (res.render(...), db.get().collection(...)), and genuine dynamic patterns this graph's name-based resolution was never meant to solve (documented in ADR-0020). Nothing here claims a higher resolution rate than what was actually measured.

docs.title: Call resolution: intra-procedural first, unsound where documented
docs.text: A call resolves to a same-file symbol first if there's exactly one; otherwise to a repo-wide unique name match; otherwise it stays unresolved (callee_id=None) rather than guessing — the same "unknown stays unknown" discipline core/reachability/index.py's three-valued Reachability already established. This is explicitly unsound for dynamic dispatch, reflection, and genuine name collisions with no local definition to disambiguate; resolve.py's own module docstring and ADR-0020 both say so.

docs.title: Persistence: deferred, on purpose
docs.text: The plan's literal wording asks for the graph to be stored in Postgres as an edges table. This week's CodeGraph is in-memory only. Building and RLS-hardening a schema with zero validating reader in the same session was judged premature risk; Week 38's taint engine will be the first real consumer, and its access pattern should inform the schema rather than being guessed at now. Recorded in ADR-0020 as an intentional sequencing decision, not a silent omission.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 954 backend tests passing (up from 949 before this week: 44 new tests for core/codeintel/ — 10 Python, 16 JS/TS, 7 Go, 7 resolution, 9 end-to-end analysis — plus 2 skipped, unrelated), 94.6% coverage; ruff/black/mypy (strict) all clean.
  • Every framework's entrypoint detection was smoke-tested directly against hand-written snippets for its specific shape (FastAPI/Flask decorators, Django urlpatterns, Express .get/.post/ member-expression handlers, Next.js App/Pages routing, Go net/http) before being formalized into tests.
  • The whole pipeline was run against a real, previously-cloned application (NodeGoat: 40 files, 120 symbols, 19 entrypoints, 417 call sites) — not just synthetic fixtures — and its measured entrypoint count and resolved-edge rate are reported above exactly as observed, including the real gaps that remain.
  • Not done: Postgres persistence of the graph (deferred to Week 38, see above); resolving calls through dynamic dispatch, reflection, or genuine cross-file name collisions (documented as permanent, not a Week 38 TODO); a fourth language beyond Python/JS/TS/Go (not in this week's scope).

docs.title: Week 38 verification — taint analysis (plan §20.3)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured — for Week 38: core/taint/, an intra-procedural data-flow analyzer with function summaries propagated over core.codeintel's call graph (Week 37), producing concrete source-to-sink paths from real HTTP entrypoints. The plan calls this "the most demanding piece of programming in the project"; see docs/adr/0021-taint-analysis.md for the design decisions and their reasoning.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text: Source/sink/sanitizer catalogs (YAML, one per language, matching the plan's own examples: request parameters as sources; cursor.execute, subprocess.run, eval, unescaped template rendering as sinks; parameterized-query helpers and escaping functions as sanitizers); a per-language intra-procedural flow analyzer (Python via ast, JavaScript/TypeScript and Go via tree-sitter) that tracks which local variables become tainted, records sink hits, and computes function summaries; and a call-graph worklist (engine.py) that composes those summaries into complete, real source-to-sink paths with a full hop-by-hop chain.

docs.title: Real-world validation, not just synthetic snippets — three independent true positives
docs.text:
Hand-written test snippets validated the algorithm's individual mechanics (branch merging, sanitizer suppression, cross-function summary composition — all covered by unit tests, 56 passing across the four language/engine test files). But the actual measure of whether this analysis finds real vulnerabilities came from running it against real, previously-known-vulnerable applications, not code written to make the analyzer look good:

Application Real vulnerability Found? Sink location Vulnerable-Flask-App SQL injection in /search (db.engine.execute(str_query) built from request.json) Yes app/app.py:265 NodeGoat eval() injection in POST /contributions (the app's own comment: "Insecure use of eval() to parse inputs") Yes app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 nodejs-goof (Snyk) Command injection in exports.create (exec('identify ' + url, ...) from req.body.content via a regex match) Yes routes/index.js:174

All three were confirmed by reading the actual source before trusting the tool's own output, not the other way around. NodeGoat's case in particular exercises the full pipeline at once: its entire route layer is written as this.handlerName = (req, res) => {...} inside a constructor function (the exact pattern Week 37 needed a dedicated fix for), registered via app.get('/login', sessionHandler.displayLoginPage) — a named-handler redirect with no body of its own, requiring engine._redirect_target to follow the call edge to the real handler before any analysis could even begin. Without that piece, NodeGoat would have produced zero findings regardless of how correct the flow analysis itself was.

docs.title: Cross-checked against Semgrep's own taint mode, as the plan requires
docs.text:
The plan's own validation instruction: "cross-check against Semgrep's taint mode on the same code; every disagreement becomes a labelled test case." Semgrep 1.178.0 (pip-installed, not this project's own pinned Docker adapter) was run against the same two files with its public registry rulesets (p/python, p/flask, p/javascript, p/nodejsscan):

  • NodeGoat's eval() case: exact agreement. ajinabraham.njsscan.eval.eval_node.eval_nodejs flagged the identical three lines (32, 33, 34) this analysis found independently.
  • Vulnerable-Flask-App's SQLi case: same vulnerability, different anchor line — explained, not papered over. Semgrep's own taint-mode rule, python.flask.security.injection.tainted-sql-string.tainted-sql-string, flagged line 261 — the string-construction site (str_query = "..." % search_term) — while this analysis reports line 265, the sink call itself (db.engine.execute(str_query)). Both tools are tracing the same tainted flow (content['search'] → search_term → str_query → execute); they differ only in which step of that flow they choose to anchor the report to. This analysis anchors at the sink deliberately: that is where the dangerous operation actually executes and where a fix (parameterizing the query) needs to happen, which is also the location this project's own SinkHit/TaintFinding model was designed around from the start (ADR-0021).
  • Semgrep's p/security-audit pack also flagged two render_template_string SSTI sites (lines 103/114, 271/281) this analysis did not find. Read directly rather than assumed away: the one inside @app.errorhandler(404) is not reachable through this analysis because core.codeintel's own entrypoint detector doesn't recognize errorhandler as a route decorator (a documented Week 37 gap, ADR-0020) — no entrypoint, no seed, no path to find. The one inside /search's except Exception as e: block builds its template from str(e), an exception message — this analysis does not model "an exception raised while handling tainted data carries that taint," a real, honest gap in scope, not a bug.

This is exactly the outcome the plan's validation step is meant to produce: real agreement on real vulnerabilities, and every disagreement traced to a specific, named, already-documented design decision rather than shrugged off.

docs.title: Real bugs found and fixed during this week's own testing
docs.text:
Consistent with the project's "measured, not assumed" standard, validating against real code (not just synthetic fixtures) surfaced genuine bugs in the analysis itself, beyond what unit tests alone caught:

  • Branch-merge order-dependence. An early version visited an if/else's two arms sequentially into one shared tainted-name map; a clean reassignment in the second arm silently erased taint the first arm had introduced, because the two arms were not independent by construction. Fixed by snapshotting the pre-branch state and visiting each arm from that same snapshot, merging the results by unioning tags afterward — caught by a direct test before this ever reached real-code validation.
  • A receiver's own taint was dropped. request.args.get('id') was computed as untainted at first, because only the call's arguments ('id', a literal) were checked — not the receiver chain (request.args) the method was called on. This is the single most common shape in real Flask/Express code and was caught immediately by the very first hand-written smoke test, before any formal test suite existed for it.
  • TypeScript's parameter grammar silently dropped every handler's source. tree-sitter-typescript wraps every function parameter in a required_parameter node — even with no type annotation at all — while plain tree-sitter-javascript never does. param_names only recognized a bare identifier, so it returned an empty list for every TypeScript arrow-function handler, meaning the param_source_positions seed (position 0, the req-like parameter) was never applied to any .ts file's entrypoint. This was invisible to every JavaScript-only synthetic test and was only caught by deliberately exercising the TypeScript path end-to-end — a .ts version of the exact same Express handler already covered for .js produced zero findings where one was expected. Fixed alongside a related gap found in the same pass: TypeScript's as/satisfies casts and the ! non-null assertion had no case in expr_taint and silently stripped taint through any type cast, a very common pattern in real TypeScript handler code (req.query.q as string). Both are now regression-tested (test_taint_js_flow.py, plus an end-to-end .ts case in test_taint_analyze.py), and neither NodeGoat nor Vulnerable-Flask-App contains any .ts files, so this gap would not have been caught by this week's own real-world corpus without the deliberate TypeScript smoke test.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1010 backend tests passing (up from 954 after Week 37: 56 new tests for core/taint/ — 19 Python flow, 15 JavaScript/TypeScript flow, 10 Go flow, 12 end-to-end analysis across all three languages), 2 skipped (unrelated), 94.2% coverage; ruff/black/mypy (strict) all clean.
  • Mutual recursion (two functions calling each other) is confirmed, by a direct test, not to hang summary computation — bounded by MAX_WORKLIST_PASSES = 50 in engine.py.
  • The same physical sink reached from one entrypoint through two different internal call paths is confirmed to produce exactly one finding, not two (de-duplicated by sink location).
  • A named-handler route redirect with no resolvable target (an undefined reference) is confirmed to produce no finding and not raise, rather than crash the whole analysis.
  • Full-repository timing on real applications: NodeGoat (40 files) in 0.07s, nodejs-goof (10 files) in 0.04s — the worklist and flow analysis add negligible time on top of Week 37's own call-graph construction at this scale.
  • Issue attachment, scoring, and the UI stepper: since landed. The initial pass of this week deferred all of this; it was completed in a follow-up pass the same week and is recorded in ADR-0022, not this document. FastAPI's typed-parameter source style, object-field-level taint (as opposed to bare-name taint), path-sensitive branch analysis, and loop-fixed-point iteration remain documented permanent limits of this design, not TODOs for a future week (ADR-0021).
  • Not done: Postgres persistence of CodeGraph/FunctionSummary data itself (as opposed to a taint path attached to a Finding, which persists today through the existing findings table's JSON column — no new table was needed) — still deferred to whenever a real consumer needs to query the graph directly rather than through a Finding it already produced.

docs.title: Week 39 verification — policy-as-code (plan §20.4)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured — for Week 39: embedded OPA, a Rego starter policy library, opa test in CI, and policy-driven pull-request check status / Action exit codes. See docs/adr/0023-policy-as-code.md for the design decisions, including what was deliberately deferred.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text: core/policy/: a subprocess wrapper around the real opa binary (opa.py), an input-document builder mapping existing Finding fields into the shape the plan's own example policy reads (input.py), the five starter policies the plan names — no reachable KEV vulnerability, no secrets, no new critical-severity issues, a license denylist, accepted risk capped at 90 days (starter/gate.rego, with a full opa test suite in starter/gate_test.rego) — and the high-level evaluate_gate() that ties them together (gate.py). bulwark ci compare gained a --policy PATH option that folds policy denials into the same exit-code/comment/$GITHUB_OUTPUT contract the severity threshold already used. action.yml gained a policy-file input, an OPA-install step gated on it actually being set, and a policy-violations output.

docs.title: Validated against the real opa binary, not a mock
docs.text: Every piece — syntax checking, evaluation, the starter library's own tests — was run against a real opa v1.21.0 binary (downloaded, checksum-verified, and used to interactively validate the design before any Python code was written), not a stubbed subprocess. The plan's own worked example (§20.4's deny contains msg if { ... in_cisa_kev ... reachable ... }) was typed in and evaluated against real input before core/policy/opa.py existed at all, to confirm the exact CLI flags and JSON output shape (opa eval -d policy.rego -I "data.pkg.deny" --format json, stdin input via -I/--stdin-input) before building around them.

docs.title: Real bugs found while writing the starter library's own tests
docs.text:
• A with keyword placement error (count(deny with input as {...}) == 1, invalid Rego — with must bind to a variable first, not appear inline inside a function call) — caught immediately by opa test itself refusing to parse the file, before it ever reached Python code.
  • An "unsafe variable" policy (deny contains msg if { false; msg := "" } used in an early CLI test) actually compiles fine in Rego (body statement order doesn't gate safety analysis the way it might in an imperative language) — confirmed directly rather than assumed, after initially suspecting it would fail.
  • A genuinely unsafe policy (an unbound msg used in the rule head with no assignment reachable in the body) does correctly fail opa check/opa eval with rego_unsafe_var_error — confirmed as the expected, correct OPA behavior for core/policy/opa.py::check_syntax's own error path, not a bug.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1049 backend tests passing (up from 1024 after Week 38's own follow-up: 25 new tests across test_policy_input.py, test_policy_opa.py, and the --policy/action.yml additions to test_ci.py/test_action.py), 2 skipped (unrelated), 94.3% coverage; tests/integration/ test_policy_opa.py is skipped automatically when opa is not on PATH, the same convention tests/integration/test_tools_docker.py already uses for Docker; ruff/black/mypy all clean.
  • action.yml's own existing static-safety test suite (tests/unit/test_action.py: no ${{ }}-interpolated shell injection, every third-party action pinned by commit SHA, every input wired to the step that uses it) passed unchanged against the new policy-file input, plus three new tests specifically confirming OPA is only installed when a policy is actually configured and the new output is correctly wired.
  • The project's own CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) now installs a checksum-pinned OPA v1.21.0 and runs opa test core/policy/starter as its own step, exactly the plan's "opa test runs the policy tests in CI" — not just something the Python test suite happens to also cover.
  • A synthetic end-to-end run through bulwark ci compare --policy: a LOW-severity secret finding (which --fail-on critical alone would pass clean) correctly fails the check once a policy denying category == "secrets" is supplied, with the denial message appearing in the generated PR comment.
  • Not done: the policy editor UI (Monaco editor, live evaluation against the last scan, "save disabled until opa test passes") — deliberately deferred, recorded in ADR-0023, not silently dropped. Also not done: Week 40's own license/SBOM data, without which the starter library's license-denylist rule is real, tested code with nothing yet to match against.

docs.title: Week 40 verification — supply-chain risk (plan §20.5)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured — for Week 40: malicious-package severity, license policy, typosquat detection, OpenSSF Scorecard for direct dependencies, and the direct/transitive dependency graph. See docs/adr/0024-supply-chain-risk.md for the design decisions, including what was deliberately deferred. This closes Milestone M8 (v1.3.0).

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/adapters/osv_scanner.py: a MAL- id now forces CRITICAL severity and 1.0 confidence instead of falling through to INFO; core/policy/input.py exposes this as malicious, and the starter policy library gained a sixth rule (no malicious packages, ever).
  • core/sbom/syft.py: summarize() now also returns SbomPackages (name/version/ecosystem/purl/ license/manifest path) and a direct/transitive dependency graph built from CycloneDX's own dependencies[].dependsOn array.
  • core/sbom/enrich.py::apply_licenses: joins the SBOM's own package licenses onto findings before policy evaluation. bulwark ci compare gained --sbom PATH; the GitHub Action's existing sbom: true input now also feeds this (its step moved before "Compare and gate").
  • core/supplychain/typosquat.py: a new Finding for any SBOM package within edit distance 1–2 of a popular package in the same ecosystem (popular_packages.json, a small curated seed).
  • core/supplychain/scorecard.py: OpenSSF Scorecard for each direct dependency, via deps.dev (purl → source repo) and the Scorecard REST API, cached for a week.
  • core/supplychain/dependency_view.py::path_to: the shortest root-to-package path over the SBOM's own dependency graph.
  • core/scoring/versions.py::smallest_safe_upgrade: a real bug fix, shared by osv_scanner.py and grype.py — both previously used whichever fixed version a scanner listed first, not the smallest.
  • bulwark supply-chain analyze --sbom PATH --output PATH: typosquats + Scorecard as a JSON report.

docs.title: Validated against real, live endpoints — not mocks
docs.text:
Every external integration was exercised against the real thing before any Python was written around it, the same discipline ADR-0023 used for OPA:

  • api.osv.dev: queried live for a known typosquat (reuests on PyPI) to confirm MAL- records are ordinary OSV records with no CVSS/severity fields — this is why the severity bug existed, not an assumption.
  • bulwark/syft:1.52.0: run via Docker against a real two-level npm project (once → wrappy, installed with real npm install) to capture the actual CycloneDX shapes this feature depends on: licenses[].license.id / .expression, the syft:location:0:path property, and — critically — that a component's dependencies[].ref is its purl plus a ?package-id=... qualifier, not the bare purl. Missing that distinction would have silently produced empty direct/transitive sets for every real SBOM; it was caught before writing summarize(), not after a test failed.
  • api.deps.dev/v3alpha/purl/... and api.securityscorecards.dev/projects/...: both fetched live (pkg:pypi/requests@2.31.0 → github.com/psf/requests; that repo's real Scorecard run, score 8.3) to confirm the exact REST paths and JSON shapes before core/supplychain/ scorecard.py was written. (Unit tests mock fetch — the module is a thin, injectable wrapper — but the shapes being mocked are real captured responses, not invented ones.)

docs.title: A real bug found and fixed while writing this, not assumed
docs.text: core/adapters/osv_scanner.py and core/adapters/grype.py both picked fixed[0] for their remediation summary — whichever fixed version a scanner's own JSON listed first. Checked against this codebase's own tests/golden/osv-scanner/raw.json: PYSEC-2023-62's flask record lists two git commit hashes and two real releases (2.2.5, 2.3.2), in that order. smallest_safe_upgrade was written to compare dotted-numeric versions and refuse to order a list where any entry doesn't parse that way — confirmed, by running it against this exact fixture, that it correctly declines to guess (returns None, and the caller falls back to the old fixed[0] behavior) rather than lexically "sorting" a git hash against a release number. The three real golden-fixture cases with mixed hash/version lists were confirmed to produce byte-identical output to before this change.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1102 backend tests passing (up from 1049: 52 new tests across test_scoring_versions.py, test_sbom_syft.py, test_sbom_enrich.py, test_supplychain_typosquat.py, test_supplychain_scorecard.py, test_supplychain_dependency_view.py, test_cli_supply_chain.py, plus additions to test_adapters.py, test_policy_input.py, test_ci.py, test_action.py), 2 skipped (unrelated), 94.4% coverage; ruff/black/mypy all clean (mypy core api, the project's own configured scope).
  • opa test core/policy/starter: 15/15 passing (13 existing + 2 new, for the malicious-package rule), against the real opa binary.
  • An end-to-end run: a real bulwark/syft:1.52.0 SBOM piped through bulwark ci compare --policy --sbom, with a policy denying issue.license == "ISC", correctly failed the gate with "x uses denylisted ISC license" in the generated PR comment — the license value came from the real SBOM, not a stub.
  • bulwark supply-chain analyze end-to-end against the same real SBOM: correctly reported zero typosquats (a two-package project, neither a look-alike name) and the real direct/transitive split (once direct, wrappy transitive) with --no-scorecard.
  • tests/unit/test_action.py's own static-safety checks (no ${{ }} shell injection, every third-party action pinned, every input wired) pass unchanged after moving the "Generate SBOM" step earlier; a new test asserts that step now runs strictly before "Compare and gate" and that SBOM_FILE is wired into it.
  • Since done, as a follow-up (ADR-0025, see below): the Dependencies screen UI, and wiring Syft into the hosted pipeline's own scan flow ("syft" in Scan.tools) -- both deferred here originally, now implemented.

docs.title: Follow-up (2026-09-30): the Dependencies screen, end to end
docs.text:
core/sbom/syft.py::SyftAdapter is now registered in core/scan.py's ADAPTERS, selectable via Scan.tools exactly like grype/checkov/gosec. core/pipeline.py::_process_sbom reshapes its raw CycloneDX output into typosquat Findings (folded into the normal correlate/finalize/persist pipeline, so they get fingerprints and Issue tracking for free) and a JSON summary persisted on a new Scan.sbom_summary column (migration 0010, one nullable JSON column -- no new table, matching FindingRow.data's own pattern). GET /assets/{asset_id}/dependencies (api/schemas.py:: DependenciesView) serves it, empty rather than 404 when no scan has opted in yet, mirroring /assets/{id}/issues's own shape. web/app/app/projects/[id]/dependencies renders it: a filterable package table (name, ecosystem, direct/transitive/root, license, OpenSSF Scorecard for direct dependencies), each row expandable to its own path-from-root (a client-side BFS over the same graph core.supplychain.dependency_view.path_to walks server-side) and its direct dependents -- no new graph-drawing library, since none existed in this codebase and the actual need (a small tree/DAG, shortest-path) didn't warrant adding one. SubmitForm.tsx gained a "Supply-chain risk" checkbox so a user can opt a hosted scan into this from the web UI, not only the API/CLI. Full design reasoning in docs/adr/0025-dependencies-screen.md.

Verified: a synthetic scan with tools=["syft"] and a fake CycloneDX raw output (a real ToolOutcome, run through the actual run_scan_job, not a mocked pipeline) correctly persisted Scan.sbom_summary (component count, per-package license/relation) and a real typosquat Finding in the findings table with reported_by=["bulwark-typosquat"] -- confirming the whole tools-loop-to-persistence path, not just _process_sbom in isolation. 7 new backend tests (1117 total), 5 new frontend tests (155 total; the dependency-path/relation-filter logic exercised against realistic fixture data matching the real API response shape), tsc --noEmit and mypy/ruff/black all clean. The new page was confirmed live in a real browser (Next.js dev server) to compile, route, and render correctly behind TokenGate -- verifying the component's own data rendering against a real backend (Postgres/Redis/Celery/a real scan) was not done this session; that path is covered instead by the automated component tests above, which exercise the exact same API response shape.

docs.title: Week 41 verification — model gateway and LLMOps (plan §21.1)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured — for Week 41: a local backend, per-task routing, privacy mode, token budgets, PII redaction, a path denylist, one schema-repair attempt, and a versioned prompt with a real evaluation suite. See docs/adr/0026-model-gateway.md for the design decisions, including what was deliberately deferred. This closes part of PHASE 10 (M9 is Weeks 41-45; this is Week 41 only).

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/llm/ollama_client.py: OllamaClient/OllamaConfig, a plain-HTTP local backend against Ollama's /api/chat -- no new SDK dependency.
  • core/llm/gateway.py: Task/Backend enums, GatewayConfig, make_gateway_client() -- the single choke point for hosted-vs-local backend selection, per task, with privacy-mode enforcement.
  • core/llm/client.py: LLMClient.complete now returns Completion(text, tokens) instead of a bare string, so real provider-reported token usage flows through to budgets. AnthropicClient populates it from the SDK's own usage.input_tokens/output_tokens.
  • core/llm/budget.py + migration 0011: Scan.llm_tokens_used (a running per-scan counter) and a new llm_usage table (per-org-per-month, RLS-protected) -- both a hard 429 stop, checked before a real call and recorded after it.
  • core/llm/pii.py: optional Microsoft Presidio redaction (bulwark-scan[pii] extra) as a second layer after scrub_secrets, explicitly pinned to the small en_core_web_sm spaCy model.
  • core/llm/pathguard.py: a path denylist (.env, *.pem, id_rsa*, ...), additive-only via BULWARK_LLM_PATH_DENYLIST.
  • core/llm/service.py: one repair attempt on a ContractError, with a fixed generic note that never echoes the rejected reply.
  • core/llm/prompts/fix/v1.md + core/llm/prompt.py::load_prompt: the system prompt moved from an inline string to a versioned, packaged file.
  • core/llm/prompts/fix/promptfooconfig.yaml + promptfoo_provider.py + promptfoo_assert.py + scripts/gen-promptfoo-fixtures.py: a real, runnable promptfoo evaluation suite.
  • api/main.py/api/deps.py: build_default_app now wires the gateway instead of the single hardcoded client; POST /scans/{id}/suggestion enforces the token budget alongside the existing call-rate limiter and records real usage after a genuine (non-cached) call.
  • cli/main.py: bulwark llm status reports gateway routing and both backends' status; bulwark llm suggest gained --privacy.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things — not mocks
docs.text:
• A real local Ollama server: pulled the real ollama/ollama Docker image, ran a real qwen2.5:0.5b model, and called OllamaClient.complete() against it directly -- got a real reply and a real token count (31) back before writing any test around it.
  • The full privacy-mode path, end to end: with a real (valid-shaped) hosted API key configured AND BULWARK_LLM_PRIVACY_MODE=1 AND a real local Ollama server ready, suggest() was run through make_gateway_client for real -- it routed to the local model, made two real HTTP calls (the original attempt plus one repair attempt, both logged), got back a real (small-model-quality) reply that correctly failed the real contract validator on both attempts, and degraded to static text with an honest degraded_reason -- the entire pipeline exercised for real, not stubbed at any layer.
  • The migration: 0011 was run up and down against a real bulwark/postgres:16-pgvector container (the same one Week 40 used), including confirming the RLS policy actually isolates one org's llm_usage row from another's (SET ROLE bulwark_app; SET app.current_org = ...) before and after a downgrade/upgrade cycle.
  • The promptfoo suite: actually run (promptfoo eval) against the real local Ollama server, not just written. This caught two real integration bugs before they could have shipped silently broken:
  • promptfoo's Python provider is a persistent worker process; an env var exported in the invoking shell after that worker starts does not reliably reach it. Fixed by driving the provider entirely from its own YAML config: block instead of ambient BULWARK_LLM_* env vars.
  • promptfoo itself reserves the provider config key timeout (milliseconds, its own per-call cap); a first draft reused that name for Ollama's own request timeout (seconds), which silently fed a seconds-based number in as a millisecond cap and timed out every call after 90ms. Renamed to request_timeout_s. Once fixed, the suite correctly exercised the real model and correctly failed two of its three fixtures against the tiny local model's genuinely malformed (fenced-JSON) output -- proof the deterministic assertion (the real parse_response) actually rejects bad real output, not just a suite that trivially always passes.

docs.title: A real design trade-off made and documented, not silently dropped
docs.text: The plan's own wording for schema validation is "validated with Pydantic: one repair attempt, then fall back to static text." The existing hand-rolled core/llm/contract.py validator (568 lines of tests, including a 20-payload hostile-input battery: bidi-override rejection, dismissal-language filtering, unified-diff structural checks) already does everything a generic Pydantic model would plus protections a plain schema wouldn't express. Rewriting it to Pydantic purely to match the plan's wording would have risked regressing exactly those protections for no behavioral gain -- deliberately not done. The repair attempt (the actually new, valuable half of that plan line) was built. Full reasoning in ADR-0026.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1151 backend tests passing (up from 1117: 34 new, across test_llm.py, test_llm_cache.py, a new test_llm_gateway.py, and test_api_suggestions.py), 2 skipped (unrelated), 94.3% coverage; ruff/black/mypy all clean (mypy core api).
  • The migration's up/down/up cycle and RLS isolation check, above, against a real Postgres container.
  • The promptfoo suite's own real run against a real local model, above.
  • bulwark llm status, bulwark llm suggest, and bulwark llm suggest --privacy were all run for real against this session's real local Ollama server and a real (deliberately invalid, to prove the refusal) hosted-key-plus-privacy-mode combination.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• No MLX backend was built. The plan names "Ollama or MLX"; only Ollama was built. See ADR-0026's "Decisions" section for why, and what would need to change to add MLX later.
  • No new frontend screen. The plan lists no UI screen for Week 41 (unlike Week 39's policy editor or Week 40's Dependencies screen); the existing "Generate AI suggestion" button already surfaces whatever message a 429 carries, but it is not itself budget-aware (no usage meter, no "X of Y tokens used this month" display). That would be new frontend work, not done here.
  • Token budgets were validated by unit test and by reading the migration's live RLS behavior, not by running a real, sustained multi-scan load against a live API + Postgres + real model calls concurrently. The check-before/record-after race window is reasoned about and documented, not measured under real concurrent load.
  • Fix quality against a real model is still formally unmeasured (Week 14's blinded evaluation). The promptfoo run above is a schema-conformance smoke test that happened to also surface a real small model's real shortcomings -- informative, but not that measurement. See docs/llm-remediation.md's own "What this does NOT prove" section, updated this week.
  • PII redaction's actual recall/precision on real code was not measured. Presidio was run once, live, against a synthetic sentence with a name/email/phone/IP/credit-card, and correctly redacted all of them (confirmed manually) -- this proves the wiring works, not that it reliably catches PII in real, messy source code and comments.

docs.title: Week 42 verification — the verified-fix agent (plan §21.2)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured — for Week 42: "the flagship v2 feature." See docs/adr/0027-verified-fix-agent.md for the design decisions, including several deliberate, disclosed scope cuts. This closes part of PHASE 10 (M9 is Weeks 41-45; this is Week 42 only).

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/fixagent/limits.py: ADR-0015's three safety limits, with real, documented numbers.
  • core/fixagent/tools.py + context.py: read_file/search_code/get_call_path, path-contained, built on a fresh core.codeintel.analyze() run per attempt (nothing about the call graph survives past the original scan, confirmed before writing this).
  • core/fixagent/agent.py: the propose-patch tool-calling loop, the first tool-calling code in this repository, hosted (Anthropic) only.
  • core/fixagent/verify.py: apply_patch (a real patch -p1 call), rerun_rule, rerun_scanners -- all reusing core.scan.scan(), none inventing new scan-scoping infrastructure.
  • core/fixagent/sandbox.py: a second, more permissive Docker sandbox for opt-in project test runs.
  • core/fixagent/github_pr.py: create_pull_request, built on GitHub's Contents API.
  • core/fixagent/workflow.py + worker.py + client.py: the Temporal workflow, its activities, the worker entrypoint, and the API's own Temporal client wrapper.
  • core/fixagent/store.py + core/persistence/models.py::VerifiedFixRun + migration 0012: persistence for one run, RLS-protected.
  • api/main.py: POST/GET /assets/{asset_id}/issues/{issue_id}/verified-fix[/approve|/reject].
  • docker-compose.yml: temporal, temporal-ui, fixagent-worker, all behind --profile fixagent.
  • web/components/VerifiedFixPanel.tsx + verified-fix-panel.css: the fix-review screen (plan §28.4), embedded in the existing issue detail page.
  • core/tokens.py: two new scopes, fixes:read/fixes:write, added only alongside the endpoints that actually check them (the file's own stated rule for adding a scope).

docs.title: Validated against real, live things — not mocks
docs.text:
• A real local Temporal server (temporal server start-dev): a hand-written hello-world workflow was run to prove basic connectivity, then specifically to prove worker-restart durability -- started a workflow, killed the worker process mid-run (before it received the human-approval signal), started a brand-new worker process with no shared memory, and it resumed and completed correctly purely from Temporal's own event history. This is the plan's own stated reason for choosing Temporal over Celery for this feature, and it was checked, not assumed.
  • VerifiedFixWorkflow.run() itself, against temporalio.testing.WorkflowEnvironment .start_time_skipping() (a real, disposable Temporal server whose clock fast-forwards through workflow timers): four scenarios run the actual workflow code end to end -- approve-opens-a-pr, reject-never-opens-a-pr, max-attempts-exhausted-never-asks-for-approval, and overall-timeout-stops-starting-new-attempts-and-reports-inconclusive. All four passed against the real engine (tests/unit/test_fixagent_workflow.py, ~42s total).
  • The context-gathering and tool layer: gather_context/read_file/search_code/ get_call_path were run against a real, on-disk two-function Python file with a real call relationship (handler calls get_user) -- core.codeintel.analyze() correctly found the enclosing function and its real caller. Path containment was checked against ../ escapes, bare absolute paths, and mixed traversal -- all correctly rejected.
  • The test-execution sandbox: a real python:3.12-slim container, a real pip install pytest over the network, a real passing test run, then a real failing one (with the actual pytest failure output captured and returned) -- both confirmed by hand before the mocked-subprocess unit tests were written around the already-proven mechanism.
  • The migration: 0012 was run up, down, and up again against a real bulwark/postgres:16-pgvector container, including confirming RLS actually isolates one org's verified_fix_runs row from another's (SET ROLE bulwark_app; SET app.current_org = ...).
  • docker compose config: the new temporal/temporal-ui/fixagent-worker services (plus every existing profile) resolve cleanly with no schema errors -- not started end-to-end (no real GitHub App or hosted LLM key configured in this environment to run a full live workflow through Temporal against real containers), but the compose file itself is proven valid, not just written.
  • The frontend: npm run build (a real Next.js production build, not just tsc --noEmit) compiled cleanly with the new route wiring; all 163 frontend tests pass (up from 155), including 8 new tests for VerifiedFixPanel that caught one real integration gap (an existing a11y test's fetch mock needed a branch for the new endpoint) before it could have shipped as a console error on a real issue page.

docs.title: A real bug caught while writing tests, not by inspection
docs.text: core.scan.scan() always recomputes Finding.fingerprint via correlate(), discarding whatever a caller set beforehand -- a first draft of test_fixagent_verify.py hand-assigned matching fingerprint strings to two fake Finding objects and got real, failing assertions back, because the correlator silently replaced both with freshly-computed (and, since the two fakes had subtly different shapes, different) values. Fixed by constructing both findings with identical path/snippet/CWE/rule-ids so they hash the same way a real rescan would. This is documented in ADR-0027 as a real, useful discipline the test uncovered, not a test-only workaround.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1216 backend tests passing (up from 1151: 65 new, across seven new test_fixagent_*.py files), 2 skipped (unrelated), 93.0% coverage; ruff/black/mypy all clean (mypy core api).
  • 163 frontend tests passing (up from 155: 8 new for VerifiedFixPanel), tsc --noEmit clean, a real next build production build clean.
  • The Temporal workflow's own live validation and the migration's live Postgres/RLS validation, both above.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• No end-to-end run against a real GitHub App installation. create_pull_request's five-call sequence was built from GitHub's documented REST v3 contract and is unit-tested against a fake, sequenced transport -- this environment has no real App credentials to exercise it against live. The request shapes are believed correct, not proven correct against the real API.
  • No end-to-end run through Temporal against a real hosted LLM key. The propose-patch tool- calling loop (core/fixagent/agent.py) is unit-tested against a fake Anthropic-shaped client covering the real control-flow paths (valid patch, invalid patch retried once, giving up, secret scrubbing on tool results) -- it has not been run against the real Anthropic API with a real key in this environment. Week 41's own AnthropicClient.complete() (the simpler, non-tool-calling path) has real-world usage from the base remediation feature; complete_with_tools is new and unproven against a live model.
  • The per-attempt-timeout scenario (a genuinely hung Temporal activity) was not validated with a live timing test. The other three ADR-0015 scenarios were; this one is covered by code review and Temporal's own documented ActivityError behavior, not a live run -- scripting a reliable, fast-running "activity hangs past its own timeout" test proved awkward in this environment.
  • No MLX/local tool-calling (ADR-0027's own cut, mirroring ADR-0026's Ollama-only decision): verified-fix does not work in Week 41's privacy mode.
  • No "Edit" action on a pending patch before approving it, unlike the plan's own three-button mockup ([Reject] [Edit] [Open pull request]) -- this ships two.
  • No precise minimal capability set for the test-execution sandbox -- it runs with Docker's default capabilities (not --cap-drop=ALL, unlike the scanner sandbox), disclosed as the honest floor for "hardened Docker, for now" rather than a guessed-at middle ground. ADR-0015/ADR-0027 both point at Firecracker (Phase 11, not yet built) as the real fix.
  • docker compose --profile fixagent up -d was not run end-to-end in this environment (no real GitHub App/LLM credentials to make a real run meaningful) -- docker compose config confirms the compose file itself is valid, not that a full stack boots and completes a real verified-fix run.

docs.title: Week 43 verification -- triage assistant and Hypotheses lane (plan §21.3/§21.4)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See docs/adr/0028-triage-assistant-and- hypotheses-lane.md for the design decisions, including the Hypotheses lane's deliberate scope narrowing (one flaw type, not three).

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/triage_assistant/: contract.py (a separate JSON contract from remediation's, on purpose -- see the ADR), prompt.py (nonce-fenced, shows the taint path + code), service.py (the propose-a-verdict call, one repair attempt, None on any failure -- never a guess).
  • core/hypotheses/: facts.py (100% deterministic candidate generation, no model), contract.py, prompt.py (shows structured facts + one route's code), service.py (assess_candidate + generate_for_checkout, the whole per-asset pass).
  • core/codeintel/models.py/python_lang.py/js_lang.py: Entrypoint.auth_markers, populated for Python decorators and Express middleware.
  • core/risk/score.py: an optional verdict parameter to score_finding/apply_risk, a bounded multiplier (0.6-1.15 depending on verdict and confidence), applied before the KEV floor.
  • core/pipeline.py: looks up stored verdicts by fingerprint before finalize(), so a verdict informs every later scan of the same asset.
  • core/persistence/models.py + migrations 0013/0014: IssueRow.assistant_verdict* columns, IssueRow.source column, the new hypotheses table (RLS via assets, same shape issues itself already has).
  • core/persistence/repo.py: verdict storage/lookup, and the Hypotheses lane's create/list/get/dismiss/promote functions -- promotion is a direct insert, never core.issues.sync (see the ADR for why).
  • api/main.py: POST/GET .../triage-assistant, POST .../hypotheses/generate, GET .../hypotheses, POST .../hypotheses/{id}/promote, POST .../hypotheses/{id}/dismiss.
  • web/components/TriageAssistantPanel.tsx + HypothesesLane.tsx (+ a new /app/projects/[id]/hypotheses route, linked from the project overview's crumb line).
  • Two new promptfoo suites, core/llm/prompts/triage/ and core/llm/prompts/hypotheses/, following the exact pattern core/llm/prompts/fix/ (Week 41) established.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
