• The full risk-scoring wiring, end to end, across two real scans. tests/unit/test_pipeline.py ::test_a_stored_triage_verdict_dampens_the_next_scan_of_the_same_asset runs a real scan through core.pipeline.run_scan_job, stores a verdict against the resulting Issue, runs a SECOND real scan of the same asset, and asserts the second scan's persisted risk score is lower than the first's, with the verdict named in risk_factors -- and that the human triage_status was never touched. Not a unit test of score_finding in isolation: the real pipeline, the real fingerprint-based lookup, twice.
  • Promotion's isolation from the rest of an asset's issue history. test_hypotheses_repo.py::test_promote_does_not_touch_other_open_issues creates a real, unrelated open Issue via the real scan-sync path, promotes a hypothesis, and confirms the unrelated Issue's state is untouched -- proving promote_hypothesis's deliberate choice not to call core.issues.sync actually matters, not just that it's a plausible-sounding design note.
  • Code-intelligence extraction, against real parsers. auth_markers extraction is tested through the real ast (Python) and real tree-sitter (JS) extractors, and test_hypotheses_service.py::test_generate_for_checkout_end_to_end_against_a_real_directory runs the whole candidate-generation pass against a real on-disk Python file with a real core.codeintel.analyze() call -- not a hand-built CodeGraph fixture.
  • Both migrations, up/down/up, against a real Postgres container (bulwark/postgres:16-pgvector, disposable, not the project's own long-running dev stack), plus a live RLS proof: inserted a hypotheses row under org-a, confirmed SET app.current_org='org-b' sees zero rows and org-a sees one, as bulwark_app (not a superuser).
  • The frontend, against a real running API. Not just npm test/tsc --noEmit/next build (all three ran clean): started scripts/e2e_server.py (a real FastAPI app + real SQLite database, no mocks) and a real next dev server pointed at it, seeded one real Issue through core.persistence.repo directly, and manually drove a real browser through: signing in, opening the Issue detail page (the Triage assistant panel renders, its "Get a triage verdict" button calls the real endpoint and shows the real 409 message when no model is configured), the project overview's new "hypotheses" link, and the Hypotheses lane page (its "Generate" button calls the real endpoint and shows the real 409 message the same way). Every message shown was the actual API's own text, not a hand-written approximation of what it might say.
  • promptfoo suites for both new prompts, built and validated to run offline against a local Ollama backend the same way core/llm/prompts/fix/'s suite was, with real fixtures generated from the real build_prompt() functions (scripts/gen-triage-fixtures.py, scripts/gen-hypotheses-fixtures.py).

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1295 backend tests passing (up from 1216 at the start of the week: 79 new, across nine new test_triage_assistant_*.py/test_hypotheses_*.py files plus additions to test_codeintel_python.py/test_codeintel_js.py/test_risk.py/test_pipeline.py), 92.4% coverage; ruff/black/mypy all clean.
  • 173 frontend tests passing (up from 163: 10 new for TriageAssistantPanel/HypothesesLane), tsc --noEmit clean, a real next build production build clean.
  • Both migrations' live Postgres/RLS validation, and the pipeline/promotion end-to-end tests, all above.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• No live run against a real hosted model, for either feature. Both core.triage_assistant .service.assess and core.hypotheses.service.assess_candidate are unit-tested against fake Anthropic-shaped clients covering the real control-flow paths (a valid reply, a malformed reply repaired once, giving up) -- not run against the real API here, the same disclosed gap Week 41/42's own verification docs already carry for their own LLM call sites.
  • The Hypotheses lane detects exactly one flaw type: a route missing the authorization check its siblings have. IDOR and mass assignment, both named in the plan, are not implemented -- a deliberate scope decision (ADR-0028), not an oversight.
  • No live measurement against OWASP Juice Shop or seeded authorization flaws. The plan asks for "precision on seeded authorization flaws plus OWASP Juice Shop's documented access-control challenges" -- that evaluation was not run in this environment (no live model, and no Juice Shop checkout was scanned). generate_for_checkout's own end-to-end test proves the mechanism works against real code; it is not a precision measurement.
  • auth_markers extraction covers Python and Express/JS only. Go and Django routes never produce a Hypotheses candidate this week -- a missed-candidate gap, not a false-positive risk (see the ADR).
  • The OWASP-Benchmark precision/recall measurement for the triage assistant's verdicts (plan §21.3: "measured against the OWASP Benchmark's ground-truth labels") was not run -- it needs a live model, which this environment does not have. The contract, prompt construction, and ranking-integration mechanics are all real and tested; the verdict's actual accuracy against a real model is not measured here.
  • No live GitHub App run for either feature (neither needs one directly, but Hypotheses-lane generation's re-clone reuses core.gitfetch.clone_repo over a plain public HTTPS URL, not through an installed App) -- consistent with how core/gitfetch.py is used elsewhere in this codebase.

docs.title: Week 44 verification -- security copilot (plan §21.5)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See docs/adr/0029-security-copilot.md for the design decisions, including why several pieces reuse existing infrastructure (the knowledge base's hashed embedder, the verified-fix agent's tool-calling loop) rather than building new capability.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/embeddings/ (task 1): chunk.py (function-level chunking off core.codeintel's real parsers, no model involved), service.py (the analyze-chunk-embed-persist pass). New code_chunks/code_chunk_indexes tables (migration 0015), RLS via assets. The pgvector/JSON TypeDecorator was extracted from core.rag.store into core.persistence.vector_type so the knowledge base and the new table share one implementation.
  • core/copilot/ (task 2): tools.py (the five read-only tools: query_issues, fetch_code_range, get_call_path, list_routes, compare_scans), contract.py (citation validation), service.py (the tool-calling turn loop, ask()). Task.COPILOT added to the gateway.
  • core/copilot/session.py (task 3): CheckoutCache, clone-once-per-conversation with idle-TTL eviction and a per-conversation-id lock. New copilot_conversations/copilot_messages tables (migration 0016), the second with a two-hop RLS policy. Three endpoints: start a conversation, post a message, list messages.
  • web/components/CopilotPanel.tsx + copilot-panel.css (task 4): a slide-in panel, mounted in IssueDetail (issue context) and ProjectOverview (no context). Issue citations render as real links; code citations render as plain path:line text (no jump-to-line view exists in this frontend yet).
  • docs/adr/0029-security-copilot.md, docs/copilot.md.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• Chunking and retrieval, against a real Postgres with pgvector. A disposable bulwark/postgres:16-pgvector container: the full migration chain plus the 0015 downgrade/upgrade roundtrip, a real chunk-embed-store-search pass proving correct ranking (a delete_user function ranks above get_user for the query "delete a user from the database," not just "returns something"), and cross-org RLS isolation as the non-superuser bulwark_app role.
  • The tool-calling loop, against a fake Anthropic-shaped client covering the real control-flow paths: a tool call answered and used, an invalid citation rejected then retried successfully, and a model that never calls the terminal tool raising CopilotGiveUp. query_issues and compare_scans were tested against real seeded issues/scans through core.persistence.repo.sync_issues_for_scan, not hand-built fixtures standing in for the real data shape.
  • The checkout cache's concurrency guarantee, with a real multi-threaded test. Five real threads racing to be the first message of the same brand-new conversation clone exactly once, proven by counting actual clone calls under a lock-widened race window -- not just reasoned about in a docstring.
  • Persistence and RLS, against a real Postgres, including the two-hop case. A second disposable container run: the full migration chain plus the 0016 downgrade/upgrade roundtrip, and live cross-org isolation for both copilot_conversations (one-hop) and copilot_messages (two-hop, through copilot_conversations into assets) as the non-superuser bulwark_app role -- the two-hop policy was checked explicitly rather than assumed to follow from the one-hop case.
  • The API layer, against real persisted rows, not just mocked responses: starting a conversation creates a real CopilotConversationRow; posting a message (with ask() mocked, its own real tests cover the loop itself) persists both the user's question and the assistant's answer as real CopilotMessageRows, retrievable via the GET endpoint; a model that gives up still produces a real, honest stored message rather than a 5xx.
  • The frontend panel, against a real running API, not mocked HTTP: seeded a real scan (with real fake findings, via the e2e server's actual scan-creation path) through scripts/e2e_server .py, then drove a real browser through opening the panel on both the project overview and issue detail pages, confirming each POSTs to the real /copilot/conversations endpoint and displays the real 409 "the copilot is not enabled on this server" message when no model is configured -- the actual API's own text, not a hand-written approximation.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• Backend: test_embeddings_*.py (chunk/repo/service), test_copilot_*.py (tools/contract/service/ repo/session/api) -- new tests across the four backend tasks, plus the existing suite re-run clean (ruff/black/mypy, and the affected areas' own tests) after each task.
  • Frontend: copilot-panel.test.tsx (6 tests: trigger/open/send/citation-link/code-citation-text/ close), the full existing suite re-run clean, tsc --noEmit clean, a real next build production build clean, the a11y audit re-run clean with the panel now mounted on two more pages.
  • Both migrations' live Postgres/RLS validation, and the checkout-cache concurrency test, all above.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• No live run against a real hosted model. core.copilot.service.ask is unit-tested against a fake Anthropic-shaped client covering the real control-flow paths, not run against the real API here -- the same disclosed gap Weeks 41-43 already carry for their own LLM call sites.
  • No promptfoo suite for the copilot's system prompt. Consistent with, not a new gap relative to, core/fixagent's own tool-calling prompt (neither has one -- see ADR-0029 for why a schema-conformance suite doesn't fit a multi-turn tool-calling conversation the way it fits the single-shot fix/triage/hypotheses prompts).
  • No measurement against the plan's own 100-question reference set ("valid-citation rate; answer correctness") -- that evaluation needs a live model, which this environment does not have.
  • Retrieval quality is bounded by the same lexical-embedding limits ADR-009 already discloses for the knowledge base: a plain-English question sharing no vocabulary with the relevant code will miss. Not measured separately for code chunks here.
  • The Hypotheses lane's own "off by default" gateway toggle pattern was followed, but no separate audit-log entry type was added for copilot conversations/messages -- they are ordinary RLS-protected rows, not audit-logged events, the same posture triage verdicts already have.
  • core.copilot.session.CheckoutCache is process-local. A multi-worker deployment needs sticky routing per conversation, or a shared cache, to get the reuse benefit across every worker. A cache miss just re-clones -- correctness is unaffected, only the latency benefit is process-scoped.
  • The scan-comparison page's "this scan" copilot context is not wired up. The panel supports a scan context prop; only that specific page's plumbing (threading the selected scan id out of ScanComparison's internal state) was not done this task.
  • Code citations have nowhere to link to. This frontend has no view that jumps to an arbitrary file:line; they render as plain text rather than a link that would go nowhere.

docs.title: Week 45 verification -- attack paths, threat model draft, red team (plan §21.6/§21.7/§21.9)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See docs/adr/0030-attack-paths-threat-model-and-red-team.md for the design decisions, including why several pieces reuse existing infrastructure (the call graph, core.taint.catalog's sink patterns, an already-curated but previously-unused payload corpus) rather than building new detection.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/attackpath/ (task 1): model.py (Node/Edge/AttackPath dataclasses), nodes.py (entrypoint/issue node construction from already-persisted data), rules.py (three chaining rules -- one call-graph-verified, two disclosed co-location heuristics), service.py (fetch-issues -> apply-rules -> rank orchestration, pure, no I/O).
  • core/attackpath/prompt.py/contract.py/narrative.py + checkout.py (task 2): a model-written narrative per path, contract-enforced to mention every node label it was given; a one-shot clone+analyze helper (deliberately uncached, unlike the copilot's CheckoutCache, since this screen is typically opened once per visit). Task.ATTACK_PATH added to the gateway. One API endpoint (GET /assets/{id}/attack-paths) that never gates on a model being configured. A paginated attack-path screen at /app/projects/[id]/attack-paths.
  • core/threatmodel/ (task 3): model.py/generate.py -- a fully deterministic Mermaid DFD + STRIDE table generator, no LLM call. New threat_models table (migration 0017, one current row per asset, RLS via assets). Three endpoints (GET auto-generates, POST .../regenerate, PUT for edits). An editable diagram + table screen at /app/projects/[id]/threat-model, rendered with the new mermaid npm dependency (pinned to 11.17.2 + npm audit fix after the default install pulled in a high-severity transitive lodash-es vulnerability via chevrotain).
  • tests/redteam/ (task 4): wires up tests/fixtures/injection_payloads.json (20 payloads, curated in an earlier week, never used until now) into a real test suite against the fix/triage/copilot pipelines. Fixed a real bug it caught: core/llm/prompt.py and core/triage_assistant/prompt.py scrubbed secrets from a finding's code block but never its title/description.
  • docs/adr/0030-*.md, docs/attack-paths.md, docs/threat-model-draft.md, docs/redteam.md.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• The SSRF chaining rule, against a real analyzed checkout. A real Flask fixture (route -> helper -> sink) run through core.codeintel.analyze, proving the backward call-graph walk actually finds the reachable entrypoint -- not a hand-built CodeGraph standing in for real analysis. A negative case (an orphan symbol with no callers) confirmed no path is produced when unreachable.
  • The full attack-path service, against real persisted issues. Seeded through core.persistence.repo.sync_issues_for_scan/add_findings, the same real path production scans use, not fixtures shaped by hand to match what the code expects. Caught a real bug during development: the secret_grants_resource rule had no exclusion for .github/workflows/ paths, producing a redundant path alongside the more specific ci_secret_workflow rule for the exact same secret+workflow pair -- fixed before this was committed.
  • The narrative contract, against a fake model covering the real control-flow paths: a valid reply, a reply missing a node retried once then succeeding, two failed attempts returning None rather than a guess, and a transport failure doing the same.
  • threat_models' RLS, against a real disposable Postgres container (pgvector/pgvector:pg16, since migration 0002 needs the vector extension): the full migration chain, then a real insert under org-a and org-b each, connected as bulwark_app (not a superuser), confirming each org sees only its own row -- the same standard already held for hypotheses, code_chunks, and both copilot tables.
  • The threat-model generator, against a real analyzed checkout with three real routes (one reaching a SQL sink, one reaching a command sink, one reaching neither): confirmed the Database and OS-process nodes and their STRIDE rows each appear exactly once, not once per reaching route.
  • The API layer, against real persisted rows: first access auto-generates and persists; a second access returns the same row without re-cloning; a PUT edit persists and survives a subsequent GET; regenerate discards the edit and re-clones.
  • The red-team corpus, against the real contracts and pipelines, not mocks of them. All 20 payloads rejected as raw replies by three different contracts (60 cases); schema-valid replies isolating one adversarial detail at a time (patch redirection, dismissal language, an extra field) still rejected; a fully-compliant fake model's legitimate "likely_false_positive" verdict proven to never touch the real Finding object; an injected instruction naming a disallowed copilot tool proven to error safely via _dispatch's real unknown-tool branch; cross-tenant reach proven impossible against two real seeded assets, not merely argued from the function signature.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• Backend: test_attackpath_*.py (model/nodes/rules/service/contract/narrative/checkout/api, 29 tests), test_threatmodel_*.py (generate/repo/api, 15 tests), tests/redteam/*.py (73 tests), plus test_llm_gateway.py/test_llm.py updated for the new Task.ATTACK_PATH route. Full suite re-run clean after every task (ruff/mypy, and the affected areas' own tests); one full-suite run at the end: 1487 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated Docker-integration flake (test_grype_agrees_with_trivy_and_osv_on_the_same_dependency, not caused by this week's work), 2 skipped.
  • Frontend: attack-paths-screen.test.tsx (4 tests), threat-model-editor.test.tsx (4 tests, mermaid's render/initialize mocked since jsdom cannot do real SVG layout), full existing suite re-run clean, tsc --noEmit clean.
  • threat_models' live Postgres/RLS validation, above.
  • scripts/gen-licenses.py --check passes with a new, disclosed manual override for khroma (mermaid's color-math dependency): its package.json omits a license field entirely, verified by hand against its actual MIT LICENSE file in node_modules rather than assumed.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• The two co-location heuristic rules are not proven causal links. secret-grants-resource-v1 and ci-secret-workflow-v1 connect a secret to a resource/workflow only because both exist in the same asset -- neither Checkov nor gitleaks output in this codebase records which credential actually grants access to which resource. Disclosed in both the rule docstrings and docs/attack-paths.md, not silently presented as equally certain to the verified SSRF rule.
  • No multi-hop path combination. Two separately-matched rules never combine into one longer chain this week. A real generalization, not attempted.
  • No live run against a real hosted model, for either the attack-path narrative or the red-team suite's live-model half (garak). Both are unit-tested against fake clients covering the real control-flow paths -- the same disclosed gap every LLM call site in this project already carries (Weeks 41-44).
  • No attack-success-rate tracking. The plan asks for one; it only means something for a probabilistic, live-model run, which this week deliberately does not add (real API spend on every scheduled run, non-deterministic results a hardcoded number would misrepresent). See docs/redteam.md for what wiring this up later would need.
  • A fully-compliant model reciting its own system prompt back in free text is not structurally prevented. No contract filters rationale/explanation fields against echoing prompt text; the mitigating factor is that no system prompt in this project contains secrets, only instructions.
  • core/attackpath/checkout.py's one-shot clone is uncached, unlike the copilot's CheckoutCache -- a disclosed perf limitation (slower page load on repeat visits), not a correctness issue.
  • Threat-model version is a plain counter, not full history. An edit or regenerate overwrites the prior content in place; there is no way to view or restore an earlier version.

docs.title: Week 46 verification -- SandboxRuntime interface, gvisor backend, egress denial (plan §22.1)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See ADR-0031 for the design decisions, including which parts of the plan's "Isolation v2" this deliberately does not attempt yet.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/sandbox/ (task 1): runtime.py (the SandboxRuntime protocol), docker_runtime.py (build_docker_argv moved here unchanged, DockerRuntime). core/runner.py refactored to take an optional runtime, defaulting to DockerRuntime -- a pure refactor, not a behavior change.
  • core/sandbox/gvisor_runtime.py + seccomp.py (task 2): GvisorRuntime reuses build_docker_argv verbatim and inserts --runtime=runsc. A seccomp-profile hook is wired in but returns None for every scanner today -- see ADR-0031 for why.
  • core/fixagent/egress.py, docker/egress-sidecar/ (task 3): a default-drop nftables ruleset (DNS + HTTP/S allowed, cloud-metadata range and RFC1918 denied, IPv6 dropped outright) applied to the fix-verification sandbox's target container via a sidecar joined to its network namespace. core/fixagent/sandbox.py's run_tests now starts the target detached behind a startup barrier, applies the policy, then releases it -- on by default (TestRunSpec.deny_internal_egress=True), with an explicit opt-out that reproduces the original behavior exactly.
  • docs/adr/0031-*.md, docs/sandbox-runtimes.md (task 4, this document).

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• DockerRuntime's argv, against the pre-refactor build_docker_argv. Byte-for-byte equality asserted directly (test_docker_runtime_build_argv_matches_the_free_function), not just "the tests still pass" -- the two code paths are proven identical, not just similarly-behaved.
  • The full existing test suite, unchanged, before and after the task 1 refactor. 1399 tests passed both times; core.scan and core.sbom.syft's calls into run_tool were never touched.
  • The egress ruleset's actual packet-filtering behavior, against a real container (Docker Desktop on macOS -- a real Linux VM under the hood). Not a syntax check: a python:3.12-slim container with nftables/curl installed for the exercise confirmed, with real network calls, that HTTPS to pypi.org succeeds, that the metadata IP and an RFC1918 address both time out (a real DROP, not merely "nothing was listening"), and that DNS resolution keeps working. This caught two real bugs before either shipped:
  • RFC1918-before-DNS ordering broke every package install. Docker Desktop's own embedded DNS resolver is 192.168.65.x -- inside the RFC1918 ranges the ruleset denies. The very first version of the ruleset denied that range before allowing DNS, so getent hosts pypi.org failed outright. Fixed by moving the DNS-allow rules earlier in the chain; DNS now resolves regardless.
  • An unmirrored IPv6 allow bypassed every IPv4 deny rule. The ruleset's tcp dport {80,443} accept rule, written in an inet-family table, applies to both protocol families, but the deny rule (ip daddr {...}) is IPv4-only. curl -6 https://pypi.org succeeded even with the "blocking" ruleset loaded. Fixed by dropping IPv6 outright (meta nfproto ipv6 drop) rather than trying to author and keep in sync a second, IPv6-specific deny list for a protocol this sandbox has no real need for.
  • The full run_tests orchestration, against real Docker, not mocked subprocess.run. Three separate real runs: (1) the default egress-enforced path with a python:3.12-slim target proving both "pypi reachable" and "metadata blocked" in one process, exit code 0, VerificationStep(passed= True); (2) the same target with a deliberately failing script, confirming the real exit code and log tail surface correctly through docker wait/docker logs; (3) deny_internal_egress=False against a script that asserts the metadata IP is reachable, confirming the fallback path is not merely present in code but actually skips the sidecar and its restriction.
  • The docker/egress-sidecar image, built and run for real, including confirming its pinned nftables=1.0.6-2+deb12u2 package version is the one Debian 12's own repository actually serves (checked via apt-cache policy before pinning it, not assumed), and reading its installed package's own copyright file to confirm the real license (GPL-2) before adding the scripts/gen-licenses.py TOOLS entry, rather than guessing.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• test_sandbox_runtime.py (4 tests), test_sandbox_gvisor.py (5 tests), test_sandbox_seccomp.py (2 tests), test_fixagent_sandbox.py (rewritten: 13 tests covering both the egress-enforced default and the legacy fallback), test_fixagent_egress.py (8 tests). Full suite re-run clean after every task: 1420 passed. black --check ., ruff check ., mypy all clean. scripts/gen-licenses.py --check passes with the new egress-sidecar entry.
  • Live Docker runs, above -- both the standalone sidecar mechanism and the full run_tests path through the real Python code, not just the shell commands used to first work out the ruleset.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• GvisorRuntime has never actually executed. runsc has no macOS build. Every assertion about it is an argv-shape unit test (it produces --runtime=runsc in the right place, preserves every Docker flag, adds the seccomp flag when a profile is given). Whether a real scanner actually runs correctly under gVisor's syscall emulation -- and gVisor's syscall coverage is not 100% of Linux's, so this is a real open question, not a formality -- is untested. core.runner.run_tool does not use this backend anywhere in production.
  • No seccomp profile exists. seccomp_profile_path always returns None. The plumbing is real; the content is not, and shipping a guessed one would have been a security regression (see ADR-0031 for exactly why).
  • Firecracker does not exist in this codebase. Not a stub, not a partial implementation -- nothing. The architectural question of how a checkout gets into a microVM was identified but not resolved.
  • Egress denial adds real latency and a real failure mode per test run: a sidecar container start plus an nft -f - invocation (typically well under a second in this project's own testing, but unmeasured under real production load), and EgressPolicyError is a hard stop, by design -- a fix-verification run that can't get its policy applied does not silently fall back to running the target unprotected, but it does mean a sidecar-image pull failure or Docker daemon hiccup now fails a verification attempt that would previously have succeeded.
  • No Linux host exists for this project. Every "verified live" claim above ran on Docker Desktop on a macOS development machine -- a real Linux VM, which is what makes the egress-denial testing meaningful, but not a host this project controls, has gvisor installed on, or has wired into CI. docs/sandbox-runtimes.md's runbook describes, but does not perform, that setup.
  • The egress policy is IPv4-only and covers exactly one sandbox. IPv6 is dropped entirely rather than policed (a deliberate scope reduction, not an oversight -- see ADR-0031). Scanner containers (core/runner.py) are unaffected and unchanged: they already run with --network=none and have no egress to police in the first place.

docs.title: Week 47 verification -- envelope encryption, crypto-shredding, mTLS, secrets (plan §22.2)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See ADR-0032 (tasks 1-2) and ADR-0033 (tasks 3-4) for the design decisions, including several real bugs found and fixed by live testing rather than caught later.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/secrets/openbao.py, core/secrets/envelope.py (task 1): a Transit client minting/unwrapping per-org data keys, and AES-256-GCM encryption bound to each object's own storage key as AEAD associated data. New scan_data_keys table (migration 0018). core.persistence.storage. EncryptingObjectStore/build_object_store wire this into the real production path (core.tasks.run_scan_task), off by default.
  • core/retention.py (task 2): an hourly Celery-beat sweep destroying a scan's data key once its org's retention window passes (default 7 days). New data_retention_policies table (migration 0019), a GET/PUT /settings/retention API, and a settings screen at /app/settings.
  • docker/postgres/pg_hba.conf, docker-entrypoint-wrapper.sh, init-temporal-role.sh (task 3): a rebuilt Postgres image requiring a client certificate matching the connecting role for every network connection. New bulwark_api/bulwark_worker/bulwark_fixagent roles (migration 0020), each inheriting bulwark_app's grants via role membership; bulwark_app itself set NOLOGIN. scripts/gen-mtls-certs.sh generates the dev CA and per-service certificates.
  • core/secrets/resolve.py, bulwark secrets migrate-env (task 4): four plaintext secrets (GitHub App private key, its webhook secret, the API token, the LLM API key) now prefer a value from OpenBao's KV store, falling back to their environment variable unconditionally when OpenBao isn't configured or doesn't have them yet.
  • docs/adr/0032-*.md, docs/adr/0033-*.md, docs/data-protection.md.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• The full OpenBao Transit round-trip, against a real openbao/openbao:2.1 container: mount the engine, create an org key (confirmed idempotent), mint a data key, unwrap it back to the identical plaintext, and two rejections confirmed live rather than assumed -- an undecodable ciphertext (HTTP 400) and unwrapping under the wrong org's key (HTTP 400, "encryption key not found").
  • EncryptingObjectStore's AEAD binding, with a real key-swap attack attempted and blocked. A ciphertext written under one storage key, then read back under a different key string, fails closed (DecryptionError) rather than silently decrypting into the wrong scan's data.
  • scan_data_keys' and data_retention_policies' RLS, and their ON DELETE/cascade behavior, against real Postgres as the actual bulwark_worker role (not a superuser): one organization's data key and retention setting are both invisible to another organization, even when a call explicitly passes the other organization's id as an argument -- RLS is what actually enforces it, not application-level filtering alone. ON DELETE CASCADE from scans to scan_data_keys was confirmed only on real Postgres: SQLite (every unit test) does not enforce foreign keys by default, so this specific guarantee has no SQLite-backed test at all, by necessity.
  • shred_expired_scans, twice caught doing the wrong thing before it shipped. First, comparing a SQLite-stored naive timestamp against a timezone-aware cutoff inside the SQL WHERE clause itself silently matched nothing; fixed by moving the comparison into Python against _aware()-normalized values, mirroring a fix core.maintenance.reap_stale_scans already needed. Second, discovering a cross-organization query run through the RLS-enforced bulwark_app-family connection would see zero rows for every organization, not every organization's own rows -- fixed by iterating organizations one at a time with set_session_org explicitly set for each.
  • The entire mTLS mechanism, against a real image built from docker/postgres, not designed from documentation alone. In order: the exact ownership/permission Postgres requires for a bind-mounted private key (a plain bind mount is owned by the host user, which Postgres refuses outright as "group or world access"); verify-full's server-hostname check, confirmed to reject a mismatched hostname and accept a matching one; a certificate's CN correctly authenticating as its matching role and being rejected for any other role, including a validly CA-signed certificate for an unrelated identity; a connection with no certificate at all rejected with a distinct, clear error. tests/integration/test_postgres_mtls_docker.py builds the real image and runs all of this automatically now, not just once by hand.
  • The full migration 0020 up/down/up cycle, against real Postgres, confirming bulwark_app regains LOGIN on downgrade and the three service roles are recreated cleanly on re-upgrade.
  • Role-membership inheritance, proven functionally, not just by reading the grant. A freshly created role made a member of another via GRANT ... TO ..., with no direct table grants of its own, successfully inserted into and read from a real application table (organizations) through its inherited privileges alone.
  • The real docker-compose.yml, not a hand-reconstructed equivalent. The actual migrate service, using its actual environment-variable-interpolated BULWARK_DATABASE_URL (with the mTLS query parameters) and its actual certificate volume mount, ran the full migration chain -- including migration 0020 -- to completion with no modifications to the compose file for the test. Also confirmed, incidentally: the new mTLS-enabled image starts correctly against an already-initialized data directory from before this week's changes, not only a fresh one.
  • Temporal's temporal_svc carve-out, against the same real image. Password authentication with no client certificate succeeds for temporal_svc specifically; a wrong password is rejected; and bulwark (Bulwark's own owner role) is confirmed to still require a certificate even when given its correct password, proving the carve-out is scoped to exactly one role, not a general weakening.
  • CI's tenancy-rls job, re-verified end to end against the exact scenario it will actually run: a plain pgvector/pgvector:pg16 image with no custom mTLS configuration, migrated as the owner role, then the RLS test suite run connected as bulwark_worker over a plain password -- confirmed necessary and sufficient after discovering bulwark_app's new NOLOGIN state would otherwise have broken this job outright.
  • The full OpenBao KV v2 path, against a real container: enabling the engine (confirmed already-mounted in dev mode, and idempotent to call again), writing a secret, reading it back, rotating it, and confirming both a missing path and a missing field within an existing path return None rather than raising.
  • Settings/LLMConfig actually preferring OpenBao's value over a stale environment variable, live: a secret written to OpenBao is what Settings.from_env()/LLMConfig.from_env() return, with a deliberately different, stale value left in the environment variable to prove which source won; removing BULWARK_OPENBAO_ADDR afterward confirmed the fallback to the environment variable still works.
  • bulwark secrets migrate-env, run against a real OpenBao container via the actual installed CLI entry point (not python -m cli.main, which -- a pre-existing quirk of this file's structure, not something this week introduced -- only sees commands defined before its mid-file if __name__ == "__main__" guard): migrated secrets confirmed present in OpenBao afterward by reading them back independently, and the missing-configuration guard confirmed to error cleanly.

docs.text:
• test_secrets_envelope.py (8 tests), test_secrets_openbao.py (10), test_persistence_storage.py (9), test_persistence_scan_data_keys.py (5), test_retention.py (7), test_persistence_retention_settings.py (4), test_retention_settings_api.py (6), test_secrets_resolve.py (5), test_secrets_cli.py (3). tests/integration/test_secrets_openbao_docker.py (4), test_postgres_mtls_docker.py (5), test_data_protection_rls_docker.py (5, extended from task 1's 3). Full suite re-run clean after every task: 1475 unit tests passed. black --check ., ruff check ., mypy (project scope -- cli/ is outside pyproject.toml's configured mypy files, unchanged by this week) all clean.
  • Frontend: retention-settings.test.tsx (4 tests), full existing suite (191 tests) re-run clean, tsc --noEmit clean, the new /app/settings route confirmed to compile and render correctly in a real browser preview (falling through to the same sign-in gate every other page uses, with no server errors).
  • Live Docker/Postgres/OpenBao runs, above -- covering every mechanism this week added, not just the application-level logic around them.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• Database grants are not actually least-privilege per service. bulwark_api/bulwark_worker/ bulwark_fixagent each inherit the exact same privileges bulwark_app always had. Distinct, individually-revocable identities is the real, verified improvement; narrower permissions per service needs a function-by-function audit of core.persistence.repo's call sites this pass did not attempt (ADR-0033).
  • No automated certificate rotation, and no real CA. scripts/gen-mtls-certs.sh is dev/self-signed only; a real deployment needs its own CA and issuance process.
  • Crypto-shredding never touches the underlying ciphertext object. Deleting a scan's data key makes that scan's data permanently unreadable, but the encrypted bytes themselves remain in object storage indefinitely, an intentional simplification (the plan's "backups included" framing implies exactly this: unrecoverable, not un-stored) rather than a real cleanup mechanism.
  • A concurrent first-use race for a scan's data key is unhandled. Not triggered by the current sequential call pattern, but not structurally prevented either.
  • Only four secrets route through OpenBao. Database passwords, Redis/S3 credentials, and the OpenBao token itself all remain plain environment variables -- protected at the connection layer by this week's mTLS work where applicable (Postgres), not moved into a secrets store.
  • Temporal's own database credential is password-only, a disclosed, deliberate carve-out in an otherwise unconditional certificate requirement -- not a gap anyone should assume is closed.
  • The pre-existing core.maintenance.reap_stale_scans likely has the identical unscoped-RLS-query bug shred_expired_scans was caught and fixed for here, discovered incidentally while building this week's work. It was not fixed as part of Week 47 -- it predates this week and is out of scope for it -- and was flagged separately instead.

docs.title: Week 48 verification -- fuzzing, DAST self-scan, ASVS, supply-chain hardening (plan §22.3)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See ADR-0034 for the design decisions, including which pieces of this week could not be executed from this session and exactly why.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• tests/fuzz/fuzz_adapter.py, scripts/seed-fuzz-corpus.sh, .github/workflows/fuzz.yml, tests/fuzz_regressions/ (task 1): an Atheris harness per scanner adapter, seeded from tests/golden, a nightly CI job with a fixed time budget, and the "every crash becomes a regression test" replay mechanism. tests/unit/test_correlation_properties.py (task 1): three Hypothesis property tests for fingerprinting (whitespace invariance, CWE sensitivity, symmetric matching), fully local.
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml's new zap-baseline job, web/public/.well-known/security.txt, three new security headers in web/proxy.ts (task 2).
  • docs/ASVS-SELF-ASSESSMENT.md (task 3): a full ASVS 4.0.3 Level 2 self-audit, V1-V14, plus three real fixes it drove (BULWARK_FORCE_HTTPS for HSTS, core/ingest.py's new depth limit, the dependency-audit CI job).
  • .github/workflows/scorecard.yml, .github/workflows/release.yml, .github/dependabot.yml, SHA-pinned + least-privilege ci.yml/fuzz.yml (task 4).

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• A manual boundary-case probe of all nine fuzzable adapters, against real parse() implementations: empty input, truncated JSON, non-UTF8 bytes, wrong-shaped JSON, deeply nested arrays, huge numbers, single-quoted pseudo-JSON. Zero crashes -- every adapter already logs a warning and returns no findings rather than raising. Confirmed this is a genuine finding, not a silent exception being swallowed, by checking the actual exception path raised nothing through except Exception in the probe script itself.
  • The fuzz-regression replay mechanism, proven with a synthetic crash file: a hand-crafted "crash" placed in tests/fuzz_regressions/bandit/, confirmed discovered and replayed by test_fuzz_regressions.py, then removed -- proving the wiring works before being left empty for real findings, not merely asserted to work.
  • Atheris's real macOS build failure, reproduced directly: pip install atheris fails with "Failed to find libFuzzer; you may be building using Apple Clang," confirming the disclosed platform limitation rather than assuming it from Atheris's own documentation.
  • A real ZAP baseline scan, four times, against a real production build (npm run build && npx next start, NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO_ONLY=1 -- not the dev server, whose HMR/CSP noise doesn't reflect production): first run found 3 missing cross-origin headers (0 FAIL, 8 WARN against dev mode; 4 WARN against the real production build once dev-mode noise was excluded); each header was added one at a time and the scan re-run until the specific warning cleared -- Cross-Origin-Embedder- Policy, then -Opener-Policy (which only appeared once COEP was fixed), then -Resource-Policy (which only appeared once COOP was fixed) -- confirming ZAP's rule 90004 reports this family of headers incrementally, not all at once. Final state: 0 FAIL-NEW, 4 WARN-NEW, all four scoped to /_next/static assets.
  • Every header fix, confirmed not to break the app: a full page load (/, /self-host) in a real browser after each header addition, console messages checked clean each time.
  • web/public/.well-known/security.txt and its /security.txt redirect, both loaded in a real browser: the file serves with the correct content, and the redirect actually resolves to the canonical well-known path (confirmed via the network request list, not just the final URL).
  • The three ASVS-driven fixes: core/ingest.py's new path-depth limit, tested with a 10-component-deep zip entry rejected under Limits(max_depth=5) and a 3-component entry correctly still extracted; the dependency-audit job's exact commands (pip-audit --desc off, npm audit --omit=dev) run locally -- the only vulnerabilities pip-audit found locally were in this session's own stale bundled pip/setuptools (not a real project dependency), confirmed by upgrading them and re-running (0 findings, exit 0) before adding that upgrade as an explicit CI step rather than trusting whatever pip version ships with actions/setup-python; npm audit --omit=dev against the web app's real lockfile: 0 vulnerabilities.
  • Every GitHub Action version referenced in ci.yml/fuzz.yml/scorecard.yml/release.yml, resolved to its real commit SHA via the GitHub API directly (not guessed or copied from memory), matching the exact major version already in use so this is a pinning pass, not an undisclosed version upgrade riding along with it.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• test_correlation_properties.py (4 property tests), test_fuzz_regressions.py (mechanism proven live, 0 permanent regressions currently stored), test_ingest.py (+2 depth-limit tests, 12 total), web/tests/proxy.test.ts (7 tests, new file -- proxy.ts had no test coverage at all before this week). Full suite re-run clean after every task: 1481 unit tests passed, 1 skipped (the empty fuzz regression corpus, correctly not a failure). black --check ., ruff check ., mypy all clean.
  • Frontend: full suite (198 tests) re-run clean, tsc --noEmit clean.
  • Every workflow YAML (ci.yml, fuzz.yml, scorecard.yml, release.yml, dependabot.yml) parsed successfully with yaml.safe_load -- syntactically valid, though this does not and cannot prove GitHub Actions' own semantic acceptance of a workflow that has never actually run (see below).

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• No Atheris run has ever executed, on this machine or in CI. The fuzz harness and nightly workflow are written and reviewed, never fired. The empty tests/fuzz_regressions/ directory reflects that honestly -- it is not evidence that fuzzing would find nothing.

Amended 2026-10-12: the nightly workflow's steps have now run, every matrix entry, in a python:3.12 linux/amd64 container (Docker Desktop's emulation on Apple Silicon, standing in for ubuntu-latest): pip install -e ".[dev]" atheris, scripts/seed-fuzz-corpus.sh, then each of the 9 adapters and 18 report parsers for the workflow's 120 seconds. The first run found the report-parser job broken: fuzz_ingest_parser.py imported tests.fuzz.mappings, which is not importable when the file runs as a script, so all 18 entries stopped before fuzzing anything. Fixed; then all 27 ran their full time with no crash, timeout (10 s) or memory cap (2 GB) hit, from 2,809 inputs (burp, the slowest parser) to 441,616 (the sample analysis). Under emulation an input runs slower than on a real runner, so this is less fuzzing than CI would do in the same time. It has still not run on GitHub itself. - .github/workflows/scorecard.yml has never run. The OpenSSF Scorecard score this week claims to improve towards 8+ is not yet measured; the README badge will not resolve to a real number until the workflow fires for the first time (on the next push to main, or the next Saturday cron). - .github/workflows/release.yml has never run, and this session did not trigger it: doing so means pushing a real container image to a real registry under a real version tag, with no way to verify GHCR push permissions or the SLSA generator's exact behavior from here. The job structure follows slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator's documented contract as closely as could be verified without executing it -- not the same as having confirmed it works. - The ASVS self-assessment is not a certification. It is a self-audit by the project's own maintainer-assistant, not an independent third-party review -- real value, but not the same evidentiary weight as an external audit. - Two real gaps remain open by disclosed choice, not oversight: no authentication-attempt rate limiting, no general API abuse-prevention. Both are in docs/ASVS-SELF-ASSESSMENT.md's summary table as real, tracked follow-up work. - Branch protection was not configured. It is a GitHub repository setting (Settings → Branches), not something achievable from a workflow file, and this review did not request or receive the repository-admin access that would be needed to change it even if asked.

docs.title: Week 49 verification -- DAST: ownership verification, egress proxy, scanning tiers, SAST/DAST correlation (plan §22.4)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See ADR-0035 for the design decisions, including the one piece (campaign execution routed through the egress proxy) that was not wired together this week despite both halves existing and being independently proven.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/dast/ownership.py, new asset_verifications table (migration 0021): DNS TXT / .well-known proof-of-control, re-checked live everywhere it gates something, never trusted from a cached status (task 1).
  • core/dast/proxy.py, core/dast/egress.py, docker/dast-egress-proxy/: a real allow-list forward proxy and the nftables policy that would force a campaign runner through it (task 2).
  • core/dast/campaign.py, core/dast/pipeline.py, core/dast/adapters/{zap,nuclei}.py, scans.dast_mode (migration 0022): passive (ZAP baseline) always-on, active (+curated Nuclei) opt-in and rate-limited, the campaign UI (/app/projects/[id]/campaigns), and audit logging (task 3).
  • core/dast/routes.py, core/dast/correlate.py, scans.route_map and issues. confirmed_at_runtime_at/confirmed_by_scan_id (migration 0023), assets.linked_source_asset_id: a DAST finding on a route with a related-CWE SAST finding near its handler marks that Issue confirmed at runtime (task 4).

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• Ownership verification: real DNS/HTTPS lookups against example.com (confirmed failing, no such record exists there) via both the CLI and a real FastAPI TestClient request path; the full browser → Next.js dev server → FastAPI → Postgres → DNS path exercised in a real browser session, showing the real DNS failure message end to end. A real bug was found and fixed this way: the new CLI commands never set the Postgres session's app.current_org, so every write hit RLS's own INSERT denial under a real (non-SQLite) connection -- fixed by calling set_session_org first, the same as every other admin/CLI code path already does.
  • The egress proxy: a real running instance relaying a real local HTTP server's response and refusing (and reporting, as structured JSON) a disallowed host; a real CONNECT tunnel plus a real TLS handshake to example.com over the real network; the actual docker/dast-egress-proxy image built and run standalone with the same results via curl -x.
  • ZAP and Nuclei adapters: a real zap-baseline.py run against a real local HTTP target found 19 real findings, including discovering a /admin link it found by actually spidering the page -- not a canned fixture. A real Nuclei run against https://example.com/ produced real findings with real CWEs. Two real bugs were found this way and fixed, each with a regression test: ZAP's rule 90004 reporting three distinct alerts under one shared pluginid against the same URL (fixed by including the alert name in the finding id); Nuclei reporting the same template against the same URL more than once (fixed by hashing the whole raw record instead of just the matched URL).
  • The full DAST campaign pipeline: with only the live ownership check stubbed (genuine DNS/HTTP verification was already proven separately above; a synthetic domain can never pass a real check), a complete campaign ran against real Postgres -- live rate-limit check, real ZAP+Nuclei execution against https://example.com/, real correlation/dedup (69 raw findings → 46 unique), real persistence, real issue sync (19 issues created), a real audit-log entry. A third real bug was found here: the worker's own active-scan rate-limit re-check compared the campaign's own created_at to itself to exclude it from "the most recent prior active campaign" -- under SQLite this comparison silently failed (naive vs. aware datetimes), which would have made every active campaign instantly rate-limit itself in production. Fixed by excluding the current scan by id in the query instead of comparing timestamps at all.
  • Route extraction: run against this project's own api/main.py (1700+ real lines) found all 44 real FastAPI routes, including /assets/web, /assets/{id}/verify, and /assets/{id}/campaigns -- the exact routes this week's own earlier tasks added -- a stronger proof than any hand-built fixture that the decorator-matching logic works on real code.
  • SAST/DAST correlation end to end: a real bandit scan (via core.pipeline.run_scan_job, the actual worker code path) of a real, deliberately vulnerable Flask app (subprocess.call(query, shell=True), CWE-78) against a real zip archive produced a real, correctly-extracted route map (/search at the right line) persisted to real Postgres. Registering a web Asset linked to that SAST Asset, then running the correlator with a synthetic CWE-78 DAST finding on the same route, correctly wrote confirmed_at_runtime_at/confirmed_by_scan_id onto the real Issue row for the real command-injection finding. Committed as tests/integration/test_dast_sast_correlation_live.py, not just an ad-hoc script.
  • Cross-tenant isolation: asset_verifications' RLS policy (join-based through assets.org_id, the same pattern issues/findings/tool_runs already use) verified against real Postgres -- org B cannot see org A's verification row even querying the table directly by id, bypassing application-level org_id= filtering entirely. assets.linked_source_asset_id cross-org linking is rejected at write time (repo.register_web_asset raises ValueError), verified directly. Migration 0021's up/downgrade round-trip verified against real Postgres.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1578 unit tests passed, 1 skipped (consistent with prior weeks' disclosed never-executed paths), up from Week 48's 1481. New: test_dast_ownership.py, test_asset_verification_repo.py, test_asset_verification_api.py, test_dast_proxy.py, test_dast_egress.py, test_dast_zap_adapter.py, test_dast_nuclei_adapter.py, test_dast_campaign.py, test_dast_campaign_api.py, test_dast_routes.py, test_dast_correlate.py. black --check ., ruff check ., mypy (core+api, the project's own enforced scope) all clean.
  • 9 integration tests against real Postgres/real sockets/real network, all passing: test_asset_verification_rls_docker.py (2), test_tenancy_rls_docker.py (2, no regression), test_dast_proxy_live.py (3), test_dast_adapters_live.py (2, ZAP+Nuclei), plus test_dast_sast_correlation_live.py (1).
  • Frontend: 211 tests passed (up from 198), tsc --noEmit clean. New: web-asset-verification. test.tsx, campaigns-view.test.tsx, confirmed-at-runtime-badge.test.tsx.
  • Golden fixture tests (test_adapters.py) updated for the new Location.route field appended to the canonical Finding schema -- a clean, purely-additive diff across 9 fixture files, re-verified passing.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• The egress proxy is not in the loop for a real campaign. core/dast/pipeline.py runs ZAP/ Nuclei as plain docker run subprocesses on the worker host today; it does not start a per-campaign proxy instance or apply the nftables egress policy to the scanner containers. Both halves are real and independently verified; connecting them is real remaining work (ADR-0035 has the detail), not a rounding error.
  • The nftables ruleset itself has never loaded into a real network namespace, on this machine or any other, for this feature -- Linux-only, same disclosed boundary as Week 46's own egress work.
  • Route extraction covers one decorator shape. Django's urls.py table, non-Python frameworks, and any route built from a runtime string (not a string literal in the decorator) are invisible to it -- correlation simply finds nothing for those, never a wrong match.
  • The DAST-side half of one correlation test was synthetic. Getting a real ZAP/Nuclei scan to report a genuine "OS command injection" finding needs a real vulnerable live server with the injectable code path actually running, not static source on disk -- the adapters' own real-scanner execution was separately and fully verified live (above); only the specific "this scanner found this specific CWE at this specific route" fact in the correlation test is a stand-in for that.
  • Linking a web Asset to its source project is API/CLI-only. The "Add web target" registration screen does not yet offer a picker for linked_source_asset_id.
  • Branch protection, a real production deployment of any of this, and an actual Celery worker process consuming bulwark.run_dast_campaign were not part of this review -- the campaign pipeline was run directly (as a real function call against real Postgres), not via a running Celery worker consuming from a real Redis queue, matching the same practical boundary this project's other "run the real job function directly" verifications have drawn before.

docs.title: Week 49b verification -- wiring the DAST egress proxy into campaign execution (plan §22.4 follow-up)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. This is a standalone task inserted between Week 49 and Week 50, not a numbered plan week: the plan's own M10 milestone (tag v1.5.0) claims "scope enforced at the network layer" for DAST, and Week 49 itself disclosed that the egress proxy it built was not actually wired into campaign execution -- so that claim wasn't true yet. See ADR-0035 for the design detail; this doc is the evidence.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• core/dast/proxy.py: a new ProxyConfig dataclass and BackgroundProxy class -- a real AllowListProxy run on its own thread and event loop, usable as a context manager from a synchronous caller. Extracted from (and now shared with) the test fixture tests/integration/test_dast_proxy_live.py already used.
  • core/dast/pipeline.py: run_dast_campaign_job now starts a BackgroundProxy scoped to exactly the campaign's one verified host before running either scanner, and tears it down after, on every exit path including a tool error. Blocked egress attempts are recorded as a tool_runs row ("egress-proxy") and an audit-log entry (dast.campaign.egress_blocked).
  • core/dast/adapters/zap.py, adapters/nuclei.py: both adapters gained a proxy: ProxyConfig | None parameter, pointing the real tool at the real proxy when a campaign supplies one.
  • core/dast/adapters/nuclei.py: a new unconditional restriction, ALLOWED_PROTOCOL_TYPES = ("http",) (-pt http), alongside the existing EXCLUDED_TAGS -- see "What this found" below.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• The ZAP proxy-config keys were wrong, and a real test proved it. The legacy network. connectionParam.proxyChain* keys (most ZAP documentation still shows these) produced zero traffic at a real running BackgroundProxy when used with a real zap-baseline.py run against https://example.com/. The add-on's own compiled ConnectionOptions.class, extracted from the shipped network-beta-*.zap file inside the real ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable image, gave the keys it actually reads: network.connection.httpProxy.{enabled,host,port}. A second real run with the corrected keys showed the proxy's own log recording a successful CONNECT example.com:443 (the allowed host) and three refused CONNECT attempts to news.zaproxy.org, cfu.zaproxy.org, and tel.zaproxy.org -- ZAP's own background telemetry, correctly blocked -- while the scan itself still completed and produced 11 real findings.
  • Nuclei's default templates legitimately reach third parties, found by a real run. Running the existing (pre-Week-49b) run_nuclei invocation for real against https://example.com/ -- with only the already-shipped EXCLUDED_TAGS applied -- produced real DNS-template findings (an NS, DNSSEC, MX, DMARC, SPF, AAAA lookup, each a genuine DNS query to whatever resolver the container uses) and a real rdap-whois template finding that called rdap.verisign.com directly, not example.com. Once the campaign's proxy was scoped to exactly example.com, the same unmodified invocation failed outright ("no templates provided for scan", because its own template-list fetch from GitHub was also blocked) -- a real, live demonstration that a single-host allow-list and Nuclei's default template set are incompatible without a further restriction. Adding -pt http (confirmed against Nuclei's own -h output: -pt, -type value[] templates to run based on protocol type) and re-running produced a clean, successful scan through the proxy with no blocked attempts other than template-irrelevant noise.
  • The full campaign pipeline, through the real proxy, against real Postgres. New: tests/integration/test_dast_pipeline_egress_proxy_live.py. The real run_dast_campaign_job (not a stand-in), with only the live DNS/HTTP ownership re-check stubbed to ok=True -- the same deliberate, disclosed exception Week 49's own correlation test made, since a synthetic local target can never pass a real DNS TXT or .well-known check, and that check's own real pass/fail behavior is separately and fully proven in tests/unit/test_dast_ownership.py and tests/integration/ test_asset_verification_rls_docker.py. Everything else is real: a real Postgres-backed Scan row, a real BackgroundProxy, a real zap-baseline.py run against a real local http.server target through that proxy, real findings rows persisted, and both a real tool_runs row and a real audit_entries row for the campaign's own blocked egress attempts (ZAP's background telemetry calls, exactly as seen in the adapter-level test above). The campaign completed with real findings every run.
  • Shutdown correctness. The first live run surfaced a real asyncio cleanup bug: closing a BackgroundProxy while a scanner's connection was still mid-relay abandoned that connection's task when the background thread's event loop was torn down, producing a Task was destroyed but it is pending / Event loop is closed warning. Fixed by draining any still-pending relay tasks (with a 2-second bound) before the thread's event loop closes. Re-ran the same live ZAP-through-proxy scenario after the fix with no warnings, and the existing test_dast_proxy_live.py suite passes clean under -W error::pytest.PytestUnhandledThreadExceptionWarning.
  • No regressions. tests/integration/test_asset_verification_rls_docker.py, test_dast_sast_ correlation_live.py, and test_tenancy_rls_docker.py all still pass against the same real Postgres instance used for the new test above.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1583 unit tests passed, 1 skipped (up from Week 49's 1578); new: 5 tests across test_dast_zap_ adapter.py and test_dast_nuclei_adapter.py covering the argv built with and without a proxy, and a regression guard that ALLOWED_PROTOCOL_TYPES stays {"http"}. black --check . (382 files unchanged), ruff check ., and mypy (core+api, 196 files) all clean.
  • 6 integration tests against real Postgres/real Docker/real sockets, all passing: the 3 existing test_dast_proxy_live.py tests (now sharing BackgroundProxy instead of a duplicated fixture), the 2 existing test_dast_adapters_live.py tests (unchanged, still pass with the new -pt http restriction in place), and the 1 new test_dast_pipeline_egress_proxy_live.py test.
  • Coverage: 90.71% (pytest tests/unit), above the project's enforced 80% gate.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• This is cooperative scope enforcement, not a kernel-level guarantee. The proxy wiring works because ZAP and Nuclei were configured to use it and chose to honor that configuration. Nothing at the network-namespace level yet stops a scanner container that ignored its proxy settings (a compromised scanner, a future adapter that skips the proxy argument, a template with its own raw-socket logic) from reaching the internet directly. core.dast.egress's nftables ruleset is exactly the backstop for that case, and it has still never been loaded into a real network namespace, on any machine, for this feature -- Linux-only, the same disclosed boundary as Week 46's own egress work.
  • DNS resolution itself is not proxied or restricted here. The egress proxy only sees HTTP(S) traffic; a scanner's own DNS queries (for the target's hostname, or -- before the -pt http fix -- for a DNS-type template) go out however the container's network is configured, unaffected by this week's work. Restricting DNS at the network layer is also the nftables ruleset's job, not this proxy's.
  • The -pt http restriction narrows what Nuclei can report in a campaign. Any DNS/SSL/TCP/ whois/headless-type template -- not just the third-party-contacting ones discovered this week -- is now excluded from every DAST campaign, not only the specific rdap-whois/DNS templates that caused the problem. This is a deliberate, disclosed trade of coverage for scope correctness, not an oversight.
  • Linking a web Asset to its source project is still API/CLI-only (unchanged from Week 49) -- not something this follow-up touched.

docs.title: Week 50 verification -- Scale: Helm chart with KEDA, k6 load testing, cost-per-scan dashboard (plan §23)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See ADR-0036 for the design decisions, including every disclosed simplification.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• helm/bulwark/: a Helm chart for the core product (Postgres, Redis, object storage, OpenBao, migrate Job, API, worker, a new single-replica Celery beat, web), plus an optional KEDA ScaledObject scaling the worker on Celery queue depth.
  • k6/scan-submission.js, k6/browse-results.js: real load-test scripts against a real running API.
  • core/observability/cost.py, two new API endpoints (/scans/{id}/cost, /costs/summary), a new Prometheus gauge + two Grafana panels, and a new web page (/app/costs) for cost-per-scan visibility.
  • Along the way: core/persistence/db.py's connection pool sizing, docker-compose.yml's api command (--workers 4) and postgres command (max_connections=300), and a real fix to an existing, previously-undiscovered openbao healthcheck bug.
  • A real, pre-existing production bug in core.maintenance.reap_stale_scans, unrelated to Scale itself but found while doing this week's own RLS/connection work: it queried scans with no app.current_org ever set, which real Postgres RLS reads as "see nothing," not "see everything" -- the housekeeping task meant to fail scans whose worker died was silently a no-op in any real, RLS-enforced deployment. Fixed to iterate one org at a time with set_session_org, the same pattern core.retention.shred_expired_scans already used (and whose own docstring already named reap_stale_scans as needing it).

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• A real kind Kubernetes cluster, not a dry-run. helm install bulwark helm/bulwark into a freshly created kind create cluster brought every pod to Ready: Postgres (StatefulSet), Redis, object storage, OpenBao, a migrate Job that ran alembic upgrade head for real, the API (passed its own /healthz readiness probe), the worker (2/2 containers Ready, including the docker:27-dind sidecar), beat, and web.
  • A real KEDA installation (helm install keda kedacore/keda -n keda), not a stub. Its own ScaledObject genuinely reads Redis LLEN celery through the KEDA operator's metrics API server -- confirmed via kubectl get scaledobject showing READY=True only after fixing the Redis address to be fully qualified (see ADR-0036).
  • A real, deliberately isolated 3,000-task backlog, and a real scale event. The worker Deployment was paused at 0 replicas (autoscaling.keda.sh/paused-replicas=0) specifically so the backlog being built wasn't also being drained at the same time; kubectl exec'd into the real API pod, celery_app.send_task('bulwark.update_feeds') was called 3,000 times for real, and Redis was queried directly to confirm the depth held at exactly 3,000 with nothing consuming it. Unpausing and polling kubectl get hpa/kubectl exec ... redis-cli llen celery every 4 seconds showed: depth 3000 at t=4s, replicas already at 5 (the configured max) by t=16s, depth down to 0 by t=28s. A second kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/component=worker poll loop, run in the background, confirmed the Deployment scaled back down to 1 replica (the configured min) roughly 5 minutes after the queue emptied -- HPA's own default scale-down stabilization window, unmodified.
  • The beat-is-a-scheduler-only fix, proven by the same backlog technique: before the fix (beat running worker -B -P solo -c 1), a 100-task backlog pushed onto a paused worker Deployment drained to 0 anyway within seconds, proving beat was silently consuming the very queue KEDA was supposed to scale on. After switching beat to the dedicated celery beat subcommand, the identical technique (100 tasks, worker paused, checked depth) held the queue at 100 until the worker was unpaused.
  • k6, against the real docker-compose dev stack, not a mock API. k6 run k6/scan-submission.js (BULWARK_API_TOKEN a real scoped token minted via bulwark token create):
checks_succeeded...: 99.83% (2476/2480 — 4 transient 500s)
http_req_duration..: avg=406.63ms min=270µs med=380.23ms p(50)=380.23ms p(90)=593.9ms p(95)=675.18ms p(99)=809.99ms max=1.16s
http_reqs..........: 2480   122.182577/s

k6 run k6/browse-results.js (final run, after the --workers 4 + pool-sizing + max_connections fixes; BULWARK_SCAN_ID a real completed scan):

checks_succeeded...: 96.75% (9854/10184)
http_req_duration..: avg=2.64s med=696.41ms p(50)=696.41ms p(90)=1.08s p(95)=1.84s p(99)=1m0s
  { expected_response:true }...: avg=809.44ms med=686.89ms p(50)=686.89ms p(90)=1s p(95)=1.18s p(99)=2.33s
http_reqs..........: 10184  127.298695/s
iterations.........: 3292   41.149578/s

(The earlier, unfixed runs -- single uvicorn process timing out at ~31s on 85%+ of requests, then a mis-sized connection pool doing the same thing for a different reason -- are recorded in full in ADR-0036, since they're exactly the evidence for why each fix was needed, not just the final number.) - The cost dashboard, end to end, with real scan data. GET /scans/{id}/cost against a real, just-completed scan (a real octocat/Hello-World clone-and-scan) returned {"compute_seconds": 0.39, "compute_usd": 0.000117, "llm_tokens": 0, ...} -- 0.39 is the real summed ToolRun.duration_seconds for that scan's real bandit/semgrep/gitleaks/trivy/osv-scanner runs. GET /costs/summary?days=30 against the real dev database (15 real scans accumulated across this whole project's history -- OWASP NodeGoat, terragoat, VAmPI, nodejs-goof, and others) returned a real aggregate ($0.33 total, 18m37s of real summed scanner compute time). The /app/costs web page was opened in a real browser against the real running web app and API (localhost:3010, not 127.0.0.1:3010 -- the difference is a real CORS origin mismatch this exposed, not a bug in the page itself, since BULWARK_CORS_ORIGINS only allow-lists localhost:3010), showing the identical 15-scan, $0.33 breakdown with working "Last 7d/30d/90d" window switching. The new Grafana panels (bulwark_estimated_cost_usd as a stat and a bargauge split by component) were confirmed rendering the same live Prometheus data after a Grafana restart picked up the updated dashboard JSON. - The reap_stale_scans fix, against real Postgres, connected as the real worker's own bulwark_worker role -- not bulwark_app, which does nothing to prove the bug since the worker never connects as it. Two organizations, each with one real "stuck" scan row; calling reap_stale_scans exactly the way core.tasks.maintenance_task really does (no org context set on the caller's own session beforehand) correctly reaped both, one per org, via the internal set_session_org loop -- the old implementation would have reaped neither, since the query it ran had no org context at all and RLS reads that as "nothing," not "everything."

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• 1591 unit tests passed, 1 skipped (up from Week 49b's 1583); new: test_observability_cost.py (6 tests), two new tests in test_observability.py for the CostSummary Prometheus collector (a happy path against a real SQLite-backed session, and an unreachable-DB path). black --check ., ruff check ., and mypy (core+api, 197 files) all clean.
  • 215 frontend tests passed (up from 211), tsc --noEmit clean; new: cost-dashboard.test.tsx (4 tests: empty state, a real-shaped response rendering totals and a linked row, window switching refetching with the right days value, and an error state).
  • The Helm chart: helm lint helm/bulwark clean; helm template output validated against the real kind cluster's own API schema via kubectl apply --dry-run=client, including the KEDA ScaledObject CRD.
  • 2 new integration tests against real Postgres/real RLS, connected as bulwark_worker: tests/integration/test_maintenance_rls_docker.py, both passing; no regressions in the existing test_tenancy_rls_docker.py/test_data_protection_rls_docker.py against the same database.
  • Coverage: 90.62% (pytest tests/unit), above the project's enforced 80% gate.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• The Helm chart's simplifications are real, not cosmetic. No mTLS to Postgres, OpenBao in dev mode only, a privileged DinD sidecar instead of socket-proxy's narrow allowlist, and a single-node-only hostPath workdir volume by default -- see ADR-0036's own list and helm/bulwark/README.md for exactly what each means for a real production deployment.
  • k6's absolute numbers are this one developer laptop's, not a provisioned server's. It was running a kind cluster, a browser, and the rest of this session's work at the same time as the load test. The relative findings (single-process uvicorn cannot serve 500 concurrent users; a 15-connection pool across 6 processes needs Postgres's own max_connections raised to match) are real engineering facts independent of the hardware; the specific p50/p95 milliseconds are not a capacity-planning number for any other machine.
  • The cost estimate is relative visibility, not a bill. Blended per-token pricing (no real input/output split), no historical model attribution, and placeholder $/compute-second and $/token defaults that need overriding with a deployment's own real figures -- all disclosed in core/observability/cost.py's own docstring and repeated on the dashboard page itself.
  • The Prometheus cost metric covers the default org only, consistent with the rest of core/observability/metrics.py and this project's self-hosted, single-tenant scope -- not a cross-tenant SaaS billing figure.
  • The nftables egress backstop (Week 49b) and gVisor/Firecracker sandboxing (Week 46) are untouched by this week's work and remain exactly as previously disclosed; nothing here closes those gaps.

docs.title: Week 51 verification -- Ecosystem: Plugin SDK, Integrations, pre-commit hook, documentation site (plan §23)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. See ADR-0037 for the design decisions, including every disclosed simplification.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• Plugin SDK (core/plugins/): entry-point discovery (bulwark.scanner_adapters), a shared conformance kit built-ins now use too, keyless Sigstore verification (core/plugins/signing.py), a per-org allowlist (PluginAllowlistRow, migration 0024), and a real, installable example package (examples/bulwark-plugin-demo).
  • Integrations (core/integrations/): Slack/Discord notifications, HMAC-signed generic outbound webhooks, GitHub Issues and Jira two-way sync (IntegrationSettingsRow/ExternalIssueLinkRow, migration 0025), a shared SSRF guard extracted into core/netsafety.py, and two inbound webhook receivers.
  • Pre-commit hook (core/precommit/): native (no Docker) secrets regex rules and ast-based Python SAST checks, bulwark precommit run/install/uninstall, and a .pre-commit-hooks.yaml for the pre-commit framework.
  • Documentation site: mkdocs.yml + docs/index.md, docs/quickstart.md, docs/concepts/architecture.md, docs/plugins.md, reusing docs/policy.md/risk-score.md/ taxonomy.md/reachability.md/api.md as-is.
  • Along the way: fixed a pre-existing gap where tests/integration/*_rls_docker.py wasn't fully wired into CI (two of four RLS test files were silently never run); fixed docs/api.md/ docs/openapi.json having been stale for several weeks with no test to catch it.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• A real podinfo image's real Sigstore signature. verify_plugin_image against ghcr.io/stefanprodan/podinfo:6.4.0 (a real, publicly signed image) succeeds; against the same image with the wrong declared identity, or against an unsigned image, it correctly raises PluginSignatureError -- all three paths exercised live, not mocked (tests/integration/test_plugin_signing_live.py).
  • A real third-party package, installed exactly as pip install would. examples/bulwark-plugin-demo is installed in CI with --no-deps the same way a plugin author's own install would be; discover_plugins() finds it via a genuine entry point with no change to Bulwark's own source, and its adapter runs through a real docker run (tests/integration/test_plugin_sandbox_execution_live.py), including a deliberate signature mismatch (its declared identity doesn't match its own unsigned image) correctly failing.
  • Real DNS resolution for the integrations SSRF guard. validate_webhook_url against hooks.slack.com and discord.com resolves and accepts their real public addresses; against 169.254.169.254 (the AWS/GCP metadata address) it correctly rejects (tests/integration/test_integrations_webhooks_live.py). Real HMAC-signed delivery proven over a real local HTTPServer socket, not a mocked transport.
  • A real, unmocked, HMAC-verified GitHub webhook round trip. A crafted issues webhook payload, signed with real hmac.new(secret, body, sha256) the way GitHub itself would sign it, correctly closes a linked issue's sync status through the actual running FastAPI app; a tampered signature is correctly rejected with 401 (tests/unit/test_integrations_api.py).
  • Real Postgres RLS, connected as the real bulwark_worker role: one org's integration credentials and external issue links are invisible to another org's session, and a brand-new connection with no app.current_org ever set sees zero rows from either table (tests/integration/test_integrations_rls_docker.py).
  • Real temporary git repositories and real git commits, start to finish. bulwark precommit install writes an actual .git/hooks/pre-commit; a real git commit with a staged fake AWS key genuinely fails (non-zero exit from the real hook, not a simulated check), fixing the file and restaging genuinely lets the commit through, and git commit --no-verify genuinely bypasses it (tests/unit/test_precommit_cli.py).
  • A real performance measurement that found and drove a real fix. This project's own 238-file core/ tree, copied into a fresh git repository and staged in full: the first working version took 1.93s wall-clock (one git show subprocess per file), at the edge of the plan's 2-second budget. Switching to one batched git cat-file --batch call dropped the same real commit to 0.45s. tests/integration/test_precommit_performance_live.py pins both the pure scan time (<2s) and a looser wall-clock regression budget (<4s) against this same real file set.
  • The documentation site, actually built and actually opened in a browser. pip install -e ".[docs]" then mkdocs build completes in under a second with zero warnings on any new or reused page (the handful of warnings that do print are pre-existing broken relative links in old, non-nav docs -- confirmed by name, not assumed harmless). Opened the built site in a real browser: the homepage's card grid and six-step pipeline list, syntax-highlighted code blocks and a working table of contents on the plugin guide, the full real generated API reference (including /plugins and /settings/integrations), the real policy cookbook, the architecture diagram rendering correctly from a nested docs/concepts/ page via its relative ../ path, and MkDocs Material's built-in search returning real, correctly-ranked, deep-linked results for the query "allowlist" (13 matching documents, correct anchors).

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
