• 1779 unit tests passed, 1 skipped (up from Week 50's 1591: +38 Plugin SDK, +78 Integrations, +70 pre-commit hook, +2 the API-docs freshness fix, +1 net from a pre-existing test fix along the way). black --check . and ruff check . clean repo-wide; mypy clean across 216 source files (up from 197 at the end of Week 50).
  • 9 new live integration tests this week (plugin signing x3, plugin sandbox execution x2, integrations webhooks x4), all passing against real Docker/network/DNS; 3 new RLS integration tests against real Postgres (test_integrations_rls_docker.py).
  • The CI gap this week found: tenancy-rls's job only ever ran two of the four tests/integration/*_rls_docker.py files; fixed to glob all of them.
  • scripts/gen-licenses.py --check clean, including the new docs optional-dependency group (correctly excluded from SHIPPED_EXTRAS, the same as the pre-existing dev extra -- a documentation build tool, not something the application image ships).
  • Coverage: 90.83% (pytest tests/unit), above the project's enforced 80% gate.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• GitHub Issue and Jira ticket creation are mocked-transport tested, not live. Nothing in this week's work has created a real issue or ticket on a real account -- that needs the account owner's own token and would be a real, visible side effect, which this session does not take unprompted.
  • A plugin's severity is INFO until someone edits core/scoring/severity.py by hand. The allowlist controls whether a plugin can run at all, not what its findings are ranked as.
  • The pre-commit hook's SAST coverage is Python-only, and its 15 secret patterns and 7 AST checks are a deliberately narrow, high-confidence subset chosen to be safe to block a commit on -- not a replacement for bulwark scan --tools gitleaks,bandit in CI, which still runs the real tools.
  • The documentation site isn't deployed anywhere. mkdocs build is verified and wired into CI; publishing it to GitHub Pages needs the repository owner to enable Pages in the repository's own settings, which this work does not do on its own.
  • Everything from prior weeks' own disclosed limits is unchanged: no mTLS to Postgres in the Helm chart, OpenBao dev mode only, the nftables egress backstop and gVisor/Firecracker sandboxing exactly as previously documented. Nothing in Week 51's work touches any of them.

docs.title: Week 52 verification -- Launch: benchmark v2, the landing page, the v2.0.0 release (plan §33)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. No new ADR this week -- unlike every other v2 week, Week 52 made no new architectural decisions; it compiled, measured, shipped, and wrote up what the previous 25 weeks already built. The closest things to a design record this week produced are docs/release-notes-v2.0.0.md (what shipped, by phase) and docs/technical-report-v2.md (the three mechanisms the plan asked to be written up: correlation, taint-based ranking, verified fixes).

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• Task 1 -- Benchmark v2 (plan §34): docs/evaluation-v2.md, compiling every row of the plan's own evaluation table. Four rows were real, already-measured work scattered across earlier weeks, collected here for the first time. One row (the taint engine) is new, real measurement work done this week. Five rows are explicitly marked not measured (need a live model), and the UX row has no before/after (the baseline study was never run) -- none of these are new findings, just a single place collecting what each feature's own week already disclosed.
  • Task 2 -- Launch landing page (plan §33): the homepage now replays a real scan of the real, public OWASP Juice Shop (271 real findings), reusing the existing ScanReport/ToolCards components unchanged -- the same ones the authenticated app's real WebSocket-driven live scan uses.
  • Task 3 -- v2.0.0 release: docs/release-notes-v2.0.0.md and docs/demo-script-v2.md (the video itself is explicitly the user's own task).
  • Task 4 -- Technical write-up: docs/blog-v2.0.0.md, docs/technical-report-v2.md, and docs/talk-outline-v2.md (giving the talk is the user's own task).
  • Two small fixes found and closed along the way, before this week's own tasks: docs/api.md and docs/openapi.json had drifted stale for several weeks with nothing checking them, and the CLI's ignored-finding count was silently dropped from the pre-commit hook's output in one branch -- both already covered in Week 51/52's own earlier commits, not repeated here.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• The taint-engine measurement: a real bulwark scan run against two real, cached repositories from the project's own 25-repo corpus (NodeGoat, nodejs-goof), with every confirmed finding hand-verified by reading the actual source. NodeGoat's three confirmations are genuine true positives -- the file's own comment reads "Insecure use of eval() to parse inputs."
  • The landing page's live replay is a real scan, not synthetic data. scripts/ gen-juiceshop-demo-data.py converts a real bulwark scan https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop run; every finding, tool duration, and severity count a visitor sees is what Bulwark actually reported. Verified live in a real browser: the replay reveals scanners in their real finish order, reaches the real "271 unique findings, 287 raw, 6% fewer" summary, and a bug found live before shipping (ElapsedTime reading a stale generation timestamp, producing an ever-growing nonsensical counter) was fixed and re-verified in the same browser session.
  • Every cross-reference in the four new write-up documents was checked against the real filesystem -- including catching one wrong citation before it shipped: a draft of the talk outline cited a local "ADR-015" for the Opengrep/hosted-mode decision that does not exist in this repository (that numbering is the external plan document's own scheme, not this repo's sequentially-assigned docs/adr/ files); corrected to describe it as a planned, not-yet-written v3 decision instead.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• Backend: ruff check ., black --check ., mypy (216 source files) all clean after each task; full unit suite green throughout, no regressions.
  • Frontend: 220 tests passing (up from 215 at the end of Week 51 -- 5 new, covering the live replay's initial state, its progression, its connection-label switch, its links, and that it never fabricates data), tsc --noEmit clean, npm run build clean (the production build's own stricter typecheck caught one test-file type error the editor-level typecheck had missed, fixed before committing).
  • scripts/gen-juiceshop-demo-data.py is outside this project's checked mypy scope (files = ["core", "api"]) but was cleaned up anyway: a bare dict annotation tightened to dict[str, Any].

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• Everything docs/evaluation-v2.md already discloses, disclosed again here rather than softened: five evaluation rows need a live model and weren't measured; the UX row has no real before/after; the taint-engine result is a 3-case spot-check, not a corpus study; scale and platform-security numbers are a single developer machine's.
  • The landing page's "live" replay is exactly that -- a replay. The underlying scan and every number in it are real; the on-screen pacing is compressed from the real ~20-second run into 6 seconds for a visitor's sake, and the copy says "replaying," never "scanning right now." No new Juice Shop scan runs per visitor or per page load.
  • The demo video and the talk itself are not part of this week's work product -- by the user's own explicit instruction, both are left to them; what's delivered here is the script and outline that would make recording/giving either one faster, not the recordings themselves.
  • No GitHub Release was created via the GitHub API or gh CLI -- neither is available in this environment. docs/release-notes-v2.0.0.md is written so it can be pasted directly into a GitHub Release description once the v2.0.0 tag is pushed.

docs.title: Week 53 verification -- Gate and hierarchy (plan Phase 13, §39.5/§40)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. First week of v3; see ADR-0038 and ADR-0039 for the real design decisions.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• Task 1 -- Verification gate (§39.5): found that the "two-tenant RLS test passes on every endpoint" gate item was false by a wide margin -- the existing test covered 4 of this API's 50+ endpoints, a scope that hadn't grown since Week 29/30. Closed with tests/integration/test_api_tenancy_coverage_rls_docker.py, extending real cross-org coverage to every /assets/{asset_id}/... endpoint and the remaining /scans/{id}/... ones (~27 more endpoints).
  • Task 2 -- ADR-0038: hosted mode runs Opengrep, not Semgrep, closing the plan's "ADR-015" gate item. New core/adapters/opengrep.py, docker/opengrep/ (a from-scratch image, since no official one exists), and an originally-written starter ruleset (docker/opengrep/rules/) -- Opengrep's own bundled rules turned out to carry the identical "no hosting as a service" restriction Semgrep's do, discovered by actually reading their LICENSE file rather than assuming the fork solved licensing by itself.
  • Task 3 -- ADR-0039: Portfolio and Engagement tables (plan §40 change C11), plus a real data migration (0026) giving every existing Asset one "ci" Engagement and linking its history to it. "Test" is deliberately not a third new table -- ToolRun already was one, gaining only an engagement_id column.
  • Task 4: RLS + the two-tenant leak test for both new tables, live-verified against real Postgres.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• The "every endpoint" gap, proven by actually trying every endpoint. Seeded one real asset/issue/hypothesis/conversation/scan for an org via direct ORM inserts, then hit all ~27 previously-untested /assets/{asset_id}/... and /scans/{id}/... routes with another org's header against a real, freshly migrated Postgres connected as bulwark_worker. All correctly 404; no leak found, but the coverage gap itself was real before this task closed it. Three real test-design bugs were found and fixed getting this to pass cleanly (a missing required query param, a client gated on the wrong AppState field, a Copilot endpoint's additional isinstance(client, AnthropicClient) check) -- documented in the task's own commit.
  • Opengrep's actual licensing, checked by fetching and reading the real files, not assumed from marketing copy: the engine's LICENSE (plain LGPL-2.1) and opengrep-rules' LICENSE (LGPL-2.1 plus a Commons Clause "no selling as a service" condition) were both fetched directly from GitHub and read before any adapter code was written. A web search's suggested Docker image names (ghcr.io/opengrep/opengrep, opengrep/opengrep) were checked against both registries' own APIs and found not to exist, before building docker/opengrep/ around the real binary-release distribution mechanism instead.
  • Every one of the 11 new Opengrep rules, hand-verified against real true/false-positive pairs inside the actual built image (docker run ... opengrep scan --config ...) before being trusted -- not assumed correct from the YAML alone.
  • A real sandbox incompatibility, reproduced and isolated, not guessed at. Opengrep's binary failed every run with "couldn't launch child (exec): Permission denied" against the sandbox's shared /tmp. Isolated to the tmpfs mount itself (a bare, unrestricted --tmpfs=/tmp mount with no flags at all still failed the same way; a totally unmounted default /tmp did not) before settling on redirecting HOME/TMPDIR to a plain writable volume instead of loosening the shared sandbox protection.
  • The Portfolio/Engagement data migration, run against real seeded data on a real Postgres: one asset with a real scan and two real ToolRuns correctly got one Engagement with both ToolRuns linked; one asset with no scans correctly got one empty, "completed" Engagement. The full migration chain (0001 through 0026) was also run against a brand-new, from-scratch Postgres, not only the incrementally-migrated one used throughout the rest of the week's work.
  • Cross-org isolation for both new tables and for the Tests (ToolRuns) inside an Engagement, live against real Postgres RLS, including the fail-closed guarantee for a connection that never set an org context at all.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• Backend: ruff check ., black --check ., mypy (217 source files) clean throughout.
  • Full unit suite: 1803 passed, 1 skipped (up from Week 52's close of 1779 -- +24: 8 Portfolio/ Engagement repo tests, 9 Opengrep/hosted-mode tests across two files, 7 miscellaneous from the golden-fixture conformance parametrization picking up the new adapter).
  • 23 tests/integration/*_rls_docker.py tests pass together against one real Postgres instance (4 of them new this week), connected as bulwark_worker.
  • THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md regenerated and passing its own policy check (scripts/gen-licenses.py --check) with Opengrep's real license correctly recorded.
  • docs/severity-matrix.md regenerated and passing its own freshness test with Opengrep's severity mapping included.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• The verified-fix agent's verification record on a real pull request (plan §39.5's own fourth gate item) is still not demonstrated -- it needs a live model, which this environment is not configured with. Not newly discovered this week; carried over from every prior week's own disclosure of the same gap.
  • Opengrep's starter ruleset is small and unmeasured at corpus scale (7 Python + 4 JS/TS rules, each hand-verified individually, not run against a labelled corpus) -- see ADR-0038's own disclosure.
  • No Portfolio/Engagement API or UI exists yet. This week's scope was the data model and its migration; the v3 screens and endpoints that read and write it are later weeks' own tasks.
  • The "every endpoint" cross-tenant test still doesn't cover /plugins, /settings/integrations, or /settings/retention's own cross-org behavior at the HTTP layer -- those are already covered, but at the repository layer (their own *_rls_docker.py files from Weeks 47/51), not by an HTTP request through the live API the way this week's new test covers the asset-scoped surface. Not a known gap so much as a different, already-covered layer -- noted for completeness, not as a new finding.

docs.title: Weeks 54-56 verification -- Ingest and reimport (plan Phase 13, §41.1/§42, Milestone M12)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run, and measured. Weeks 54 (ingest endpoint and reimport), 55 (standard parsers) and 56 (import screen and fuzzing) were done as one body of work in eight tasks, because each depends on the one before. The design decisions are in ADR-0040; the user-facing description is docs/ingest-api.md.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text: # Task Result 1 Schema and ADR-0040 engagement_tests, import_records, outbox_events (migration 0027); amends ADR-0039 2 Repo layer and RLS helpers plus a two-tenant leak test for all three tables 3 Reimport engine core.imports.reimport.plan_reimport: new / unchanged / reopened / closed (+ detached) 4 Ingest service preview, apply (idempotent, row-locked), revert; native scans moved onto the same decision 5 Parser framework and SARIF IngestParser, registry, sandboxed parsing (docker/ingest-parser) 6 CycloneDX, SPDX, OSV; fuzzing three more parsers, an XXE corpus, an Atheris harness 7 Ingest API POST /v2/ingest and six more endpoints, worker job, scopes, migration 0028 8 Import screen and close-out the §55.1 screen, docs, this record

docs.title: Bugs found and fixed along the way
docs.text:
Most of these were found by running things for real, not by reading code. Several would have shipped green on SQLite and mocks.

  1. A cross-tenant leak that predates this work (the serious one). A database session could run as another organization after a commit. Row-Level Security reads app.current_org from the connection, but a session hands its connection back to the pool on every commit and takes whichever is free next, and the org had been set once per session at session level -- so it landed on a connection the session might never see again and stayed there for the next session to inherit. Reproduced on real Postgres with two overlapping sessions: the first one's next statement after a commit ran as the second org (it could read, and write into, the other tenant). It needs concurrent requests from different organizations, which is why every single-session test missed it; single-org self-hosting was never exposed. Fixed in core/tenancy.py (the org is re-applied, transaction-local, at the start of every transaction); five regression tests interleave sessions on a two-connection pool, one reads back real rows, and all five fail without the fix. See the changelog entry.
  2. A whole report collapsed into one Issue. Parsed findings have no fingerprint until correlate() runs; reimport matches by fingerprint, so four findings all matched the empty one. Found by the first end-to-end API test (my unit-test helper correlated, hiding it). Now an explicit step, core.imports.prepare; removing it fails 7 tests.
  3. Uploaded secrets would have been stored. A scan's Gitleaks redacts at the source; an uploaded file carries no such guarantee. redact_secret_findings now runs before correlation, so no function of a secret is fingerprinted either. Removing it fails 3 tests.
  4. Every applied upload leaked onto disk: apply_import clears the path the job then needed to delete. Found by an assertion that the upload directory is empty afterwards.
  5. Findings were inserted before the Issues they reference. SQLite does not enforce foreign keys and never noticed; Postgres refused. Found only by running against real Postgres.
  6. The parser sandbox's input directory had to be the shared scratch path, because in the worker container the Docker daemon is on the host (as run_tool already does for its output).
  7. JSON and XML disagreed on a real file: XML lost every finding's file path, and counted the document's own subject as a component. Found by comparing the two on a real Grype file; they are now byte-identical.
  8. The periodic scratch cleanup would have deleted a previewed upload while a person was deciding. It removes anything under the uploads directory after two hours, and a preview keeps its file until confirmed. Ingest uploads now live in their own directory with a lifetime tied to the import's status (core.maintenance.expire_stale_imports: a preview nobody confirms in 24 h is cancelled and its file deleted; an import a worker never finished is failed rather than left "in progress"; finished imports are never touched). Found by reading what else touched that directory, not by a failing test.
  9. Smaller: google-re2 has no IGNORECASE constant (caught at import by the tests); a maintenance RLS test asserted on the whole database and failed on rows other tests left; the shared SARIF mapper dropped region-less results and missed lower-case CWE tags.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• Real files from real tools. Syft (CycloneDX JSON and XML, SPDX 2.3), Grype (CycloneDX 1.7 with a vulnerabilities section, as JSON and XML), Semgrep (SARIF) and OSV-Scanner, generated by the project's own images (tests/golden/ingest/README.md). Grype's JSON and XML give identical findings (19 each). A real Semgrep SARIF imports to exactly what the native path reads from it, and OSV-Scanner output through the new parser equals the native adapter's.
  • Real Postgres under Row-Level Security as the non-superuser bulwark_worker: 53 integration tests pass together. They cover the three new tables (another org cannot read, enumerate, dispatch or forge rows), the whole ingest flow over HTTP, another org getting 404 on every import endpoint, two orgs importing interleaved, and two simultaneous uploads of one file applying exactly once (it fails 3 of 3 times if the row lock is removed).
  • The real sandbox container. Parsing runs in bulwark/ingest-parser: same findings as in-process; hostile, oversized and truncated files refused inside the container; a container that cannot start reads as an error, never an empty report; and from inside it the network, DNS, /app and /etc are all unreachable, the user is non-root, and the database layer is not in the image.
  • XML attacks: external entity (file and network), external DTD, parameter entity, billion laughs, quadratic blowup and a harmless internal entity are all refused in under 2 s, nothing from /etc/passwd surfaces, no connection is attempted -- in-process and inside the container.
  • Ground-truth property tests for the reimport decision: Hypothesis replays random import sequences into two Tests and compares every count against an independent set-arithmetic oracle; no strict prefix of any real report ever reads as complete; mutated real reports and arbitrary bytes never raise.
  • Mutation checks. Each deliberate regression makes the tests fail: ignoring other sources, ignoring close_missing, widening the close scope, stdlib XML, swallowing truncation errors, letting an SBOM close issues, dropping redaction, dropping correlation, removing the row lock, and (in the screen) changing the confirmation wording, saving on upload, and showing counts before the format is confirmed.
  • Fuzzing, for real (but briefly). Atheris was built from source in a Linux container (scripts/fuzz-ingest-docker.sh) and run for 90 s per parser seeded from the real files: 1.80 million executions (SARIF 901,207; CycloneDX 168,919; SPDX 670,743; OSV 62,759), no crash or hang, each corpus growing (65-232 entries).
  • A real browser against the real stack. The import screen was driven in a browser against the real API on the real Postgres with the real parser container: a Semgrep SARIF previewed as "3 new" and was imported ("Imported: 3 new, 0 reopened, 0 closed"); a second report previewed as "0 new, 2 unchanged, 0 reopened, 1 closed", imported with the same numbers, and the database showed 1 fixed / 2 open; Undo restored all three; an unrecognised file asked which format it was and showed no counts; a truncated file failed with a readable message and an Import button never appeared.
  • Backend: ruff, black, mypy (234 source files) clean; 1942 unit tests pass (1803 at the start of Week 54), 2 skipped. Web: 236 tests (+16), tsc clean, npm run build clean.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• The fuzzing is a smoke run, not a campaign. 90 s per parser found nothing, which is weak evidence. The nightly CI job (fuzz-ingest) is written and the harness is proven to run, but that job has never executed on a CI runner; the real depth comes from it running for weeks.
  • Each format is exercised against the producers I could run. CycloneDX and SPDX: Syft and Grype only (other generators, e.g. cdxgen or Trivy, may use features not seen). SARIF: real Semgrep output plus a hand-written file shaped like CodeQL's (results before rules, ruleIndex, lower-case CWE tags, security-severity); no real CodeQL file was tested. OSV: OSV-Scanner results only -- a bare OSV advisory record is deliberately not importable.
  • SPDX imports no findings, by design, and reads only SPDX 2.x JSON (not tag-value, RDF or 3.0). An SBOM becomes useful as a component inventory in a later week; until then it is recognised, validated, and cannot close anything.
  • "Your own runners switch to the same ingest path" is true at the decision-and-writer level, not the HTTP level. Native scans now call the same plan_reimport and the same Issue writer (and emit the same outbox events), but a scan does not POST to /v2/ingest. The plan's wording could mean either; this is the version that removes the duplicated logic without routing every scan through an upload.
  • The outbox has no consumer. Events (issue.created, issue.reopened, issue.closed, scan.completed, import.reverted) are written in the same transaction as the change, which is the property that matters, but nothing dispatches or prunes them yet; the first consumers are the SLA, rules and notification weeks. Until then the table only grows.
  • Per-source deduplication (plan §42.3) is not built (Week 58). wait_for_dedup is accepted and dedup_complete is always true; every source matches by the same project-level fingerprints, and the screen's Matching row is read-only text for that reason. source only accepts upload.
  • The screen is thinner than the wireframe in two places. Issues are listed by the first eight characters of their id (there is no human-friendly ISS-311 numbering yet), and "Into [Change]" edits a Test name and a choice of engagement type rather than browsing existing engagements (that list arrives with Week 64). It was verified in a real browser once and by 15 jsdom tests with axe; there is no Playwright journey (Week 74).
  • Issue identity is still project-level and fingerprint-based, so two tools describing one defect in different words import as two Issues until the matching work in Week 58.
  • detached is not shown as a fifth big number on the screen (it appears as a sentence), because the plan's wireframe has four.
  • The §39.5 gate item that needs a live model is still open (the fix agent's verification record on a real pull request), unchanged from Week 53.
  • Preview expiry is 24 hours, fixed. It is a constant in the maintenance task, not a setting, and the sweep is covered by unit tests but has not run under a live Celery beat.

docs.title: Weeks 57-59 verification -- Ported parsers and deduplication (plan Phase 14, §42.2-§42.3)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run and measured. Weeks 57 (ported parsers, batch 1), 58 (batch 2 and per-source deduplication) and the dedup half of 59's neighbourhood were done as one body of work in seven tasks (the universal mapper and manual findings -- Week 59 -- are separate, later tasks). Decisions: ADR-0041 (what identifies a DAST or network finding) and ADR-0042 (deduplication per source).

docs.title: What was built
docs.text: # Task Result 1 ZAP, Nuclei; DefectDojo fixtures; DAST identity two parsers, a vendoring script that reads DefectDojo's expected results out of its tests, ADR-0041 2 Burp, Nessus, OpenVAS three parsers; the first parser to admit a DTD (Burp's own), and only that 3 Sandbox hardening and throughput the parser container streams its result; an ingest throughput benchmark; fuzz runs 4 Grype, Trivy, Snyk parsers that read a report with the function a native scan uses (Grype, Trivy) or a two-pass reader (Snyk) 5 GitLab security reports, Checkov one parser for GitLab's five report types; Checkov 6 Dedup engine five strategies, versioned per-source settings (migration 0029), applied to imports and scans 7 Dedup dry run, API and screen preview/apply with merges and splits, wait_for_dedup, the Matching screen

docs.title: Bugs found and fixed along the way
docs.text:
1. DAST findings were merged, collapsed and made quadratic (the serious one; it predates this work and affected the native DAST campaigns). Found by importing a real ZAP report, and it was three separate mechanisms: correlation saw every DAST finding "at the same place" (no file, no line) and merged any two alerts sharing a CWE; the fingerprint ignored the route; and the location-independent fallback key matched every URL an alert fired on to the first Issue made for it -- 130 findings of one report became 15 Issues. All three fixed (ADR-0041); the regression tests fail without each fix, the quadratic one in 34 s. One consequence: existing DAST Issues are re-created once.
  2. The parser sandbox ran out of memory at ~250,000 findings and said "try again." Found pushing 95 MB reports through the real container. The worker built three copies of the findings; it now writes them as it parses (300,000 findings in 18 s), partial findings of an unreadable file are never built, and a timed-out or killed container says so instead of "try again".
  3. Burp's own DOCTYPE would have made every real Burp file unreadable under the rule that refuses all DTDs. iter_xml(allow_dtd=True) admits an internal element declaration and nothing else; an entity or an external DTD is still an error (tested, including inside the container).
  4. A stdlib HTML parser used to strip markup from ZAP descriptions took 2.3 s on 20,000 characters of hostile markup (quadratic); replaced by RE2.
  5. -1 (ZAP's "no CWE") was read as CWE-1 by a too-loose pattern.
  6. A Nessus CSV in DefectDojo's own samples has 75 where 7.5 was meant; as a CVSS score that turned a High into a Critical. Impossible scores are now ignored, with a warning.
  7. Trivy showed NVD's CVSS beside a severity another source (GitHub) had decided; it now shows the score of the source that decided (found by comparing with DefectDojo's expected results).
  8. Test-suite finds (not product bugs, but they would have lied): three "no prefix reads complete" property tests had a wrong boundary condition and failed intermittently under Hypothesis; found by running them repeatedly, and fixed by saying precisely what a cut at a row boundary is.
  9. Three of my own mutation checks silently mutated nothing (a pattern that matched a docstring, a git checkout on an untracked file, a str.replace that did not match after reformatting) and "survived"; each was redone until it really changed the code and was killed.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• DefectDojo's own sample reports and the results its tests expect. scripts/sync-dd-fixtures.py reads the expected values (counts, titles, severities, rule ids, CWEs, CVSS, locations, components) out of DefectDojo's unit tests with ast and vendors the samples from a pinned commit. 156 sample files, 135 count expectations and 319 field expectations across the ten ported parsers all agree, except 12 differences and 2 deliberate refusals, each recorded in tests/unit/test_ingest_defectdojo.py with its reason (examples: DefectDojo titles a Tenable.io finding with the asset's name; folds every licence into a finding; folds same-text SAST findings on different lines; keeps GET and DELETE of one URL apart). Two Grype samples over 3 MB are not vendored; they were checked locally against the pinned hashes (1,509 and 1,567 findings, both matching).
  • Same function as a native scan. An uploaded Grype, Trivy or Checkov report yields exactly the findings the native adapter yields from the same bytes (golden outputs of the project's own images); the ZAP and Nuclei readings are shared with the native DAST adapters.
  • Independent oracles, not our own parser: a ZAP reimport's new/unchanged/closed counts equal the set arithmetic of the XML (stdlib ElementTree); a Nessus reimport after removing one plugin from one host closes exactly that one; after a real dedup change on real Postgres, reimporting the second ZAP scan gave 4 new / 14 unchanged / 1 closed, equal to a title-set oracle computed from the XML.
  • Real Postgres under Row-Level Security as the non-superuser worker role: 61 integration tests pass, including a dedup merge and its inverse split (foreign keys, the (project, category, fingerprint) uniqueness) and another org being unable to read, preview or apply anything to a project it does not own.
  • The real sandbox container: every ported parser, smallest and largest vendored sample, gives the same findings in the container as in-process; a Burp entity and a ZAP external entity are refused inside it; a dense 300,000-row CSV parses; 525,000 rows is refused for the findings limit with that reason.
  • Fuzzing, for real, briefly. Atheris in a Linux container, 10 parsers: batch 1 (zap, nuclei, burp, nessus, openvas) 246,598 runs, batch 2 (grype, trivy, snyk, gitlab, checkov) 422,471 runs in 60 s each; no crash or hang. (Batch 1's wall clock ran long because the machine slept mid-run; the run counts are what libFuzzer reported.)
  • A real browser against the real stack (local API and Next dev server on the throwaway Postgres): the Matching screen listed the sources, a preview of hashing ZAP by title said "would merge 75 issues into 9 and split none" (81 Issues -> 15), applying it moved all 130 occurrences, recorded version 1 with its effect, an outbox event and an audit entry, and a reimport afterwards matched by the new key.
  • Throughput (benchmarks/ingest_throughput.py, results in benchmarks/results/ingest-2026-10-04.json, files tiled from real samples to ~95 MB, Postgres under RLS, Apple silicon laptop):
Report Records Parse only (peak) Parse + prepare (peak) Whole import to Postgres (peak) Nessus XML, 95 MB 27,342 1.4 s, 19,000/s (31 MB) 2.3 s (236 MB) 11.4 s, 2,400/s (516 MB) SARIF, 95 MB 117,504 3.9 s, 30,000/s (31 MB) 7.7 s (745 MB) 32.0 s, 3,700/s (1.5 GB)
  • Mutation checks. Each of these makes tests fail: removing the DAST correlation guard, the host or route from the fingerprint, the DAST fallback exclusion; Burp's DTD allowance; the Nessus score bands; the OpenVAS "not Done" rule; CSV strictness and the ragged-row check; the Checkov counters-only rule; the GitLab location classifier; the dedup digest check, triage reset, ticket repointing, fallback clearing and oldest-survivor rule; and, in the screen, preview clearing on edit, the apply guards, the digest, and the field requirement.
  • Backend: ruff, black, mypy (251 source files) clean; 2,322 unit tests collected, all pass (the one pre-commit CLI test needs .venv/bin on PATH). Web: 247 tests, tsc clean, npm run build clean.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• Deduplication quality is not measured. The plan's evaluation is precision and recall against hand-labelled duplicate pairs from three tools across ten repositories. That corpus does not exist. benchmarks/dedup_strategies.py measures only what each strategy changes on real reports (for example tool_id merges GitLab's 467 SAST findings into 109 Issues; on the DAST tools it changes nothing, by design) -- not whether the change is right.
  • Real ZAP and Nuclei output was not produced here. Their samples are DefectDojo's; ZAP's JSON report has no real sample (the JSON test is built from a real XML one), and the images to run them were not pulled. Everything else was checked against real files, but ZAP versions after 2.16 and Nuclei's newest JSON are untested. (2026-10-08: real ZAP 2.17.0 JSON reports of Juice Shop are now vendored in tests/fixtures/dast. They showed ZAP lists only a sample of an alert's places, so reimport was closing Issues at places still affected; a place now closes only once its rule is gone from the host -- ADR-0041's amendment.)
  • Closing is not scoped to the hosts a report covers: a Nessus or OpenVAS report covering fewer hosts than the last one lists the missing hosts' Issues as closed. The preview shows the count, and the docs say so; making it host-aware is not done (ADR-0041).
  • The fuzzing is minutes, not weeks, and the nightly job (now 14 parsers) has not run on CI.
  • Throughput numbers are for tiled real files, more uniform than a real 100 MB scan, on one laptop; the whole import at 117,000 findings peaks at 1.5 GB in the importing process, and the dry run has not been measured on a very large project.
  • Request and response bodies in ZAP and Burp reports are not stored (one line each is kept); the HTTP method is not part of a DAST finding's identity, so GET and POST of one URL with one check are one Issue.
  • CI results for these commits have not been observed (no gh here), and nothing is pushed or tagged.
  • The fix agent's verification record on a real pull request and the five LLM-gated evaluation rows are still open (they need a live model).

docs.title: Weeks 59-60 verification -- Universal mapper, manual findings, connectors (plan Phase 14, §42.4-§43.2)
docs.text:
Honest record of what was built, run and measured, done as four commits. Decisions: ADR-0043 (a saved mapping is a deterministic, sandboxed parser), ADR-0044 (manual findings are an ingest source; evidence is encrypted and only downloaded), ADR-0045 (connectors pull through the ingest path and never close on a pull they cannot trust).

M13 is closed and v2.2.0 is tagged (2026-10-05). The round trip with a real DefectDojo, the one item open after the first three commits, was run in a fourth -- and found two bugs that every recorded-shape test had passed (below).

docs.title: What was built
docs.text: # Commit Result 59.1 Universal mapper MappingSpec + a small path language; UniversalParser streams in the parser sandbox; sample analysis in the sandbox; drafts by the model (checked against the sample) or by name matching; versioned, tenant-isolated mappings (migration 0030); the Map a format screen; saved mappings offered on the import screen 59.2 Manual findings CVSS 4.0 (cvss library); CWE picker; routes from code intelligence (scans.entrypoints, migration 0031); correlation to automation's taint path; evidence sniffed, encrypted with OpenBao, downloaded only through a signed link; the Record a finding form and a panel on the issue page 60 Connectors GitHub code scanning and Dependabot (GitHub App), GitLab (GraphQL), DefectDojo in and out; SSRF-guarded client; health, backoff, run history (migration 0032); Celery beat; the Connectors screen M13 DefectDojo round trip Run against DefectDojo 3.3.300; two connector bugs fixed; tests/integration/test_defectdojo_live.py; a recorded page of real findings as a unit-test fixture

docs.title: The DefectDojo round trip (M13)
docs.text:
DefectDojo 3.3.300 (the latest release, 2026-09-28), from its own docker-compose.yml with the images pinned to that tag, on localhost:8180; an API v2 key minted for its admin user inside the container. tests/integration/test_defectdojo_live.py runs Bulwark's real API, connector service and HTTP client (with its SSRF guard, private hosts allowed) against it; it makes fresh products each run.

Direction What happened In DefectDojo's own parsers imported a Bandit, an Anchore Grype and a ZAP report (DefectDojo's sample files) into a product: 13 active findings. The import connector pulled all 13 in 6 requests (the product, then five pages of 3 -- the test's page size; Bulwark asks for 100 -- by DefectDojo's own next links) and made 13 Issues -- code, package and web findings each read as such: file and line, package and CVE, severity. Pulled again: the same pull, not applied twice. A finding closed in DefectDojo (active: false) was closed in Bulwark on the next pull. Out A project's 3 open Issues (a real Semgrep SARIF) were exported: DefectDojo created the product, engagement and a "Bulwark Scan (SARIF)" Test, with the 3 findings on the same files and lines. Bulwark then closed one; the next export reimported into the same Test and DefectDojo closed it there: 2 active. Back That product pulled into a second project: 2 Issues on the files, lines and severities they left from, and none of them exported again (no echo). Screen The Connectors screen against the same instance: the export and import connectors Healthy (2 sent, 12 pulled, "12 new, 0 reopened, 0 closed"), and a connector for a product that does not exist Failing with "DefectDojo product 424242: not found (HTTP 404)". A wrong key: "the credential was refused (HTTP 403)".

docs.title: Bugs the round trip found (every recorded-shape test had passed)
docs.text:
1. The import connector pulled every product's findings. DefectDojo's findings API ignores a filter it does not know, and ?product=<id> -- what the connector sent, and what the documented example shapes could not reveal -- is not one: each of three products returned all 39 findings of the instance. A connector for one product would have imported every product its key can read. The filter is now test__engagement__product; the product is fetched first (a wrong id is a 404, not "fetched nothing"); and every finding is asked for with its related_fields, so one from another product refuses the whole pull. Checked live: with the old filter put back on the wire, the guard refuses ("finding 1 from outside product 7 ... nothing was imported").
  2. The export could not create its product: HTTP 400, "Product ... does not exist and no product_type_name provided". It now sends a product type (default "Bulwark", settable on the screen), and a 4xx's reason now reaches the connector's health instead of a bare "HTTP 400".

Also from the real data: newer DefectDojo lists CWEs in cwes ([{"cwe": "CWE-614"}], where ZAP's is; the old cwe field was 0), now read; and fix_version becomes the remediation. One real page -- a Bandit, a Grype and a ZAP finding as DefectDojo 3.3.300 returns them -- is now a unit-test fixture (tests/golden/connectors/defectdojo-3.3.300-findings-page.json), so CI checks the real shape.

After the fixes: 2,438 unit tests pass (4 skipped, coverage 92%), 274 web tests, the three live round-trip tests; ruff, black, mypy (272 files) and tsc clean. Versions are 2.2.0 in pyproject.toml and web/package.json (both had stayed at 2.0.0 through v2.1.0; the changelog's 2.1.0 section is now separated out too).

docs.title: Found, not fixed here
docs.text: • On SQLite (the scratch and end-to-end servers) timestamps lose their time zone, so the screen read a run from seconds earlier as "6 hours ago" in IST. Postgres keeps the zone; this affects every screen on SQLite, not connectors, and is queued as its own task.

docs.title: M13, item by item
docs.text:
• "At least 15 formats." The plan's own list (§42.2, "Order of work") counts "generic JSON and CSV through the universal mapper" as one item, beside SARIF, CycloneDX, SPDX, OSV and the ported tool formats. Built: SARIF, CycloneDX (JSON and XML), SPDX, OSV, ZAP, Burp, Nuclei, Nessus, OpenVAS, Grype, Trivy, Snyk, GitLab security reports, Checkov (14 parsers), and generic JSON, CSV and XML through saved mappings: 15 by the plan's count. (Without the mapper it is 14.)
  • "3 connectors." Five kinds are built (GitHub code scanning, GitHub Dependabot, GitLab, DefectDojo in, DefectDojo out). Only DefectDojo has run against a live instance with data; see below for what that leaves unproven about the others.
  • "Deduplication can be changed per source with a dry run" -- Week 58 (ADR-0042).
  • "A round trip with a real DefectDojo instance is recorded" -- above.

docs.title: Bugs found and fixed along the way (Weeks 59-60)
docs.text:
1. Correlation dropped a copied taint path. correlate() rebuilds each finding without its taint_path (scans attach theirs later, in finalize), so the path a manual finding inherited from automation vanished. Found by its own test; now attached after preparation.
  2. The issue page could not open an Issue only an import or a person reported -- "issue not found in the latest scan", for every imported Issue since Week 54. Found driving the manual finding flow in a browser. It now shows the Issue's most recent occurrence from any source; regression test added.
  3. GitLab hides what a viewer cannot read instead of refusing. A live, anonymous request to gitlab.com returned a valid page with no vulnerabilities and hasNextPage: true. The connector would have paged through a hundred empty pages and then failed with a misleading message. It is now reported as a permissions error on the first page (the real response is a fixture).
  4. Three tests that task 1 should have updated (the model gateway's task list, the fuzz matrix) were caught by the full suite and fixed in the next commit -- the task 1 commit ran only a subset.
  5. Layout: the mapper's path inputs were unreadably narrow, and CVSS options wrapped into the label column; both found by looking at the screens, both fixed.

docs.title: Validated against real, live things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• CVSS 4.0 against FIRST's own calculator. Eight vectors (9.3, 7.1, 5.3, 1.0, 8.1 with E:U, 8.7, 7.0, 6.3) scored on first.org/cvss/calculator/cvsscalc40; the library agrees on all eight and they are fixed in tests/unit/test_manual_findings.py.
  • GitLab against gitlab.com. The exact connector query ran against gitlab.com without a schema error; every field it selects is checked against an extract of gitlab.com's published GraphQL schema (tests/golden/connectors/gitlab-schema-extract.json). A connector with a bad token, run against gitlab.com through the real client and SSRF guard, reported "the credential was refused (HTTP 401)".
  • The real parser sandbox (Docker). A mapped report of 200 records parses to the same findings in the container as in-process; sample analysis is identical in both; a mapped XML report with an entity is refused inside the container (36 sandbox tests pass).
  • Real Postgres under Row-Level Security, as the non-superuser worker role, migrated to 0032: 50 integration tests pass, including new ones for mappings, manual findings and evidence, and connectors and their runs. Undoing the import that recorded a manual finding removes the finding and its evidence through the foreign-key cascade (which SQLite tests cannot exercise).
  • Fuzzing. Atheris in a Linux container, 60 s each: universal-json 151,760 runs, universal-csv 134,698, universal-xml 140,086, analyze 324,935; no crash or hang. The four targets joined the nightly matrix.
  • A real browser against the real API (local API with the real Docker sandbox, Next dev server): a JSON sample was described in the sandbox, drafted, edited (rule, a custom severity), previewed live (1.2 s per preview), saved, suggested on the import screen ("Closest match: Acme scanner (95%)") and imported ("Imported: 4 new"). A manual IDOR finding was scored 7.1 by the calculator, placed on its route's handler, linked to the seeded opengrep finding and its taint path, and shown on the issue page; its disguised HTML evidence was listed as text/html, "can contain script", and its signed download carried attachment, nosniff, a sandbox CSP and no-store; a forged link got 404. The Connectors screen showed a failing GitLab connector (HTTP 401) and a GitHub one ("the GitHub App is not configured"), with the verdict naming both.
  • Mutation checks. Removing the empty-pull hold-back, or the GitLab empty-page check, fails a test; the taint-path fix and the issue-page fix were each found by a failing test or screen first.
  • Backend: ruff, black, mypy (272 files) clean; 2,432 unit tests pass (4 skipped), coverage 90%. Web: 273 tests, tsc clean.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• One DefectDojo version. The round trip ran against 3.3.300 only. Older versions name the same things differently (cve and vulnerability_ids are both read); a version without related_fields would now be refused rather than trusted. DefectDojo's Endpoints (a web finding's URLs) are still not fetched, so a DAST finding from DefectDojo has no route.
  • No GitHub App is registered here, so the GitHub connectors were never run against GitHub. They are tested against response shapes taken from GitHub's documented examples. Dependabot does not report the installed version, so a Dependabot Issue uses the vulnerable range and will not merge with an OSV-Scanner Issue for the same package.
  • GitLab was reached, but never with a token that can read a vulnerability report (that needs GitLab Ultimate). The mapping of real nodes is tested on nodes shaped from the schema.
  • The mapping assistant's prompt was not evaluated (no local model here); its eval set exists (core/llm/prompts/mapper/). The draft's safety does not depend on its quality: every path is checked against the sample, a person saves the mapping, and imports never call a model.
  • Without OpenBao, connector credentials and evidence are stored unencrypted (the API and the screen say so), the same posture as scan artifacts. Encrypted paths are tested with a fake OpenBao, not a live one in this run.
  • Download links are signed with a deployment-wide key (BULWARK_LINK_SECRET, else derived from the API token), not a per-org key; serving them from a separate origin is configuration, not shown here.
  • "15 formats": there are 14 built-in parsers reading more than 20 file layouts, plus any number of saved mappings. Whether mappings count toward the milestone is a judgment call; they are not counted here.
  • CI results for these commits have not been observed (nothing pushed), and the one web test run that showed 10 failures under load did not reproduce on three re-runs.

docs.title: Weeks 61-62 verification -- SLA engine and risk acceptance (plan Phase 15, §44.1-§44.2, §55.3)
docs.text: Honest record of what was built, run and measured, done as two commits. Decision: ADR-0046 (deadlines are computed, never stored; accepting a risk takes a second person). Neither week ends a milestone: M14 and v2.3.0 come after Week 64.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text: # Commit Result 61 SLA engine Versioned SLA policies per project by severity (migration 0033, RLS); the clock from first detection, sla_started_at for restarts; on track / due soon / breached, met / missed, paused; issue.sla on every issue response and ?sla= on the issues table; a five-minute sweep announcing each crossing once (outbox event + Slack, Discord, webhook); the SLA page, an SLA column and filter, the deadline on the issue page 62 Risk acceptance risk_acceptances and their Issues (migration 0034, RLS); request, four-eyes approve and reject, withdraw, expire now, reinstate, extend, lapse; an expiry job that reopens Issues and can restart their SLA; proof links and encrypted proof files; triage can no longer accept alone; legacy acceptances migrated; the request form (§55.3), the Approvals queue and a page per acceptance

docs.title: Bugs found and fixed along the way
docs.text:
1. CORS refused every PUT, PATCH and DELETE -- found saving the SLA policy in a browser. Preflight allowed only GET and POST since the first CORS commit, so from the web app on its own origin (the default: web and API on different ports) these had never worked: threat model, retention, plugin allowlist and integration settings saves, and turning off or deleting a connector (Week 60). It now allows every method a route uses; a test enumerates them.
  2. A one-person bypass: triage's "accepted" action would have let anyone skip approval. It now answers 409 and points at the request; the old test that accepted through triage was rewritten.
  3. The issue page crashed on a non-list response for its acceptances (a real API error could do the same); guarded, as Week 59's manual-finding panel was.
  4. Found in the browser: people showed as token prefixes ("token:bulwark_083076"); responses now carry token names. The issue page showed two banners for one acceptance; now one. The request form's SLA checkbox sat above its text and the file picker had a redundant label; fixed.

docs.title: Validated against real things -- not mocks
docs.text:
• Real Postgres under forced Row-Level Security, as the worker role, migrated to 0034 (and down to 0032 and back up): 52 integration tests pass, two new. Another org sees no policy, no acceptance, and its sweep and expiry job touch nothing of the first org's; the issues-table SLA filter does its deadline arithmetic in Postgres and agrees with the rules.
  • The legacy migration on real Postgres under forced RLS (the migration sets each org's scope itself): two Issues accepted by one person with one reason and expiry became one approved legacy acceptance covering both; one past its date became an expired one; an untouched Issue was left alone; no Issue's triage or expiry changed.
  • A real browser against the real API (the end-to-end server, SQLite, Next dev server):
  • SLA: the starter policy saved as version 1; a Critical first seen 10 days ago showed "Breached · 3 days overdue", a High at 25 days "Due soon · 4 days left"; the Breached filter showed only the first; the issue page read "SLA: Breached · 3 days overdue (due 02/10/2026)".
  • Risk acceptance, with two personal tokens (Alice, Bob): Alice requested from the issues table (the approver list offered only Bob; "56 days · Policy maximum: 90 days"); the Issue stayed open. Alice's own approve call got 403 ("you requested this; someone else has to approve or reject it") and her page offered only Withdraw. Bob approved; the Issue became accepted until 30/11/2026 and its history read "Risk acceptance requested", "Risk acceptance approved". A second request with a link and a PNG proof file was approved by Bob and expired now: the Issue reopened, Reinstate was offered, and the trail read requested, proof added, approved, expired -- by name.
  • Mutation checks. Removing the "not the requester" rule fails three tests; removing the "not the shared token" rule fails two.
  • Backend: ruff, black, mypy (280 files) clean; 2,489 unit tests pass (4 skipped), coverage 92%. Web: 288 tests, tsc clean.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• "Someone else" is another API token, not another person. One person with two tokens can approve their own request. Real identities arrive with SSO and SCIM (Week 75).
  • Notifications were not delivered to a real Slack or Discord. Message text and routing are tested with the senders replaced; the senders themselves are the ones scan notifications use.
  • The sweep and the expiry job were run by tests and by hand, not by a running Celery beat; they are scheduled the same way as the connectors job (Week 60).
  • Priority bands (§44.1's alternative SLA basis) are not built; they need the priority engine (Week 63).
  • Scale. The sweep and expiry job read every open Issue of every org every five minutes; nothing here measured that on a large dataset.
  • Proof files without OpenBao are stored unencrypted, as manual-finding evidence is; the encrypted path is the same code, tested with a fake OpenBao in Week 59.
  • CI results for these commits have not been observed (nothing pushed).

docs.title: Week 63 verification: the priority engine v3 (plan Phase 15, §44.3, §55.7)
docs.text: This is a factual record of what was built, run and measured. Decision: ADR-0047. Week 63 does not end a milestone; M14 and v2.3.0 come after Week 64.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• Engine (core/priority/engine.py, pure): weights per factor as exponents, the KEV floor scaled by its weight, business context that only lowers, P1-P4 bands, and every factor recorded with its weight and multiplier.
  • Storage (migration 0035): priority_policies (versioned, forced RLS) and four new columns on issues. Every existing Issue is backfilled with its latest occurrence's v2 score, one organization at a time.
  • Writers: ingest (scan, import, DAST, manual finding), runtime confirmation, assistant verdict, hypothesis promotion, and the background recomputation (bulwark.recompute_priority, or in the API process when there is no worker).
  • API: GET/PUT /v2/projects/{id}/priority, POST …/priority/preview, issue.priority on every issue response, ?priority= on the issues table, sorting by priority, and SLA basis priority.
  • Web: the Priority page (business context, a slider per factor, the before-and-after top 50, Issues leaving it, band counts, recompute progress, history), a Priority column and P1-P4 filter on the issues table, weights in "Why it's ranked here", and severity or priority band on the SLA page.

docs.title: Found and fixed along the way
docs.text:
1. Business context inflated whole projects into P1. The first design boosted exposed projects (internet-facing ×1.2, restricted ×1.3, critical ×1.3). In the browser, on a seeded 2,500-Issue project, that moved 770 Issues to P1 and tied the whole top 50 at 100. Context now only lowers, and unset means the worst case. On the same project, describing it as an internal, low-criticality wiki took P1 from 84 to 9. All 9 left are CISA KEV entries, whose floor ignores context by design.
  2. A promoted hypothesis never stored its risk score (since Week 43), so it sorted last. It now does, and gets a priority.
  3. Found in the browser:
  4. The new table column broke the issues table's grid: titles were pushed right and "Rule" wrapped. The grid now has the column, with narrower tracks on phones.
  5. A global label style rendered every factor description as uppercase monospace.
  6. The History table made the page scroll sideways on a phone.
  7. The sliders did not report a server field error to assistive technology. A web test caught this one.

docs.title: Checked against real systems, not mocks
docs.text:
• The v2 score is reproduced exactly. More than 1,000 findings (every severity, CVSS or not, KEV, EPSS from 0.04% to 90%, no exploit data, no CVE id, code findings by confidence, three reachability states, every assistant verdict) are scored by core.risk.score_finding, then by the engine with v2's weights. Every score is equal.
  • Real Postgres with forced RLS, as the worker role: 53 integration tests pass, one of them new. Another org sees no policy. A recompute run the way the worker runs it re-ranks only its own project. The preview sees no other org's Issues, and the band filter runs in Postgres. With RLS turned off on priority_policies, the new test fails.
  • Migration 0035 on Postgres with seeded data from two orgs:
  • An Issue with occurrences scored 40 (older) and 85 (newer) got 85 and P1.
  • A score of 59 got P3, at the boundary.
  • An Issue with no occurrence stayed unranked.
  • The second org was backfilled too.
  • Downgrade to 0034 removed the columns, and upgrading again worked.
  • The backfill statements, run as the worker role, update 0 rows without the org scope and every row with it. That is why the migration sets the scope per organization (the container's owner role is a superuser, so the migration run itself does not prove this).
  • A real browser against the real API (SQLite, 2,500 seeded Issues, Next dev server):
  • Preview, save, then "Waiting to apply…" followed by "Applied to 2,500 issues; 1,586 changed band".
  • The issues table sorted by the new priority.
  • An issue's panel read "P4 · 15/100" with each factor's weight and multiplier. The arithmetic was checked by hand: 100 × 0.95 × 0.95 × 1.1 × 0.36 × 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.65 = 14.9.
  • An SLA by priority band saved as version 1.
  • Speed at this size (SQLite, one process, 2,500 Issues): recompute 227 ms, preview 169 ms.
  • Unit tests:
  • 53 new tests covering the engine, validation, the lock, a stale lock taken over, two saves racing, superseded and failed jobs, a job taken over mid-run, ingest under a policy, rescoring, the preview, org isolation, and the SLA by band.
  • Removing the lock check, or the unique-version guard, fails a test.
  • Web: 298 tests (10 new, including axe), tsc clean.

docs.title: What this does not prove
docs.text:
• Scale. No project larger than 2,500 Issues was measured, and none on Postgres. The preview loads every open Issue's latest occurrence in one request.
  • The Celery path was not run with a live worker. The task is a thin wrapper around the same service.recompute the tests and the browser run exercised.
  • The lock was not seen holding in the browser. A 2,500-Issue recompute finished before a second save could be sent. The 409 is covered by API tests.
  • The new factor strengths are judgment calls, as v2's were, and are not validated against outcomes.
  • Recomputation uses EPSS and KEV as stored at scan time, not today's feeds.
  • CI results for this commit have not been observed (nothing pushed).

docs.title: Week 64 verification: assessments, retests and collaboration (plan §43.1, §43.3, §49, §55.2)
docs.text: A factual record of what was built, run and measured. The decision is ADR-0048. This week ends Phase 15 (Governance); milestone M14 is assessed at the end.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• Assessments. Scope, lead and testers, dates, and a lifecycle (planned, in progress, reporting, closed). An optional OWASP checklist: WSTG 4.2 (114 tests) or ASVS 4.0.3 at L1, L2 or L3 (128, 259 or 278 requirements), shipped from OWASP's tagged releases with credit.
  • The engagement screen (§55.2). Every finding the engagement's uploads reported, with what else reports it and where its retest stands; its tests; "Add a finding" and "Import results" into it; "Close and write the report". There are also a project's engagement list and the checklist page.
  • The report. A snapshot taken on closing, downloadable as Markdown or HTML.
  • Retests. Mark ready, confirm fixed, reproduce (with a note), or cancel. The next scan or upload decides for scanner Issues. A targeted retest runs one rule against one file, or one DAST template against one URL.
  • Notes. Threaded, plain text, with @mentions, a Mentions page and files on notes.
  • The attachments origin is enforced when configured; the setting is now in Compose and Helm.
  • Tags on portfolios, projects and Issues, inherited downward, with ?tag= on the issues table. A project can belong to a portfolio.
  • Migration 0036. Four new tables, all under forced RLS, and new columns on engagements, Issues, assets and attachments.

docs.title: Found and fixed along the way
docs.text:
1. Found by the browser run:
  2. The issue page scrolled sideways whenever an issue had a long title (Opengrep's titles are full sentences). Two causes: the root grid's implicit column grew to its widest line, and the title had no min-width: 0. This predated the week.
  3. The targeted-retest line's long rule id widened the sidebar.
  4. The tests table on the engagement screen inherited the global table-header band.
  5. The portfolio dropdown was four lines tall: a flex rule meant for a row was setting its height.
  6. "Fix first" on the project overview still listed an Issue a targeted retest had just confirmed fixed. It now skips those, as the issues table does.
  7. The report named its author as a token prefix, gave UTC dates without saying so, and over-escaped Markdown (api\.acme\.example). It now names the person, labels UTC, and escapes only what Markdown acts on.
  8. "Also found by sarif" named a parser; it now names the other Test ("Also found by Nessus").
  9. Found by the tests:
  10. A token named "Arjun K." got the handle arjunk., so @arjunk mentioned nobody.
  11. Weight sliders never reported a field error to assistive technology (Week 63; fixed then, and the same wiring was used here).
  12. An unexpected API response would crash the whole issue page through the tags panel. Every new panel now checks a response's shape.
  13. Undo. Undoing an upload did not undo the retest outcome it had decided. The undo record now carries the retest state.

docs.title: Checked against real systems, not mocks
docs.text:
• A real targeted retest. A sample repository was scanned by the real bulwark/opengrep image (2 findings).
  • From the Issue page, "Run the targeted retest" re-ran only rule bulwark-py-subprocess-shell-true on only app/report.py, on a fresh copy of the repository. The result was "still fires on app/report.py:5": the retest failed and the Issue stayed open.
  • After the code was fixed, the same button gave "no longer fires": the retest passed and the Issue was marked fixed.
  • The Issue's history records both runs.
  • A pen test end to end, in a browser against the real API (SQLite, Next dev server, two named test tokens):
  • Created "Q4 external pentest" through the form.
  • Recorded a CVSS 4.0 IDOR finding through "Add a finding", which went into the engagement.
  • Imported a two-result SARIF report into a "Burp Suite" test.
  • Recorded a pass and a fail, with a note, on the WSTG checklist ("2 of 114 done").
  • Priya marked the IDOR ready for retest, with a note.
  • Arjun, signed in separately, found Priya's @mention under Mentions. He reproduced the IDOR; the button stayed disabled until he wrote a note.
  • Built a portfolio "Payments" with tag pci-dss; the project then showed it as inherited.
  • Closed the engagement with a summary. The Markdown report has the scope, team, the failed checklist item with its note, the three findings with reproduction steps and CVSS vector, the tests, and OWASP credit.
  • The attachments origin, over real HTTP. An HTML "capture" containing a script was attached to a note; the server sniffed it as active content.
  • Its signed link pointed at attachments.localhost, which returned the bytes as application/octet-stream with attachment, nosniff and a sandbox CSP.
  • The same link on the API's own host returned 404, and the attachments host returned 404 for an API route.
  • Real Postgres under forced RLS, as the worker role: all 54 integration tests pass, one of them new.
  • Another org sees none of the new rows (checklist results, notes, targeted runs, tags, Issues, engagements), cannot open the engagement by id, and its tag filter matches nothing of the first org's.
  • With RLS turned off on issue_notes, the new test fails.
  • Migration 0036 on Postgres with two orgs' engagements:
  • Standing ci and import engagements kept "active"; an active pen test became "in progress" and a completed audit became "closed"; lists were set to empty.
  • Downgrade restored "active" and "completed", and upgrading again worked.
  • Its data updates, run as the worker role, change 0 rows without the org scope and 2 with it.
  • Mutation checks. Each of these, removed, fails a test: enforcing the attachments origin, the author-only rule on notes, scans deciding retests, and HTML escaping in the report.
  • Totals.
  • Backend: 2,591 unit tests pass (55 new), coverage 92%. ruff, black and mypy are clean, except one older import-order warning in tests/unit/test_dedup_strategies.py that also fails on a clean main.
  • Web: 307 tests (9 new, with axe checks) and tsc are clean.

docs.title: What this does not prove
docs.text:
• People are API tokens. A lead, a tester and a mention are names, and one person with two tokens is two people. Real accounts arrive in Week 75.
  • The DAST targeted retest was not run against a live target. Its plumbing (verification first, egress proxy, one Nuclei template via -id) is tested with the runner replaced.
  • The Celery path was not run with a live worker, for targeted retests or anything else this week. The task wraps the same targeted.run the browser exercised.
  • Downloads were checked over HTTP, not by clicking. The download buttons for attachments and reports were not clicked in the browser, to avoid saving files. They call the endpoints checked above.
  • The Import results page was not driven through its file picker. The import used the same endpoint the page calls. The page's engagement wiring is covered by its code path and tests.
  • Mention and retest notifications are outbox events only. Delivery to Slack, email and an inbox is Weeks 65–66.
  • Scale. Mentions are found by reading an org's notes, and an engagement's findings by reading every upload into it. Neither was measured at size.
  • CI results for this commit have not been observed (nothing pushed).

docs.title: Milestone M14: Governance
docs.text:
The plan's test: "A pen test runs end to end inside the platform. SLAs and risk acceptance are enforced, and every decision is in the audit log."

  • End to end. The browser run above covered scope, findings, import, checklist, retest, notes and the report.
  • Enforced. The server enforces SLAs and risk acceptance, including four-eyes approval (Weeks 61–62).
  • Audited. Every decision a person makes is a hash-chained audit entry. That covers triage, risk acceptance, SLA and priority policies, engagement changes and checklist results, retest decisions, notes and tags. Outcomes decided by a scan or upload are outbox events, because they are results rather than decisions.

M14 is met, with the limits above.

docs.title: Week 65 verification: the rules engine (plan §45, threat T26)
docs.text: A factual record of what was built, run and measured. The decision is ADR-0049.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• Rules. WHEN a trigger, IF a Rego condition, THEN up to eight actions, for one project or every project, with a confirmation threshold. Versioned, audited, deletable (history kept).
  • Triggers. Issue found, back, fixed, assigned; retest requested or decided; SLA due soon or breached; risk acceptance expiring within seven days (new: announced once by the expiry sweep) or expired; scan or import completed; no scan for N days; schedules (hourly, daily, weekly, UTC).
  • Conditions. Rego bodies against input.issue, input.project, input.event, evaluated in batches by OPA with http.send, net.lookup_ip_addr and opa.runtime removed and no network.
  • Actions. Assign, set a priority band (a new override that wins wherever a band is read), add tags, mark ready for retest, request a verified fix, notify Slack, Discord and the outbound webhook.
  • Safety. Dry run over the last seven days, bulk confirmation, a depth limit of three, the AI budget and a daily cap on fix requests, the rules:write scope, an audit entry per run and per change, and redelivery that never acts twice.
  • The outbox dispatcher (core.dispatch), every ten seconds on the worker, under a per-org advisory lock; the rules sweep every five minutes.
  • Screens. An Automation page (held runs first, rules as WHEN / IF / THEN, "Test this rule", on and off, delete, run history) and an Owner panel on the issue page (assignee and a priority by hand, naming the rule when a rule set them). Creating and editing rules on screen is Week 66.
  • API. /v2/rules (catalogue, CRUD, enable, test a draft or a rule), /v2/rule-runs (list, confirm, dismiss) and /v2/issues/{id}/assignee and /priority.
  • Migration 0037. automation_rules and rule_runs under forced RLS; assignee and priority override on Issues; when an acceptance's expiry warning went out; waiting outbox events marked dispatched.
  • OPA in the app image, pinned to 1.21.0 and checked against the published SHA-256.

docs.title: Found and fixed along the way
docs.text:
1. Found by the tests:
  2. Runs first de-duplicated by subject within a cause. Two assignments of the same Issue in the same minute (a person, then a rule) are one cause, so the second was silently skipped. Runs now record (event, subject) pairs; the depth-limit test caught it.
  3. An action that failed rolled back the session, and with it the uncommitted record of the run it belonged to: the run vanished. The run is now committed before it acts.
  4. A quiet stretch was keyed to the second; two scans in the same second looked like one stretch. It is keyed to the full timestamp.
  5. Found in the browser:
  6. Confirming a held run did not update the rule's "last acted" time.
  7. The history said "Priority set by hand by the rule …"; it now says "Priority set by the rule …".
  8. Found while reading the code: issue titles go into Slack and Discord messages, and titles come from scanners reading other people's code. Slack text is now escaped (<!channel> cannot ping a channel) and Discord gets an empty allowed_mentions (@everyone pings nobody).

docs.title: Checked against real systems
docs.text:
• OPA 1.21.0 evaluates every condition in the unit tests (no mock). http.send, opa.runtime and net.lookup_ip_addr fail to compile with OPA's own message; line numbers in errors are the condition's own.
  • Speed. One opa eval for 1, 100 and 500 inputs: median 12, 12 and 15 ms (p95 14, 13, 15 ms) on this Mac. A scan with 500 new Issues through a rule that matched 50 of them: 551 events dispatched, 50 priorities set, one run and 52 audit entries, in 0.1 s on in-memory SQLite.
  • Postgres under forced RLS (throwaway pgvector container, worker role): 55 integration tests pass, one new. A rule fires from the outbox through the advisory lock (a second dispatcher holding the lock gets nothing); another org sees no rules, runs, tags, Issues or events, cannot open the rule, and its dispatcher finds nothing. With RLS turned off on automation_rules, the new test fails.
  • Migration 0037 on Postgres: three waiting events in two orgs were marked dispatched; downgrade removed the tables and columns; upgrading again worked. alembic check reports nothing for the new tables or columns (its other differences predate this week).
  • The app image builds for arm64 with the checksum verified, and opa version runs inside it.
  • In a browser against the real API (SQLite, a thread standing in for Celery beat, three named tokens; Meera holds rules:write):
  • Three rules existed before a second scan brought five new Issues. "Critical issues go to Priya, as P1" assigned, set P1 and tagged the one new critical Issue; "Tag every new issue" (threshold 3) held its five.
  • The Automation page showed the held run first with its five Issues; "Apply to all 5" tagged them.
  • "Test this rule" said "would have matched 2 issues in the last 7 days" -- including the critical Issue from before the rule existed, which the rule itself (correctly) never touched.
  • The issue page named the rule for the assignment and the P1, with "computed P3"; its history named both rules. Reassigning to Arjun from the dropdown saved and showed Arjun.
  • At phone width the Automation page has no sideways scroll of its own (the shell's header still overflows, as before this week).
  • Totals. Backend unit tests: 2,610 pass (19 new for rules), coverage 92%; ruff (apart from the older import-order warning), black and mypy clean. Web: 312 tests (5 new, with axe), tsc clean.

docs.title: What this does not prove
docs.text:
• No Celery worker ran. The dispatcher and sweep tasks wrap the same drain and sweep the tests and the browser run used.
  • Request a verified fix was tested with the agent's start replaced: Temporal was not running.
  • Notify was tested with Slack and Discord replaced; nothing was posted anywhere.
  • Rule latency under sustained load (plan §60) was measured later, with a synthetic event stream: benchmarks/README.md (2026-10-12).
  • "Admin" is a token scope until roles exist (Week 75).
  • The rule editor, its template gallery, notification channels and ticket actions are Week 66.

docs.title: Week 66 verification: rules editor, notifications, tickets (plan §49, §45, §55.7)
docs.text: A factual record of what was built, run and measured. The decision is ADR-0050.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• The rules editor (§55.7). Trigger, condition and action builders; a Rego view showing the module OPA runs; "Test this rule" on the unsaved draft; OPA's errors by the condition; editing an existing rule. A gallery of nine templates on the Automation page, each saying what it still needs.
  • New rule actions: put in a group, file or update its ticket; notify can name people.
  • Notifications (§49). Watchers (automatic from taking part, or by hand). An inbox with an unread count in the header. Email through the operator's SMTP server. For each of eight kinds of event, in-app off or instant and email off, instant or daily digest, per person, with an address and a digest hour. For the team channels -- Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams (new) and the outbound webhook -- four kinds, each off, instant or digest. A settings page for both.
  • Tickets (§49). Per-project settings: Jira or GitHub Issues, who owns the status, and a status map. Filing (an Issue, or its group), syncing both ways by webhook, a ten-minute poll, and "Sync now". A ticket panel on the issue page with its status, assignee and group.
  • Issue groups, one ticket each, made on the issue page or by a rule.
  • Migration 0038. notifications, issue_watchers, notification_prefs, issue_groups and ticket_configs under forced RLS; issues.group_id; what a ticket last said on its link; a Teams webhook in integration settings.
  • Deployment. BULWARK_SMTP_* and BULWARK_PUBLIC_URL in Compose and the Helm chart (password in the chart's secret); helm lint passes.

docs.title: Found and fixed along the way
docs.text:
1. Found by sending real email to Mailpit: an issue title containing a line break stayed out of the headers (Python's email package folded it into the Subject, no Bcc header was added), but in the plain-text body it started a new line, so a title could fake a line of a digest. Titles are now one line wherever they go.
  2. Found in the browser:
  3. A native scan's completion event carried no counts (only an import's did), so a rule reading input.scan.counts.new -- which the catalogue advertises -- never matched a scan. Scans now count their new, reopened and closed Issues.
  4. After a ticket sync marked the Issue ready for retest, the retest panel on the same page still said "no retest requested". The panels that show it now reload.
  5. A new ticket showed "not read yet, synced never" until someone pressed Sync. Filing now reads it once (a first read never acts).
  6. When a ticket asked for a retest, the watcher got two notifications saying the same thing, one of them naming the actor as ticket:PAY-1. Now one, in words; the retest panel says "asked by its ticket, PAY-1".
  7. The editor's dropdowns were each a full line wide (a global stylesheet sets every select to 100%); rows now sit on one line. The settings table's row labels had the global table-header style. The template hint read "action 1, to"; it now says "choose who action 1 assigns to". "No rules yet." appeared twice.
  8. The assignment email's body said "Critical in the project."; it names the project.
  9. Found by the tests:
  10. The GitHub webhook handler reused the name of the app state for the issue state (mypy).
  11. Typing a second tag or person in the editor was impossible: the input dropped the trailing space.
  12. Found while reading the code: Jira's address was never checked by the SSRF guard (only the webhook URLs were), and the new poll calls it on a schedule. It is now checked when saved and before every call.

docs.title: Checked against real systems
docs.text:
• Email, through a real SMTP server (Mailpit v1.31.4 in Docker, axllent/mailpit@sha256:b68349e3…): an instant mention email, a daily digest with the pending assignment, and in the browser run the rule's assignment email to Priya. Raw messages read back: text/plain, Auto-Submitted: auto-generated, a link built from BULWARK_PUBLIC_URL, and no injected header.
  • In a browser against the real API (SQLite, a beat thread, Mailpit for email, three named tokens; Jira answered by the recorder below; Slack and Teams captured locally, nothing posted):
  • As Meera (Admin): opened "Critical issues go to the on-call" from the gallery; "Test this rule" without a person showed "Name a person by their @handle." under that action; with Priya chosen, "This rule would have matched 1 issue in the last 7 days"; the Rego view showed the module; saved.
  • As Priya: set email at once for assignments. A scan brought a new critical Issue: the rule assigned it to her and set P1; her inbox showed it with the unread count, and Mailpit received the email. On the issue page: watching (as assignee), "File a ticket in Jira" made PAY-1 and showed "To Do" at once; the ticket moved to "In Review" (mapped), "Sync now" showed it, the Issue became ready for retest "asked by its ticket, PAY-1", the history said "Marked ready for retest by its ticket, PAY-1", and her inbox said so once. A new group "Secrets in settings" from the panel.
  • A "scan completed" rule with the message <!channel> look at these reached Teams as an Adaptive Card with \<!channel\> and Slack as <!channel>: no channel was pinged.
  • At phone width the editor has no element wider than the page (the shell header still overflows, as before).
