This runs in a more permissive sandbox than every scanner (core/fixagent/sandbox.py): network enabled (to install dependencies), a writable checkout, default Docker capabilities rather than the scanner sandbox's --cap-drop=ALL/read-only/no-network. This is the plan's own "hardened Docker runner, for now" — ADR-0015 named Firecracker as the properly-isolated version of this: on a Linux host with KVM, BULWARK_TEST_SANDBOX=firecracker runs the tests in a microVM with no network at all, so the image must already hold the dependencies (sandbox-runtimes.md).

docs.title: Limits (ADR-0015)
docs.text:
Limit Value Env var Per attempt 10 minutes BULWARK_FIXAGENT_PER_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_S Overall (verification phase only — excludes the human-approval wait) 30 minutes BULWARK_FIXAGENT_OVERALL_TIMEOUT_S Attempts 3 BULWARK_FIXAGENT_MAX_ATTEMPTS Concurrent runs per organization 3 BULWARK_FIXAGENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_PER_ORG

A run stopped by a timeout resolves to inconclusive, never failed — a timeout is evidence verification didn't finish in time, not evidence the patch was wrong (ADR-0015). ended_reason on the run's own record says which limit ended it: overall_timeout, per_attempt_timeout, max_attempts_exhausted, or approval_timeout (a run nobody reviewed within 7 days — a hygiene limit, not one of ADR-0015's three).

docs.title: What leaves your machine
docs.text: The same things Week 41's remediation feature already sends (title, description, CWE/OWASP ids, file path, the code snippet — secret-scrubbed and PII-redacted first), plus: whatever the model asks read_file/search_code for during its tool-calling turn (also scrubbed and redacted before being sent back to it), and, once a human approves, the patched file's full content to GitHub via the Contents API.

docs.title: What this does NOT prove (read before relying on it)
docs.text:
• No live GitHub App run. create_pull_request is unit-tested against a fake transport, built from GitHub's documented API contract — not run against a real installation in this environment.
  • No live run against a real hosted model. The tool-calling loop is unit-tested against a fake Anthropic-shaped client covering the real control-flow paths — not run against the real API here.
  • No MLX/local tool-calling. Privacy mode (Week 41) does not cover verified-fix.
  • No "Edit" action on a pending patch — the plan's own mockup shows [Reject] [Edit] [Open pull request]; this ships the first and third.
  • No precise sandbox capability set for test execution — see above.

Full account in ADR-0027 and v2-week42-verification.md.

docs.title: VEX: telling customers which vulnerabilities do not affect them
docs.text: A VEX document (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) goes with an SBOM: for each vulnerability in the product's components, it says whether the product is affected, and if not, why. Bulwark writes a project's VEX from what the organization has decided, as OpenVEX v0.2.0 or CycloneDX 1.6 VEX. The design is ADR-0053.

docs.title: Where statements come from
docs.text:
For every vulnerability the advisory engine finds in the project's current SBOM, at every library version:

What the organization decided Exported as A person confirmed a VEX statement not_affected, its justification, the evidence and its limits, who confirmed it The dependency Issue was marked not a risk not_affected, with the justification chosen (or the reason, if none was) Nothing, and the version matches affected, with the fix ("Upgrade x to 1.2.3 or later") Nothing, and the version could not be compared under_investigation A confirmed statement the latest scan contradicts under_investigation, saying so

Only PyPI, npm, Go and Maven vulnerabilities are included (what the advisory engine covers).

docs.title: Marking a dependency Issue not a risk
docs.text:
On a dependency Issue, "Mark as not a risk" offers OpenVEX's five justifications:

OpenVEX CycloneDX Meaning component_not_present code_not_present The vulnerable component is not in the product vulnerable_code_not_present code_not_present The component is there, but not its vulnerable code vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path code_not_reachable The vulnerable code is never executed vulnerable_code_cannot_be_controlled_by_adversary requires_environment An attacker cannot control the vulnerable code's input inline_mitigations_already_exist protected_by_mitigating_control Built-in protections already stop it

The CycloneDX column is Bulwark's mapping (neither specification defines one); CycloneDX statements also carry the OpenVEX value in bulwark:openvex:justification.

docs.title: Draft VEX for the others
docs.text:
On an advisory's page, Draft VEX proposes not_affected / vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path for each use where Bulwark has evidence, and nothing where it has none. Two kinds of evidence:

  • Vulnerable functions not called (Go). Go's vulnerability database names the vulnerable functions. When Bulwark scans a project it reads its Go source (parsed, never built or run) and records which names the code uses from each package it imports, and every method name it calls. If none of the vulnerable functions is used, the use is proposed. Matching is by name and errs towards "used": any call of a method called Next counts as a call of Tokenizer.Next.
  • Package not imported (Python, JavaScript, and Go records that name no functions). The package is a declared dependency no application source file imports, or only tests do.

Nothing is proposed for Maven packages, versions that could not be compared, malicious packages, or projects Bulwark has not scanned (an imported SBOM has no source to read).

What the evidence does not cover, and every statement says so:

  • Code inside other dependencies is not analysed. If another library calls the vulnerable function on the project's behalf, the claim is wrong.
  • Calls through reflection, plugins or function values obtained elsewhere are not seen.
  • Import-level evidence does not know which functions are vulnerable.

A proposal is exported nowhere until a person confirms it, with their own API token. Confirming also marks the matching Issue not a risk with the same justification; reopening that Issue withdraws the statement. Rejected proposals are not proposed again until a scan changes the evidence. Every step is in the audit log.

docs.title: Downloading
docs.text:
On the project's VEX page, or:

GET /v2/projects/{id}/vex/openvex
GET /v2/projects/{id}/vex/cyclonedx

The product is identified by the project's repository URL (or a urn:uuid: for other projects), each component by its package URL. The documents validate against the OpenVEX v0.2.0 and CycloneDX 1.6 JSON schemas, and vexctl filter applies them to SARIF results.

docs.title: How good are the proposals?
docs.text: Not yet measured. The plan asks for 100 proposals reviewed blind; scripts/vex-review-kit.py makes the review sheet (proposals mixed with uses that were not proposed, Bulwark's answer hidden) and scores the answers. It needs a reviewer and real projects.

docs.title: ADR-001: SARIF 2.1.0 as the canonical intermediate format
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-24)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Each scanner emits its own format and severity vocabulary. We need one intermediate representation before mapping to our internal Finding model.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Bespoke schema.
  2. SARIF 2.1.0 (OASIS standard).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Every tool's output is converted to SARIF 2.1.0, then to Finding. Tools with native SARIF (Semgrep, Trivy, Gitleaks, OSV-Scanner) share one ingestion path; others (Bandit) are converted by their adapter.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• GitHub Code Scanning consumes our export with no extra work.
  • One SARIF ingestion path is reused across adapters.
  • SARIF is verbose and lacks some fields we need (EPSS, KEV); those live on Finding, not SARIF.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-09-24, Week 4)
docs.text: SARIF is lossy for SCA: it carries no package identity, CVSS vector or CWE list. The Trivy and OSV-Scanner adapters therefore parse each tool's richer native JSON straight into Finding. SARIF remains the ingestion path for tools that emit it natively (Semgrep) and will be the export format generated from Finding (Week 10, for GitHub Code Scanning).

docs.title: ADR-002: One sandboxed Docker container per scanner
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-24)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The scanner ingests attacker-controlled code and runs third-party tools over it (threats T1, T2, T6, T10).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Each tool runs in its own ephemeral container with: --network=none, --read-only, --cap-drop=ALL, --security-opt=no-new-privileges, non-root UID, --memory=2g --cpus=1.0, PID limit, wall-clock timeout, target mounted read-only, and a single writable output dir. Images are pinned by SHA-256 digest in production. Dependencies are never installed. Production hardening: rootless Docker or gVisor.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Tools needing network (OSV-Scanner online mode, Trivy DB) must use pre-fetched offline databases.
  • Per-container overhead is accepted for isolation.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-09-24, Week 5): running inside docker compose
docs.text:
The worker must launch scanner containers, i.e. it needs Docker access. Mounting the raw socket would make a compromised worker equivalent to root on the host, so it instead reaches the daemon through tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy, allowing only container create/start/kill, image inspect and volumes. Scan workspaces live in a directory bind-mounted at the same path in the worker and on the host, because sibling containers are started by the host daemon.

Residual risk (accepted for v0.x, must be addressed before any public deployment): the proxy still permits creating containers with arbitrary host bind mounts. Production should use a dedicated runner service on an isolated host, or gVisor/rootless Docker, with the worker holding no Docker access at all.

docs.title: ADR-003: No DAST in v1.0
docs.text:
Status: Accepted (2026-09-24)

DAST requires a target-ownership verification system that must exist before the feature, not after. Deferred to v1.1 behind domain verification (ZAP, Nuclei). Architecture must not preclude it.

docs.title: ADR-004: Cross-tool correlation and fingerprinting scheme
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-25)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Five scanners over one repository produce overlapping reports of the same defects, and they disagree on almost everything a naive comparison would use:

  • Line numbers. Bandit reports the assignment building a SQL string (line 6); Semgrep reports the execute() call that uses it (line 7).
  • Snippets. Bandit quotes numbered context lines; Semgrep quotes only the matched expression.
  • Identifiers. OSV reports GHSA-… with CVE aliases; Trivy reports the CVE-… directly. Trivy says ecosystem pip, OSV says PyPI.
  • CWEs. Bandit calls a hardcoded password CWE-259; Gitleaks calls the same line CWE-798.
  • Granularity. Semgrep fires two rules on one subprocess.call(..., shell=True).

Exact-match fingerprinting fails on all of these. The goal is to merge reports of one defect without merging two different defects.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Findings are correlated in core/correlation (pure functions over Finding; no I/O).

docs.title: Matching (same_defect)
docs.text:
SCA (findings with a package): merge iff same (ecosystem, name, version) and they share a vulnerability identifier (any of CVE / GHSA / PYSEC / ..., compared case-insensitively over taxonomy.aliases ∪ taxonomy.cve). Ecosystems are normalized (pip/PyPI → pypi). Grouping is transitive, so one OSV advisory covering CVE-A and CVE-B absorbs Trivy's two separate findings.

Code, IaC and secrets: merge iff all of the following hold: 1. same file path; 2. compatible category (sast↔sast; sast↔secrets allowed, nothing else crosses); 3. overlapping CWE family (a small explicit parent/child map: 259, 260, 321 → 798); 4. line ranges within LINE_WINDOW = 3 lines of each other (distance between ranges, not points); 5. snippet evidence: token-set overlap coefficient ≥ 0.8 over normalized snippets, or, when a snippet is a redaction placeholder or has fewer than MIN_TOKENS = 4 tokens (no evidence either way), the findings must be on adjacent lines (distance ≤ 1).

Snippet normalization strips line-number prefixes and comments and masks identifiers, strings and numbers, so query = "SELECT " + user_id and q = "SELECT x" + uid compare equal.

Overlap coefficient, not Jaccard. One tool routinely quotes more context than another, so the smaller snippet is usually a subset of the larger. Jaccard punishes that; containment does not.

Never merge a tool with itself. Two findings from the same tool and the same rule are distinct occurrences (two identical call sites are two defects) even when a third tool's finding spans both. The cluster union refuses any merge that would put one (tool, rule) in a cluster twice. Different rules from the same tool on one defect (Semgrep's two shell=True rules) do merge, and both rule ids are kept.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
• Severity: the maximum across members; every tool's native label is kept in scoring.native_severity.
  • Confidence: noisy-OR over the members, 1 − Π(1 − cᵢ), capped at 0.99. Agreement between independent scanners raises confidence; two rules from the same tool do not raise agreement_count, which counts distinct tools.
  • Primary member (title, location, description): highest severity, then confidence, then a fixed tool priority. CWE / OWASP / CVE / alias / reference lists are unioned.

docs.title: Fingerprints
docs.text:
• SCA (exact): sha256(ecosystem | name | version | primary_id) where primary_id is the smallest CVE, else the smallest alias. Identical whichever tool reported it.
  • Code: sha256(smallest CWE in family | path | hash of normalized snippet); for placeholder snippets, the line number replaces the snippet hash. Survives whitespace, comment and renaming changes and line movement. It is best effort across different tool sets, because the quoted snippet depends on which tool led the merge.

docs.title: Ordering and safety
docs.text: Correlation runs before redaction. Redaction placeholders are identical strings and would otherwise look like matching snippets, merging unrelated defects that merely sit near a secret (covered by a regression test).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Exact (cwe, path, line) match. Fails on the ±1–3 line disagreement seen in the very first real example (Bandit 6 vs Semgrep 7).
  • Line-only proximity. Merges unrelated defects on neighbouring lines.
  • ML / embedding similarity. Non-deterministic, unexplainable to a user who asks "why were these merged?", and unnecessary given the structure above.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every merge decision is explainable from the rules above; the UI shows "Flagged by 2 of 2 code scanners" with each tool's own severity and rule.
  • The thresholds (LINE_WINDOW, SNIPPET_OVERLAP, MIN_TOKENS) are recorded alongside every benchmark run, so they can be tuned against evidence rather than intuition.
  • Known limits: no cross-file matching (a taint flow spanning files is reported at each end); CWE families beyond the credential group are not mapped; IaC/Dockerfile findings have no CWE, so they only ever merge within Trivy.

docs.title: Measured results (2026-09-25)
docs.text:
Baseline over five public repositories (benchmarks/README.md, benchmarks/results/): 2552 raw findings -> 1824 unique, a 28.5% deduplication rate, ranging from 6.9% (Terraform-only) to 49.2% (dependency-heavy), with all five repos completing.

Evidence about the matcher itself: on NodeGoat, 291 of OSV-Scanner's 292 findings were matched to a Trivy finding once both scanned the same scope, and the single miss was a genuinely different advisory. The first run's apparently poor overlap (83 of 292) was a scanner-scope difference (Trivy skips dev dependencies by default), not a matching failure, which is why the Trivy adapter now passes --include-dev-deps. Lesson recorded: when cross-tool agreement looks low, check that the tools are scanning the same thing before tuning the matcher.

docs.title: ADR-005: No blockchain for report integrity; Sigstore, in-toto and RFC 3161 instead
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-25)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The original concept included a blockchain to make scan reports tamper-evident. The real requirements are narrower: a reader must be able to verify that (1) a report was produced by this system, (2) it was not modified afterwards, and (3) it existed at a given time.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Public or private blockchain / distributed ledger. Stores a hash on-chain.
  2. Sigstore (cosign) signatures + in-toto attestations + RFC 3161 timestamps.
  3. Do nothing (plain files).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Option 2, scheduled for Phase 5. Reports are signed with cosign, wrapped in an in-toto attestation describing the inputs (source digest, scanner image digests, tool versions) and timestamped by an RFC 3161 authority.

docs.title: Why not a blockchain
docs.text:
• It provides no property this system needs that signatures and timestamps do not: integrity comes from the hash and signature; time comes from the timestamp authority; provenance comes from the attestation. A ledger adds a fourth mechanism for a problem already solved by the first three.
  • Consensus, immutability and decentralisation are valuable when parties distrust one another. Here one operator produces reports for its own users; there is no adversarial multi-party write.
  • It adds operational cost (nodes, fees or a private network), latency and a new attack surface to a system whose whole job is to reduce attack surface.
  • The industry already uses Sigstore, in-toto and timestamping for exactly this: verifiable software supply-chain artifacts. Tooling, verifiers and auditors already exist.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Verification works offline with standard tools (cosign verify-blob, in-toto-verify).
  • If a future requirement genuinely needs multi-party, publicly auditable history (for example a transparency log across organisations), Sigstore's Rekor transparency log already provides an append-only, publicly verifiable log without introducing a blockchain.
  • This decision is reversible; reversing it should be a deliberate, documented act.

docs.title: ADR-006: Semgrep rules are fetched at build time and never redistributed
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-24) — needs a decision before the public demo (Week 10)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The design document assumed Semgrep "community rules" were usable in a platform offering. In practice the Semgrep engine is LGPL-2.1, but the semgrep/semgrep-rules repository is under the Semgrep Rules License v1.0, which permits use "only for your own internal business purposes" and does not allow distributing the rules or making them available to others as a service. (Verified against semgrep.dev/legal/rules-license, 2026-09-24.)

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Rules are never committed to this repo (docker/semgrep/rules/ is git-ignored).
  • A multi-stage docker/semgrep/Dockerfile clones a pinned commit at image build time; each user builds their own image locally for their own use. The image is never pushed to a registry.
  • The Semgrep adapter stays in the codebase: it is the reference for the shared SARIF path.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Self-hosted / local CLI use: fine (internal use by the person who built the image).
  • A public hosted demo or SaaS running these rules would violate the licence. Before Week 10, either (a) disable Semgrep on the hosted instance, (b) ship our own rules, or (c) evaluate a fork with permissively licensed rules, checking its rule licence separately, or (d) get legal advice / a commercial licence.
  • THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md must record this distinction.

docs.title: ADR-007: Any S3-compatible store for raw artifacts; RustFS in the dev stack
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-24)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The design doc specified "MinIO/S3" for raw tool output. When building Week 5, the official minio/minio Docker Hub image no longer exists and the quay.io/minio/minio mirror returns 401, so MinIO cannot be pulled by a clean docker compose up.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The code depends only on the S3 API (boto3 with a configurable endpoint), never on MinIO. The compose stack uses RustFS (Apache-2.0, S3-compatible, multi-arch). Production can point BULWARK_S3_ENDPOINT at AWS S3, Cloudflare R2 or any compatible service.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Swapping the store is a config change; verified by exercising bucket creation and put/get.
  • RustFS is younger than MinIO; the image is currently :latest and must be pinned by digest before any production use (ADR-002).

docs.title: ADR-008: Product name "Bulwark"; distribution name bulwark-scan
docs.text: Status: Proposed (2026-09-25); the owner may override

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The design doc says to check name availability in Week 1 and to secure the GitHub organisation and package names. Checked on 2026-09-25 against public registries:

Name PyPI npm GitHub bulwark taken (bulwark 0.6.1, an unrelated data-analysis package) taken (empty placeholder) taken (user, 0 repos) bulwark-security n/a n/a taken kavach, palisade taken taken taken bulwark-scan free free free kavach-scan, usebulwark, bulwarkscan free free free

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Keep Bulwark as the product name (it is the name used throughout the project and UI) and use bulwark-scan for the Python distribution, the npm scope/package and the GitHub organisation. The installed CLI command stays bulwark. Import packages (core, cli, api) are unchanged.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• pip install bulwark-scan cannot be confused with the unrelated bulwark package.
  • Nothing in the codebase depends on the distribution name, so renaming again is cheap.
  • Action for the owner: register the bulwark-scan GitHub organisation, PyPI project and npm name soon (names are first-come). The VS Code Marketplace and trademark register were not checked.

docs.title: ADR-009: Remediation knowledge base on pgvector, with a model-free embedder
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-25, Week 11)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The LLM remediation layer (Weeks 12-14) needs grounding text per finding: what the weakness is (CWE) and how to fix it (OWASP cheat sheets). The design doc asks for a local corpus and a vector store that avoids adding another service.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Corpus: 211 CWE entries (every CWE in the OWASP Top 10 table plus those scanners emitted in our real scans) and 1,697 chunks from 59 OWASP cheat sheets. Built by scripts/build-corpus.py, committed under core/rag/corpus/, versions pinned in SOURCES.json. Nothing is fetched at scan time.
  2. Store: two tables in the existing PostgreSQL (kb_chunks, kb_meta). pgvector vector(1024) with an HNSW cosine index. SQLite (tests, quick local runs) stores the vector as JSON and searches in Python; both produce identical rankings (checked on real Postgres). The Postgres image is postgres:16-alpine plus pgvector v0.8.0 compiled from source (docker/postgres/Dockerfile), so existing data volumes keep working.
  3. Embedder: hashed, IDF-weighted bag of words and bigrams (core/rag/embed.py), no ML model, offline, deterministic. IDF is fitted at load time and stored with the index. An Embedder protocol allows a neural model later; the index records which embedder built it and refuses to be queried by another.
  4. Retrieval (core/rag/retrieve.py): exact CWE lookup first, then cheat-sheet chunks that address the finding's CWEs (else its OWASP categories) ranked by similarity, else pure similarity. The query uses the finding's title and description, never its code snippet.

docs.title: Why not a neural embedding model
docs.text: No embedding model ships with this stack. An API call would send finding text to a third party and make a network dependency of something that should work offline; a local model (sentence-transformers) pulls in PyTorch (hundreds of MB) for a 2k-chunk corpus. The corpus is keyword-rich, and lexical retrieval plus CWE/OWASP metadata is enough to be useful. The cost is real and measured (below).

docs.title: Measured (80 real findings, tests/fixtures/rag_eval.json; see docs/rag.md)
docs.text: Without metadata, the right sheet is first 52.5% of the time and in the top 5 84% of the time. With CWE metadata the first guidance item is a relevant sheet in 100% of cases. Dimension was chosen by sweeping 384 to 2000 on this same set (384: 71% top-5; 1024: 84%; 2000: 84%); it is one parameter, but it is tuned on the data it is reported on.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Plain-English queries without shared vocabulary miss (for example, "server fetches a URL supplied by the user" does not find the SSRF sheet). Findings with a CWE or OWASP tag do not depend on this.
  • Changing the embedder or dimension means a new migration and bulwark kb load.
  • CC BY-SA share-alike applies to the cheat-sheet chunks (core/rag/corpus/NOTICE.md); the rest stays Apache-2.0.
  • Everything retrieved is passed to a model as data, never instructions (T8).

docs.title: ADR-010: LLM remediation as a validated annotation, never a decision
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-25, Week 12)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The plan wants plain-English explanations and suggested patches from a model. The scanned repository is attacker-controlled input to that model (threat T8), and sending code to a third party is a privacy decision.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Annotation only. The model receives one existing finding and returns a separate object. It has no field that can change severity, triage or taxonomy, and Finding is never modified.
  2. Structural defences over trust. Instructions in the system message only; repository text in random-nonce fenced data blocks; the reminder after the data; strict output contract that rejects extra keys, dismissal language and patches outside the finding's file; any failure returns static reference text.
  3. Provider-agnostic. Code depends on an LLMClient protocol. An Anthropic implementation ships behind an optional extra; the model id comes from configuration.
  4. Opt-in, minimal, scrubbed. Off by default; secrets findings send no code; other code is scrubbed first; bulwark llm prompt shows exactly what would be sent.
  5. Reject, do not repair. A malformed reply is discarded whole. Partially trusting a reply an attacker may have influenced is riskier than showing the deterministic text.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Some legitimate replies will be rejected (for example one that discusses "false positives" in a way the phrase filter matches); the user then sees static text, which is always safe.
  • Structural safety is tested with simulated attackers. Real-model behaviour is unmeasured until a key is available (Week 14 evaluation).
  • Patch correctness is not verifiable by Bulwark; patches are labelled and never applied.

docs.title: ADR-011: Pin Redis to 7.2 (the last BSD-licensed line)
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-26, Week 22)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Generating THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md forced a look at every image the compose file runs. redis:7-alpine is a floating tag and currently resolves to 7.4.11. Redis 7.4 and later are no longer BSD-3-Clause: they are RSALv2 / SSPLv1 (and Redis 8 adds AGPLv3). Neither RSALv2 nor SSPL is an OSI open-source license, and Bulwark's license policy denies SSPL.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Pin redis:7.2-alpine, the last BSD-3-Clause line, in docker-compose.yml and the README.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Existing dev stacks that ran 7.4 hold an RDB file in the image's anonymous volume that 7.2 refuses to load ("Can't handle RDB format version 12"), so the container restarts in a loop. Redis here holds only queues and transient results: docker compose rm -sfv redis && docker compose up -d discards the volume and fixes it. Hit and fixed for real while making this change.
  • The compose stack uses only what Bulwark needs from Redis (Celery broker, results, pub/sub, a list length for queue depth). All of it works on 7.2, and the full stack was brought up and a scan run against it.
  • 7.2 receives fewer updates than current Redis. Valkey (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) is the maintained drop-in alternative and the better long-term answer; it was not adopted now because it changes the datastore and needs its own soak test.
  • The license report lists the pin and the reason, and scripts/gen-licenses.py --check fails a build that introduces an unknown or network-copyleft license among the dependencies it can see (it cannot see image contents: the tool table is maintained by hand and checked against the Dockerfiles).

docs.title: ADR-0012: Split Finding into Issue (stable identity) and Occurrence (one sighting)
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-27, Week 28). Verified live end to end; see docs/v2-week28-verification.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
core/persistence/models.py today has Scan → ToolRun → FindingRow, and FindingRow is scoped entirely to one scan_id. Every scan is an island: there is no way to ask "is this the same SQL injection we saw last week?", "did the fix work?", or "is this new in this pull request?" without re-deriving it from scratch each time, because nothing persists a finding's identity across scans — only its fingerprint (core/correlation) within one.

v2 needs all three of those questions answered: incremental/PR scanning (§20.1 of the plan), the fix-verification loop (§21.2), and the trend data the UI shows ("5 fixed, 2 new, 1 returned", §28.1). None of it is possible without something that outlives a single scan.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Split the concept in two:

  • Issue — one vulnerability, identified once, that persists across scans of the same project. Carries the current state (new / open / fixed / reintroduced), first-seen and last-seen timestamps, and (later, Week 62) risk acceptance.
  • Occurrence — one sighting of an Issue in one scan. What FindingRow is today, minus the parts that are really Issue-level (state, first-seen). An Occurrence always belongs to exactly one Issue and one scan.
Scan ──< ToolRun
Scan ──< Occurrence >── Issue

docs.title: Issue identity (matching)
docs.text:
Reuses the fingerprint from ADR-0004 as the primary key, plus a fallback so moving a function to another file doesn't manufacture a spurious "new" Issue and a spurious "fixed" one:

  1. Primary: the existing Finding.fingerprint (package-level exact match for SCA; normalized CWE+path+snippet hash for code). If two Occurrences in successive scans share a fingerprint, they're the same Issue.
  2. Fallback, code findings only: sha256(cwe + rule_family + normalized_snippet) with no path component, so a function moved to a new file still matches. Used only when the primary fingerprint has no match in the project's existing open Issues, to avoid over-merging unrelated findings that happen to share a snippet hash with no CWE context.

Matching is scoped to one project (one Scan's lineage, i.e. repeated scans of the same source_ref), not global — a CWE-89 in payments-api and one in internal-wiki are different Issues even with an identical snippet.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
new/open → fixed (no matching Occurrence in the next full scan of the same project)
fixed → reintroduced (a matching Occurrence reappears later)

accepted_risk and not_a_risk states are deferred to Week 62 (risk acceptance), matching the plan's own sequencing — v2's Phase 8-9 don't need them yet, and adding an incomplete version now would be a state machine Week 62 has to migrate away from.

docs.title: What does NOT change in Week 28
docs.text:
• ToolAdapter, execute_tool, correlation, redaction, finalize() — none of it. Issue/Occurrence sits above the existing pipeline; a scan still produces Finding objects exactly as it does today, and the persistence layer is what learns to turn a batch of them into Occurrences against existing or new Issues.
  • The CLI's one-shot scan() path keeps returning Findings with no persistence; Issue/Occurrence only applies where scans are stored (the API/worker path), matching how raw_object_key already only exists there.

docs.title: What was actually built, and where it differs from the design above
docs.text:
• FindingRow was not renamed to Occurrence. It gained issue_id and issue_state columns instead of becoming a new table under a new name. A rename would have touched every reader of findings (the API, the CLI JSON/HTML/PDF exporters, the web app, the golden-fixture tests) for zero behavioural gain in one week; the table already is an Occurrence in every way ADR-0012 describes, just under its original name. If a future week needs Occurrence as a distinct, separately-queryable concept (e.g. the plan's IssueGroup, §41.2 of the later system-of-record design), rename then, with a reason that isn't just "the ADR said so".
  • A real collision was found and fixed: Issue identity is scoped by (asset, category, fingerprint), not just (asset, fingerprint). fingerprint() (ADR-0004) doesn't hash category, by design — correlate() checks category compatibility separately via same_defect() before ever comparing fingerprints. Used alone for Issue identity, that means two findings of different categories (say a SAST rule and a secrets rule) can hash identically when both lack a CWE and land on the same redacted line, and would otherwise collide on the database's uniqueness constraint. Caught by a real test failure the first time two such findings landed in the same scan (tests/unit/test_issues.py::test_different_categories_never_collapse_even_with_the_same_raw_fingerprint), not by inspection.
  • No /v2 API namespace. Standing up a parallel versioned API and freezing /v1 read-only, as the plan's C5 proposes, is a bigger structural change than one week justifies, and nothing yet depends on /v1 staying frozen (the VS Code extension and GitHub Action are still pre-Marketplace). Instead, GET /scans/{id} gained an additive issue_counts field and each finding an additive issue field; existing clients that don't know about either simply ignore them. Revisit real API versioning when there's a second client (the plan's own GitHub App in v2, or the Marketplace-published extension) that needs /v1's exact shape to keep working while /v2 moves.
  • Only "new" and "reintroduced" are surfaced as UI badges, not "fixed" — a fixed Issue has no Occurrence in the current scan to attach a badge to, so showing it needs a history view (the plan's scan-comparison screen, §28.6) that doesn't exist yet. ScanReport shows a one-line "N new, M reintroduced since the last scan of this project" summary instead, quiet when there's nothing to say.
  • The historical backfill is a standalone script (scripts/backfill-issues.py), not baked into the Alembic migration. The migration (migrations/versions/0004_issues_assets.py) only creates tables and columns. Turning 13 real pre-existing scans' stored JSON into a lifecycle history needs the same core.issues.sync() logic the live pipeline uses, replayed oldest-scan-first per asset — that's application logic that will keep changing, and Alembic migrations are meant to stop changing once shipped. Run once with --apply; dry-run by default.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A migration must backfill: every existing FindingRow becomes one Occurrence under a new, freshly-minted Issue (there's no history to reconstruct "first seen" from, so first-seen = the existing scan's timestamp). Done via scripts/backfill-issues.py, run live against the 13 pre-Week-28 scans in this environment: 5 assets, 1,468 issues, 4,652 occurrences, with the same repo's repeat scans correctly collapsing to open instead of each counting as new.
  • The API's finding-list endpoint returns Occurrences (one row per scan, unchanged), each carrying which Issue it belongs to and that Issue's current state. A dedicated Issues endpoint (list issues for a project, independent of any one scan) is not built yet — nothing in the current UI needs it before the scan-comparison and fix-first screens (§28.1, §28.6) exist to consume it.
  • Nothing here requires multi-tenancy (ADR-0013) to land first, but both touch core/persistence/models.py, so Week 28 (data model) intentionally comes before Week 29 (tenancy) to avoid migrating the same tables twice.
  • Only a "completed" scan syncs issues (core/pipeline.py). A "partial" or "failed" scan leaves every finding's issue_id unset: absence during a partial scan doesn't mean fixed, it might mean the tool that would have found it never ran.

docs.title: ADR-0013: Multi-tenancy enforced by Postgres Row-Level Security
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-27, Week 29). Verified live end to end; see docs/v2-week29-verification.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every table in core/persistence/models.py (Scan, ToolRun, FindingRow) is global: there is one shared bearer token (SECURITY.md, "known limits") and no concept of who a scan belongs to. That is fine for a single-user, self-hosted tool, which is what v1.0 is and remains (the self-host page is explicit: one token, one machine, not for untrusted multi-user hosting).

v2's collaboration features (§19.1: organizations, projects, roles) need real isolation between tenants sharing one deployment. The risk if that isolation lives only in application code — a query handler that forgets a WHERE org_id = ... clause — is a cross-tenant data leak, which for a security-findings product is about as bad a bug class as exists.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Enforce tenancy at the database layer with Postgres Row-Level Security, not only in the application:

ALTER TABLE scans ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE scans FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;  -- FORCE: applies even to the table owner

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON scans
  USING (org_id = current_setting('app.current_org')::uuid);

-- per request, inside the transaction, before any query:
SET LOCAL app.current_org = '<the authenticated org id>';
  • org_id is added to Scan (and cascades to ToolRun/FindingRow/Occurrence through the foreign key, so a join can never cross tenants even if a query forgets to filter).
  • The API's database role has no BYPASSRLS. Only a separate, narrowly-scoped migration role does.
  • SET LOCAL app.current_org is set once per request from the authenticated identity, inside the same transaction as every query that request makes, so there is no window where the session has no tenant context.

docs.title: The test that proves it, not just documents it
docs.text: An automated test creates two organizations, authenticates as the first, and requests every resource ID belonging to the second across every endpoint. Every request must return 404 (never 403 — a 403 confirms the resource exists, which is itself a leak of information about another tenant). This runs on every pull request, not just once at ship time, because RLS policies are exactly the kind of thing a later migration can silently weaken.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Application-level filtering only (every query handler adds .filter(org_id == current_org)). Rejected: one omitted filter in one endpoint, ever, is a full cross-tenant leak, and there is no structural way to catch a missing filter except by testing every endpoint — which is exactly what RLS makes unnecessary for the common case (the two-tenant test in the previous section is then a belt-and-suspenders check, not the only line of defense).
  • Separate database per tenant. Rejected for v2: correct isolation, but no shared connection pool, migrations fan out per tenant, and it's a much bigger operational jump than a single self-hosted or small-multi-tenant deployment needs. Revisit if/when the project ever needs to scale past what one Postgres instance with RLS comfortably serves.

docs.title: What was actually built, and where it differs from the design above
docs.text:
• org_id lives on assets and scans only, not on tool_runs/findings/issues. Those three get a Row-Level Security policy that joins back to the table that does carry it (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM scans WHERE scans.id = findings.scan_id AND scans.org_id = ...)), which is what "cascades through the foreign key" in the original design actually means in a working policy, not a literal duplicated column. Application-level code enforces the same shape: every client-facing lookup resolves and org-checks the Scan first (api/main.py's _get_scan), and everything else scoped by that scan_id is safe without its own check.
  • assets needed org_id too, which the original design didn't mention. Two organizations scanning the same public repository would otherwise share one Asset row (identity is keyed on (source_type, key) alone, ADR-0012) — meaning one org's Issue lifecycle history and counts would leak into the other's. Caught by working through the design before writing code, not by a test failure. Fixed by scoping Asset identity to (org_id, source_type, key).
  • The non-superuser API/worker role is real, not a stated intention. bulwark_app (NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS) is created by the migration itself and is what docker-compose.yml now points the api and worker services at; migrate keeps connecting as the table-owning role so it can alter schema and manage that role. This is load-bearing, not cosmetic: this project's Postgres image makes its initial role a superuser, and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is a documented no-op against a superuser or any BYPASSRLS role regardless of policies — every policy below would have silently protected nothing if the app kept using the original role. Verified directly (see the verification doc): the superuser sees all rows regardless of app.current_org; bulwark_app with no org set sees zero rows (fails closed, not open); bulwark_app with the right org set sees exactly that org's rows.
  • No org-management API. There is no endpoint to create an organization, list them, or assign a caller to one — matching the plan's own sequencing (real identity is §19.2). organizations rows exist only as the migration's bootstrap default plus whatever is inserted directly for now. A caller selects scope with an X-Bulwark-Org header (core/tenancy.py); the single shared bearer token still authenticates that a caller may use the API at all, so a caller that knows the token can claim any org id that exists. This is a known, explicit limitation, not an oversight — it proves the isolation mechanism is correct, and real org membership binds to it later without changing RLS or the application-level filtering at all. The header is also not part of the OpenAPI schema (it's read directly from Request.headers, not declared as a FastAPI Header() parameter), since it isn't a stable public interface yet.
  • Two real bugs found live, beyond the design itself:
  • set_config(..., true) (transaction-local) was the first implementation, matching the ADR's own SET LOCAL framing — and it broke the very first real request. Several repo.py functions commit internally more than once within one request/session (create_scan commits the asset, then commits the scan; the worker's completed-scan path commits issues via sync_issues_for_scan, then commits findings via add_findings in the same session). A transaction-local setting resets at the first of those commits, leaving the rest of the same request running with no org context — which RLS then reads as "see nothing," not "see everything." Fixed by switching to set_config(..., false) (session-scoped): safe because every consumer of a session sets it immediately after opening, before any other statement, so a stale value from a previous occupant of a pooled connection can never actually be read.
  • The worker was still fully broken after that fix, for a different reason: nothing had ever told it which org a scan belonged to. It connects as the same non-bypass bulwark_app role as the API, so every write it made (mark_running, add_tool_run, add_findings, finish_scan) would be silently rejected or simply match zero rows under RLS. Reading the scan's own org_id first doesn't work either — the worker has no bypass privilege, so it can't SELECT a row it hasn't already identified the org for. Fixed by threading org_id through the dispatch path the API already has it on: AppState.enqueue gained a second argument, run_scan_task and run_scan_job both gained org_id, and core.tenancy.scoped_sessions wraps the worker's session factory to set app.current_org on every session it opens, the same job api.deps.db does for the API.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every new table added from Week 29 onward needs org_id and its own FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY policy from day one; this ADR is the checklist a reviewer should hold new tables to.
  • The CLI's local, unauthenticated scan() path is unaffected — RLS only applies to the API/worker's database access. A self-hosted single-user deployment can run with exactly one organization and never notice the isolation exists.
  • This does not, by itself, migrate v1.0's single-shared-token auth into real per-organization accounts; that is separate identity work (the plan's §19.2, GitHub sign-in / passkeys / TOTP), not part of this ADR.

docs.title: ADR-0014: Taint analysis scope cut — intra-procedural, single language, prefer existing engines
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-27). Design only; not yet implemented. Scopes down the v2 plan's tree-sitter code intelligence + taint analysis phase before any of it is built, so the cut is on record before the pressure of a slipping schedule makes it tempting to quietly cut it later instead.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The v2 plan calls for a taint analysis engine that propagates function summaries over a call graph, across Python, JavaScript, and Go. That is a description of what CodeQL and Semgrep Pro's proprietary engines do, built by dedicated teams over multiple years. Bulwark ships in weekly increments with no research team. Committing to the full version as written risks the single most common failure mode of ambitious security tooling projects: the taint engine never quite finishes, and it stalls every other v2 feature scheduled after it.

This ADR exists to make the scope decision explicit before that phase starts, not to record a retrospective excuse after it has already slipped.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Cut scope on three axes, in order of how much complexity each removes:

  1. Intra-procedural only, not interprocedural. Track source → sink dataflow within a single function body. No function summaries, no call graph construction, no cross-function propagation. This is a materially different (and dramatically simpler) problem: no summary computation, no recursion/cycle handling in the call graph, no whole-program fixpoint analysis.
  2. One language first: Python. Bandit already gives Bulwark a mature Python AST pipeline and tree-sitter's Python grammar is the most battle-tested of the three. JavaScript and Go are deferred to their own, separately-scoped weeks rather than built in parallel with Python — building three at once triples the surface area for the exact kind of subtle bug (wrong scope resolution, wrong sanitizer recognition) that a partially-working taint engine produces silently.
  3. Build vs. configure: check Semgrep's existing taint mode first. Semgrep already ships bounded, intra-file taint tracking (mode: taint, source/sink/sanitizer rules) as a configuration surface, not something Bulwark has to implement. Before writing a custom engine, evaluate how much of the intra-procedural, single-language scope above is already covered by authoring Semgrep taint rules through the existing adapter. Only build custom tree-sitter-based analysis for what Semgrep's taint mode demonstrably cannot express for Bulwark's use cases — and record what that gap actually is, rather than assuming one exists.

Interprocedural analysis and the other two languages remain a real goal — they move to v3 (or a later, explicitly re-scoped v2 week) once the intra-procedural, single-language, configure-before-build version has shipped and proven the approach.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Build the full cross-language interprocedural engine as originally planned. Rejected for v2: correct long-term ambition, wrong thing to put on the critical path of a single release. Every other v2 feature scheduled after this phase inherits its risk of never finishing.
  • Drop taint analysis from v2 entirely, defer everything to v3. Rejected: the intra-procedural, single-language, configure-first version above is small enough to actually ship, and shipping something real (even narrow) gives v3's more ambitious version a working baseline and real usage data to design against, instead of starting from zero.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Whichever week implements this must budget time to first evaluate Semgrep taint-mode coverage before writing new analysis code — that evaluation is part of the week's scope, not a shortcut around it.
  • Marketing/docs language about "taint analysis" for v2 must describe the actual shipped scope (intra-procedural, Python) accurately, the same way ADR-0012 documents where the Issue/Occurrence implementation differs from its original design — no silent over-claiming.
  • JavaScript and Go taint support, and interprocedural analysis for any language, need their own future ADR (or an explicit amendment to this one) with real scoping before they start, not an assumption that "the engine already exists, just extend it."

docs.title: ADR-0015: Verified-fix agent — wall-clock limits, per-attempt timeouts, and an inconclusive state
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-27). Design only; not yet implemented. Records the safety limits the verified-fix agent's Temporal workflow must have from its first version, before the workflow itself is built.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The v2 plan's verified-fix agent proposes a patch, then loops (up to three times): rerun the specific rule that flagged the finding, rerun the full scanner suite, run the project's own unit tests, and only then request human approval. Each of those steps, for a real project, can run inside a Firecracker microVM — meaning a single fix attempt can spin up a sandboxed environment, install dependencies, and execute an arbitrary, untrusted-until- verified test suite, up to three times per finding.

A hung test suite (an infinite loop, a test that waits on a network call that will never resolve, a fixture that deadlocks) inside that loop is not a hypothetical: it is what test suites occasionally do even in well-maintained projects. Multiplied by three retries and by however many findings are queued for verified-fix concurrently, an unbounded workflow is a direct path to resource exhaustion and a real cost spike, not just a slow response.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Three limits, all present from the first version of the workflow, not added reactively after an incident:

  1. A wall-clock timeout on the entire Temporal workflow, covering all three attempts together. If verified-fix for one finding is still running past this timeout, Temporal cancels it outright.
  2. A separate, shorter wall-clock timeout on each individual attempt (patch → rerun rule → rerun scanners → run tests), enforced independently of the overall workflow timeout. Without this, one hung attempt can consume the entire workflow budget before a second or third attempt ever starts, silently turning "up to three tries" into "one long hang."
  3. A concurrency cap on verified-fix workflows per tenant, enforced by Temporal's workflow execution limits or an equivalent queue-depth check before starting a new one. This bounds the worst case (many findings triggering verified-fix at once) independently of any single workflow's own timeout.

A workflow that is cancelled by either timeout resolves to a distinct terminal state — inconclusive, not failed. A timeout is evidence that verification didn't finish in time, not evidence that the patch was wrong; conflating the two would show the user a false "this fix doesn't work" when the true story is "we don't know." The UI and API must surface inconclusive as its own state, not silently fold it into failed.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Overall workflow timeout only, no per-attempt timeout. Rejected: a single hung attempt (e.g. a deadlocked test fixture) would exhaust the whole budget, and every subsequent attempt would report as skipped for a reason indistinguishable from "ran and failed" unless the per-attempt boundary exists separately.
  • Rely on Firecracker/microVM resource limits (CPU/memory quotas) alone, no wall-clock timeout. Rejected: resource quotas stop a runaway process from consuming unbounded CPU or memory, but do nothing for a process that is idle-blocked (waiting on a network call, a lock, a fixture) rather than resource-hungry — that failure mode burns wall-clock time and workflow slots, not CPU, so only a timeout catches it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Whichever week implements the verified-fix agent must pick and document concrete numbers for both timeouts and the concurrency cap as part of that week's own verification (the same way Week 28's verification doc records real numbers, not just the mechanism) — this ADR fixes the shape of the limits, not the specific values, since sensible values depend on real test-suite runtimes this project hasn't measured yet.
  • The workflow's audit trail (whatever records what verified-fix attempted) must record which of the three limits ended a given run, not just that it ended, so a pattern of hitting the per-attempt timeout on a specific project's test suite is visible and actionable rather than looking identical to an outright failure.
  • This ADR does not address cost limits beyond concurrency (e.g. a per-tenant or per-day spend cap on verified-fix usage) — that is a billing/quota concern for whichever week wires verified-fix into the product's plan limits, not a workflow-safety concern this ADR covers.

docs.title: ADR-0016: Detect upstream scanner output drift via pinned versions and scheduled bump tests, not daily schema polling
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-09-27). Design only; no new automation implemented yet. Applies to all current and future ToolAdapter implementations (currently Bandit, Semgrep, Gitleaks, Trivy, OSV-Scanner, plus opt-in Grype, Checkov, gosec, Dockle), and to the import-format side of ingestion.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Bulwark wraps the output of a growing number of upstream open-source scanners. None of them publish a formal, versioned output schema to validate against — their "schema" is whatever the currently-installed version happens to emit. When an upstream tool changes its output shape (a renamed field, a new severity string, a restructured JSON envelope) between releases, the adapter that parses it can silently misparse or drop findings without raising any error, and nothing currently in the pipeline would notice before a user does.

A proposal to catch this via "automated daily schema validation against the upstream repositories" is solving the right problem with a mechanism that doesn't fit it: there is no upstream schema to validate against, and daily polling doesn't match how often these tools actually release (most cut a new version every few weeks to months, not daily).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Two changes, layered:

  1. Pin exact tool versions in the scanner Docker images, if not already fully pinned, so an adapter never silently starts parsing a different tool version than the one it was written and tested against. Drift then only happens on a deliberate version bump, never on an unattended latest pull.
  2. A scheduled CI job (weekly, not daily) that bumps one tool's pinned version at a time in an isolated branch and runs the existing golden-fixture adapter tests against it. If the new version's output breaks parsing or changes shape in a way the golden fixtures catch, the job fails loudly and opens a tracked issue, instead of the drift surfacing as an unexplained drop in findings in production. This reuses the adapter test infrastructure that already exists rather than building a second, parallel validation system.

Weekly cadence, not daily: matches how often these tools actually cut releases, and avoids spending CI minutes re-checking versions that haven't changed.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Daily validation against upstream repositories' published schemas, as originally proposed. Rejected: most of these tools don't publish a formal output schema at all (their output shape is implicitly whatever the code emits), so there is nothing concrete to validate against short of actually running the tool — which is exactly what the golden-fixture bump job does, on a cadence that matches real release frequency instead of an arbitrary daily poll.
  • Do nothing extra; rely on user bug reports to catch drift. Rejected: for a security tool, a silent drop in findings is a false sense of safety, which is a worse failure mode than a visible error — the whole point of catching this proactively is to fail loudly in CI instead of quietly in someone's real scan.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Each ToolAdapter's existing golden-fixture tests become dual-purpose: they already verify correctness today, and now also gate the scheduled version-bump job. A ToolAdapter added without golden fixtures is not covered by this drift detection, so fixtures are a checklist item for any new adapter, not optional test coverage.
  • The version-bump job runs against a branch, never main directly — a version bump is only fast-forwarded once its own fixtures pass, keeping this consistent with how dependency bumps are handled elsewhere in the project.
  • This does not cover drift in imported formats (SARIF, other scanners' native JSON ingested rather than executed by Bulwark itself) — that surface has no pinned version to bump in the first place, since Bulwark doesn't control when an external CI pipeline upgrades the tool producing that import. Import-format drift stays a runtime validation concern (reject/flag unrecognized shapes on ingest) rather than something a scheduled job can pre-empt.

docs.title: ADR-0017: GitHub App integration for automatic PR scanning
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-27, Week 30), except live verification against a real, registered GitHub App — that half is gated on registering one, which is the user's action, not mine. See docs/v2-week30-verification.md for exactly what was and wasn't proven live.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Bulwark already has a GitHub Action (core/ci/*, docs/github-action.md): a repo owner adds a workflow file, CI runs bulwark scan, and core/ci/github.py posts a PR comment using the token Actions hands that one workflow run. That requires the repo owner to write and maintain a workflow file, and only runs when their CI actually executes it.

A GitHub App is a different, complementary mechanism: install it once on an org or repo, and GitHub pushes webhook events (a PR opened, synchronized, ...) to a server Bulwark controls, with no workflow file for the user to write at all. This is what the plan's Week 30 asks for.

docs.title: Two-step GitHub auth, not the Action's borrowed token
docs.text: The App authenticates itself to GitHub with a JWT it signs (RS256, its own private key), then exchanges that for a short-lived (~1h) installation token scoped to exactly the repos/permissions that installation granted (core/github_app.py: app_jwt, installation_token, cached in-process per installation until near expiry). This is GitHub's own documented flow for an App acting on its own behalf, as opposed to the Action's model of "the CI job already has a token, just use it."

docs.title: An installation IS a tenant, for now
docs.text:
There's no org-management API yet (ADR-0013 already deferred that). Rather than block the App integration on building one, installing the App on an account creates that account's Organization the first time a webhook mentions it (GithubInstallation maps installation_id -> org_id, core/persistence/repo.py's get_or_create_installation). Real membership/sign-in (§19.2) can attach to this mapping later without changing it.

github_installations deliberately carries no Row-Level Security policy, unlike every table that holds actual tenant content. Resolving which org a webhook belongs to has to happen before any org-scoped query can run at all — RLS-gating the very table that answers "which org is this" would be a chicken-and-egg deadlock. It's a directory table, like organizations itself: knowing "installation X belongs to org Y" isn't a cross-tenant data leak the way a scan's findings would be. Once resolved, core.tenancy.set_session_org scopes the rest of that session's writes correctly — this is exactly the kind of subtle RLS interaction ADR-0013 didn't anticipate, caught here by reasoning through the sequence before writing the webhook handler, not by a test failure.

docs.title: Scanning a PR's actual commits, not the default branch
docs.text: core/gitfetch.clone_repo gained a ref parameter, but restricted to one specific, tightly-matched shape: refs/pull/<n>/head — GitHub's own stable name for a PR's current head commit. A shallow git clone --branch can't target it directly (that only resolves refs/heads/refs/tags), so the ref path instead does init -> remote add -> a scoped fetch --depth=1 -> checkout FETCH_HEAD, keeping every one of the existing SSRF/hardening flags (IP pinning, no redirects, no credential helper, ...) on every one of those four git invocations, not just the first.

docs.title: PR-triggered scans don't feed the asset's Issue lifecycle
docs.text: A pull_request scan targets the same Asset a push-triggered scan of the repo would (same asset_key), but core/pipeline.py only calls sync_issues_for_scan (ADR-0012) when scan.ref is None. A PR previews code that might never merge; treating its findings as the asset's real current state would corrupt fixed/reintroduced detection the moment the PR closes without merging — a finding only present on the PR branch would show as "new," then falsely "fixed" the next time the real branch is scanned and it's correctly absent. This is a real risk that isn't obvious until you trace through what sync_issues_for_scan assumes about "absence means fixed."

docs.title: Result delivery reuses the Action's comment poster, not a second one
docs.text: core/ci/github.py's upsert_comment already exists, is tested, and only needs a token — it doesn't care whether that token came from Actions' GITHUB_TOKEN or an App's installation token. The App path builds its own comment body (core/github_app.pr_comment_body, a plain per-PR summary, not a diff — see "what was actually built" below for why) and calls the same upsert_comment. No Check Runs API this week; a PR comment is a smaller, already-built surface that does the job.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Diff the PR against the base branch, like the Action's core/ci/compare.py does. Rejected for this week: that needs a scan of the base branch to diff against, and running two scans per PR (base + head) doubles cost for a feature that's supposed to make scanning more automatic, not more expensive. pr_comment_body shows a plain summary of the PR's own findings instead. Real base-vs-head diffing for the App path is a reasonable future upgrade once there's a cheaper way to get a base-branch baseline (e.g., reusing the asset's last completed non-PR scan).
  • Check Runs API instead of a comment. Rejected for this week: a genuinely nicer UI (shows in the PR's Checks tab, can annotate specific lines), but it's a new results-rendering surface to build and test, and this week's job is the App's plumbing (auth, webhooks, tenant resolution), not a new UI.
  • Bypass privilege for the worker to look up a scan's org_id itself, instead of threading it through the enqueue call (as Week 29 already does for exactly this reason). Not reconsidered here; Week 29's scoped_sessions mechanism is reused as-is for PR-triggered scans, since the API always knows the org before dispatching regardless of why it's creating the scan.

docs.title: What was actually built, and where it differs from the design above
docs.text:
• Nothing significant differs from the design — this ADR was written after implementation (like ADR-0012/0013), so "design" and "built" line up more closely than usual. The real surprises were bugs, not design gaps; see the verification doc.
  • One explicit limitation, stated plainly rather than glossed over: live verification against a real, registered GitHub App was not possible this week. Registering an App (getting an App ID, generating its private key, setting a webhook URL) is the user's action on their own GitHub account, the same way pushing to origin/main has stayed theirs through this whole project. What was verified live: real RS256 JWT signing/verification with a real (test) RSA keypair, the full webhook receiver against the real running API and Postgres (including real Row-Level Security), and — using a real, existing public GitHub pull request — the ref-based git clone path against the actual GitHub API, not a mock. What remains unverified: an installation token actually accepted by GitHub, and a PR comment actually posted and visible on a real pull request.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The web app has no UI for this yet (no "connected repositories" page, no installation management) — API/webhook only, consistent with how this project's API has repeatedly shipped ahead of its UI.
  • A caller who already knows the shared v1.0 bearer token cannot forge a webhook (a different trust mechanism, HMAC-verified against a secret only GitHub and this server know) — but per-installation authorization of which repos a given webhook may act on is entirely GitHub's own responsibility (the installation token itself is scoped by GitHub to only what that installation was granted).
  • Uninstalling the App removes the GithubInstallation mapping but never the Organization or its scan/issue history (ADR-0013's durability guarantee, unchanged). Reinstalling gets a new installation id and therefore a new org — there is no way to prove it's "the same" account asking, so this doesn't attempt to guess.
  • core/config.py's three new settings are all optional and all-empty by default: an existing self-hosted deployment that never sets them is completely unaffected, and the webhook endpoint simply 404s.

docs.title: ADR-0018: Scoped, hashed, prefixed API tokens
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-28, Week 29 backfill). Verified live against real Postgres; see docs/v2-week29-backfill-verification.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
v1.0/Week 29 authenticated every request with one shared BULWARK_API_TOKEN — "the whole deployment," full access, org selected only by a client-suppliable X-Bulwark-Org header (ADR-0013). ADR-0013 documented this as a known limitation, not a finished access-control story: a caller who knows the token can claim any org id that exists.

The plan's §19.2 asks for real per-token identity: a recognizable prefix plus a checksum (GitHub's own token format), shown once, stored only as a hash, carrying scopes, and expiring.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
core/tokens.py (pure logic) generates bulwark_<40 hex chars>_<6-char base62 checksum>:

  • The checksum (CRC32-derived) is a typo/truncation check, not a security property — it lets a clearly-malformed token be rejected before it ever reaches a database lookup.
  • Only sha256(raw) is ever persisted (ApiToken.token_hash); the raw value is returned exactly once, by core.persistence.repo.create_api_token, and the CLI that calls it never logs it.
  • display_prefix (the first 14 characters) is safe to show afterwards in a token listing, so an operator can tell tokens apart without the secret ever being reconstructable from it.

Scopes are real and enforced, not decorative. SCOPES = {"scans:read", "scans:write"} today — deliberately smaller than the plan's own example (issues:read), because there is no dedicated issues endpoint yet (ADR-0012's own deferred item) to gate with it. A scope that nothing checks would be a scope that lies about what it does; new scopes get added alongside the endpoint they actually restrict, not ahead of it.

A scoped token's org is authoritative, not client-suppliable. api/deps.py's AuthContext carries org_id and scopes from whichever credential authenticated the request:

  • The legacy shared token: org_id=None, scopes=None — "the whole deployment," exactly ADR-0013's existing behavior, X-Bulwark-Org still selects scope as before.
  • A real scoped token: org_id fixed to the token's own org, X-Bulwark-Org ignored entirely for it. Trusting a client-suppliable header over what the token actually authenticated as would defeat the entire point of scoping the token — this is the concrete fix for the exact limitation ADR-0013 named.

api_tokens carries no Row-Level Security policy, for the same structural reason github_installations doesn't (ADR-0017): authenticating a request with a token is what resolves org context in the first place, so the lookup that does it can't itself require org context to already exist. It's a directory/credential table, not tenant-owned content.

Token management is CLI-only (bulwark token create/list/revoke), not a self-service API endpoint. There is no per-user identity yet for a "your tokens" page to belong to (that's the deferred piece below) — an operator with direct database/container access mints tokens for now, the same trust boundary bulwark kb load already operates at.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• A separate lookup table keyed by a short public id, instead of hashing the whole token and looking up by hash directly. Rejected: unnecessary complexity — token_hash is already a fixed-length, indexed, exact-match value; there's no scan-the-table cost to avoid.
  • Letting the org header override a scoped token's org when explicitly requested. Rejected: no legitimate use case needs it, and it reintroduces exactly the trust-the-header problem this ADR exists to close.

docs.title: What was actually built, and where it differs from the design above
docs.text:
• No custom Gitleaks rule for the platform's own token format, despite the plan explicitly asking for one ("the scanner protects its own credentials"). This needs mounting a custom .gitleaks.toml into the gitleaks scanner container, but the sandboxed runner (core/runner.py) launches sibling containers via the host's Docker daemon (Docker-outside- of-Docker, the same reason BULWARK_WORKDIR must be host-visible) — a bind mount path has to exist on the host, not just inside the api/worker container, and no such mechanism exists yet for a one-off config file. A real, small follow-up (extend ToolSpec with a read-only mount, materialize the config into scratch_dir()), deliberately not rushed into the sandboxing code in the middle of an already-large backfill.
  • No self-service token API, no web UI for tokens — CLI-only, as decided above; not a deviation so much as the plan's own identity work (§19.2's sign-in) not existing yet to hang a self-service page off of.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• AuthContext.actor (e.g. "token:bulwark_5c83e8") is available for audit-log attribution (ADR-0019) wherever an authenticated API request should be logged — not wired into every endpoint yet, since most of the plan's own example audit actions (role changes, triage, fix approvals) don't exist as features yet either.
  • A future org-management/self-service API, when it exists, should reuse require_scope and AuthContext rather than inventing a second auth layer alongside them.

docs.title: ADR-0019: Tamper-evident audit log (hash chain + Rekor checkpoints)
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-28, Week 30 backfill), except a real, published Rekor checkpoint — that step is a real, permanent, public write to a third-party transparency log, done only with explicit confirmation each time, not automatically as part of this backfill. See docs/v2-week29-backfill-verification.md for exactly what was and wasn't verified live.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Nothing in Bulwark records that a security-relevant action happened in a way that survives someone with database access editing or deleting the record afterward. The plan's §19.3 (and its own ADR-008 slot) asks for a hash-chained log with periodic checkpoints signed and published to Sigstore's Rekor transparency log — "the original blockchain idea done properly": tamper-evidence without a distributed ledger, using infrastructure the software supply-chain world already depends on (this project already uses cosign/Sigstore for SBOM attestation, ADR-009).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
core/audit.py (pure logic, no DB access — mirrors core/issues.py's split):

entry_hash = SHA256(seq || prev_hash || timestamp || actor || action || target || payload_digest)
  • payload_digest, never the payload itself: deleting the underlying record later (a revoked token, a removed installation) must never break the chain, since the chain never depended on that data still existing.
  • seq is application-assigned, not a database autoincrement — the chain needs to know the exact sequence number before the row exists, to hash it. core/persistence/repo.py's append_audit_entry handles the read-latest-then-insert race with a bounded optimistic-retry loop, not a database lock: an accepted, documented simplification at this project's current scale (one API process, one worker), not a claim that a concurrent-write race is impossible.
  • verify_chain checks each entry's prev_hash against the actual previous entry's entry_hash — not against that entry's own prev_hash field, which an attacker could edit to agree with a forged entry_hash on the same row. Editing any stored field is caught at that entry; deleting an entry is caught at the next one, whose prev_hash now points at a hash that doesn't exist.

A single, global, operator-facing ledger — not per-organization. There's no per-org sign-in yet for a per-org audit screen to gate access to (that's the deferred identity work, §19.2/ADR-0018's own deferred item); building per-org filtering ahead of the UI that would need it is speculative scope.

Checkpointing (core/audit_rekor.py) is key-based signing with real Rekor upload, not keyless. The plan's own architecture diagram mentions "keyless signing through Sigstore's Fulcio CA," but keyless signing needs an OIDC identity provider this project doesn't integrate with for a long-running self-hosted server (GitHub Actions gets this for free via its own ambient OIDC token; a Docker Compose deployment does not). Rekor's transparency-log guarantee doesn't require keyless signing — a key-based cosign sign-blob still uploads to the public log unless told not to, which is exactly this module's job. This reuses the same cosign generate-key-pair / COSIGN_PASSWORD setup core/attest already documents, in a new, separate module rather than extending core/attest/cosign.py: that module signs scan artifacts completely offline (--network=none, --tlog-upload=false) by design, and a checkpoint's entire purpose is the opposite of offline.

bulwark audit verify walks the whole chain and recomputes every hash; bulwark audit checkpoint signs the current head and publishes it. Neither runs automatically yet (see below).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Keyless (Fulcio-issued, OIDC-bound) signing, as the plan's diagram suggests. Rejected for now: no OIDC identity provider integration exists for a long-running server outside GitHub Actions' own workflow context. Revisit if/when Bulwark runs as a GitHub Actions-triggered job for this specific purpose, or integrates a real OIDC provider for other reasons first.
  • A DB-level lock (advisory lock or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) around append_audit_entry, instead of an optimistic retry loop. Rejected for this week: more moving parts (and a dialect difference between SQLite tests and Postgres) for a race that's currently unlikely at this project's scale. Documented as an accepted simplification, not hidden.

docs.title: What was actually built, and where it differs from the design above
docs.text:
• A real, live-tested, genuine bug was caught building this: SQLite (and possibly a differently-configured Postgres session) can hand back a naive datetime even for a DateTime(timezone=True) column. compute_hash's original .astimezone(timezone.utc) on a naive value assumes the local zone, silently shifting it — meaning verify_chain would recompute a different hash than the one written, and report a perfectly untampered chain as broken. Fixed by treating a naive timestamp as already UTC (every timestamp this codebase writes is UTC, core.persistence.models._now) before hashing. Caught by a real, live test failure against actual data, not by inspection — and confirmed fixed against both SQLite and real Postgres afterward.
  • Automatic checkpointing (every hour or every N entries, per the plan) is not wired up. bulwark audit checkpoint exists and works, run by hand or from external cron/CI, but nothing in core/tasks.py's Celery beat schedule calls it yet. A deliberate Week 30 scope cut: wiring a scheduled task is small, but this ADR's job was proving the checkpoint mechanism itself works (including a real, deliberately-confirmed publish to the public Rekor instance) before automating when it fires.
  • No audit log screen in the web app. Backend + CLI only, consistent with how this project's API has repeatedly shipped ahead of its UI.
  • Only two real integration points log anything today: installation.created / installation.deleted (the GitHub App webhook, ADR-0017) and token.created / token.revoked (ADR-0018's CLI). Most of the plan's own example actions to log — role changes, triage decisions, accepted risk, policy changes, fix approvals, DAST authorizations — don't exist as features yet. The log is real and ready for them; there is nothing to log for a feature that isn't built.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every future feature the plan lists as auditable (risk acceptance, policy changes, fix approvals, DAST authorization) should call repo.append_audit_entry when it ships, not retrofit it later — this ADR is the checklist a reviewer should hold new security-relevant actions to.
  • A real Rekor checkpoint, once published, is permanent and public. bulwark audit checkpoint should not be run against production data without deliberately intending that — there's no --undo.
  • audit_entries/audit_checkpoints carry no org_id and no RLS; if this ever needs to become per-organization (a customer-facing audit screen, not just an operator one), that's a schema migration and a scoping decision this ADR does not make for it.

docs.title: ADR-0020: Code intelligence — symbols, call graph, entrypoint detection
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-29, Week 37), in-memory only — Postgres persistence deferred to Week 38 (its first real consumer). See docs/v2-week37-verification.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The plan's §20.2/§20.3 (taint analysis, Week 38) needs to answer "is this sink reachable from an HTTP entrypoint, and by what path?"
