That needs three things that don't exist yet: a way to find functions in source code, a way to know which functions call which, and a way to find the functions a web framework actually exposes as routes. This week builds all three, general enough for the taint engine to walk next week, without yet building the taint engine itself.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
core/codeintel/, structured in four pieces:

  • models.py: Symbol (one function/method definition), CallEdge (one call site, resolved to a Symbol or not), Entrypoint (a route: framework, method, path, the Symbol it enters), CodeGraph (the whole analysis, plus callers_of/calls_from for the one-hop queries a reachability walk needs).
  • One extractor per language (python_lang.py, js_lang.py, go_lang.py): parses one file into raw Symbols and (caller_id, callee_name, line) call sites, plus any entrypoints that file's own decorators/exports/registrations reveal.
  • resolve.py: turns every file's raw calls into a CodeGraph's resolved edges, intra-file first, then by name across the whole repository.
  • __init__.py: analyze(root)/analyze_or_none(root), walking the tree once and dispatching by extension — the same never-raises contract core/reachability already established.

docs.title: Python uses ast, not tree-sitter-python
docs.text: The plan's own wording says "parse Python... with tree-sitter." This deviates from that, on purpose: core/reachability/imports.py already made the same choice for the same reason — Python ships a real, maintained parser (ast) in the standard library, so there's nothing tree-sitter would add here except a dependency. JavaScript/TypeScript and Go have no such built-in, so they use tree-sitter (tree-sitter-javascript, tree-sitter-typescript — already a dependency; tree-sitter-go, added this week).

docs.title: Entrypoint detection is shape-based, not import-based
docs.text:
@app.get("/path") is recognized as FastAPI by the shape of the decorator (an HTTP-verb method call with a string first argument), not by confirming app really came from fastapi import FastAPI. The same is true of Flask's @app.route, Express's app.get(...), and Go's http.HandleFunc. Resolving the real import chain reliably (through aliasing, re-exports, dependency-injected app objects) is a much larger analysis than decorator/call inspection, and would still be wrong for a hand-rolled function that merely happens to be named get. This is a documented, deliberate approximation: a false positive is a function that looks like a route but isn't; a false negative is a route registered through enough indirection that its shape doesn't match (a factory function building the decorator, for instance).

Next.js is the exception — it uses file location, not code shape (app/**/route.ts exporting GET/POST/etc., or pages/api/**/*.ts's default export), because that is what Next.js's own routing is actually keyed on; there is no decorator to inspect. The path derived from the file's location is a close but not exact match to Next.js's own resolution (route groups like (marketing) are not stripped, and [...slug] catch-alls are left as literal path segments) — documented in js_lang.py's own docstring, not silently wrong.

docs.title: Call resolution is intra-procedural first, then name-based — and is unsound where the plan says it will be
docs.text:
A call site's name is matched against symbols defined in the same file first (so a file that defines its own process resolves to it, even if another, unrelated process exists elsewhere). Failing that, it's matched against every symbol with that name across the whole repository only if there is exactly one — an ambiguous or absent match stays unresolved (callee_id=None), the same "unknown stays unknown, never guessed" principle core/reachability/index.py uses for package reachability. This cannot and does not handle:

  • Dynamic dispatch (getattr(obj, name)(), calling a value stored in a dict/list).
  • Reflection (importlib.import_module(computed_name)).
  • Genuine name collisions with no local definition to disambiguate — the exact case the plan asks to be honest about, not silently resolved to an arbitrary candidate.

An inline callback (an anonymous arrow function passed to .map(), setTimeout, etc. — everywhere except the one place an anonymous function needs its own identity, an inline route handler) has its calls folded into the enclosing named function rather than becoming its own graph node: for the reachability question this graph exists to answer, a call made from inside a closure is exactly as reachable as the function that created it, so nothing is lost by not giving every closure literal its own place in the graph.

docs.title: Persistence: deferred, on purpose
docs.text: The plan says "store the graph in Postgres as an edges table." This week's CodeGraph is in-memory only, not yet written to a database. A Postgres schema (code_symbols, call_graph_edges, entrypoints, asset-scoped like issues, with the same Row-Level Security pattern) is a bounded, well-understood addition on its own, but it has no real reader yet — Week 38's taint engine is the first thing that will actually query this data, and its access pattern (does it read whole-graph per asset? walk edges lazily? cache in memory per scan?) should inform the schema rather than being guessed at now. Building and RLS-hardening a table nothing reads yet, in the same week as the graph construction itself, traded a genuine but premature piece of the plan's literal wording for real risk to a security-sensitive migration with no validating consumer in this session. Deferred explicitly, not silently dropped.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Reachability today (core/reachability, SCA-only: "is this package imported") is unaffected; this is new, separate infrastructure for a different, broader question ("is this code called from an entrypoint") that Week 38 will connect to scoring.
  • The taint engine's function summaries (plan §20.3) can be built directly on CodeGraph.symbols/ edges/entrypoints without re-parsing anything.
  • Every unresolved edge, every unparsed file, and every entrypoint whose shape didn't match is something Week 38 (and any future consumer) must treat as "don't know," not "not reachable" — the same discipline core/reachability/index.py's three-valued Reachability already established.

docs.title: ADR-0021: Taint analysis — sources, sinks, function summaries, concrete paths
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-29, Week 38), in-memory only, not yet wired to Issues/scoring. See docs/v2-week38-verification.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: core.codeintel (Week 37, ADR-0020) can find functions, resolve calls between them, and detect HTTP entrypoints — but it says nothing about what a function actually does with the data it receives. The plan's own framing calls this next piece "the most demanding piece of programming in the project": precise intra-procedural data flow, plus function summaries propagated over the call graph with a worklist until a fixed point, so a source-to-sink path can be reported step by step without re-analysing a function once for every caller.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
core/taint/, five pieces:

  • models.py: SinkHit (one place a tainted value reached a sink, plus the hop chain that led there), FunctionSummary (what a function does with its own parameters, computed once, independent of any caller), TaintFinding (a complete source-to-sink path from a real entrypoint).
  • catalog.py + catalogs/{python,javascript,go}.yaml: sources, sinks, and sanitizers, matched by name the same way core.codeintel's own call graph already extracts a callee name — not a giant table of attribute-access patterns (see "Sources are literally parameters" below).
  • One flow analyzer per language (python_flow.py via ast, js_flow.py/go_flow.py via tree-sitter): the actual intra-procedural algorithm, detailed below.
  • engine.py: the call-graph worklist — compute_summaries (pass 1) and find_taint_paths (pass 2).
  • __init__.py: analyze(root)/analyze_or_none(root), the same never-raises contract core.codeintel and core.reachability both already established. Every file that contributed a Symbol is re-parsed here, independently of core.codeintel's own pass, to recover the actual function bodies — the same "each analysis parses its own files" precedent ADR-0020 already set, now extended one layer further.

docs.title: A tainted value's provenance is a set of tags, not a boolean
docs.text: One mechanism has to answer two different questions: "if this function's parameter 2 is ever tainted, does it reach a sink?" (a hypothetical, caller-independent question — a FunctionSummary) and "starting from this real entrypoint, does a sink actually fire?" (a TaintFinding). Both questions are answered by the exact same per-function analyzer; only the seed differs — parameter indices ({0}, {1}, ...) for the first, the literal tag SOURCE for the second. A SinkHit found while seeded with parameter tags becomes part of that function's summary; the same code path, re-run later seeded with SOURCE from a real entrypoint, produces a real TaintFinding.

docs.title: Sources are literally "request parameters," per the plan's own wording
docs.text: Not a table of attribute-access patterns (request.args.get, req.body.x, ...). Concretely: a catalog names either a global_sources entry (a bare name that is always tainted wherever it's referenced — Flask's imported request object, which also covers a Django view's request parameter for free, since ast/tree-sitter can't tell a parameter from a global reference; both are just a name) or a param_source_positions entry (the position of an entrypoint handler's request-like parameter — Express's (req, res) => {}, Go's func(w, r) {} — position, not name, since a handler is free to call it anything). FastAPI's typed-parameter style (a request body arriving as a Pydantic model parameter, not an attribute access) needs the parameter's type annotation, not its name or position, to know it carries external input — a documented gap this catalog format doesn't express, not a silent guess.

docs.title: The algorithm: may-taint, not must-taint — over-approximate on purpose
docs.text:
A call's result taint is the union of its argument taints (plus, for a method call, the taint of its own receiver — request.args.get('id') must come out tainted because request.args is, even though 'id' the literal argument plainly is not). A branch (if/try) is walked once per arm from the same starting state, and the resulting states are merged by unioning each name's tags — not visited sequentially into one shared map, which would let one arm's clean reassignment wrongly erase taint another arm introduced (a real bug caught and fixed during this week's own testing, see verification doc). A loop body is visited once, not iterated to a fixed point. An unresolved call (no summary, not in any catalog) is assumed to pass taint through its arguments rather than drop it.

Every one of these choices trades recall for precision in the safe direction for a security tool: a reviewable false positive costs far less than a silently missed real vulnerability. This is not free, and the plan's own validation instruction — cross-check against Semgrep's taint mode — is what this week actually measured that trade-off against, not just asserted it (see verification doc).

docs.title: Function summaries compose across the call graph via a bounded worklist
docs.text:
compute_summaries seeds every function with its own parameters (hypothetically tainted, one tag per parameter) plus any real global_sources, analyses it once, and re-queues its callers (CodeGraph.callers_of) whenever its summary changes — a caller can only need re-analysis because a callee it calls changed, so re-queuing exactly those callers is what keeps this from being O(passes × graph size). Capped at MAX_WORKLIST_PASSES = 50 so a call cycle (direct or mutual recursion, tested explicitly) cannot loop forever; summaries only grow via union operations, so this is monotonic and converges well inside that cap for any repository this was tested against.

Each SinkHit re-exposed from a callee's summary into a caller carries a hops tuple, one TaintHop prepended per level — so by the time a TaintFinding is built from an entrypoint's own analysis, the chain already reads in call order (the entrypoint's own hop, then each intermediate call, in the order they were actually made), fulfilling the plan's "each hop... rendered step by step" without needing a second reconstruction pass.

docs.title: Named-handler route registrations are followed to their real body
docs.text: app.get('/login', sessionHandler.displayLoginPage) (Express) and a Django urlpatterns entry both make core.codeintel mint a synthetic symbol that is nothing but a redirect — a route registration call with no body of its own. engine._redirect_target follows that symbol's one outgoing call edge to the function that actually has a body to seed. Without this, none of NodeGoat's own routing (entirely written this way) would produce a single finding — confirmed directly, see verification doc.

docs.title: Persistence, and Issue/scoring integration: deferred, on purpose
docs.text: This week's TaintFindings are in-memory only, returned from analyze(), not written to Postgres or attached to an Issue. Building that integration (which findings become which Issue fields, how a taint path renders in the UI per plan §28.3, whether Postgres persistence happens now or is deferred again) is real, separable work that benefits from being scoped on its own rather than appended to an already-large week — the same reasoning ADR-0020 gave for deferring CodeGraph persistence to this week.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every finding's hop chain, source, and sink location is real and traceable to actual source positions — never fabricated or estimated — but the rate of resolved findings depends entirely on core.codeintel's own call-resolution soundness (ADR-0020): a call this project's own resolver can't attribute to a symbol, taint can't follow either.
  • The catalogs are intentionally small and named after the plan's own examples (cursor.execute, subprocess.run, eval, parameterized queries, escaping functions) rather than an exhaustive sink/sanitizer library; extending them is additive, low-risk work for a future week, not a redesign.
  • Anything this analysis cannot express — dynamic dispatch, reflection, FastAPI's typed-parameter sourcing, object-field-level taint (as opposed to bare-name taint), path-sensitive branches, loop fixed points — is a documented "doesn't know," the same discipline core.reachability and core.codeintel both already established, not a silent wrong answer.

docs.title: ADR-0022: Taint findings attach to Issues, feed scoring, and reach the UI
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-29, follow-up within Week 38). Closes the three items ADR-0021 deferred: "Taint paths attached to Issues; reachability v2 feeds scoring; UI: the taint-path stepper goes live" (plan's own Week 38 line item).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR-0021 built the taint engine itself but stopped at core.taint.analyze() returning an in-memory list[TaintFinding] — nothing connected it to an actual scan's Findings, to risk scoring, or to the UI. This closes that gap.

docs.title: Enrichment, not a new finding type
docs.text: core/taint/reachability.py::attach_taint_paths() never creates a Finding. It matches an existing SAST Finding (already produced by Semgrep, Bandit, or another SAST tool) to a taint sink by exact (path, start_line), and only then attaches the path — the same role core.reachability's package-level reachability already plays for SCA findings: "is something another tool already flagged actually reachable," never "here is a vulnerability nothing else found." A SAST finding whose own location has no matching taint sink is returned completely unchanged.

docs.title: The confidence field, not a new scoring formula
docs.text:
core/risk/score.py::score_finding already has a rule for exactly this situation: a finding with no CVE/EPSS/KEV data (true of essentially every SAST finding) uses scoring.confidence directly as its likelihood. Rather than adding a second, parallel "taint reachability" multiplier that would need to be kept consistent with the existing CVE/EPSS/KEV/confidence logic, attach_taint_paths raises confidence to a fixed TAINT_CONFIRMED_CONFIDENCE = 0.9 (never lowers it) when a concrete path is found, and lets the existing formula do the rest. Measured effect on a synthetic HIGH-severity SAST finding: risk_score 56 → 71 once a real taint path is attached — a meaningful, correctly-directed change, not a cosmetic one.

scoring.reachable is set separately, through the same Assess composition core.reachability already uses: core/postprocess.py::finalize() builds one combined assess callable that tries TaintIndex.assess (SAST) then falls back to ReachabilityIndex.assess (SCA) — the two never both apply to the same finding, so trying taint first costs nothing when a finding is SCA.

docs.title: No new database table
docs.text: FindingRow.data (core/persistence/models.py) already stores a Finding's full to_dict() output as JSON. Adding taint_path: tuple[TaintPathStep, ...] to the Finding dataclass (core/models/finding.py) means every taint path persists automatically through that existing column — no migration, no new table. CodeGraph/FunctionSummary themselves are still not persisted (ADR-0021's own deferral stands); only the final, already-attached path on a Finding is.

docs.title: Per-step code snippets are captured at scan time, not fetched later
docs.text: The plan's own UI mockup (§28.3) shows the code view changing as each step is clicked, including steps in files other than the sink's own. There is no "fetch arbitrary file content" API, and building one is a larger, separable piece of work. Instead, attach_taint_paths takes the scanned workspace's root path (still on disk at that point in the pipeline — core/scan.py/ core/pipeline.py call finalize(..., root=target)) and reads a few lines of context around each hop directly, storing it on TaintPathStep.snippet. This is the one point in the whole pipeline where the checked-out source is guaranteed to still exist; capturing it here is strictly cheaper than building a new on-demand file-serving endpoint, at the cost of a fixed, non-configurable context window (2 lines either side) rather than letting the UI request more.

docs.title: The UI stepper already existed, built ahead of the data
docs.text: web/design-system/taint-stepper.tsx was built in an earlier week explicitly "static until Phase 9 supplies real paths," rendering the finding's own location as the one honest step until then. This change is almost entirely on the data side: IssueDetail.tsx now maps finding.taint_path (when non-empty) into the stepper's existing TaintStep[] shape, defaults the active step to the sink (not step 1 — matching the plan's own mockup, where the code view opens on the dangerous call), and passes each step's own path/line/snippet to CodeView as it's clicked. The one real component change: the sink's ◄ marker used to be tied to whichever step was currently clicked (activeIndex), which meant it would move away from the sink the moment a user clicked a different step and lose its meaning; it's now driven by TaintStep.isSink, a fact about the data, independent of what the user has clicked.

docs.title: Backward compatibility with data persisted before this change
docs.text: A Finding written to the database before this change has no taint_path key in its stored JSON. Both the Python (finding_from_dict's d.get("taint_path", ())) and TypeScript (finding.taint_path ?? []) sides default it to empty rather than raising — found directly by an existing accessibility test whose fixture predated this field and crashed on undefined.length until the fallback was added, not by inspection.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A repository's real, currently-unpatched SQL injection or command injection reachable from an HTTP entrypoint now visibly outranks an otherwise-identical but unreachable finding — the "Why it's ranked first: Reachable from POST /login, a public route" line from the plan's own mockup is now real output, not illustrative copy.
  • The taint engine's own precision limits (ADR-0021: no FastAPI typed-parameter sourcing, no object-field taint, not path-sensitive) apply here unchanged — a finding this doesn't enrich is not "confirmed unreachable," it is "no confirmed path found," and its score is unaffected either way, the same "unknown, not false" discipline the rest of this project already holds to.
  • The next real gap is Postgres persistence of the graph itself, for a consumer that needs to query it directly rather than through a Finding it already produced — still not this week's problem.

docs.title: ADR-0023: Policy-as-code — embedded OPA, a starter Rego library, and policy-driven PR gates
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-29, Week 39), core engine and CI/Action integration done; the policy editor UI (Monaco, live evaluation, save) is explicitly deferred — see "Deferred" below.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Every gate this project has had until now is a severity threshold (fail_on): fail the check if any new finding is at or above some severity. That can't express "no secrets, ever, regardless of severity" or "an accepted risk expires after 90 days" or "no denylisted license" — real organizational rules that aren't about severity at all. The plan's answer (§20.4) is to embed Open Policy Agent and let an organization write these as Rego, evaluated against the scan's own Issue set, with deny messages driving the pull-request check.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
core/policy/, four pieces:

  • opa.py: a thin subprocess wrapper around the real opa binary — check_syntax, eval_deny, run_tests.
  • input.py: builds the OPA input document ({"new_issues": [...]}, the plan's own field name) from a scan's existing Finding dicts — no new data collection, only reshaping what already exists.
  • starter/gate.rego + gate_test.rego: the plan's own five example policies, each its own deny contains msg if {...} block in one gate.pull_request package (Rego unions same-named rules automatically), with a full opa test suite.
  • gate.py: evaluate_gate(), the one function both bulwark ci compare and (eventually) a policy editor call.

docs.title: OPA runs directly, not through the sandboxed scanner runner
docs.text: Every other external tool in this project (core.runner, gVisor-sandboxed) exists to run against untrusted repository content. OPA evaluates this platform's own already-computed output — a scan's findings — against a policy that is either the bundled starter library or something an org admin wrote. There is nothing here for a sandbox to protect against that core.risk.score (which also runs directly, unsandboxed, over the same kind of data) doesn't already face. Running opa as a plain subprocess, not a Docker-sandboxed adapter, is the same trust boundary this project already draws elsewhere, applied consistently.

docs.title: The input schema only sends fields that already have a real source
docs.text:
issue_document() (core/policy/input.py) maps directly from an existing Finding's own fields — severity, category, cwe, in_cisa_kev, reachable (Week 38's own taint work), entrypoint (read from a taint path's own entrypoint hop, when one exists). Two fields the starter library's own example rules reference have no real source yet anywhere in this codebase, and are handled honestly rather than faked:

  • license — needs Week 40's SBOM/license work (plan §20.5). Until then, no Finding/Package carries a license at all, so the field is simply absent from the input document, never sent as null or "unknown". The starter library's license-denylist rule is real, tested Rego — it is just dead code in practice today, the same way the UI taint stepper was real code fed no real data for several weeks before Week 37/38 landed.
  • triage_expires_at — lives on IssueRow (a database row keyed by asset), not on the standalone Finding JSON a bulwark scan --format json file contains. build_input() accepts an optional issues_by_fingerprint map so the hosted pipeline (which has database access) can supply it; the standalone CLI/Action gate (which only ever sees two JSON files, no database) genuinely cannot, and does not pretend to.

docs.title: bulwark ci compare --policy folds into the existing exit-code contract, not a new one
docs.text: ci_compare already had a well-defined contract (exit 0/1/2, --fail-on, a markdown comment, a $GITHUB_OUTPUT block) that action.yml's "Enforce the threshold" step and every downstream consumer already understands. Adding --policy composes into that same contract rather than inventing a parallel one: failed = bool(severity_breaches) or bool(policy_denials), one exit code, one markdown comment with a new "Policy violations" section only when there are any, one new policy-violations GitHub Actions output (only emitted when --policy was actually passed — a scan running without a configured policy gets no new noise in its output). A syntactically invalid policy exits 2 (the same "unusable input" code load_scan already uses for a corrupt scan file), not a silent pass.

docs.title: action.yml's new policy-file input only pays for OPA when it's used
docs.text: The OPA binary is only downloaded when policy-file is non-empty (if: ${{ inputs.policy-file != '' }}) — a repository that hasn't configured a policy pays nothing extra. The project's own CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) always installs a checksum-pinned OPA and runs opa test core/policy/starter, exactly the plan's own "opa test runs the policy tests in CI"; the reusable Action's own install is unpinned (no single fixed architecture to pin a checksum against, unlike the project's own ubuntu-latest CI runner), a deliberate, smaller trade-off than the project's own pipeline makes for itself.

docs.title: Deferred: the policy editor UI
docs.text: Plan §28.6: "Monaco editor for Rego on the left, live evaluation against the last scan on the right... Save is disabled until opa test passes." Not built this session. This needs real, separable design work of its own — an org-scoped policy storage table and migration, two new API endpoints (evaluate a draft policy against the latest scan; save one, gated on check_syntax passing), and a new frontend page with a Monaco integration — comparable in size to everything above it in this ADR, and better scoped on its own than appended to an already-large week. Today, an organization can use policy-as-code in full by committing a .rego file to their repository and pointing the Action's policy-file input at it — no UI is required for the mechanism itself to work end to end, matching how OPA and most policy engines are actually used in practice.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A finding's severity alone no longer decides everything: a LOW-severity secret now fails a configured gate the exact same way a leaked credential should, regardless of how any individual scanner happened to rate it.
  • The starter library's license-denylist and 90-day-risk-acceptance rules are real, tested, and will start actually firing the moment their data sources land (Week 40's SBOM work; already-live for triage data in the hosted pipeline) — no code change needed when that happens, only real data flowing into fields that were always there.
  • The next real gap is the policy editor UI itself, and, separately, Week 40's own license data — neither is this week's problem.

docs.title: ADR-0024: Supply-chain risk — malicious-package severity, license policy, typosquats, Scorecard
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-29, Week 40), core detection and CLI done; the Dependencies screen UI is explicitly deferred — see "Deferred" below.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Plan §20.5 names four checks: dependency health (OpenSSF Scorecard), malicious packages (OSV's MAL- advisories), typosquatting, and license compliance against the SBOM — plus a "dependency view" showing direct versus transitive packages, which path pulls in a vulnerable one, and the smallest upgrade that fixes it. This closes Milestone M8 (Weeks 37–40: reachability, Issue lifecycle, policy gates, supply-chain risk), tagged v1.3.0.

docs.title: Malicious packages needed a severity fix, not a new pipeline
docs.text: Before this week, running osv-scanner --offline-vulnerabilities (already Bulwark's default SCA tool) against a package with a reported MAL- id already produced a Finding — OSV's database includes OSSF's malicious-packages reports as ordinary records, confirmed live against api.osv.dev (reuests, a real typosquat of requests, returns MAL-2022-7441). The bug: such a record carries no CVSS score and no severity label, so it fell through to normalize()'s default — INFO, the lowest severity — exactly backwards from what a confirmed malicious package deserves. core/adapters/osv_scanner.py now detects a MAL- id in a group's aliases and forces CRITICAL severity, 1.0 confidence, and a title/remediation that says "malicious package," not "upgrade to fix." core/policy/input.py exposes this as malicious (always present, false by default, the same shape as in_cisa_kev), and the starter library gained a sixth rule: no malicious packages, ever, the same reasoning as its existing "no secrets, ever" rule.

docs.title: License policy needed license data to exist somewhere first
docs.text: core/policy/input.py::issue_document already read package["license"] — ADR-0023 left the field wired but unpopulated, honestly noting it needed this week's SBOM work. core/sbom/syft.py now parses each CycloneDX component's own licenses[] (both the expression and license.id/.name forms) into a new SbomPackage, and core/sbom/enrich.py::apply_licenses joins that onto a finding's package by (ecosystem, name, version) — enrichment only, the same discipline core.taint.reachability established: a package the SBOM has no license for is left unchanged, not given a fabricated "unknown". bulwark ci compare gained --sbom PATH; the GitHub Action reuses its existing sbom: true input rather than adding a second one, and the "Generate SBOM" step moved earlier (before "Compare and gate", not after) since gating is now something the SBOM can feed, not only an artifact produced alongside it.

docs.title: Typosquat detection is genuinely new, not an enrichment
docs.text: Nothing else in Bulwark looks at a package's name on its own, so core/supplychain/typosquat.py produces new Findings directly from an SBOM's packages: a name within Levenshtein distance 1–2 of a popular package in the same ecosystem, and not itself that name. The reference set (popular_packages.json) is a small, hand-curated seed per ecosystem — there is no single canonical "top N packages" API the way EPSS/KEV are canonical feeds, so this is honestly a starting point, not a live popularity ranking.

docs.title: Scorecard is scoped to direct dependencies and split from the policy gate
docs.text:
core/supplychain/scorecard.py resolves a purl to its GitHub source repo via deps.dev (api.deps.dev/v3alpha/purl/<purl>) and fetches that repo's own weekly Scorecard run (api.securityscorecards.dev/projects/<repo>) — both validated against their live endpoints (github.com/psf/requests, github.com/sirupsen/logrus) before any Python was written around them, the same discipline ADR-0023 used for OPA. Two deliberate scope limits:

  • Direct dependencies only (the plan's own wording): both because that is what an organization can act on directly, and because it bounds a scan to one request pair per direct dependency, not one per transitive package, which can number in the hundreds.
  • A separate command (bulwark supply-chain analyze), not folded into ci compare: a typosquat or a Scorecard score is not a deny/allow policy decision the way a severity threshold or a Rego rule is — it is a report. Forcing it through the pass/fail gate would mean inventing a policy for data that is not itself a violation. It runs over an SBOM directly and writes a JSON report; a future policy could read that report's own fields the same way it reads issue.license today, once there is a real reason to gate on it.

Both cross network boundaries the sandboxed scanner runner deliberately does not (core.risk.feeds already draws this same line for EPSS/KEV): API/worker side only, cached (a week for Scorecard, matching its own refresh cadence), and best-effort — a network error yields None/an empty result, never a failed scan.

docs.title: Direct-versus-transitive and "smallest safe upgrade" are two different, reusable pieces
docs.text: core/sbom/syft.py::summarize now also derives direct_purls/transitive_purls/graph/roots from CycloneDX's own dependencies[].dependsOn array — real only when the lockfile format Syft read already recorded the tree (validated against a real bulwark/syft:1.52.0 run: a component's bom-ref is its purl plus a ?package-id=... qualifier, not the bare purl, which the summarizer translates before building the graph). core/supplychain/dependency_view.py::path_to walks that graph to answer "which path pulls in this package." Separately, core/scoring/versions.py's smallest_safe_upgrade fixes a real, if minor, existing bug: both osv_scanner.py and grype.py picked fixed[0] — whichever fixed version a scanner listed first, not the smallest — and a real OSV record can list a version out of order, or list git commit hashes alongside real releases (this codebase's own golden fixture has both cases). The fix compares dotted-numeric versions and refuses to order a mixed list rather than silently mis-comparing a hash against a release.

docs.title: Deferred: the Dependencies screen UI
docs.text: Plan §46/the supply-chain UI: a screen showing the dependency graph, the path to a vulnerable package, and the smallest safe upgrade. Not built this session. The data it would render is real and already tested (Sbom.graph/.roots, dependency_view.path_to, scoring.versions. smallest_safe_upgrade, the supply-chain analyze JSON report) — this is a rendering problem, not a data problem, the same relationship ADR-0023's deferred policy editor has to the policy engine it would sit on top of.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A malicious package now fails a default-severity gate the same way a leaked credential does, regardless of what severity label (if any) the underlying OSV record carries.
  • License policy, typosquat detection, and Scorecard enrichment are all real and usable today from the CLI/Action without any UI — an organization runs bulwark sbom, then bulwark ci compare --sbom and/or bulwark supply-chain analyze, the same "mechanism before UI" shape ADR-0023 used for policy-as-code.
  • The next real gaps are the Dependencies screen UI and, separately, wiring Syft into the hosted pipeline's own scan flow so license data exists there without a separate manual step — neither is this week's problem.

docs.title: ADR-0025: Dependencies screen — hosted SBOM/supply-chain integration
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-30), a follow-up to ADR-0024's supply-chain risk mechanism, which explicitly deferred this: "The data it would render is real and already tested... this is a rendering problem, not a data problem." This closes that gap end to end: pipeline, persistence, API, and a real frontend screen.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR-0024 built the supply-chain risk mechanism (SBOM parsing, typosquat detection, Scorecard enrichment, the dependency graph) as pure library code, reachable only via CLI commands. Nothing persisted it, no API served it, and no page rendered it — core/sbom/enrich.py's own docstring said so outright: "the hosted pipeline does not yet run Syft as part of a scan." This closes that gap: an organization opts a hosted scan into syft, and the result shows up as its own screen alongside Issues/Compare, the same way every other piece of scan data already does.

docs.title: One toggle for the whole feature area, reusing the existing per-scan tool mechanism
docs.text:
There is no feature-flag mechanism anywhere in this schema (Asset/Scan carry no settings columns) — the existing, consistent way every other optional tool (grype, checkov, gosec, dockle) opts in is Scan.tools. core/sbom/syft.py::SyftAdapter is now registered in core/scan.py's ADAPTERS under "syft", selectable exactly like any other tool from the API (ScanRequest.tools) or the web UI's own scan-creation form. Opting "syft" in gets the SBOM artifact and typosquat detection and Scorecard enrichment as one bundle (core/pipeline.py::_process_sbom) — not three separate flags, matching how the plan frames "supply-chain risk" as one feature, not three.

SyftAdapter needed one override: the base ToolAdapter.applies_to default (ctx.languages & spec.languages) is always false for it, since Syft catalogs manifests/lockfiles, not source files in core.adapters's "language" sense — without the override, opting "syft" in would have silently run it on nothing, on every repo.

docs.title: The raw SBOM reuses the existing artifact mechanism; the summary is one JSON column, not a table
docs.text:
Two different things needed persisting, so they got two different treatments, matching what each one actually needs:

  • The raw CycloneDX document: Syft runs through the exact same per-tool loop as every other scanner in core/pipeline.py::_run_scan_job (a ToolOutcome with raw bytes), so it already gets a ToolRun row and an ObjectStore artifact (_store_raw) for free — zero new schema.
  • The queryable summary (every package's identity/license/relation/graph edges, Scorecard results): a new nullable Scan.sbom_summary: JsonType column (migration 0010), not a normalized table. This matches FindingRow.data/RemediationCache.payload's own "keep the full document, index only what needs server-side filtering" pattern — nothing about the Dependencies screen needs SQL-level pagination or filtering; it renders one scan's whole SBOM summary at once, the same way ProjectOverview renders several pre-assembled pieces in one response. A typical SBOM is hundreds, not hundreds of thousands, of packages.
  • Typosquat findings: find_typosquats() already returns ordinary Findings (Category.SCA, evidence.reported_by = ["bulwark-typosquat"]), so they are folded into the same correlate/finalize/repo.add_findings pipeline as every other tool's — they get fingerprints, Issue tracking, and show up in the existing Issues table with no new code there at all. No parallel table for these either.

docs.title: Best-effort at every layer, matching the tools loop's own "a dying tool is data" principle
docs.text: core/pipeline.py::_process_sbom catches SbomError (a corrupt or malformed Syft document) and a Scorecard/deps.dev failure separately, logging and degrading (sbom_summary = None, or an empty Scorecard map) rather than failing the whole scan — the same discipline the per-tool loop already applies to a scanner that crashes. repo.set_sbom_summary treats None as "leave the column unset," never a fabricated empty summary.

docs.title: The API endpoint mirrors /assets/{id}/issues exactly: empty, not 404
docs.text: GET /assets/{asset_id}/dependencies (api/schemas.py::DependenciesView) follows the identical shape /assets/{id}/issues already established: look up the asset's latest scan, and if there is none (or it never populated sbom_summary), return an empty view rather than a 404 — a project that simply hasn't opted into syft yet is a normal, expected state, not an error.

docs.title: The frontend needed a graph, but not a graph library
docs.text:
No graph/tree-visualization library exists anywhere in this codebase (confirmed: no d3, react-flow, dagre, cytoscape). Adding one for a single screen was a bigger commitment than the actual need: Sbom.graph is a small tree/DAG (roots → direct → transitive), and "which path pulls in this package" only needs a shortest-path walk, not force-directed layout. web/components/ DependenciesView.tsx implements pathTo() client-side — the same BFS core.supplychain. dependency_view.path_to runs server-side — over the graph edges the one API response already carries (DependencyPackage.depends_on), rendered as an expandable per-row detail (path breadcrumb, direct children, Scorecard checks) rather than a drawn graph. This is a deliberately smaller commitment than a full graph-drawing library for what plan §20.5 actually asks for.

The page reuses every existing frontend convention rather than introducing new ones: the same TokenGate/AppShell/thin-server-component-plus-client-component shape every other project page uses, the same plain-fetch-in-useEffect data pattern (lib/api.ts::getDependencies), and adds itself to ProjectOverview's existing crumbline the same way "compare scans" was added — no new nav component invented for one more link.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Supply-chain risk is now a real, persisted, navigable feature for hosted scans, not only a CLI workflow — an organization ticks one box on a new scan and the Dependencies screen has real data.
  • The SBOM/Scorecard/typosquat mechanism itself is unchanged from ADR-0024; this is entirely plumbing (pipeline → persistence → API → frontend) on top of it.
  • The next real gap, if this feature area grows further, is a drawn dependency graph (not just the expandable-row path view) — deliberately not built here, the same "defer the fancier UI, ship the real mechanism" shape ADR-0023's policy editor and this ADR's own predecessor both used.

docs.title: ADR-0026: Model gateway and LLMOps
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-30), Week 41 (plan §21.1), building on Week 12/13's LLM remediation feature (ADR-0010) rather than replacing it.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Week 12/13 built one hardcoded provider (core.llm.client.AnthropicClient) behind an LLMClient Protocol the rest of the code already depended on only through that interface (ADR-0010 §3 stated provider-agnosticism as an intent, without a second provider to prove it). Nothing routed by task, nothing tracked spend in tokens (only call counts, process-local), nothing removed personal data before sending text off the machine, and there was no way to guarantee "this specific call never leaves my machine" beyond simply not setting an API key. Week 41 closes those gaps: a real second backend, per-task routing, token budgets, PII redaction, a path denylist, one schema-repair attempt, and a versioned prompt with an evaluation suite gating changes to it.

docs.title: A gateway layer on top of client.py, not a rewrite of it
docs.text:
core/llm/gateway.py is the new single choke point for "which backend does this task use," sitting above the existing make_client() (hosted) and the new make_ollama_client() (local, core/llm/ollama_client.py) rather than merging them into one class. client.py's existing AnthropicClient/LLMConfig are untouched apart from the Completion return type below — every existing call site that only ever used one hardcoded provider still works exactly as before if it calls make_client() directly; only the two production call sites (the API's build_default_app, the CLI's llm suggest) were moved onto the gateway.

Task is a real enum keyed by name (Task.FIX, the only member), not a hardcoded string, so Week 43's triage assistant and Week 44's copilot register their own routes later without changing this module. The plan names "explanations" and "triage" as candidate per-task routes; neither has a model-calling consumer yet, so no route was fabricated for either — inventing configuration for a task nothing calls would be dead weight, not a real per-task routing story.

docs.title: Local backend: Ollama, not MLX
docs.text: The plan says "Ollama or MLX." Ollama exposes a plain JSON HTTP API (/api/chat), needs no new dependency (core/llm/ollama_client.py reuses the same urllib.request approach core.risk.feeds.http_get already uses elsewhere in this codebase), and runs identically on any platform with Docker. MLX is an Apple-Silicon-only in-process Python inference library with no network surface at all — supporting it would mean a second, structurally different client implementation (loading model weights in-process, not calling a server) for a platform-specific gain the plan's own goal ("a local model, so the code never leaves the machine") doesn't need MLX specifically to achieve. Validated against a real, live ollama/ollama container during development (a real qwen2.5:0.5b pull, real HTTP calls, real token counts back) — this is real prior art for a second backend if MLX is wanted later, not a stub.

docs.title: Privacy mode forces local and refuses, never silently falls back to hosted
docs.text: BULWARK_LLM_PRIVACY_MODE=1 (or bulwark llm suggest --privacy) overrides every task's route to Backend.LOCAL, and make_gateway_client raises PrivacyModeViolation — loudly, at the call site, never returning a hosted client instead — when no local backend is ready. A silent fallback would quietly defeat the one guarantee privacy mode exists to make. Validated live: with a real (working) hosted API key configured AND privacy mode on, the gateway still refuses rather than using the key.

docs.title: Token budgets: two tables, not one, because they have different lifetimes
docs.text:
Scan.llm_tokens_used (migration 0011, a plain integer column, same "counter on the row it describes" shape as sbom_summary in migration 0010) tracks one scan's own spend. A new LlmUsage table, keyed by (org_id, period), tracks an organization's spend across every scan in a calendar month — there is no single Scan row a month-spanning total could live on. llm_usage gets org_id and Postgres RLS exactly like assets/scans (migration 0005), unlike api_tokens (migration 0007), which deliberately has none: org context here is already known (a scan's own org_id) before any read or write happens, unlike a token lookup, which is what resolves org context in the first place.

Enforcement is check-before / record-after: core.llm.budget.check() refuses before a call if either cap is already at or past its limit; record() adds the real token cost (from the provider's own usage field, now on LLMClient.complete's Completion return type) after a genuine, non-cached call. This can overshoot by at most one call's worth of tokens under concurrent requests — the same class of imprecision UsageLimiter (call-rate limiting, ADR-0010) and RemediationCache.hits's own non-atomic increment already accept elsewhere in this codebase. A cache hit is free: core.llm.cache._store strips tokens_used from what gets cached, so replaying a cached answer never re-reports (or re-charges) a token cost it didn't actually incur this time.

docs.title: Redaction: Presidio as a second, best-effort layer after scrub_secrets, path denylist as a third
docs.text:
core/llm/pii.py wraps Microsoft Presidio (pip install 'bulwark-scan[pii]', plus a separate python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm no pip extra can express) to catch free-text personal data — names, emails, phone numbers — that scrub_secrets's pattern-based scrubbing was never meant to catch. It runs strictly after scrub_secrets, never before, so Presidio's NER models never see raw key material. It is optional and lazy exactly like AnthropicClient: absent, or its language model not downloaded, or any internal failure, all degrade to a no-op rather than blocking a suggestion or crashing suggest() — confirmed by explicitly wiring en_core_web_sm rather than trusting Presidio's own default, which downloads en_core_web_lg (~400MB) the first time it runs with no config at all; that surprise was caught by actually running AnalyzerEngine() during this feature's own development, not assumed.

core/llm/pathguard.py adds a third, independent layer: a small denylist (.env, *.pem, id_rsa*, ...) checked against a finding's path before any code from it is even considered for scrubbing or redaction — the same "withhold entirely" treatment secrets-category findings already get, extended to any file whose path alone is reason enough, regardless of what a scanner's category happened to label it.

docs.title: Structured-output validation: keep the hand-rolled contract, add the repair attempt
docs.text:
The plan says "Structured outputs validated with Pydantic: one repair attempt, then fall back to static text." core/llm/contract.py's existing hand-rolled validator already does everything a generic Pydantic model would (required keys, types, lengths) plus hostile-input protections a plain schema wouldn't express on its own (bidi-override rejection, control-character rejection, a dismissal-language filter, unified-diff structural validation) — all covered by 568 lines of existing tests, including a 20-payload hostile-input battery. Rewriting a security-hardened, thoroughly tested validator to Pydantic purely to match the plan's wording would risk regressing exactly the protections that matter here, for no behavioral gain. The genuinely new, valuable half of that plan line — "one repair attempt" — is what got built: core.llm.service.suggest now makes one additional call with a fixed, generic repair note ("Reply again with exactly the single JSON object...") on a ContractError, before falling back to static text.

The repair note never echoes the rejected reply or the rejection reason back into the next prompt. Both could carry model- or attacker-influenced text — the reply already failed validation, which is exactly the trust boundary prompt.py's nonce-fencing exists to police — so feeding either back in would open a second-order injection channel the rest of this feature was built to avoid. Cost: tokens from a failed contract check now count twice (original + repair) toward budgets, which core.llm.budget accounts for by summing every real call's usage, not just the last one.

docs.title: Prompt registry: a real versioned file, moved under core/llm/, not repo-root prompts/
docs.text: The plan's own example path is prompts/fix/v3.md (repo root). pyproject.toml only packages core*/cli*/api* ([tool.setuptools.packages.find]) for a real pip install — a repo-root prompts/ directory would silently not exist outside a git checkout. core/llm/prompts/fix/v1.md instead, declared in [tool.setuptools.package-data] exactly like core.rag's own bundled corpus (core/rag/corpus/*.jsonl), for the identical reason. core/llm/prompt.py now loads SYSTEM from that file (core.llm.prompt.load_prompt) instead of an inline string constant; PROMPT_VERSION still hashes the loaded content, not the "v1" label, so a cache-busting version change never depends on someone remembering to bump a filename.

docs.title: Evaluation: promptfoo, driven through the real gateway, gated by the real contract validator
docs.text:
core/llm/prompts/fix/promptfooconfig.yaml is a real, runnable promptfoo eval suite — validated during development against a live local Ollama container, not just written and assumed to work; two real bugs were caught doing that (below). Its custom Python provider (promptfoo_provider.py) calls core.llm.gateway.make_gateway_client directly, so an eval run exercises the exact backend-selection code production uses. Its assertion (promptfoo_assert.py) calls the real core.llm.contract.parse_response — the same validator suggest() uses — rather than a second, divergence-prone reimplementation of the same rules, matching the plan's own framing: "correctness is always decided by deterministic checks," not an LLM judge. Fixtures (fixtures/*.txt) are pre-rendered real build_prompt() output (scripts/gen-promptfoo-fixtures.py regenerates them), not hand-written approximations that could drift from the real prompt format.

Two real integration bugs surfaced only by actually running this against a live model, not by inspection: - promptfoo's Python provider runs as a persistent worker process; an env var exported in the invoking shell after that worker starts does not reliably reach it. The provider's backend choice is therefore driven entirely by its own YAML config: block, not ambient BULWARK_LLM_* env vars, so an eval run is reproducible regardless of that. - promptfoo itself reserves the provider config key timeout (milliseconds, its own per-call worker timeout) — a first draft that also used timeout for Ollama's own request timeout (seconds) silently fed a seconds-based number in as a millisecond cap, timing out every call after 90ms. The Ollama-side setting is request_timeout_s instead, with a comment at the collision site.

Running the suite against a real (small, local) model during development produced two real contract-validator failures — the model wrapped its JSON in a fenced block in a shape the validator correctly rejected — which is itself the intended outcome: the suite is a real gate that can fail a real model's real output, not a suite that always trivially passes. Per docs/llm-remediation.md, fix quality against a real model remains formally unmeasured (Week 14's evaluation pipeline, unchanged by this ADR); this suite is a schema-conformance gate for prompt changes, not that measurement.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A hosted deployment is unaffected by default: GatewayConfig.default_backend is hosted, so behavior is identical to before this week unless an operator opts into local routing or privacy mode.
  • Token budgets are best-effort, not byte-exact, under concurrency — documented, not hidden, and the same tolerance this codebase already accepted for call-count limiting.
  • Presidio is optional; a deployment that never installs bulwark-scan[pii] (or never runs python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm) gets exactly Week 12's original secret-only scrubbing, silently — this is by design (best-effort, not a hard requirement to send text) but worth knowing before assuming PII redaction is active.
  • MLX support, if ever wanted, has no code to build on here beyond the Backend enum itself — it would be a structurally different, in-process client, not an extension of OllamaClient.
  • The Dependencies-screen-style "full hosted integration" question doesn't apply the same way here: this ships as backend/CLI plumbing only. No new frontend screen was built this week — the plan lists no screen deliverable for Week 41 (unlike, e.g., Week 39's policy editor or Week 40's Dependencies screen) — the existing "Generate AI suggestion" UI already surfaces whatever error message a 429 (rate or budget) carries; it isn't budget-aware beyond that.

docs.title: ADR-0027: Verified-fix agent
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-30), Week 42 (plan §21.2) — "the flagship v2 feature." Builds on ADR-0015 (workflow safety limits, design-only), ADR-0017 (GitHub App), ADR-0020/0021 (call graph, taint analysis), and Week 41's model gateway (ADR-0026).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The plan describes a loop: propose a patch for one Issue, verify it for real (rerun the rule, rerun every scanner, optionally the project's own tests), and only then ask a human to approve opening a pull request — never auto-merged. It asks for this to be implemented as a Temporal workflow specifically, the first one in a codebase that has used Celery for scan fan-out since v1.0. Nothing of this existed before this week: no core/agent/-style module, no PR-creation code anywhere (confirmed before writing this — core/github_app.py only mints tokens and posts PR comments), and ADR-0015 (Week 28) had deliberately fixed only the shape of the safety limits, leaving concrete numbers to whichever week built the real thing.

docs.title: Temporal, stood up and validated live, not stubbed
docs.text:
The user chose the full option over deferring Temporal to plain Celery orchestration. temporalio is a new dependency (fixagent extra, plus dev). Every claim below about Temporal's behavior was checked against a real local Temporal server (temporal server start-dev, then temporalio.testing.WorkflowEnvironment for the test suite) before being relied on:

  • Worker-restart durability (the plan's own stated reason for choosing Temporal): started a workflow, killed the worker process mid-run, started a brand-new worker with no shared memory, and it resumed and completed correctly from Temporal's own event history — not assumed from Temporal's documentation, actually done.
  • The three ADR-0015 scenarios that don't need real wall-clock minutes to test (approve, reject, max-attempts-exhausted, overall-timeout) run against WorkflowEnvironment.start_time_skipping(), a real (disposable) Temporal server whose clock fast-forwards through workflow timers — tests/unit/test_fixagent_workflow.py exercises the actual VerifiedFixWorkflow.run() code, not a reimplementation of its control flow. The fourth (a genuinely hung activity exceeding its own start_to_close_timeout) is covered by Temporal's own documented ActivityError semantics and code review, not a live timing test — that one proved awkward to script reliably in this environment; see docs/v2-week42-verification.md.
  • Two real integration mistakes were caught building this, not assumed away: a workflow file containing top-level side-effecting code gets re-executed by Temporal's workflow sandbox on import (a first throwaway script called asyncio.run() at module scope and broke); and a workflow/activity file needs its heavy, non-deterministic imports (anthropic, sqlalchemy, subprocess) kept OUT of module-level imports and lazily imported inside each @activity.defn function instead, or the sandbox's determinism checks complain about the workflow module itself.

docker-compose.yml gets temporal/temporal-ui/fixagent-worker, all behind a new --profile fixagent, pointing Temporal's own Postgres storage at the SAME Postgres instance bulwark already runs (separate databases, auto-created) rather than a second Postgres container.

docs.title: The five allowlisted tools: four are real, one is deliberately not a tool
docs.text:
read_file, search_code, get_call_path are real, path-contained functions (core/fixagent/tools.py) the model can call freely while composing a patch — validated live against real, on-disk Python source, including confirming path-containment rejects ../ escapes, absolute paths, and empty input. propose_patch is the terminal call that ends the turn.

run_verification — the fifth tool the plan names — is not exposed as something the model can call mid-turn. Verification means applying an untrusted patch to a real checkout and executing scanners (and optionally the project's own tests) against it: a materially heavier, more security-sensitive operation than reading text. The workflow (core/fixagent/workflow.py), not the model, decides deterministically when that happens — after a turn ends, always, every attempt — rather than leaving "when do we mutate and execute a sandboxed checkout" to model discretion. This is a real interpretation choice, not an oversight: the plan's flow diagram shows verification as workflow-level control flow (loop-back arrows into "propose patch" carrying feedback), consistent with this reading.

docs.title: Tool-calling is new infrastructure, hosted-only, and extends client.py rather than replacing it
docs.text:
No tool-calling code existed anywhere in this repository before this week (confirmed: LLMClient .complete is single-shot text in, text out). AnthropicClient.complete_with_tools is new but additive — every existing caller of complete() (Week 12/13's remediation feature, Week 41's gateway) is untouched. Only the hosted (Anthropic) backend implements it: native tool-calling is a provider-specific protocol, and building it against the local Ollama backend too would have doubled this week's newest, least-proven surface for a capability privacy mode doesn't strictly need (a verified-fix run already touches a live GitHub App and the public internet via a PR; "the code never leaves the machine" isn't the promise verified-fix makes in the first place). Consequence: verified -fix does not currently work as a local-only pipeline the way Week 41's remediation suggestions now can.

Every tool result the model sees is scrubbed for secrets (core.llm.scrub) and redacted for PII (core.llm.pii) before being sent — the same two layers Week 41 built, reused rather than duplicated. The system prompt states, in the same plain terms prompts/fix/v1.md already uses, that tool output is data from an untrusted repository, never instructions. A repair-style retry exists at the contract level (an invalid propose_patch call is told "rejected: " as its own tool result and the model gets to try again within the same turn budget) but the rejected reply is never itself echoed back, for the same reason Week 41's one-repair-attempt design avoids it: a rejected reply already failed validation, so feeding it back would open a second-order injection channel.

docs.title: Verification reuses core.scan.scan() wholesale; "changed files" is a filter, not new scan scope
docs.text: Nothing in this codebase can scope a scan to a subset of files (confirmed: ToolAdapter.applies_to filters by language, not by file list). Rather than build that, rerun_rule/rerun_scanners (core/fixagent/verify.py) run a full core.scan.scan() of the whole patched checkout and filter the result: rerun_rule checks whether the finding's own fingerprint still turns up when only the originating tool runs again; rerun_scanners checks whether any finding on the changed file(s) has a fingerprint that wasn't already present in the pre-patch baseline. A real, non-obvious fact surfaced while testing this: core.scan.scan() always recomputes Finding.fingerprint via correlate(), even for a single, unmerged finding — a fingerprint hand-assigned on a fake Finding in a test is silently discarded and replaced with the correlator's own value, so verifying "the same defect is gone" only works when the rescanned content actually hashes the same way (same path, snippet, CWE, rule ids) as the original. This is real, useful discipline, not a workaround: it means the check is honestly tied to what a real rescan would report, not to a label a test (or, worse, a future caller) could set arbitrarily.

docs.title: A second, more permissive sandbox for tests — not a mode of the scanner sandbox
docs.text:
core/runner.py's scanner sandbox is --network=none, read-only, non-root, all capabilities dropped: correct for reading code, useless for installing a project's own dependencies and running its test suite. core/fixagent/sandbox.py is a deliberately separate, more permissive function (network on, writable tree, default Docker capabilities rather than --cap-drop=ALL) rather than a runtime branch inside the existing one — validated live against a real python:3.12-slim container (pip install pytest, a real passing run, then a real failing one, both with real captured pytest output). This is explicitly the plan's own "hardened Docker runner, for now": ADR-0015 already named Firecracker (Phase 11, not yet built) as the eventual, properly-isolated execution environment for this; picking a precise minimal capability set for arbitrary language ecosystems' build tooling is real, ecosystem-specific work this pass does not attempt, and the gap is disclosed rather than papered over with a guessed-at middle ground.

Gated by two independent conditions, both required: the caller opts in (run_tests: true plus an image and command), and the asset is "verified owner" — defined as Scan.github_installation_id is not None, i.e. it was scanned via an installed GitHub App, which is GitHub's own proof that the installer has admin rights on that repository. No new ownership-verification column was added; this reuses data that already exists for exactly the reason the plan's wording implies (hardened Docker runner... verified-owner repositories only). Asking for run_tests on a non-verified asset is a normal request, silently downgraded to "no tests," never a 4xx — the same shape decision Week 40's Dependencies screen made for an unopted-in syft.

docs.title: GitHub PR creation via the Contents API, not local git
docs.text: core.gitfetch.clone_repo deletes .git from every checkout it makes (an existing, unrelated isolation choice) — there is no local git history a verified-fix checkout could commit from. Since every patch this feature ever produces touches exactly one file (core.llm.contract.validate_patch already enforces that, reused as-is), the GitHub REST Contents API (create/update a file in one call, given its current sha) is sufficient and far simpler than the lower-level git-data blob/tree/ commit API a multi-file change would need. core/fixagent/github_pr.py's five-call sequence (read the default branch, read its head sha, create a branch ref from it, read the target file's current sha on that branch, update it, open the PR) was built by reading GitHub's documented, long-stable REST v3 contract, and is unit-tested against a fake, sequenced Transport (the same injection pattern core.ci.github.upsert_comment already uses) — but not validated against a real, live GitHub App installation: this environment has no App credentials to test against. This is an honest, disclosed gap, not a hidden one; see docs/v2-week42-verification.md.

docs.title: Persistence: a new table, not an overload of IssueRow.triage_status
docs.text: IssueRow.triage_status's own docstring already says it is "a human decision layered on top of [scan-derived] state" — conflating "an automated agent is mid-attempt, or awaiting human approval" with that would blur two concepts this schema has deliberately kept separate since Week 34. A new verified_fix_runs table (migration 0012) carries org_id directly and gets the same tenant_isolation RLS policy assets/scans/llm_usage already have (validated live against a real Postgres container: inserted a row as one org, confirmed a different app.current_org sees zero rows, then confirmed the migration's down/up cycle is clean). latest_patch/ verification_record are JSON blobs, matching FindingRow.data/RemediationCache.payload's established "keep the full document" pattern — the fix-review screen renders one run's whole record at once, nothing here needs server-side filtering.

docs.title: ADR-0015's three numbers, picked and documented (core/fixagent/limits.py)
docs.text: Per-attempt: 10 minutes. Overall: 30 minutes, excluding the human-approval wait (started as its own, separately-timed phase in the workflow, so a reviewer taking an hour doesn't itself trigger inconclusive — the plan's own worked example, in fact: "took 2 attempts," a normal, unhurried review). Concurrency: 3 per organization, enforced by core.fixagent.store.count_running_for_org before starting a new run — checked, not merely asserted, since the whole point of a cap is refusing the (n+1)th request, not just counting. A fourth, pragmatic (not an ADR-0015 limit) 7-day approval timeout exists so a run nobody ever reviews doesn't live in Temporal forever; it resolves to inconclusive with its own distinct ended_reason (approval_timeout), never folded into the other three.

docs.title: The fix-review screen matches the plan's own mockup (§28.4), with one named cut
docs.text: Verification record before the diff ("trust before content," the plan's own words) — implemented exactly that way in VerifiedFixPanel.tsx. Failed attempts are shown, not hidden (attemptSummary surfaces the first failed attempt's own feedback). The action that opens a pull request is labelled "Open pull request," not "Approve," matching the plan's UI copy exactly, even though the API call underneath is the same /approve signal. "Edit" (revising the patch by hand before submitting) was not built — the plan's mockup shows three actions ([Reject] [Edit] [Open pull request]); this ships two. Editing a pending patch would need a new mutate-in-place endpoint and workflow signal this pass didn't build, and reasoning about a human-edited-then-verified patch (was the edited version actually reverified, or only the AI's original?) is a real design question of its own, not a small addition — deliberately deferred, not silently dropped.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The verified-fix agent is real, hosted-only, and gated behind a compose profile — a base deployment is completely unaffected until an operator opts into --profile fixagent and sets a hosted LLM key.
  • Local/privacy-mode users get Week 41's remediation suggestions but not verified-fix, since tool-calling is hosted-only this pass.
  • The next real gaps, if this feature area grows further: MLX/local tool-calling (mirrors ADR-0026's own Ollama-only cut), a precise capability set for the test-execution sandbox (mirrors ADR-0015's own Firecracker deferral), an "Edit" action on a pending patch, and end-to-end validation against a real GitHub App installation once one is available to test against.

docs.title: ADR-0028: Triage assistant and Hypotheses lane
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-30), Week 43 (plan §21.3/§21.4), building on Week 41's model gateway (ADR-0026) and Week 42's verified-fix agent (ADR-0027) rather than inventing new LLM plumbing.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Week 43 is two related but distinct plan sections bundled into one week: §21.3 (a model reads one finding's taint path and code and returns a likely_real/likely_false_positive/unsure verdict that feeds the ranker) and §21.4 (an off-by-default lane where a model reasons over structured route/authorization facts to hypothesize about flaws SAST can't express, promotable to a real Issue only by a person). Both ship this week; the Hypotheses lane's scope is deliberately narrower than the plan's own three-example list, for reasons below.

docs.title: Two separate LLM contracts, never one shared with core.llm.contract
docs.text: core/triage_assistant/contract.py and core/hypotheses/contract.py are each their own small, hand-rolled JSON validator, structurally identical in shape to core.llm.contract.parse_response (reject unknown fields, control characters, oversized replies) but NOT importing or reusing it. The reason is not code organization: core.llm.contract's _DISMISS regex exists specifically to REJECT a fix suggestion that claims a finding is a false positive, because a remediation reply must never suppress a finding. The triage assistant's entire purpose is to say exactly that when it believes it. Sharing one validator between "must never dismiss" and "must be able to dismiss" would mean one of the two call sites has to punch a hole in the other's guarantee. Three separate contracts, three separate call sites, is what lets all three promises hold at once without any of them trusting the others not to regress.

docs.title: The triage verdict is advisory, stored per-Issue, and only ever dampens/nudges a score
docs.text:
IssueRow.assistant_verdict* (migration 0013) is a new, separate set of columns, never triage_status (migration 0009's human decision) and never a new value inside it. Nothing in this codebase lets a model write triage_status; the only writer of that column remains repo.triage_issue, called only from the human-facing /triage endpoint.

core.risk.score.score_finding takes an optional verdict: TriageVerdict | None and applies a bounded multiplier -- 0.6-0.9 for likely_false_positive, 1.0-1.15 for likely_real, depending on the model's own stated confidence, unsure a deliberate no-op -- before the KEV floor is applied, so a KEV-listed CVE's guaranteed minimum score is never affected by a verdict. This satisfies the plan's "never suppresses an issue on its own" literally: even a high-confidence false-positive verdict can only ever produce score * 0.6, never zero, and the finding is never hidden or removed.

A verdict cannot retroactively change a score already computed and persisted. It is generated on demand (mirroring how "Generate AI suggestion" and the verified-fix agent both work: a model call happens on request, not automatically for every finding on every scan, which would multiply model cost by the finding count on every single scan). It takes effect starting with the asset's next scan: core.pipeline._run_scan_job looks up every stored verdict for the asset by fingerprint (repo.assistant_verdicts_for_asset) before calling finalize(), and passes it through as a verdict_lookup callback -- the same shape core.postprocess.finalize's existing assess (reachability) callback already uses. Validated live, end to end, not just at the unit level: tests/unit/test_pipeline.py::test_a_stored_triage_verdict_dampens_the_next_scan_of_the_same_asset runs two real scans of the same repo path through the real pipeline and proves the second scan's risk score is lower than the first's, with the verdict named in risk_factors.

The CLI path (core.scan.scan, used with no database) always passes verdict_lookup=None: there is no asset, no history, and nothing to look a verdict up against there.

docs.title: The Hypotheses lane's v1 scope: one hypothesis type, not three
docs.text: The plan names three flaw types for this lane: a route missing the authorization check its siblings have, IDOR (an object id from the request used without an ownership check), and mass assignment. Only the first ships this week. IDOR and mass assignment both need reasoning about object identity and field binding across a request/response boundary that a deterministic, testable candidate generator cannot produce responsibly in the time this week has -- building a heuristic detector for either badly (high false-positive rate, no real evidence) would cost more trust in the lane than shipping one well-specified type does. This is the plan's own Cut Order v2 item #4 ("Hypotheses lane, part of Week 43") exercised as a scope narrowing rather than a wholesale cut: the lane exists, is real, and is fully wired end to end, just for one flaw type. Deferred, not abandoned.

docs.title: Candidate generation is 100% deterministic; the model's only job is to judge it
docs.text:
core.hypotheses.facts.missing_auth_candidates needs no model call: group a repository's HTTP entrypoints (core.codeintel) by the file they're defined in, and flag any route with no auth-looking marker in a file where a sibling route has one. This is exactly the plan's own framing, "the model reasons over facts rather than guessing from raw text" -- the facts are computed first, by ordinary code, and are independently unit-tested with no model involved (tests/unit/test_hypotheses_facts.py). The model's job is purely downstream: given one candidate's facts and its own code, decide whether it's worth a person's time (surface: bool) and, if so, write the evidence and a suggested manual check. A model that always said "surface: true" would still be bounded by a real, inspectable candidate list; a model that never ran at all (client is None) short-circuits to zero hypotheses rather than fabricating one.

The keyword heuristic (AUTH_KEYWORDS) that decides whether a marker "looks like" authorization is exactly that: a heuristic, disclosed as such in facts.py's own docstring, prone to both false positives (a decorator that merely mentions "auth" in its name) and false negatives (an unconventionally-named in-house check). Narrowing that judgement is explicitly left to the model step, not fixed by growing the keyword list indefinitely.

docs.title: core.codeintel.Entrypoint.auth_markers: a new field, populated for Python and Express only
docs.text:
Extending code intelligence (Week 38) to capture "which decorators/middleware apply to this route" needed a new Entrypoint.auth_markers: tuple[str, ...] field. Populated for: - Python (python_lang.py): every decorator on a route function OTHER than the one recognized as the route registration itself (@app.get(...)/@app.route(...)) -- @login_required or @auth.requires_role("admin") both contribute a name, matched by shape, not resolved to a real definition. - Express/JS (js_lang.py): every argument between the path and the final handler in a route registration call -- router.get(path, requireAuth, checkAdmin, handler) -- including a called middleware factory (passport.authenticate('jwt') contributes "authenticate").

Not populated for Go or Django this week, a disclosed gap: Go's ecosystem has no single dominant middleware convention the way Express does, and Django's decorator-based views (as opposed to urlpatterns) weren't in scope for the route-registration work Week 38 already did. A Go or Django route simply never becomes a Hypotheses candidate today, which is a false-negative gap (missed candidates), not a false-positive risk.

docs.title: Promotion is a direct, narrow insert -- never core.issues.sync
docs.text:
repo.promote_hypothesis builds one real IssueRow (source="llm-confirmed", a new column, migration 0014) and one FindingRow occurrence attached to the asset's latest scan, as if that scan had reported it. It deliberately does NOT call core.issues.sync (the function every real scan uses to reconcile a full scan's findings against history): handed just one synthetic finding, that function would read every other currently-open Issue as "absent from this scan, therefore fixed" and silently mark the whole asset's issue history wrong. tests/unit/test_hypotheses_repo.py:: test_promote_does_not_touch_other_open_issues proves this against a real second, unrelated Issue.

The promoted Issue is scored with the same core.risk.score_finding every scanner-sourced finding uses (Feeds(), empty -- there's no CVE or scanner-agreement signal here), with the model's own stated confidence (high/medium/low) mapped to a fixed 0.8/0.6/0.4 scoring-confidence value: a documented, honest floor, not a precisely-calibrated number nothing here has evidence for.

HypothesisRow.snippet stores the exact code shown to the model at generation time specifically so promotion never needs to re-clone the repository a second time.

docs.title: Generation re-clones the repository; it is on demand, gated by the gateway, not a new toggle
docs.text:
POST /assets/{id}/hypotheses/generate re-checks out the asset's latest scan's git source (core.gitfetch.clone_repo, the same SSRF-guarded clone the verified-fix agent already uses) into a throwaway directory, runs core.codeintel.analyze fresh, and cleans up unconditionally. "Off by default" is enforced the same way triage and fix already are: Task.HYPOTHESES has no route unless an operator configures one (core.llm.gateway), so app_state.llm_hypotheses is None and the endpoint returns 409 -- no separate per-org feature-flag table was built for this, since the gateway's own task routing already is that toggle, and a second one would just be two ways to express the same on/off state.

Model-call budget is checked once per generate call (UsageLimiter.acquire()), not once per candidate inside it: candidates are processed as one batch triggered by one user action, not N independent requests, and MAX_CANDIDATES_PER_RUN (30) bounds the worst case regardless.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A hosted deployment is unaffected by default, same as Week 41/42: nothing here calls a model unless Task.TRIAGE/Task.HYPOTHESES are explicitly routed to a backend.
  • The Hypotheses lane's real coverage is narrower than the plan's own three-example list (IDOR and mass assignment are not detected); revisiting this needs a genuinely new candidate-generation approach for each, not just a bigger keyword list.
  • Go and Django routes never produce a Hypotheses candidate this week (no auth_markers extraction for either yet) -- a false-negative gap, not a false-positive risk.
