  • A triage verdict changes ranking starting with an asset's next scan, never retroactively; the issue detail screen shows the verdict immediately (advisory text), but the numeric risk score shown for the CURRENT scan is unaffected until a new one runs.
  • No live hosted-model run for either feature in this environment (no API key here); both are unit-tested against fake clients covering the real control-flow paths (a valid reply, a malformed reply repaired once, a give-up), the same posture Week 41/42 already documented for their own LLM call sites. Both promptfoo suites (core/llm/prompts/triage/, core/llm/prompts/hypotheses/) are real, runnable, schema-conformance gates, following the exact pattern core/llm/prompts/fix/ established.

docs.title: ADR-0029: Security copilot -- tool-calling chat grounded in issues, code, and scan history
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-30), Week 44 (plan §21.5), building on Week 41's model gateway (ADR-0026), Week 42's tool-calling agent (ADR-0027), and Week 43's retrieval-adjacent work.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The plan asks for grounded chat: "Which routes accept file uploads?", "Why is ISS-142 ranked above ISS-98?", "What changed since last week?" -- answered by calling tools over real data, every answer citing issue IDs and file:line, citations checked before the answer is shown. Retrieval uses pgvector embeddings of function-level chunks, always filtered by tenant.

docs.title: Retrieval reuses the knowledge base's hashed embedder, not new gateway plumbing (task 1)
docs.text:
core/embeddings/ chunks a checkout at function granularity off core.codeintel's real parsers (CodeGraph.all_symbols) and embeds with core.rag.embed.HashingEmbedder -- the same model-free, hashed/IDF embedder ADR-009 chose for the remediation knowledge base, not a new neural-embedding capability on the LLM gateway. Checked first: no LLMClient implementation anywhere in this codebase can embed today: every gateway Task (FIX/TRIAGE/HYPOTHESES) assumes chat-completion (complete(system, user) -> Completion). Adding real embedding support would mean a new protocol method, a new Anthropic embeddings call, and a new Ollama /api/embeddings call -- genuine new surface area for a corpus (source code identifiers, route paths) that ADR-009's own reasoning already covers: keyword-rich technical text, where lexical retrieval works, at no network/dependency cost. One HashingEmbedder fit per asset (CodeChunkIndexRow), not one global fit like the knowledge base's KbMeta, since each asset's code is its own small corpus, never compared against another's.

The Vector/_PgVector pgvector TypeDecorator moved out of core.rag.store into core.persistence.vector_type so the new code_chunks table and the existing kb_chunks table share one implementation instead of two copies of the same ~25 lines.

docs.title: The tool-calling loop reuses core.fixagent.agent.propose_patch's exact shape (task 2)
docs.text:
core/copilot/service.ask is structurally identical to Week 42's propose_patch: bounded turns (MAX_TURNS), native tool use via AnthropicClient.complete_with_tools (hosted-only, ADR-0027 -- local-model tool-calling was not built then and still isn't), every tool result framed to the model as untrusted data never instructions, and a terminal tool (give_answer here, propose_patch there) as the only way a turn produces a real result. This is the second tool-calling loop in the codebase; rather than generalize an abstraction from one example, it was copied and adapted, the same "kept as its own small copy" reasoning core.hypotheses.service._safe_read already documents for smaller cases.

query_issues and compare_scans are thin wrappers around core.persistence.repo .list_asset_issues/compare_scans -- the exact functions the issues table and scan-comparison screen APIs already call. No new filtering or diffing logic was written for the copilot.

Retrieval is wired in as automatic pre-loop grounding (the top-k similar chunks from task 1's index, prepended to the first user message, labelled as data), not a sixth callable tool -- matching the plan's own separate treatment of "the model answers by calling tools" and "retrieval uses pgvector embeddings" as two distinct mechanisms.

No promptfoo suite for the copilot's system prompt, consistent with (not a new gap relative to) core/fixagent: neither tool-calling agent's system prompt has one. A promptfoo suite's schema-conformance fixtures fit a single-shot "prompt in, JSON out" contract (core/llm/prompts/fix, /triage, /hypotheses) far better than a multi-turn tool-calling conversation, which has no single input/output pair to snapshot against fixtures.

docs.title: Persistence: two tables, one with a two-hop RLS policy (task 3)
docs.text: copilot_conversations (asset-scoped) and copilot_messages (no asset_id of its own) follow migration 0014/0015's RLS-via-assets pattern, but copilot_messages' policy is a two-hop EXISTS (through copilot_conversations into assets), since a message's only path to a tenant is through the conversation it belongs to. Verified live against a disposable Postgres, including cross-org isolation for both tables as the non-superuser bulwark_app role -- the two-hop case was checked explicitly, not assumed to follow from the one-hop case already proven for hypotheses.

docs.title: Clone once per conversation, not once per message
docs.text:
core/copilot/session.CheckoutCache clones an asset's latest scan's source once when a conversation starts and reuses it (checkout + CodeGraph) for every later message in that same conversation, process-local with idle-TTL eviction, rather than re-cloning on every turn the way Hypotheses-lane generation and the triage assistant each do their own one-shot re-clone. A chat panel is interactive; paying a full clone-and-analyze cost per question would make every follow-up question slow. The checkout is a snapshot as of the conversation's first message -- a scan finishing mid-conversation does not change what later messages in that conversation see; a new conversation always sees the asset's current latest scan.

A per-conversation-id lock prevents the one real race this design introduces: two concurrent first-messages for the same brand-new conversation must not both clone (the loser's checkout would never be tracked or cleaned up). Proven with a real multi-threaded test, not just reasoned about.

A local (non-Anthropic) backend routed to Task.COPILOT is rejected with a 409 at the point of use (an isinstance check mypy itself surfaced as a real gap when ask()'s AnthropicClient parameter was checked against the gateway's general LLMClient | None return type) rather than crashing -- tool-calling stays hosted-only, the same constraint core/fixagent already lives with.

docs.title: The frontend panel's citation limits (task 4)
docs.text: Issue citations render as real links to the issue detail page. Code citations (path:line) render as plain monospace text, not a link: this frontend has no view that jumps to an arbitrary file:line today (code is only ever shown inline on pages that already fetched it themselves, e.g. IssueDetail's taint-path steps) -- a link with nowhere real to go would be worse than no link. The panel is mounted in IssueDetail (issue context) and ProjectOverview (no context, general project chat); the scan-comparison page's own "this scan" context is deferred, since wiring it needs threading the currently-selected scan id out of ScanComparison's internal state, a change to an existing component this task didn't make.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A hosted deployment is unaffected by default: nothing here calls a model unless Task.COPILOT is explicitly routed to a backend, same as every other Week 41-43 LLM feature.
  • Retrieval quality is bounded by the same lexical-embedding limits ADR-009 already discloses for the knowledge base (plain-English queries without shared vocabulary with the code miss) -- not measured separately here; no evaluation run against the plan's own 100-question set in this environment (needs a live model).
  • core.copilot.session.CheckoutCache is process-local: a multi-worker deployment needs sticky routing per conversation, or a shared cache, to get the reuse benefit across every worker. A cache miss just re-clones -- correctness is unaffected, only the latency benefit is process-scoped.
  • The scan-comparison page's copilot context wiring, and code-citation navigation (no jump-to-line view exists yet), are both disclosed gaps, not silent omissions.
  • No live hosted-model run for the copilot in this environment (no API key here); the tool-calling loop is unit-tested against a fake Anthropic-shaped client covering the real control-flow paths (a tool call, a rejected citation retried, a give-up), the same posture Weeks 41-43 already document for their own LLM call sites.

docs.title: ADR-0030: Attack paths, threat model draft, and the LLM red-team suite
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-09-30), Week 45 (plan §21.6/§21.7/§21.9), building on Week 44's copilot (ADR-0029) and the code intelligence/taint infrastructure from Weeks 20-21 rather than inventing new scanning or analysis passes.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Week 45 is three plan sections bundled into one week: §21.6 (a ranked attack-path graph chaining an asset's own open issues into a narrative from entry point to impact), §21.7 (a deterministic Mermaid data-flow diagram plus a STRIDE table, a starting point for a person's own threat-modeling review, not an assessment), and §21.9 (a red-team suite proving the LLM-consuming features hold up against adversarial content). All three deliberately reuse existing infrastructure rather than building new detection: core.codeintel's entrypoints and call graph, core.taint.catalog's sink patterns, and an adversarial payload corpus that had been sitting unused since an earlier week.

docs.title: The attack-path graph has exactly one verified rule and two disclosed heuristics
docs.text: ssrf_reachable_from_entrypoint (core/attackpath/rules.py) is the one rule that is fully real: it walks CodeGraph.callers_of backward from an SSRF finding's location to prove a public route can reach it, then connects to a synthetic "cloud metadata service" node representing a well-documented technique (SSRF against 169.254.169.254), not something any scanner reports directly. secret_grants_resource and ci_secret_workflow are explicitly labelled heuristics in their own docstrings: neither Checkov nor gitleaks output in this codebase records which specific credential grants access to which specific resource, so "a cloud-flavored secret and an IAC issue both exist in this asset" is the only real signal available, not a proven causal grant. Mixing verified and heuristic rules under one AttackPath.rank_score was deliberately not smoothed over: likelihood is HIGH only for the verified rule, MEDIUM for the heuristics, so the ranking itself discloses the difference rather than presenting three rules as equally certain.

docs.title: One AttackPath per rule match; no multi-hop combination yet
docs.text: A single rule application (e.g. entrypoint → SSRF issue → metadata service) becomes one AttackPath. Combining two separately-matched rules into one longer chain (an SSRF path continuing on into a secret-grants-resource path, say) is a real generalization this week does not attempt — a disclosed scope boundary in core/attackpath/service.py's own docstring, not an oversight.

docs.title: Narrative generation never gates the graph on a model being configured
docs.text: Unlike the copilot (409 when no model is routed for its task), GET /assets/{id}/attack-paths and GET /assets/{id}/threat-model both return their real, computed structure regardless of whether Task.ATTACK_PATH has a client. The graph, the ranking, and the diagram are useful and correct on their own; the model-written narrative is strictly additive. core/attackpath/contract.py enforces this at the content level too: a narrative must mention every node's label it was given (plan §21.6: "the graph is the source of truth; the narrative only describes it"), checked by string containment, not by re-deriving the graph from the prose.

docs.title: The threat model draft makes no model call at all
docs.text: core/threatmodel/generate.py is pure, deterministic computation: entrypoints become DFD processes, a sql_injection-category sink (per core.taint.catalog) reachable from a route implies a Database node, a command_injection-category sink implies an OS-process node — the exact same sink patterns the taint engine already uses for vulnerability detection, reused for a different question (which external systems exist) rather than reimplemented. The STRIDE table is a fixed set of starter questions per element kind, not a model's per-project judgment, matching the plan's explicit framing as "a starting point for a person, not an assessment." One current row per asset (asset_id is the primary key), editable, with an explicit /regenerate that discards edits rather than a background job silently overwriting them — verified live against a real disposable Postgres container that org-a and org-b are isolated on threat_models via bulwark_app (not a superuser).

docs.title: The red-team suite is deterministic-only; garak is deferred, not faked
docs.text: Wiring up garak (or any live-model probing) needs a real API key, real spend on every scheduled run, and produces a result that can differ between runs — none of which a hardcoded "attack success rate" would honestly represent. tests/redteam/ instead runs the 20-payload adversarial corpus (tests/fixtures/injection_payloads.json, curated in an earlier week, never wired into a test until now) against the real fix/triage/copilot pipelines with worst-case compliant fake models, proving the architectural guarantees hold even when a model is fully fooled. This caught a real bug during development: core/llm/prompt.py and core/triage_assistant/prompt.py scrubbed secrets from a finding's code block but never from its title/description, fixed in the same change. No new CI job was needed — pyproject.toml's testpaths already picks up the new directory, so the suite runs on every push and pull request now, exceeding the plan's "nightly."

docs.title: ADR-0031: SandboxRuntime interface, the gvisor backend, and egress denial for fix verification
docs.text: Status: Partially implemented (2026-10-01), Week 46 (plan §22.1, "Isolation v2"). Tasks 1-3 of 4 shipped; task 4 (a real Linux host to exercise gvisor/Firecracker on, and Firecracker itself) is explicitly deferred -- see "What is NOT done" below. This is not the full Phase 11 target state (milestone M10's "scanners run under gvisor and code runs in Firecracker on the Linux host"); it is the architecture that state will be built on, plus the one piece of it (egress denial) that didn't need a Linux host to ship for real.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every scanner container has run under plain Docker (runc) since v1: namespaces and cgroups enforced by the host's real kernel. That boundary is solid but not layered -- if a scanner's parser has a real exploit (ADR-002's threats T1/T2), the contained process still executes every syscall in the host kernel itself. gVisor (runsc) interposes a userspace kernel in front of that: it intercepts and re-implements the syscalls it allows, so an escape from the scanner process still has to escape runsc before reaching a real host syscall. Firecracker goes further still (a microVM, hardware-virtualization boundary) for the fix-verification agent's "run this project's own tests" step, which is a fundamentally more permissive posture (network access, a writable tree) than scanning ever needs.

Both runsc and Firecracker are Linux-only. Development on this project happens on macOS. The plan is explicit about the consequence: keep developing with the existing Docker setup locally, run the hardened runtimes on a Linux host. Week 46 is the first pass at that architecture.

docs.title: One interface, chosen by configuration, not by branching call sites
docs.text: core.sandbox.runtime.SandboxRuntime is a Protocol with a single method, build_argv(adapter, target, out_dir, container_name, ctx) -> list[str]. core.runner.run_tool takes an optional instance of it and defaults to DockerRuntime, so every existing call site (core.scan, core.sbom.syft) and every existing test keeps its exact prior behavior -- Week 46 task 1 is a pure refactor, not a new feature, verified by running the full existing suite unchanged before and after (1399 tests, byte-identical build_docker_argv output).

docs.title: gvisor is docker run --runtime=runsc, nothing more exotic
docs.text: core.sandbox.gvisor_runtime.GvisorRuntime reuses build_docker_argv verbatim and inserts one flag. This was a deliberate choice over building a separate execution path: gVisor's own documented, standard integration point for the common case is docker run --runtime=runsc -- there is no separate CLI most deployments need. Reusing the argv verbatim also means the gvisor backend can never accidentally loosen the container contract (mounts, resource limits, no-new-privileges, cap-drop=ALL); it can only add a deeper enforcement layer underneath it. This cannot be executed on this dev machine (no macOS build of runsc), so verification here is argv-shape tests only, disclosed as such rather than claimed as a real run.

docs.title: No custom seccomp profile ships yet -- a naive one would be a regression, not hardening
docs.text: --security-opt=seccomp=<file> replaces Docker's own default seccomp profile; it does not layer on top of it. Docker's real default is a deny-by-default allowlist of roughly 300 syscalls, curated and battle-tested upstream. The only custom profile safe to author without a Linux host to verify it against is the "mostly allow, deny a few dangerous syscalls" shape -- which is strictly weaker than Docker's real default, not stronger. Shipping that as "hardening" would be a real security regression dressed up as one. core.sandbox.seccomp.seccomp_profile_path is fully wired into GvisorRuntime but returns None for every scanner today: Docker's real default stays in effect, unmodified. Building a genuinely tighter profile needs either a vendored-and-trimmed copy of Docker's actual default.json or syscalls observed via strace on a real run -- both real, disclosed, deferred work, matching the precedent core/fixagent/sandbox.py already set for capability sets in Week 42.

docs.title: Egress denial is applied from outside the target container, by a purpose-built sidecar
docs.text:
The fix-verification sandbox's target image (TestRunSpec.image) is caller-supplied and arbitrary -- python:3.12-slim, node:20-slim, anything. Nothing guarantees it has nftables installed, and installing it at runtime would need network access before any restriction exists: a chicken-and-egg problem for the very thing being restricted. docker/egress-sidecar is a small, purpose-built image (Debian slim + nftables, pinned) that joins the target's network namespace via docker run --network=container:<name> and loads a ruleset into it from the outside. nftables rules are a property of the network namespace, not of any one container's filesystem, so this works regardless of what the target image contains -- verified live against a real python:3.12-slim target with no nftables of its own.

To close the window between the target container starting and the policy landing, the target is started detached, behind a startup barrier (while [ ! -e /bulwark-egress/ready ]; do sleep 0.05; done; <command>, backed by a bind-mounted file the orchestrator touches only after the sidecar confirms the ruleset loaded). A caller that genuinely needs the old, fully-open-network behavior (e.g. a private registry on a non-standard port) can set deny_internal_egress=False, which reproduces the original single-container code path exactly; the project's own default posture is deny.

docs.title: The egress ruleset's exact shape came from live testing, not from writing it once and trusting it
docs.text:
Two real bugs were found and fixed before this shipped, both by running the ruleset against a real container rather than reviewing it by eye: - Denying all of RFC1918 before allowing DNS broke every package install, because Docker Desktop's own embedded DNS resolver lives in RFC1918 space (192.168.65.x on the machine this was verified on). Fixed by moving the DNS-allow rules before the denied-range check. - An inet-family table's tcp dport {80,443} accept rule applies to both IPv4 and IPv6, but the deny rule was IPv4-only (ip daddr {...}) -- so curl -6 reached a host the IPv4 rule fully blocked. Fixed by dropping IPv6 outright (meta nfproto ipv6 drop) rather than trying to keep two rule sets in sync for a protocol this sandbox has no real need for.

See docs/v2-week46-verification.md for the full verification record.

docs.title: Firecracker is explicitly descoped this pass, not silently dropped
docs.text: Firecracker needs a kernel image, a rootfs image, and a resolved architectural choice for getting a project's checkout into a microVM at all -- bake it into the rootfs per run (simple, slow), pass it via virtiofs (needs a vhost-user-fs daemon), or fetch it over network inside the guest (reintroduces exactly the network exposure this ADR's egress-denial decision exists to close). None of these can be chosen and then verified without a Linux host with KVM, which this pass does not have. The plan's own risk register (R12, R13) and its "drop in this order if time runs short" list both name Firecracker as the first thing to cut, in favor of exactly what task 3 did instead: harden the existing Docker sandbox. This is tracked as real, open, Linux-host-blocked work -- not something this ADR claims to have solved.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• No gvisor run has ever actually executed. Every gvisor-path assertion in this codebase is an argv-shape test. The backend is not selected by anything in production; core.runner.run_tool still defaults to DockerRuntime everywhere.
  • No seccomp profile is applied. The hook exists; it always returns None.
  • Firecracker does not exist in this codebase at all -- not even as an unused stub. Building one without being able to verify it was judged worse than not building it.

Amended 2026-10-12: built (core.sandbox.firecracker), for the fix agent's test runs only, because most of it could be verified after all. The checkout is baked in per run, as a second ext4 disk; the guest has no network; init reports the exit code on the serial console after killing every other process. The guest side was booted for real -- under QEMU's software emulation, with disks this module built from a real image -- and behaved as designed. Firecracker itself still needs a KVM host: tests/integration/test_firecracker_live.py runs there and skips here. - No Linux host exists yet. Nothing here was run anywhere but this macOS dev machine's Docker Desktop (a real Linux VM under the hood, which is what makes the egress-denial live testing meaningful -- but it is not a host this project controls, has gvisor installed, or can be wired into CI as a runner). - Egress denial only covers the fix-verification sandbox. Scanner containers already have --network=none and don't need it; nothing else in this codebase runs untrusted code with network access.

Closing these needs a real Linux host: install Docker + runsc + (eventually) Firecracker, smoke-test GvisorRuntime for real, resolve and build the Firecracker checkout-delivery mechanism, then wire the host into CI so this doesn't regress silently. That work is described, not performed, in docs/sandbox-runtimes.md.

docs.title: ADR-0032: Envelope encryption and crypto-shredding
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-10-01), Week 47 tasks 1-2 (plan §22.2), the first half of "Data protection" -- mTLS and secrets management (tasks 3-4) are ADR-0033.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Raw scanner output stored in object storage (core.pipeline._store_raw) has been plaintext since v1: readable by anyone with S3 credentials, and unrecoverably deletable only by finding and erasing every copy, including in backups. The plan asks for envelope encryption -- each organization holds a key-encryption key (KEK), each scan gets its own data key (DEK) wrapping the actual bytes -- and "deletion by crypto-shredding": destroying a scan's DEK makes its data permanently unreadable without needing to reach the ciphertext itself, backups included.

docs.title: OpenBao's Transit engine mints and unwraps data keys; this project never re-implements envelope encryption's key math
docs.text: core/secrets/openbao.py's generate_data_key/unwrap_data_key call Transit's own /datakey/plaintext and /decrypt endpoints -- Vault/OpenBao's built-in primitive for exactly this pattern, not something assembled from a lower-level encrypt call. The plaintext DEK exists only for the duration of one core.secrets.envelope.encrypt/decrypt call; OpenBao itself never sees a scan's actual data, only ever wraps and unwraps a 32-byte key. Every method's exact request/response shape, and two things that would have been wrong guesses (Transit key creation is idempotent, but mounting the engine itself is not; a bad ciphertext comes back as a clean HTTP 400, not a connection-level failure), were confirmed against a real openbao/openbao:2.1 dev-mode container before being written, not assumed from documentation alone.

docs.title: The storage key itself is authenticated, not just the payload
docs.text: core.persistence.storage.EncryptingObjectStore passes the object's own storage key (e.g. scans/<id>/raw/bandit.json) as AES-GCM associated data. This means a ciphertext can never be copied onto a different object's key and still decrypt -- verified with a real test that swaps one scan's stored ciphertext onto another scan's key and confirms decryption fails closed (DecryptionError), not a wrong-but-plausible plaintext.

docs.title: Encryption is wired into the real production path, off by default
docs.text: core.tasks.run_scan_task builds its ObjectStore through core.persistence.storage. build_object_store, which returns a plain S3Store unless BULWARK_OPENBAO_ADDR/ BULWARK_OPENBAO_TOKEN are both set -- the same "off means off, not a silent partial feature" posture the GitHub App integration and LLM gateway already use. A scan's data key is minted once (first put) and reused for every object that scan writes, looked up and unwrapped again on every subsequent read; this needed its own care about Postgres RLS (see core.persistence.storage. _resolve_scan_data_key's docstring) since scan_data_keys carries the same tenant-isolation policy every other RLS table does.

docs.title: Crypto-shredding destroys the key, never touches the ciphertext or the scan/issue rows
docs.text: core.retention.shred_expired_scans deletes a scan's scan_data_keys row once its organization's retention window has passed (core.persistence.repo.get_retention_days, default 7 days, plan §22.2). This is the entire mechanism: the encrypted object itself is never located or deleted, and neither is the Scan row or any IssueRow/FindingRow -- the plan is explicit that issues are kept regardless ("keep issues"). A scan whose data key is gone is functionally indistinguishable from one that never had encryption enabled in the first place, from the object-storage side; only get_scan_data_key returning None reveals which case applies, and callers are not meant to distinguish them.

docs.title: The sweep iterates one organization at a time, not one query across all of them
docs.text: scans and scan_data_keys both carry FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY policies keyed on app.current_org (migrations 0005/0018), and the worker's bulwark_app-family connection is NOBYPASSRLS by design (ADR-0013). A single unscoped query across every organization's rows would see zero rows under RLS, not every organization's -- an unset session variable satisfies no policy, not all of them. shred_expired_scans discovers the full list of organizations from the organizations table (the one table with no RLS, ADR-0013/0017), then opens a session scoped to each org in turn via core.tenancy.set_session_org before querying that org's own rows. This exact gap was caught and fixed here before shipping; the same gap in the older, pre-existing core.maintenance.reap_stale_scans was found along the way and flagged separately rather than fixed inline, since it's outside this week's scope.

docs.title: Time comparisons happen in Python, not in the SQL WHERE clause
docs.text: SQLite (every unit test) stores timestamps as naive text; comparing a stored naive value against an aware cutoff inside a database-level WHERE clause silently matches nothing under SQLite, even though the same comparison is correct under real Postgres. core.maintenance.reap_stale_scans already worked around this by filtering in Python against _aware()-normalized values; shred_expired_scans follows the same pattern rather than reintroducing the bug in new code.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• No object-storage cleanup. Crypto-shredding leaves the ciphertext bytes in place forever (permanently unreadable, but still occupying storage). Deleting the underlying S3 objects too would be a reasonable follow-up but was not in this week's scope.
  • A concurrent first-use race for one scan's data key is unhandled. Two parallel calls to _resolve_scan_data_key for the same never-before-seen scan_id could both attempt to insert a scan_data_keys row; the current call pattern (_store_raw writes sequentially within one scan) never triggers this, but it is not defended against structurally.
  • No manual, user-triggered "delete my data now" endpoint. Only the automatic per-organization retention sweep exists; an explicit right-to-erasure-style API was not built this pass.

docs.title: ADR-0033: mTLS between services and secrets in OpenBao
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-10-01), Week 47 tasks 3-4 (plan §22.2), the second half of "Data protection" -- envelope encryption and crypto-shredding (tasks 1-2) are ADR-0032.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Every service connected to Postgres as one of two shared, password-only roles: bulwark (the table-owning role, used by migrate) or bulwark_app (shared by api, worker, and fixagent-worker). A leaked or misconfigured credential for one service was indistinguishable from any other's, and nothing but the Docker network boundary stood between a connection and the database. Separately, several real secrets (the GitHub App private key, its webhook secret, the API bearer token, the LLM API key) lived only in plain environment variables, closing over from v1 and never revisited once OpenBao existed as real infrastructure (ADR-0032).

docs.title: Every network connection to Postgres requires a client certificate, with no exceptions for Bulwark's own services
docs.text: docker/postgres/pg_hba.conf requires Postgres's cert authentication method (clientcert=verify-full) for every hostssl connection: a client must present a certificate signed by the project's own CA, and that certificate's CN must exactly match the role it connects as. This was verified against a real built image, not assumed from Postgres's documentation: the exact ownership and permission Postgres requires for a bind-mounted private key (a bind mount from the host is owned by the host user, which Postgres refuses outright), verify-full's server-hostname check against the actual compose service name, and that a certificate signed by the right CA but for the wrong CN is rejected as cleanly as no certificate at all.

docs.title: Each service gets its own identity by role membership, not by duplicating grants
docs.text: bulwark_api, bulwark_worker, and bulwark_fixagent (migration 0020) replace the single shared bulwark_app connection every one of api/worker/fixagent-worker used before. None of the three duplicates bulwark_app's table grants: each is simply a member of bulwark_app (GRANT bulwark_app TO <role>), which -- Postgres roles default to INHERIT -- gives it every privilege bulwark_app already has, automatically, including whatever a future migration grants to bulwark_app later. bulwark_app itself is set NOLOGIN: it still holds every grant, but nothing can connect directly as it anymore. This was the deliberate alternative to actually auditing and narrowing each service's specific table-level privileges: this codebase's core.persistence.repo module is shared by both the API and the worker code paths, and confidently splitting exactly which operations each one performs, table by table, without breaking production on a wrong guess, is real, separate work this pass does not attempt. Distinct, individually-revocable identities is the genuine, verified improvement shipped here; true least-privilege grants per service is disclosed as deferred, not silently assumed to have happened.

docs.title: The one disclosed carve-out: Temporal's third-party image can't present a certificate
docs.text: docker-compose.yml's temporal service (temporalio/auto-setup, the opt-in fixagent profile) is a third-party image with no support for client certificates. Rather than weakening the rule for every service to accommodate one, it connects as its own dedicated role, temporal_svc (docker/postgres/init-temporal-role.sh, created once at first init, CREATEDB for its own temporal/temporal_visibility databases), authenticated by password and carved out by role name in pg_hba.conf ahead of the catch-all certificate rule. Every role Bulwark's own code connects as -- bulwark, bulwark_api, bulwark_worker, bulwark_fixagent -- keeps the certificate requirement unconditionally.

docs.title: The per-service roles also get a password, unused by production, so CI can keep testing RLS without a parallel mTLS setup
docs.text: docker/postgres/pg_hba.conf's cert method never checks a role's password, so setting one changes nothing about what production actually enforces. It does mean .github/workflows/ci.yml's tenancy-rls job -- which needs real Postgres and real RLS, not the SQLite application-level tests -- can keep running against a plain pgvector/pgvector:pg16 image with no custom certificate configuration, connected as bulwark_worker over an ordinary password, instead of bulwark_app, which migration 0020 makes NOLOGIN. Building a full parallel mTLS-capable CI environment just to test RLS policy correctness (a concern this ADR's certificate work is orthogonal to) was judged not worth the added CI fragility.

docs.title: Secrets prefer OpenBao's KV store, with an unconditional environment-variable fallback
docs.text: core.secrets.resolve.resolve_secret checks OpenBao's KV v2 engine (secret/data/<path>) first when BULWARK_OPENBAO_ADDR/BULWARK_OPENBAO_TOKEN are both set and the secret actually exists there, falling back to the named environment variable in every other case: OpenBao unconfigured, OpenBao unreachable, or the secret simply not migrated yet. core.config.Settings and core.llm.client. LLMConfig both route their sensitive fields (the GitHub App private key and webhook secret, the API bearer token, the LLM API key) through it. This is additive, not a breaking change: every existing deployment that has never touched OpenBao keeps reading exactly the environment variables it always has, unconditionally -- the same "off means off" posture as every other optional integration in this project, verified by confirming an OpenBao-configured-but-secret-not-yet-written case still falls through to the environment variable, not an error.

docs.title: A CLI command moves existing plaintext secrets into OpenBao; nothing does this automatically
docs.text: bulwark secrets migrate-env reads each of the four secrets resolve_secret knows about from the current environment and writes them into OpenBao's KV store, reporting which it migrated and which it skipped (not set). It is a one-time, explicitly operator-triggered action -- nothing in this change silently moves a secret on its own, and a deployment that never runs this command behaves identically to one from before this task existed.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• True least-privilege database grants per service. The three new roles inherit the exact same privileges bulwark_app always had; narrowing what each one can actually do requires auditing core.persistence.repo's call sites function by function, which this pass explicitly did not attempt (see the decision above).
  • No automated certificate rotation or a real CA. scripts/gen-mtls-certs.sh is a dev/self-signed generator; a real deployment needs its own CA and issuance process (cert-manager or equivalent), not this script.
  • Database connection strings (passwords, URLs) are not migrated into OpenBao. Only the four secrets named above route through resolve_secret; APP_DB_PASSWORD and the Postgres/Redis/S3 connection strings still come from plain environment variables, now additionally protected by mTLS at the connection layer (this ADR) rather than by being moved into a secrets store.
  • Temporal's own Postgres credential remains password-only, an explicitly disclosed gap in an otherwise unconditional certificate requirement, not an oversight.

docs.title: ADR-0034: Verifying the platform itself
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-10-01), Week 48 (plan §22.3).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Bulwark scans other projects for security issues. Week 48 is the project turning that same scrutiny on itself: fuzzing its own parsers, running its own DAST tooling against its own web app, auditing itself against OWASP ASVS, and scanning its own dependencies the same way it scans others'.

docs.title: Fuzzing infrastructure is real and reviewed; actually running it is not
docs.text: tests/fuzz/fuzz_adapter.py (Atheris) cannot run on this project's macOS dev machine at all -- confirmed by trying, not assumed: Atheris needs a real Clang+libFuzzer build, and Apple's shipped Clang deliberately omits libFuzzer. The harness, the golden-file-seeded corpus (scripts/seed-fuzz-corpus.sh), the nightly CI job (.github/workflows/fuzz.yml, Ubuntu, where Atheris ships a prebuilt wheel), and the "every crash becomes a regression test" mechanism (tests/fuzz_regressions/, tests/unit/test_fuzz_regressions.py) are all real and were verified as far as this machine allows: the regression-replay mechanism was proven with a synthetic crash file before being left empty, and a manual boundary-case probe of all nine fuzzable adapters (empty input, truncated JSON, non-UTF8 bytes, deeply nested structures) found no crash -- every adapter already fails closed by logging a warning, not raising. Real coverage-guided fuzzing explores inputs no hand-picked case would think to try, which is the entire reason this task exists; the corpus starting empty is an honest state, not evidence of completeness.

docs.title: DAST against the platform's own web app found real gaps; they were fixed, not just logged
docs.text: Running a real ZAP baseline scan against the actual production build (not the dev server, whose HMR/CSP noise would misreport findings that don't exist in production) found three missing cross-origin isolation headers on every real page: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, -Opener-Policy, and -Resource-Policy. Each was added to web/proxy.ts and verified twice -- once by re-running the ZAP scan until the specific warning cleared, once by loading the app in a real browser to confirm nothing broke (this app loads no cross-origin fonts/images/scripts, so require-corp had nothing to break). The warnings that remain are all scoped to /_next/static assets, which intentionally skip the per-request middleware for performance -- a disclosed, deliberate tradeoff that predates this week, not a newly-found gap left unaddressed.

docs.title: The ASVS self-assessment is scoped at the control level, with real citations, not a 280-row checkbox exercise
docs.text: OWASP ASVS 4.0.3 Level 2 has on the order of 200+ individual numbered requirements. Rather than producing a superficially complete table with 200+ rows of unverified or guessed status, docs/ASVS-SELF-ASSESSMENT.md organizes by ASVS's own V1-V14 chapters with one row per genuinely distinct control area, each citing real file:line evidence gathered by actually reading the code (not inferred from docstrings or assumed from architecture). Three real, previously-undiscovered gaps were found and fixed as part of writing it, not left as findings for someone else to act on later: HSTS was only ever set for the public demo build (fixed with an explicit BULWARK_FORCE_HTTPS opt-in, not forced on for every production build, which would break the documented plain-HTTP self-hosted path); Bulwark had no vulnerability scanning of its own dependencies despite shipping that exact capability as a product feature (fixed: a new dependency-audit CI job plus Dependabot); and SECURITY.md's claim of archive "depth limits" was not actually implemented in core/ingest.py (fixed for real, not just corrected in the doc). Two real gaps were found and deliberately left open, disclosed rather than hidden: no rate limiting on authentication attempts, and no general API abuse-prevention beyond the existing LLM-cost limiter -- both judged lower-severity for the project's current single-operator trust model than for a multi-tenant deployment, but real, tracked gaps either way.

docs.title: Supply-chain hardening: real, verifiable pieces shipped; the release pipeline itself is disclosed as unexecuted
docs.text: GitHub Actions across ci.yml and fuzz.yml are now SHA-pinned (not floating major-version tags) and carry explicit least-privilege permissions: contents: read blocks, matching the precedent .github/workflows/bulwark.yml already set. .github/workflows/scorecard.yml runs OpenSSF Scorecard weekly and publishes results publicly (the README badge). .github/workflows/release.yml builds bulwark/app, generates SLSA Build Level 3 provenance via slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator's own reusable container workflow, and signs the image keylessly with cosign (GitHub's own OIDC identity for the run, no stored private key) -- but this workflow has never actually run: triggering it means pushing a real container image to a real registry under a real version tag, which this session has no credentials for and would not do without being explicitly asked to cut a release regardless. The job structure follows slsa-github-generator's documented contract as faithfully as can be verified without running it; the one deliberate exception to "always SHA-pin" is the generator reusable-workflow reference itself, pinned by tag per that project's own stated requirement that callers reference one of their published, audited releases, not an arbitrary commit.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• No real Atheris run has ever executed, on any platform, for this project. The nightly CI job has never fired.
  • release.yml has never run. SLSA provenance and a signed image for a real Bulwark release do not yet exist.
  • scorecard.yml has never run. The README's Scorecard badge will show nothing resolvable until it does.
  • Branch protection rules (a Scorecard check, and a repository setting, not a workflow) were not configured as part of this ADR -- that is a GitHub repository-settings change, outside what a workflow file can do, and outside what this review changed.
  • Rate limiting on authentication attempts and general API abuse-prevention remain open, disclosed gaps (docs/ASVS-SELF-ASSESSMENT.md's own summary table), not silently accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0035: DAST -- ownership verification, scope-enforcing egress, safe scanning tiers, SAST/DAST correlation
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-10-01), Week 49 (plan §22.4); egress-proxy wiring completed in a Week 49b follow-up (2026-10-01), a standalone task inserted before tagging v1.5.0 specifically because the plan's own M10 milestone claims "scope enforced at the network layer" and that wasn't true yet.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Everything Bulwark has scanned through Week 48 is something the user handed it directly -- a git URL, an uploaded archive. A web target is different: it's someone's live, internet-reachable site, and nothing about possessing a domain name proves the person asking Bulwark to scan it actually controls it. Scanning it without permission is not a scanning feature, it's an attack. Week 49 is the whole DAST feature, built around that constraint from the start rather than bolted on after.

docs.title: Ownership verification is a live gate, never a cached status
docs.text: core/dast/ownership.py supports two standard proof-of-control methods -- a DNS TXT record at _bulwark-challenge.<domain>, or a fixed file at /.well-known/bulwark-verification.txt -- the same mechanisms CDNs and cert issuers use for the same reason. The critical design choice: a "verified" status stored in asset_verifications is never trusted on its own. Every place that gates on it -- POST /assets/{id}/campaigns, the CLI's campaign-start, and the worker's own core.dast.pipeline.run_dast_campaign_job -- re-runs the real DNS/HTTP check at that exact moment. A domain can be reassigned, a DNS record removed, five minutes after it last passed; a campaign starting on stale trust is the exact failure mode this is designed to prevent. Verified live: real DNS/HTTPS lookups against example.com (confirmed failing, since no such record exists there), and the full browser → Next.js → FastAPI → Postgres → DNS path in a real browser session.

docs.title: Scope enforcement is two independent layers: one is now in the loop, the other is still a disclosed gap
docs.text:
core/dast/proxy.py is a real allow-list forward proxy (CONNECT tunneling for HTTPS, plain HTTP relaying) -- exact-host-match only, reporting every refused attempt as structured JSON. core/dast/egress.py denies all direct 80/443 in a runner's network namespace except to that proxy, via the same nftables-sidecar mechanism core.fixagent.egress already uses for Week 46's fix-verification sandbox. Week 49 built and verified both independently but wired neither into an actual campaign; Week 49b (below) wires the proxy in. The nftables half remains exactly as it was: unit-tested only, never loaded into a real namespace, Linux-only.

Week 49b: the proxy is now in the campaign runner's actual path. core.dast.pipeline. run_dast_campaign_job starts a core.dast.proxy.BackgroundProxy -- a real AllowListProxy on a background thread, scoped to exactly the campaign's one verified host -- before invoking either adapter, and tears it down after, on every exit path including a tool error (core/dast/proxy.py's BackgroundProxy is a context manager for exactly this). core.dast.adapters.zap.run_zap_baseline and nuclei.run_nuclei both gained a proxy: ProxyConfig | None parameter: ZAP is pointed at it via -z "-config network.connection.httpProxy.enabled=true -config network.connection.httpProxy.host=... -config network.connection.httpProxy.port=...", and Nuclei via its native -proxy flag; both containers get --add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway so the hostname resolves identically on macOS Docker Desktop and real Linux (Docker Engine >= 20.10).

Two real findings came out of making this actually work, not just compile:

  • ZAP's config keys had moved. The legacy network.connectionParam.proxyChain* keys (what most ZAP documentation and forum answers still reference) are silently ignored by the Network add-on this image ships; a real zap-baseline.py run with those keys showed zero traffic reaching a real running proxy. Inspecting the add-on's own compiled ConnectionOptions.class inside the shipped network-beta-*.zap file found the keys it actually reads: network.connection.httpProxy. {enabled,host,port}. A second live run with the corrected keys showed the real scan's CONNECT to the target succeed through the proxy, and ZAP's own background "check for updates"/telemetry calls (news.zaproxy.org, cfu.zaproxy.org, tel.zaproxy.org) correctly refused with 403 -- proof the enforcement is real, not just a passthrough, and that the scan completes and reports findings normally regardless.
  • Nuclei's default templates legitimately contact third parties that are not the target. A real run (before the proxy was scoped down) showed dns-type templates querying whatever DNS resolver the container uses, and an http-type template (rdap-whois) calling rdap.verisign.com to look up the target's WHOIS record -- by design, not a bug, and not covered by the dos/fuzz/ intrusive/bruteforce tag exclusions Week 49 already had. A single-host allow-list can't permit this without widening the scope past the one host ownership verification actually covers, so core.dast.adapters.nuclei.ALLOWED_PROTOCOL_TYPES = ("http",) now restricts every campaign run to -pt http unconditionally, the same kind of non-negotiable restriction as EXCLUDED_TAGS. This is arguably a correction to Week 49's own curation, caught only once egress was actually constrained enough to expose it.

Both fixes are proven by tests/integration/test_dast_pipeline_egress_proxy_live.py (new): the real run_dast_campaign_job, against real Postgres, running a real zap-baseline.py through a real BackgroundProxy against a real local HTTP target, asserting the campaign completes with real findings and that the blocked call-home attempts land as both a tool_runs row ("egress-proxy") and an audit-log entry (dast.campaign.egress_blocked) -- Task 4 of this follow-up, so a blocked attempt during a real campaign is visible to an operator instead of only appearing in a log line nobody reads.

What is still NOT done. This wiring is cooperative, not a kernel-level backstop: it works because ZAP and Nuclei were configured to use the proxy and chose to honor that configuration. Nothing at the network-namespace level yet stops a scanner container that ignored its proxy settings entirely (a compromised scanner, a future adapter that doesn't take a proxy argument, a template with its own raw-socket logic) from reaching the internet directly -- that backstop is exactly what core.dast. egress's nftables ruleset is for, and it has still never been loaded into a real network namespace, on any machine, for this feature. Linux-only, the same disclosed boundary as Week 46's own egress work; closing it needs a real Linux host or CI runner, not this (macOS) dev machine.

docs.title: Safe-by-default scanning tiers: passive always, active is opt-in and rate-limited
docs.text:
A DAST campaign is a Scan row with source_type="web" and a new dast_mode column ("passive"/"active") -- no new table, because scans/tool_runs/findings already hold everything a campaign's result is. Passive mode runs ZAP baseline only -- it spiders and observes, never sends an attack payload. Active mode adds curated Nuclei, with dos/fuzz/intrusive/bruteforce template tags excluded unconditionally in the adapter itself (core.dast.adapters.nuclei. EXCLUDED_TAGS), not as a caller-controlled option -- "active" authorizes probing more thoroughly, not authorizing degrading the target. Active campaigns are limited to one per asset per 24h (core.dast.campaign.check_active_scan_rate_limit), checked both at campaign creation (API/CLI) and again by the worker itself before running (defense in depth against two requests racing past the first check).

Live-verified extensively, with three real bugs found and fixed: ZAP's rule 90004 reporting three alerts under one shared pluginid (fixed the finding-id derivation); Nuclei reporting the same template against the same URL more than once (fixed by hashing the whole raw record); and the worker's own rate-limit re-check comparing timestamps in a way that would have made every active campaign instantly rate-limit itself under SQLite's naive-datetime behavior (fixed by excluding the current scan by id instead of by timestamp equality). The full pipeline -- live ownership re-check, rate limiting, real ZAP+Nuclei execution, correlation, persistence, issue sync, audit logging -- was run end to end against real Postgres with RLS.

docs.title: SAST/DAST correlation needs an explicit link between a live site and its source, because nothing else provides one
docs.text:
A web Asset (what a DAST campaign runs against) and the git/archive Asset for the same application's source (what a SAST scan runs against) are different rows with different identities -- nothing in the existing schema connects "this live site" to "this repository." assets. linked_source_asset_id is that explicit, optional, same-org-enforced link. Without it, correlation has nothing to check against and does nothing, silently -- a missing confirmation is correct; a wrong one is not. Week 49 left the link API and CLI only; the "Add web target" screen offers it since 2026-10-12, listing the organization's git and archive projects.

The "code intelligence" matching a DAST finding's route to source is a small ast-based extractor (core/dast/routes.py) recognizing the FastAPI/Flask decorator shape (@app.get("/path"), @app.route(...)) -- verified live against this project's own 1700+ line api/main.py (44 real routes found, including every route this week's own work added). It runs as part of every ordinary SAST scan (core.pipeline._extract_route_map, best-effort, never fails a scan) and the route map is persisted on the Scan row, since nothing else keeps a scan's source around afterward. core/dast/correlate.py matches a DAST finding's route (via the route map) and CWE (via core.correlation.engine.cwe_family, the same grouping the ordinary cross-tool correlator already uses) against existing SAST findings near that route's handler, marking the matching Issue confirmed_at_runtime. Verified live end to end: a real bandit scan of a real vulnerable Flask app (CWE-78 command injection) produced a real route map in real Postgres, and a DAST finding on the same route/CWE correctly confirmed the right Issue.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-10-08): Nuclei's egress, templates and timeouts
docs.text:
Measured against OWASP Juice Shop v17.3.0 with Nuclei v3.11.1:

  • Interactsh went around the proxy. By default Nuclei registers with a public interactsh server and plants its URLs in payloads; a run held an open connection to oast.me (178.128.209.14) straight from the container. That is a third party, and the target is asked to call it. Every run now passes -ni; the OAST templates are excluded with it, so blind out-of-band issues are not found.
  • Templates came from GitHub on every run, also around the proxy. The upstream image ships none (about 86 MB, 14,036 files, fetched each time). bulwark/nuclei:3.11.1 (docker/nuclei) bakes in templates v10.5.0 and runs with -duc; it lists 11,278 HTTP templates with networking off.

  • A timeout lost everything. run_nuclei now reads output as it comes; a run that hits its deadline raises NucleiTimeout carrying the findings reported so far, the campaign keeps them and ends partial (so it closes nothing), and the container is killed by name -- stopping the docker client alone left it running. ZAP's adapter kills its container the same way.

  • Nuclei stalled through the proxy (fixed 2026-10-12). Through BackgroundProxy it stopped making progress after about five minutes (17 findings, then 75-81 tunnels open with no traffic for over 30 minutes), while the same scan without the proxy finished in 111 s. Every stuck goroutine was in rawhttp 0.1.91's CONNECT dialer (raw/unsafe templates; the rest of Nuclei uses Go's own client). That code reads the reply's status line and then peeks 5 bytes, to skip a repeated status line some devices send. The proxy replied HTTP/1.1 200 Connection Established\r\n\r\n, which leaves only 2. The target sends nothing until the client speaks, so the peek waited forever with no deadline. It was not Docker Desktop: the same stall happened with the proxy in a container on a plain Docker network (16 findings, 98%, 28 minutes). The reply now carries a Proxy-Agent header. Through the proxy, Nuclei finished against Juice Shop in 101 s and 108 s (two runs), 17 findings each; its attempts to reach www.rdap.net and login.microsoftonline.com were refused, as they should be. Direct, it found 19.

  • The two missing findings were the proxy's, not the refusals (fixed 2026-10-12). Diffed against a direct run on the same target, the missing two were robots-txt-endpoint and security-txt: plain GETs to the allowed host. The plain-HTTP relay rewrote only a connection's first request and then piped raw, so a request reusing the connection (keep-alive) reached the target still in absolute form (GET http://host/robots.txt), which Juice Shop answered with its app page -- and it was never checked against the allow-list, and the client's Host header always went through untouched. The TCP connection was pinned to the allowed host, but a shared front end routes by Host header. Now one request per plain connection: origin form, Host set to the allowed target, Connection: close both ways, so the next request comes on a new connection and is checked. Through the proxy: 19 findings, the same 19 as direct, in 105 s; the proxy now also refuses requests naming oast.me, interact.sh, localhost and random hosts that host-header and SSRF templates send, which the raw pipe used to carry.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• The egress proxy is now wired into the campaign runner (Week 49b), but only at the application layer -- a scanner's own cooperation, not a network-namespace-level guarantee. The nftables policy that would make bypassing it a dropped packet rather than a policy violation has never been loaded into a real network namespace on any machine; Linux-only, the same disclosed boundary as Week 46's core.fixagent.egress.
  • A web asset's link to its source project (linked_source_asset_id) is set when the site is registered, or later on its verification page, by PUT /assets/{id}/source or by bulwark asset link-source (since 2026-10-12), which keep its verification; each change is an audit entry. The source must be a git or archive project of the same organization, not a site.
  • Route extraction (since 2026-10-12) reads the HTTP entrypoints code intelligence finds for FastAPI, Flask, Django (the view a urls.py entry names), Express, Next.js and Go's net/http, and falls back to the FastAPI/Flask decorator shape when code analysis did not run. A route carries the prefixes its router is mounted under, across files and chained (Django include(), also of a list in place; FastAPI include_router and APIRouter(prefix=); Flask register_blueprint and Blueprint(url_prefix=); Express use(path, router) with require or import; a prefix written as a constant, when exactly one value is found by that name), and a Django regex route is read when it is a plain path with capture groups. Still invisible: a route built from a runtime string, a regex route with optional parts or alternation, a mount whose router is passed through a variable or function the extractor does not follow, Go's StripPrefix and router libraries' Mount, and Next.js's basePath. Such a route is matched by the part written where it is registered, so a full URL misses it. A conservative miss, never a false match.
  • Nuclei's own request concurrency could not reach a target through host.docker.internal on this Docker-Desktop-for-Mac machine -- reproduced directly, a host-networking limitation, not an adapter bug (tests/integration/test_dast_adapters_live.py's own docstring has the detail).

docs.title: ADR-0036: Scale -- Helm chart with KEDA autoscaling, k6 load testing, cost-per-scan dashboard
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-10-01), Week 50 (plan §23).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Everything Bulwark has run on through Week 49 is a single Docker Compose stack on one machine. Week 50 is the plan's own "Scale" week: package the product for Kubernetes with autoscaling on real demand, measure its actual capacity under load rather than assuming it, and give an operator visibility into what a scan costs. All three turned up real, fixable problems that only existed because nobody had ever generated real concurrent load or a real Kubernetes deployment before.

docs.title: A Helm chart, built from scratch, with two deliberate simplifications and one real architectural split
docs.text:
helm/bulwark/ packages Postgres, Redis, S3-compatible object storage, OpenBao, a migrate Job, the API, the Celery worker, a new single-replica Celery beat, and the web app. Live-verified end to end against a real kind cluster: every pod reaches Ready, and a real KEDA installation scales the worker Deployment from 1 to 5 replicas on a real 3,000-task Redis backlog, draining it in under 30 seconds, then scaling back to 1 once idle.

Two things docker-compose.yml's dev stack has were deliberately not reproduced, both disclosed in helm/bulwark/README.md: - Postgres has no mTLS. The custom bulwark/postgres:16-pgvector image needs client certificates a chart would have to generate and distribute itself (cert-manager or an equivalent CA Job); the default here is the plain upstream pgvector/pgvector:pg16 image with password auth, matching the substitution this repo's own CI already makes for its RLS tests. RLS enforcement itself (FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, ADR-0013) is unaffected either way. - The shared upload workdir is a hostPath volume. The API writes an uploaded archive and the worker reads it by the same path (core/config.py's BULWARK_WORKDIR); a hostPath PersistentVolume only works when both pods land on the same node, true by construction on a single-node cluster like kind, false on a real multi-node one. workdir.existingClaim lets an operator supply a real ReadWriteMany-backed PVC (NFS, EFS, Longhorn) instead.

The one real architectural change, not a simplification: Celery's embedded beat (-B) had to be split into its own fixed-at-1-replica Deployment. docker-compose.yml's own comment already says why -- run exactly ONE process with -B, or scheduled jobs (feed updates, retention housekeeping, crypto-shredding) fire once per replica instead of once. That constraint was compatible with compose's single worker container; it is not compatible with a Deployment KEDA might scale to 5 replicas. The worker's own scanner-launching capability (docker run, via core.dast's and core.scan's existing code) needed a Kubernetes-native stand-in for docker-compose.yml's socket-proxy service, since a Kubernetes node doesn't expose a host Docker socket the way a compose host does: templates/ worker.yaml runs a privileged docker:27-dind sidecar in the worker Pod instead, a real, commonly used pattern (the same one CI systems use to run Docker-based jobs on Kubernetes) -- with the real, disclosed trade-off that it needs a broader privilege than socket-proxy's deliberately narrow API allowlist.

Two real bugs surfaced only by actually deploying and driving the chart, not by writing it:

  • A Helm pre-install hook Job ran before the chart's own Secret existed. templates/migrate-job. yaml's first version was a pre-install,pre-upgrade hook; Helm creates hook resources before its normal resource-ordering pass (which is what creates the Secret), so the very first helm install failed with secret "bulwark-secrets" not found. Fixed by making it a plain Job with its own wait-for-postgres init container instead of relying on hook ordering at all -- Secrets and PVCs are created before Jobs/Deployments in Helm's normal ordering, which is what the chart actually needed.
  • KEDA's Redis trigger needs a fully-qualified address, not the short Service name. bulwark-redis alone resolved from the keda-operator Pod's own namespace (keda), not this release's namespace -- confirmed live as dial tcp: lookup bulwark-redis: no such host in the ScaledObject's own events. Fixed by qualifying it as bulwark-redis.<release-namespace>.svc.cluster.local.
  • Celery beat's first implementation was still a worker, not a scheduler. Splitting -B out (above) first ran celery worker -B -P solo -c 1 for beat, reasoning in its own comment that "this process runs no task workers of its own" -- which was false: worker -B is still a worker. This was caught directly during the KEDA demo: a 100-task backlog, pushed onto Redis while the real worker Deployment was deliberately paused at 0 replicas to build an isolated backlog to scale from, quietly drained to 0 anyway -- beat's own solo worker was consuming it one task at a time, and KEDA never saw the depth it was supposed to react to. Fixed by using Celery's dedicated beat subcommand (scheduler only, never a consumer) instead.

docs.title: k6 load testing found two real capacity bugs that had nothing to do with the test scripts
docs.text:
k6/scan-submission.js (50 concurrent virtual users hitting POST /scans for 20s) and k6/ browse-results.js (500 concurrent VUs ramped over 15s, held 30s, browsing /scans, /scans/{id}, and /scans/{id}/findings) both run against the real docker-compose dev stack, not a mock server. Final measured numbers (docs/v2-week50-verification.md has the full k6 output): scan submission p50=380ms, p95=675ms, ~122 req/s, 99.84% success; browsing p50=696ms, p95=1.18s (successful requests), ~127 req/s, 96.75% success.

Getting to those numbers surfaced two real, previously-invisible bugs, because nothing had ever put real concurrent load on this API before:

  • A single uvicorn process cannot serve 500 concurrent requests. The first browse-results.js run against an unmodified docker-compose.yml mostly timed out at k6's own 30s HTTP timeout -- p50 was ~31 seconds, not milliseconds. The API ran as one uvicorn process with no --workers flag; every synchronous request handler (api/deps.py's db() dependency) runs via Starlette's run_in_threadpool, whose default AnyIO thread-pool capacity is nowhere near 500. Fixed by adding --workers 4 to docker-compose.yml's api command -- safe because core/events.py's scan-progress relay is Redis pub/sub, not in-process memory, so a client's WebSocket connection landing on a different worker process than the one that published an event still receives it.
  • SQLAlchemy's default connection pool (5 + 10 overflow) was never sized for this concurrency, and neither was the fix tried first. Raising it to pool_size=20, max_overflow=30 (compensating for the newly-added 4 processes) immediately hit a second ceiling: 4 processes × 50 connections each attempted 200 total against Postgres's own default max_connections=100, failing as "FATAL: sorry, too many clients already" on 71% of requests. Shrinking the per-engine pool alone (12/engine = 48 total) traded back the other way -- requests queued for a connection and hit the pool's own 30s checkout timeout again. The real fix needed both halves: Postgres's own max_connections raised to 300 (docker-compose.yml's postgres service), and a core/persistence/db.py default (pool_size=15, max_overflow=10, both env-overridable via BULWARK_DB_POOL_SIZE/ BULWARK_DB_MAX_OVERFLOW) sized to add up sensibly against that raised ceiling across 4 API processes, the worker, and beat together.

Two more real bugs were found and fixed along the way, both pre-existing and unrelated to this week's own code, surfaced only because getting the dev stack healthy enough to run k6 against required actually exercising paths nothing had exercised in a while:

  • OpenBao's own healthcheck used localhost, which resolves to ::1 first in this image, but -dev-listen-address only binds the IPv4 0.0.0.0:8200 -- the healthcheck failed every time even against a genuinely healthy, unsealed server, which blocked the api service from ever starting at all (depends_on: condition: service_healthy). Fixed by pointing the healthcheck at 127.0.0.1 instead.
  • Three per-service Postgres roles (bulwark_api/bulwark_worker/bulwark_fixagent, migration 0020) were missing from this dev database, even though Alembic considered itself at head -- historical drift from an earlier manual debugging session, not something this week's work caused, but something it had to notice and fix (re-running migration 0020's own role-creation SQL directly) before the API could authenticate at all.

docs.title: Cost per scan: an estimate, computed on demand, never stored
docs.text:
core/observability/cost.py combines two numbers this project already tracked -- ToolRun. duration_seconds (every scanner's own wall-clock time, summed per scan) and Scan.llm_tokens_used (every real LLM call's token count) -- into an estimated USD figure, using a small, explicitly placeholder pricing table (MODEL_PRICING_USD_PER_1K_TOKENS, DEFAULT_COMPUTE_USD_PER_SECOND), both overridable per deployment via BULWARK_LLM_COST_PER_1K_TOKENS_USD/ BULWARK_COMPUTE_COST_PER_SECOND_USD. The cost is computed fresh on every call (GET /scans/{id}/ cost, GET /costs/summary?days=N) rather than written once at scan-completion time, because a scan's LLM spend keeps growing after the scan job itself finishes -- remediation suggestions, hypotheses, and copilot messages are all requested later, independently of the scan pipeline.

Disclosed, not hidden, imprecision: Scan.llm_tokens_used is a combined input+output count (core. llm.client.Completion.tokens sums them before this project ever sees the split), so pricing is one blended $/token figure per model, not real provider pricing's separate and usually very different input/output rates; a token count carries no record of which model it was spent against if BULWARK_LLM_MODEL changes mid-month, so every token is always priced at whatever model is configured now; and the whole figure is explicitly an internal visibility estimate, not a reconcilable bill.

Surfaced in three places: a new web page (/app/costs, linked from the app shell's own nav bar) with per-window totals and a per-scan breakdown table; two new Prometheus panels on the existing Grafana dashboard (bulwark_estimated_cost_usd{component="compute"|"llm"}, read from Postgres at scrape time the same way QueueDepth already reads Redis); and the same two API endpoints the web page itself calls. The Prometheus metric is scoped to the bootstrap default org only, consistent with every other metric in core/observability/metrics.py (none of them carry an org label) and with this project's own stated scope as a self-hosted, single-tenant deployment, not a multi-tenant SaaS -- a cross-org aggregate would need set_session_org called once per org, since RLS hides every other org's rows from a session with no org context set.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• The Helm chart doesn't reproduce Postgres mTLS, OpenBao's production (non-dev) mode, the verified-fix agent (Temporal + fixagent-worker), or the observability stack (Prometheus/Jaeger/ Grafana) -- all disclosed cuts, not oversights, in helm/bulwark/README.md.
  • The worker's DinD sidecar needs a privileged container, a broader security surface than socket-proxy's narrow allowlist; worker.dind.enabled: false turns it off (and scanning off with it) for a cluster policy that forbids privileged Pods.
  • web.publicApiUrl in the Helm chart's values only reaches server-side code (web/proxy.ts); the browser-side bundled API_URL constant (web/lib/api.ts) is baked in at image build time via web/Dockerfile's ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL, unaffected by a runtime value.
  • The nftables egress backstop from Week 49b and the gVisor/Firecracker sandboxing from Week 46 remain exactly as disclosed there; nothing in this week's Kubernetes work touches them.
  • k6's own numbers were measured on a single developer laptop running this chart's dev stack alongside a kind cluster, a browser, and everything else this session had open concurrently -- not a provisioned, isolated load-test target. The relative findings (a single process can't handle 500 concurrent requests; a 15-connection pool can't either) are real; the absolute throughput numbers are this machine's, not a production server's.

docs.title: ADR-0037: Ecosystem -- Plugin SDK, Integrations, pre-commit hook, documentation site
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-10-02), Week 51 (plan §23).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Week 51 is the plan's own "Ecosystem" week: four tasks that each extend where Bulwark's findings can come from or go to, rather than changing scanning or scoring itself -- a third-party scanner (Plugin SDK), an organization's existing tools (Integrations), the moment before a commit even happens (pre-commit hook), and a real documentation site instead of scattered markdown files. The plan's own Cut Order names the Plugin SDK as the first of the four to drop if time runs short; all four were built.

docs.title: Plugin SDK: entry points, not a registry Bulwark controls
docs.text: A plugin is an ordinary pip-installable package declaring a bulwark.scanner_adapters entry point (importlib.metadata.entry_points() -- the first use of entry-point discovery anywhere in this codebase; [project.scripts] was the only prior packaging mechanism). It runs through the identical sandboxed docker run a built-in scanner does, proves itself with the same four golden-file conformance checks a built-in's own test suite runs (literally the same functions, extracted into core/plugins/conformance.py, not a parallel reimplementation), and is trusted via a real keyless Sigstore identity check (cosign verify --certificate-identity=... --certificate-oidc-issuer=..., needing network -- the one place in the codebase a cosign container runs with it, kept out of the otherwise fully offline core/attest/cosign.py). That signature is re-verified on every resolution, not cached from whenever an organization allowlisted the plugin: the allowlist is trust in a publisher's identity, not trust in a one-time image hash.

docs.title: Integrations: shared SSRF guard, asymmetric two-way sync
docs.text: Webhook destinations (Slack, Discord, generic outbound) pass through the exact DNS-resolve-and-reject logic core.gitfetch.validate_git_url already uses for cloning -- extracted into core/netsafety.py so the two call sites provably share one security-critical primitive rather than two similar-looking ones. GitHub Issues and Jira sync is deliberately asymmetric: Bulwark's own scan-derived state (IssueRow.state) is the only thing that can mark an issue fixed; closing or reopening the external ticket by hand only updates sync metadata (ExternalIssueLinkRow.external_status), never the authoritative state. The alternative -- trusting the external system's status both ways -- would let someone hide a still-present vulnerability by closing the wrong ticket.

docs.title: Pre-commit hook: a narrower, native complement, not a faster version of the same tools
docs.text: Gitleaks and Bandit both run in Docker (300-600s timeouts) -- nowhere near a commit-time budget. core/precommit/ is pure Python with no subprocess for the scan itself: ~15 high-confidence, vendor-prefixed secret patterns by regex, and 7 high-confidence checks over the stdlib ast tree for Python files, explicitly scoped narrower than the full scanners they complement rather than attempting to approximate them faster. The one real performance bug this surfaced -- reading staged files via one git show subprocess per file -- was found by actually timing a 238-file commit (1.93s, at the edge of the budget) and fixed by batching every blob into one git cat-file --batch call (0.45s on the same commit), not by assumption.

docs.title: Documentation site: curate the existing docs/ folder, don't fork a new one
docs.text: mkdocs.yml points docs_dir at the repository's existing docs/ folder and curates a nav across it, rather than creating a separate site-source tree that content would need to be copied into (and drift from). The already-thorough docs/policy.md, docs/risk-score.md, docs/taxonomy.md and docs/reachability.md are reused verbatim; the "API reference generated from OpenAPI" requirement is docs/api.md, which already was exactly that (scripts/gen-api-docs.py, now freshness-tested -- see below) -- mapped straight into the nav instead of standing up a second OpenAPI renderer alongside it. The 60-plus other files already under docs/ (ADRs, weekly verification records, UX research) still build and are reachable by direct URL; they're simply not in the nav, because they're engineering history, not user-facing documentation, and enumerating them in an nav: block that needs updating every week would be its own maintenance burden for no reader benefit.

docs.title: A gap found and closed along the way: generated docs had no freshness check
docs.text: Regenerating docs/api.md/docs/openapi.json while building the docs site (sanity: do they still match the live app?) surfaced that both had been stale for several weeks -- missing the Week 48-50 asset/threat-model/copilot/cost endpoints and this week's own /plugins and /settings/ integrations. Nothing had been checking them, unlike docs/severity-matrix.md, which tests/unit/test_correlation.py already does. Fixed in two steps: regenerate (commit 2716b0f), then add the missing test (commit 10e0e9b) by extracting openapi_spec()/api_doc() out of scripts/gen-api-docs.py's main() so a test can re-derive each file's expected content from the running app and compare, rather than re-implementing the derivation a second time and risking the two drifting apart from each other.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• A plugin with no row in core/scoring/severity.py's matrix has every finding normalize to INFO regardless of the tool's own severity label -- registering a plugin's severities still means a change to Bulwark's own source, not something a plugin declares for itself.
  • No per-org private plugin registry. A plugin is whatever's installed in the worker's Python environment; the allowlist is the only "org A can, org B can't" mechanism, not package visibility.
  • GitHub Issue and Jira ticket creation are unit-tested against a mocked transport, not live. Creating a real issue or ticket needs the account owner's own token and would create a real, visible side effect on their account -- outside what this session verifies unprompted. The inbound half (a signed webhook closing a linked issue) is live-verified, since it needs no third-party credentials, only a crafted, correctly-HMAC-signed request against this project's own API.
  • Jira sync never drives a workflow transition (per-project-configurable, no universal id to assume) -- it closes via a comment, not a real status change.
  • The pre-commit hook's SAST checks are Python-only. Secrets patterns apply to any file; the ast-based checks do not generalize to JavaScript/Go/Terraform the way Semgrep/gosec/Checkov do in bulwark scan itself.
  • No GitHub Pages deployment for the documentation site. mkdocs build runs in CI; publishing it needs Pages enabled in the repository's own settings, a repository-owner action this ADR doesn't take on its own.

docs.title: ADR-0038: Hosted mode runs Opengrep, not Semgrep
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-10-02), Week 53 task 2 (plan §39.5/§40, "ADR-015" in the plan's own numbering -- renumbered to this repository's real, sequential ADR series).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR-006 already established that Semgrep's community/Pro rules (docker/semgrep/) are licensed under the Semgrep Rules License v1.0: internal business use only, no redistribution, no offering them as a service. That was a non-issue for v1/early v2, since Bulwark has never offered hosted scanning -- the self-host page says so explicitly.
