Week 53's own pre-Phase-13 gate (§39.5) makes it a real one: "ADR-015 is implemented: the hosted deployment no longer runs Semgrep-maintained rules" is a precondition for starting v3's multi-tenant, ingest-anything platform work, since that work is explicitly heading toward a shape a hosted deployment could someday actually run.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A new Settings.hosted_mode flag (BULWARK_HOSTED_MODE, default off -- nothing about today's self-host deployment changes). When set:

  • The default SAST tool becomes Opengrep (HOSTED_DEFAULT_TOOLS in core/scan.py) instead of Semgrep.
  • An explicit request for "semgrep" (POST /scans, /scans/upload, or a GitHub App pull-request scan) is refused with a 422 naming the reason and the alternative, not silently substituted -- an operator should never be surprised about which tool actually ran.

Opengrep (github.com/opengrep/opengrep) is a community-maintained, LGPL-2.1 fork of the Semgrep engine with no such restriction. Verified directly, not assumed from its own marketing: its engine repository's LICENSE is plain LGPL-2.1, confirmed by fetching it.

docs.title: The rules still needed solving separately
docs.text:
Opengrep's own bundled ruleset, github.com/opengrep/opengrep-rules, is not a safe substitute for Semgrep's rules just because the engine is clear: its LICENSE file (fetched and read, not assumed) adds a Commons Clause condition on top of its own LGPL-2.1 -- "the License does not grant ... the right to Sell the Software," where "Sell" is explicitly defined to include "a product or service whose value derives ... from the functionality of the Software," i.e. exactly offering it as a hosted service. This is the same restriction, differently packaged, as Semgrep's own rules license. The plan's own wording ("Opengrep with the project's own rules") turns out to be load-bearing, not a stylistic choice: the engine alone does not solve the licensing problem.

docker/opengrep/rules/ is therefore a small, originally-written starter ruleset (7 Python rules, 4 JavaScript/TypeScript rules), Apache-2.0 licensed under this project's own license (docker/opengrep/rules/LICENSE states this explicitly), covering the same high-confidence patterns core/precommit/sast_scan.py's own AST-based checks already cover for the pre-commit hook (eval/ exec, shell=True, weak hashes, unsafe deserialization, disabled TLS verification) -- the same underlying security judgment, expressed as Semgrep/Opengrep-syntax YAML instead of Python ast walks, for a different execution context.

docs.title: No official Docker image; one real packaging problem to solve
docs.text: Opengrep ships signed platform binaries via GitHub Releases, not a container image. Unlike every other adapter's image (which pulls or lightly wraps an upstream image), docker/opengrep/Dockerfile downloads the pinned v1.30.0 binary for the target architecture and verifies it against a sha256 obtained by downloading and hashing it directly, not copied from a third party's claim (an earlier search surfaced a plausible-looking but nonexistent ghcr.io/opengrep/opengrep and opengrep/opengrep Docker Hub image; both were checked against the registries' own APIs and found not to exist before this Dockerfile was written around the real distribution mechanism instead).

docs.title: A real sandbox incompatibility, found and fixed live
docs.text: Opengrep's binary self-extracts a child opengrep-core executable and executes it from a temp directory. The sandbox's shared /tmp is a noexec tmpfs for every adapter (core.sandbox.docker_runtime) -- confirmed live, this fails every single Opengrep run with "couldn't launch child (exec): Permission denied" (and, before raising tmp_size from the default 64m, "couldn't unpack file to target path: No space left on device"). The fix is not to loosen the shared /tmp protection (tried and reverted -- it would weaken every other adapter's sandbox for one tool's sake, and on investigation turned out not to be the real cause of the exec failure anyway: a bare, unrestricted --tmpfs=/tmp mount with no flags at all still failed the identical way, which a totally unmounted default /tmp did not). docker/opengrep/Dockerfile instead points HOME/TMPDIR at /scratch, a plain writable Docker volume (the same ToolSpec.writable_volumes mechanism Trivy already uses for its own /db) -- not tmpfs, so not noexec. /tmp itself stays exactly as restrictive as it is for every other tool.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Hosted mode's SAST coverage is intentionally narrower than self-host's: 11 original rules across 2 languages versus Semgrep's full community ruleset across 4+. This is the stated trade-off, not an oversight -- growing docker/opengrep/rules/ is future, incremental, low-risk work (add a rule, add a golden-fixture case), not a blocker to this decision.
  • core/adapters/opengrep.py is registered in core/scan.py's ADAPTERS (selectable by name in self-host mode too, for testing or by choice) but not in self-host's own DEFAULT_TOOLS -- self-host keeps getting Semgrep by default, unchanged.
  • Severity normalization reuses Semgrep's own ERROR/WARNING/INFO -> HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW mapping (core/scoring/severity.py): same engine lineage, same vocabulary.
  • BULWARK_HOSTED_MODE is the only new operator-facing setting; nothing about an existing self-host deployment's behavior, defaults, or .env changes.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• The starter ruleset is deliberately small (Python + JavaScript/TypeScript only -- no Go, Java, Terraform, or Dockerfile rules yet, all of which Semgrep's own default set covers for self-host).
  • No precision/recall measurement of the new ruleset against a labelled corpus (the same disclosed gap docs/evaluation-v2.md already names for several other v2 features) -- each rule was hand-verified against a real true/false-positive pair while building it (docker/opengrep/rules/ commit's own verification record), not measured at corpus scale.
  • BULWARK_HOSTED_MODE gates tool selection only. Nothing else about running Bulwark as a genuine multi-tenant hosted service (billing, per-tenant resource isolation beyond the existing RLS/ sandbox boundaries, a terms-of-service/abuse policy) is addressed by this decision -- it closes exactly the one gate item the plan named before Phase 13, nothing more.

docs.title: ADR-0039: Portfolio and Engagement -- "Test" is a ToolRun, not a new table
docs.text: Status: Implemented (2026-10-02), Week 53 task 3 (plan §40 change C11, "ADR-016"/"ADR-017" in the plan's own numbering -- renumbered to this repository's real, sequential ADR series, the same renumbering ADR-0038 already explains).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Everything built through v2 is Organization -> Asset -> Scan -> Finding/Issue: flat, one scan at a time. v3's own stated model (plan §40 change C11) adds structure above and around that: "teams group projects by business unit" (Portfolio) and "pen tests and audits are time-boxed engagements; imported reports need a home that isn't a scan" (Engagement). The plan also names "Test" -- one tool's results within an engagement -- as a concept the rest of v3 (reimport semantics, the import screen's "new/unchanged/reopened/closed" counts, SLAs, dashboards) is built on top of.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Two new tables, Portfolio and Engagement, scoped by org_id directly (same RLS shape as Asset/Scan). An Engagement belongs to one Asset and optionally one Portfolio; engagement_type is ci | pentest | audit | adhoc.

"Test" is not a third new table. ToolRun (migrations 0001/0005) already is exactly that: one row per tool per scan, with its own status, duration, exit code, and error. Adding a Test table with the same shape next to it would mean two places holding what's structurally the same fact, with no way to guarantee they'd ever agree once either one changed independently -- the exact "parallel reimplementation instead of one shared mechanism" failure mode this codebase has consistently avoided elsewhere (the plugin conformance kit, the pre-commit hook's shared scan logic, core.netsafety's single SSRF primitive). Instead, ToolRun gains one new column, engagement_id, and every existing and future ToolRun is "the Test" the plan's later weeks (ingest, reimport, the import screen) will read and write.

docs.title: The migration is data, not just schema
docs.text:
migrations/0026_portfolio_engagement.py does what the plan's own wording asks literally: "one CI engagement per project with one Test per scanner." For every existing Asset, it creates one "ci" Engagement ("active" if the asset has ever been scanned, "completed" if not) and links every one of that asset's existing ToolRun rows to it. Verified live against a real, freshly migrated Postgres: a seeded asset with a real scan and two real ToolRuns got exactly one Engagement, with both ToolRuns correctly linked; a seeded asset with no scans at all got one "completed" Engagement with nothing linked to it (correctly empty, not an error).

core.persistence.repo.get_or_create_ci_engagement keeps this invariant going forward: add_tool_run calls it for every new ToolRun, so an Asset created after this migration gets the exact same lazily-created, singleton "ci" Engagement an Asset that existed before it got eagerly. Verified live: two scans of the same Asset (by its own computed identity, core.assets.asset_key, not a raw id) share one Engagement, never create a second; create_engagement explicitly refuses engagement_type="ci" from anyone else, so a person (or a later v3 import flow) can't accidentally split a project's standing CI history across two competing "ci" engagements.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No API surface yet (GET/POST /portfolios, /engagements, a "Tests" tab on the project screen). This week's scope is the data model and the migration it depends on; the v3 UI/API work that reads and writes it is later weeks' own tasks, not pulled forward here.
  • ToolRun.engagement_id is nullable, and stays that way: tool_runs' own RLS policy (migration 0005, an EXISTS join through scans.org_id) is unchanged and remains the real tenancy boundary. A null engagement_id is a historical/edge-case state (a scan with no asset -- create_scan always resolves one in practice, but the column is nullable), never a leak.
  • Growing Engagement types later (e.g. a dedicated "import" type for a report that didn't come from a Bulwark scan at all, per the plan's own C13 "manual findings as a first-class source") needs no schema change -- engagement_type is already a free-text column, not an enum constraint.

docs.title: What is NOT done
docs.text:
• Portfolios are created but nothing assigns an Asset's Engagements to one automatically, and nothing in the UI surfaces them yet -- purely organizational scaffolding for now.
  • SLA tracking, risk acceptance, and the configurable priority engine (plan §40 changes C15-C17) are separate, later decisions; nothing here anticipates their schema.
  • RLS on the new tables themselves (as opposed to the existing, unchanged tool_runs policy) and the two-tenant leak test covering them is Week 53 task 4, verified separately.

docs.title: ADR-0040: One ingest path -- import is reimport with an empty history
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-04), Weeks 54-56 (plan §41-§42, §55.1; "ADR-017" in the plan's own numbering -- renumbered to this repository's real, sequential ADR series, as ADR-0038 explains). Amends ADR-0039 on what a "Test" is.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Everything through v2 enters the system one way: a Bulwark scan runs, produces a complete snapshot of one asset, and core.issues.sync compares that snapshot against the asset's Issues. v3 has to accept findings from sources that are not that: a penetration tester's Nessus export, a CycloneDX file, a SARIF file from a tool Bulwark does not run, a report uploaded last quarter. The plan's rule (§39.3, §41, C12) is one code path for matching, closing and reopening, so "one place to get it right" -- and §42.1 spells the semantics out: import is reimport with an empty history; the same file into the same Test twice is a no-op; close_missing is scoped to the Test by default; the four counts are the product; the most recent import into a Test can be reverted.

docs.title: An import is a real Scan, plus an ImportRecord
docs.text:
Each upload creates a Scan row (source_type="import", status completed) that owns its findings exactly like a native scan's, and an ImportRecord carrying what a Scan does not: the file digest, the parser, the four counts, and changes (the prior state of every Issue the import touched).

This avoids a second way to store an Occurrence. findings.scan_id stays NOT NULL, the findings/tool_runs RLS policies (an EXISTS join through scans) keep working unchanged, and every existing reader of "the findings of a scan" works on an import without knowing it is one. Making findings.scan_id nullable would have been smaller on paper and would have made imported findings invisible under RLS, so it was rejected.

docs.title: A persistent Test, and what that does to ADR-0039
docs.text:
ADR-0039 said "Test is a ToolRun, not a new table." That is right for CI and wrong for imports, and Week 54's real requirement exposed it: a ToolRun is unique per (scan_id, tool), so it is per-run, but §42.1 needs a Test that outlives every upload ("every later upload is compared against that Test's previous Occurrences"), and tool_runs' RLS goes through scans, so a Test without a scan cannot be a ToolRun at all.

So both are true, one per engagement kind:

  • CI engagements: a Test is still a ToolRun, one per tool per pipeline run -- the plan's "each run of your own pipeline creates one Test per scanner." Unchanged.
  • Assessment and Import engagements: a Test is an EngagementTest row (unique per (engagement_id, name)), created once and reimported into. Named EngagementTest, not Test, so pytest never tries to collect it.

The two are not duplicate state: they hold different things (a per-run result versus a standing container), and neither can stand in for the other.

docs.title: A Test's "previous Occurrences" is its latest applied import's snapshot
docs.text: A Test's current occurrences are the findings of its most recent applied ImportRecord. A new upload is therefore compared against exactly one snapshot, the same snapshot semantics ADR-0012 already gives a scan, and a revert is "delete the latest import's scan and restore the Issues it changed" -- no per-occurrence open/closed bookkeeping to keep consistent.

docs.title: Issue identity stays at project level; counts are Issue outcomes
docs.text:
An Issue is still (asset, category, fingerprint) (ADR-0012). A SQL injection found by CI and again by a pen tester is one Issue with two Occurrences (§41.2). The four counts are about Issues:

Count Meaning new the incoming finding matches no Issue: a new Issue is created unchanged it matches a live Issue (whether or not this Test already reported it) reopened it matches a fixed Issue: the Issue becomes reintroduced closed the previous snapshot had the Issue, this one does not, close_missing is on, and no other source still reports it: the Issue becomes fixed

A fifth number, detached, is recorded but is not one of the four on the screen: Issues this file stopped reporting that stay open because another source (the CI scan, another Test) still does. Calling those "closed" would tell a reader something is fixed when it is not, which is the failure the plan's risk R20 ("reimport bugs silently closing or reopening issues") names.

"Another source still reports it" means the Issue has a finding in the latest snapshot of any other source on the same asset: the latest completed native scan, or the latest applied import of any other Test. The same rule must also apply to native scans, so sync_issues_for_scan stops marking an Issue fixed while an import still reports it (Week 54 task 4).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: close_missing has two scopes. test (the default) considers only the Test's own previous snapshot -- one tool's report cannot close another tool's findings, which is why it is the default. engagement considers every Test in the engagement and exists for assessments that must reconcile as a whole.

docs.title: Events go through an outbox
docs.text: outbox_events rows (issue.created, issue.closed, issue.reopened, scan.completed, ...) are written in the same transaction as the change that caused them, then dispatched. A crash between "saved" and "announced" cannot lose an event.

docs.title: Parsers
docs.text:
core/imports/parsers/ holds the IngestParser interface (sniff(head) -> confidence, streaming parse(stream)), a registry, and one parser per format. Decisions, and where this departs from the plan's wording:

  • A parser yields canonical Findings, not a separate RawOccurrence type. A second intermediate type would need its own mapping into Finding and so a second place that mapping can drift. SARIF results go through core.sarif.result_to_finding, the function native scans already use, so an uploaded Semgrep SARIF and a Semgrep run Bulwark did itself cannot disagree.
  • A parse that did not reach the end of the file is an error, never a smaller report. Reimport closes what a file no longer lists, so a truncated or half-parsed file would read as "everything was fixed." parse never raises on bad input; it records ctx.error, and ParseResult.complete is false. Callers must refuse to apply an incomplete result. The same holds for a sandbox that fails or times out: that is an error, not an empty report.
  • Limits are enforced while reading, not after: byte size, JSON/XML nesting depth, wall-clock time and finding count (parsers/safe.py), so a hostile file is stopped before it exhausts memory. XML goes through defusedxml with DTDs, entities and external references refused; identifiers are extracted from free text with RE2 and bounded input.
  • Streaming is real for JSON (ijson): memory is bounded by the largest record. SARIF is read twice (rule metadata, then results) because SARIF does not say which a file lists first.
  • Parsing runs in the scanner sandbox. docker/ingest-parser holds only the parser modules (no API, no database layer, no credentials); core.runner.run_tool runs it with the same no-network, read-only, all-capabilities-dropped flags as every scanner, through a pseudo-adapter, so there is no second sandbox to keep as strict as the first. In-process parsing exists for tests and local development and is an explicit opt-out, never the default.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An import is stored as a scan (source_type="import", Scan.tools holds the parser name), so anything that reads "the findings of a scan" works on one. Two places must not treat it as a scan someone ran and exclude it: "the latest/previous scan of an asset" (the project overview and trend deltas) and the recent-scans list. Its own scan page still opens by id, and its history is listed under its Test (GET /v2/tests/{id}/imports).
  • Retention deleting an import's scan leaves its ImportRecord (scan_id becomes null): the audit trail that an import happened and what it changed outlives the findings.
  • A reverted ImportRecord is kept with status="reverted"; its Scan and findings are removed, so it no longer counts as the Test's previous snapshot.
  • Reverting restores each touched Issue from changes. It only reverts the most recent import into a Test: reverting an older one would have to re-derive every later import's diff.
  • The "other sources" rule makes sync_issues_for_scan slightly more expensive (one query per scan to find live sources). That is a correctness cost, accepted.

docs.title: What is NOT done here
docs.text:
• Parsers (SARIF, CycloneDX, SPDX, OSV) are Week 55; the endpoint is Week 54 task 7; the import screen is Week 56. This ADR and migration 0027 are the schema and the decision only.
  • Per-source deduplication strategies (§42.3) are Week 58. Until then every source matches by the existing project-level fingerprints.
  • A component inventory (Week 67): an SPDX/CycloneDX file that lists packages but no vulnerabilities produces no Occurrences yet.

docs.title: ADR-0041: Where a DAST or network finding is, is its identity
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-04), Week 57 (plan §22.4, §42.2). Amends ADR-0004 (correlation) and ADR-0012 (Issue identity) for one category.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Week 57 ports the first DAST and network parsers (ZAP, Nuclei, then Burp, Nessus, OpenVAS) from DefectDojo. Feeding a real ZAP report to the import path showed that Bulwark's identity rules, written for source code, were wrong for findings with no file, no line and no snippet -- and had been wrong for the native DAST campaigns (Week 49) all along, because nothing had put more than a handful of alerts through them. Three independent mechanisms each got it wrong:

  1. Correlation merged different alerts. core.correlation.same_defect compares code findings by path, CWE and line. A DAST finding has path "" and line 0, so every DAST finding was "in the same place". Two alerts that share a CWE (ZAP's X-Frame-Options and CSP rules are both CWE-1021) were folded into one finding, and which rule survived depended on input order. Every DAST finding also fell into one candidate bucket, so correlation was quadratic in the size of the scan.
  2. The fingerprint ignored the route. It hashed CWE, path, snippet and rule. One alert fired on fifty URLs shared one fingerprint.
  3. The location-independent fallback key matched every URL to the first. fallback_key exists so a function moved to another file is not "new" plus "fixed"; it deliberately omits the path. For DAST it omitted the only thing that distinguished findings, so 130 findings of a real ZAP report became 15 Issues.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A DAST or network finding's place is its identity, and it is carried explicitly:

  • Location.host (new, default ""): scheme://host[:port] for a web target (lower-cased, the scheme's default port dropped), the bare host or IP for a network scan. Location.route is the URL path, or port/protocol (443/tcp, or host for a finding about the machine) when there is no URL. Query string and fragment are never part of it: scanners generate them on the fly.
  • DAST findings are never merged by correlate(), and are never even compared (each gets its own candidate bucket). Cross-tool merging of dynamic findings is not defined by ADR-0004, and the obvious rule (same route and CWE) is wrong as soon as one tool reports two weaknesses with a CWE in common. The existing SAST-to-DAST confirmation (core.dast.correlate) is separate and unchanged.
  • The fingerprint of a DAST finding is dast | CWE | host | route | rule ids. Tool names are deliberately not in it: ZAP run by Bulwark and a ZAP report uploaded later are one defect.
  • fallback_key is None for DAST, as it already was for SCA: the primary fingerprint is already location-independent in the only sense that applies.
  • One Finding per instance (per URL or per host/port), not one per alert. DefectDojo folds a ZAP alert hit at fifty URLs into one finding with fifty endpoints. Here each place is its own Finding and its own Issue: fixing /a closes that Issue and not /b, which a folded finding cannot express. tests/unit/ddview.py regroups our output by DefectDojo's folding key so the two can be compared like for like.
  • The map from a tool's record to a Finding lives in core/dast/mapping.py and is shared by the native campaign adapters and the import parsers, so a defect has one reading however it arrives.

docs.title: Parsing policy for the batch
docs.text:
• Burp's DOCTYPE. Burp writes <!DOCTYPE issues [<!ELEMENT ...>]> at the top of every export, so refusing every DTD (the rule for all other XML) would refuse every real Burp file. iter_xml gains allow_dtd, used only by the Burp parser, which admits an internal subset without entity declarations: an <!ENTITY> (which is all XXE and entity expansion need) and an external DTD (SYSTEM/PUBLIC) are still errors.
  • A report must have reached something to close anything. A scanner report that is a sample of a scan, not a complete one -- an OpenVAS scan that is not Done, a report with no hosts, a CSV with no rows, an empty Nuclei file -- imports what it has and closes nothing.
  • CSV truncation. A row with fewer fields than the header, or an unterminated quoted field, is an error. A cut exactly between two rows is a valid shorter CSV and cannot be detected.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-10-08): a ZAP place closes only when its rule leaves the host
docs.text:
"Fixing /a closes that Issue and not /b" assumed a report lists every place an alert fires. ZAP's does not. Measured on one unchanged OWASP Juice Shop v17.3.0 with ZAP 2.17.0 (zap-baseline.py):

  • ZAP lists at most five places for a systemic alert (a missing header, site-wide), marked "systemic": true in the JSON report; with alert.systemicLimit raised, the CSP alert has 11-12.
  • Its spider reaches different pages each run: with every limit lifted, two runs disagreed on 26 places. Two runs with default settings: 4 of 36 places in the first were missing from the second.
  • DefectDojo's own two ZAP samples: 17 places drop out of the second; for 16 of them the same rule still fires on the same host.

So for a tool that crawls (ZAP natively, a ZAP report, GitLab's DAST report, which is ZAP's), a place missing from a run is held, not closed, while the same rule still fires on the same host (core.dast.mapping.crawl_samples, repo.issues_at_sampled_places, plan_reimport's held_issue_ids). Once the rule is gone from the host, every place of it closes, including those held. An import records which Issues it held (import_records.held_issue_ids, migration 0051) and they stay part of its Test's snapshot, so a later file can still close them; the preview counts them as "held". Nuclei is unchanged: its templates request fixed paths, so a missing place is a real absence.

Costs, accepted: a place fixed while the same rule still fires elsewhere on the host stays open until the rule is gone from the host; a run that lists a different sample adds the new places as new Issues. Native campaigns keep ZAP's default limits, since raising them multiplies Issues for one site-wide header (11-12 places instead of 5) without making any closure more correct.

Not covered: a crawl that misses a rule entirely (the spider never reached the one page with the problem; "Vulnerable JS Library" appeared in 2 of 3 runs on 2026-10-07) still reads as the rule gone, and closes its places. Telling that apart needs the list of pages a run reached, which a ZAP report does not carry. Burp also crawls, but was not measured, so it is not treated as sampling.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One-time churn for existing DAST Issues. Native DAST Issues created before this change have route-free fingerprints. The next campaign (or import) against the same asset will not match them: they are closed as fixed and the same defects reappear as new Issues, one per place. Triage state recorded on the old Issues (false-positive marks, suppressions) does not carry over. This was judged better than carrying forward the bug (which would keep collapsing fifty places into one Issue); it only affects instances that ran a DAST campaign on v2.0.0 or v2.1.0, and a migration could not recover it because the old fingerprint never contained the route.
  • The Issue list for a DAST scan is longer than DefectDojo's finding list for the same report -- by design (see above) -- and a Nuclei result on the same host at two ports is two Issues where DefectDojo folds on hostname alone.
  • Location gains a field; stored findings are JSON, so existing rows are unaffected, but every golden expected.json gained "host": "".

docs.title: What is NOT done here
docs.text:
• Request and response bodies are not stored. A ZAP "XML plus requests and responses" report is read; the finding keeps the method, parameter, attack, evidence and the response's status line, not kilobytes of HTTP. Evidence attachments belong with the manual-findings work (Week 59, §43.2).
  • The HTTP method is not part of a DAST finding's place. GET /v1/trees and POST /v1/trees with the same check are one Issue with two findings. Location.route is matched against code handlers by path (core.dast.correlate), and adding the method to it would break that; for an API where the method decides what the endpoint does this under-splits, and it is a known limitation.
  • Closing is scoped to the Test, not to the hosts a report covers. A Nessus or OpenVAS report that covers fewer hosts than the last one lists the missing hosts' Issues as closed. The preview shows the count before it is saved, and the docs say to read it; making closure host-aware needs a coverage set on the parse result and a host column on stored findings, and is not done.
  • Cross-tool merging of DAST findings (ZAP and Nuclei both seeing the same missing header) is not attempted. It would need per-weakness rules and is better done as an explicit, previewed deduplication strategy (Week 58, §42.3) than as an implicit merge.

docs.title: ADR-0042: Deduplication is chosen per source, versioned, and changed only through a dry run
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-04), Week 58 (plan §42.3, §55.1; "ADR-018" in the plan's own numbering -- renumbered to this repository's sequence, as ADR-0038 explains). Builds on ADR-0004 and ADR-0040; the DAST identity it relies on is ADR-0041.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Every finding is matched to an Issue by one rule: its fingerprint (ADR-0004), with a path-free fallback for code. That is right for source code, where a defect moves, and arbitrary for everything else. A Nessus export has a stable plugin id and a host; a pen tester's tool may have neither; an SCA report has an exact package and version. DefectDojo lets a project choose how each source is deduplicated, and the plan (§42.3) asks for the same, with one non-negotiable property: changing it must be previewed -- "switching Nessus to tool_id would merge 212 issues into 97 and split none" -- because a deduplication change rewrites Issue identity, the thing every state, ticket and triage decision hangs on.

docs.title: Five strategies, as key functions (core/dedup/strategies.py)
docs.text:
A strategy turns a Finding into a key; findings with equal keys are one Issue.

Strategy Key For fingerprint_v2 the finding's existing fingerprint SAST (and the default) tool_id category, source, the rule id(s), and where (file, URL, or package without version) tools with stable ids hash_fields source plus the chosen fields (a closed list of thirteen) tools without stable ids tool_id_or_hash tool_id, or hash_fields for a finding with no rule id mixed quality package the SCA fingerprint (ecosystem, package, version, vulnerability id) SCA

package is fingerprint_v2 for a package -- an SCA fingerprint already is that key -- and is selectable so a package source's setting says what it means. Every other key is namespaced (dd1:<strategy>:<sha256>): it cannot collide with a fingerprint, and the 1 versions the key scheme. hash_fields takes a closed list of fields, not free text, so a setting cannot be a way to read anything off a finding and a dry run can always explain it.

docs.title: A setting is per (project, source) and versioned by insertion
docs.text:
dedup_settings (migration 0029, tenant-isolated): a change is a new row with the next version, never an edit, so the table is the history -- who, when, why, and what it did (effect). With no row a source uses fingerprint_v2, which is what every Issue was matched by before settings existed, so nothing changes until someone chooses. The strategy each parser suggests (IngestParser.default_dedup: tool_id for the DAST and network parsers, package for the SCA ones) is only a recommendation shown beside the choice.

A source is whatever tool the finding says reported it (evidence.reported_by[0]). For a SARIF import that is the driver's name (semgrep-oss), not the parser's; a native Semgrep scan's source is semgrep. They are different sources with different settings, and the screen lists the names that actually occur in the project.

docs.title: Applied before matching, for imports and native scans alike
docs.text: core.dedup.settings.rekey overrides a finding's key just before it is matched to an Issue -- in apply_import/preview_import and in sync_issues_for_scan -- so a source is matched the same way however its findings arrive, and an import preview shows the counts the setting will produce. A chosen key also switches off the path-free fallback: that fallback matches findings across files, which is exactly what a project that put path in its key said it does not want.

docs.title: The dry run, and what applying does (core/dedup/change.py, service.py)
docs.text:
Existing Issues are re-keyed by the same rule, judged by each Issue's latest occurrences (the findings of the last scan that saw it); older history stays attached to the Issue it was recorded against. For a source's Issues:

  • one new key: the Issue takes it (re-key);
  • several keys among one Issue's occurrences: it is split -- it keeps the key most of them have, and each other key becomes a new Issue, a copy of this one as it is now;
  • one key across several Issues: they are merged -- the oldest survives, the others' occurrences move to it and they disappear.

preview_change reads and writes nothing and returns counts, examples and a digest of the exact plan. apply_change takes the digest, recomputes the plan inside one transaction under a lock on the project's Issues, refuses (409) if it differs -- the project moved since the preview -- and otherwise applies it, records the next setting version with its effect, stages a dedup.changed outbox event, commits, and appends the audit-chain entry. The preview is ingest:read, the apply ingest:write.

What a change never loses, tested: every occurrence (they move between Issues; none disappear); external ticket links and verified-fix runs of an Issue that is merged away (they move to the survivor, except a second ticket on the same tracker); and no open Issue is ever hidden behind a decision made about another one -- if the members of a merge disagree about triage, the merged Issue is reopened for triage and the preview counts those merges.

wait_for_dedup on POST /v2/ingest is now real: it holds the response until the import has been matched (it leaves queued/processing), up to 20 s, and dedup_complete on an import is false exactly while it is still queued or processing.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An Issue that two tools reported (reported_by has more than one entry) belongs to neither source's setting and is left alone, with a count in the preview. Cross-source merging is not a strategy.
  • A merge is not reversible one-for-one -- the merged-away Issues' own first-seen dates and triage history are folded into the survivor. Choosing the previous strategy again splits what it can and loses nothing, but it does not resurrect the exact Issues that disappeared. The screen says so.
  • The tool_id key for a package omits the version, so the same vulnerability in two versions of one package is one Issue under it and two under package. That is its definition, and the dry run shows the effect on real data (benchmarks/results/dedup-strategies-2026-10-04.json): on DefectDojo's Snyk sample it merges 3 Issues into 2.
  • The dry run reads the latest occurrences of every Issue of the source; on a very large project that is a scan of its findings. It has not been measured at scale.

docs.title: What is NOT done here
docs.text:
• No precision or recall. The plan's evaluation is "hand-labelled duplicate pairs from three tools across ten repositories". That corpus does not exist; benchmarks/dedup_strategies.py measures only what each strategy changes on real reports (a tool_id that merges more is not thereby better), and the evaluation says so. Until the corpus exists, the dry run and the person reading it are the safety, not a measured accuracy.
  • The matching settings screen offers the strategies and fields; it does not suggest a strategy from the data, and it cannot yet scope a change to one engagement.

docs.title: ADR-0043: A saved mapping is a deterministic, sandboxed parser; the model only drafts it
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-05), Week 59 (plan §42.4, §50 "Mapping assistant"). Builds on ADR-0040 (one ingest path) and ADR-0042 (deduplication per source).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Fourteen parsers cover the standard formats and the most-used tools. Every organization also has a report nobody wrote a parser for: an in-house scanner's JSON, a vendor's CSV export, a pen-test tool's XML. The plan (§42.4) asks for a universal mapper: upload a sample, "the model proposes field mappings ... a person reviews and edits them, with a live preview ... the saved mapping is a deterministic parser. The model helped write it; it is never in the import path."

Three things had to be decided: what a mapping can express, where it runs, and what the model is allowed to see and do.

docs.title: A mapping is data, compiled into an IngestParser (core/imports/parsers/universal.py)
docs.text:
A MappingSpec names the format (JSON, CSV, XML), where the records are, the tool's name (the source: what "reported by" says and what deduplication settings are chosen for), a category, and one path per field: title (required), severity, description, path, line, rule, CWE, CVE, URL, package, version, ecosystem, recommendation, references. A severity map turns the tool's own words into ours; anything still unknown is Info and said so, as every ported parser does.

UniversalParser(spec) is an IngestParser like the others: it streams, it never raises on bad input, a file not read to the end is an error (so it can never close anything), and it builds web and dependency findings with the same helpers the built-in parsers use (dast_finding, package identity), so a mapped Nessus-like CSV and the real Nessus parser agree on what identifies a finding.

docs.title: The path language is deliberately smaller than JSONPath
docs.text:
$, .key, ["key"], [n], [*] for JSON; child/grandchild, @attr, . for XML (local names); a column name for CSV. No filters, recursive descent, slices or scripts.

Considered: jsonpath-ng (the plan's own resource list). Rejected for the import path because a mapping is evaluated against attacker-controlled files, and everything JSONPath adds beyond this subset -- filter expressions, .. -- is either code-like or has a cost that depends on the data. The subset covers every real report in the evaluation, its cost is linear in the record, and a person can read any path at a glance. A records path must be keys and [*] ending in [*], because it is turned into an ijson streaming prefix: a mapped file is never loaded whole.

docs.title: It runs in the parser sandbox
docs.text: The spec is written beside the uploaded file and the same container runs it (worker.py --mapping), so a mapped import has exactly the isolation of a built-in one. Describing a sample's shape for the mapping screen (analyze.py, worker.py --analyze) also reads uploaded bytes and runs there too.

docs.title: Saved mappings are versioned by insertion and tenant-isolated (migration 0030)
docs.text: ingest_mappings follows dedup_settings: an edit adds a row with the next version and never changes an earlier one. An import names the exact row (universal:<id>), so what parsed a past import is always known. Direct org_id with the forced RLS policy; a mapping id from another org resolves as unknown. A mapping's source cannot be a built-in parser's or scanner's name, or the two would share deduplication settings. Saving is audit-logged.

docs.title: The model drafts from a description, and its draft is checked against it
docs.text:
The model is shown the analysis -- candidate record paths, field paths, three short examples each -- with secrets scrubbed and the whole thing nonce-fenced as untrusted data, never the file. Its reply is then checked against that same analysis (mapper.sanitize): a records path or field path the sample does not have, a field that does not exist, or a severity that is not one is dropped and listed in the draft's notes. With no model configured, the budget spent (check_org/record_org, the org's monthly cap), or a reply that does not hold up, the draft comes from name matching instead, and says so. The prompt is versioned (core/llm/prompts/mapper/v1.md) with a promptfoo evaluation whose assertion is the same sanitize.

Either way the draft is only a draft: saving needs a person (and ingest:write), the preview runs the mapping exactly as an import would, and the import itself never calls a model.

docs.title: Suggested, never picked
docs.text: When nothing built-in recognises an upload with confidence, saved mappings whose sniff matches it are offered among the "detected" formats; one is used only when named. A mapping that half-fits a file would otherwise silently produce half the findings.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An unsupported format is an afternoon's mapping, not a parser and a release -- and the plan's "15 formats" milestone can count saved mappings honestly only as what they are: mappings.
  • Fuzzed like a parser: three fixed mappings and the sample analysis are fuzz targets (tests/fuzz/mappings.py) in the nightly matrix.
  • Not supported, deliberately: computed fields (concatenating two paths), per-record categories, and filters. A report that needs them needs a parser.
  • The model's draft quality is measured by its eval set, which was not run in this environment (no local model); the draft's safety does not depend on its quality, because nothing it says reaches an import without a person and a deterministic parser in between.

docs.title: ADR-0044: Manual findings are an ingest source; evidence is encrypted and only ever downloaded
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-05), Week 59 (plan §43.2, §52 threat T24). Builds on ADR-0040 and the runtime correlation of ADR-0035.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Pen testers and code reviewers find things no scanner does. The plan (§43.2) asks for a form: title, a searchable CWE, severity from a CVSS 4.0 calculator "with the vector stored alongside the score", a location that "can be a route picked from code intelligence" -- so a manual finding on POST /orders "links to that handler's code and taint paths automatically" -- steps, impact, recommendation, and evidence "encrypted at rest and never rendered inline". Threat T24: an HTML or SVG evidence file that runs script.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
One more ingest source, not a parallel store. A manual finding becomes a canonical Finding and is applied through core.imports.service.apply_import (source manual) into a Test -- "Manual review" in the project's standing import engagement unless an engagement is named. It is therefore an ordinary Issue: triage, deduplication, tickets and every later v3 feature apply to it, and the import that created it can be reverted. close_missing is always off. Its rule id is a hash of what it says and where, so submitting the same finding twice is one Issue (the import is idempotent) and two different findings on one handler are two. What the Finding has no field for -- the CVSS vector, the steps as written, the location kind, the automated Issue it matched -- is kept in a manual_findings row (migration 0031, forced RLS) beside the Issue, cascading away with it.

CVSS 4.0 from one implementation. The cvss library (RedHatProductSecurity, LGPL-3.0, used unmodified) scores vectors; the calculator screen asks POST /v2/cvss/v4 for every score instead of re-implementing FIRST's lookup tables in the browser. Eight vectors were checked against FIRST's own calculator and are fixed in the tests. A 0.0 ("None") score is Info. A person may set a severity without CVSS; the vector is then simply absent.

Routes come from code intelligence. Every scan now stores its HTTP entrypoints (any framework the code graph knows, with the verb and the handler's file and line: scans.entrypoints); older scans fall back to the Python-only route map. A picked route puts the finding at its handler. Linking to automation reuses core.dast.correlate, the conservative match that marks a static finding "confirmed at runtime": same handler, nearby line, related CWE family. When it matches, the manual finding records the automated Issue and carries its taint path as evidence. No CWE, or no static finding there, means no link -- never a guess.

Evidence: sniffed, encrypted, downloaded. Attachments are stored in the database (so RLS covers them), at most 10 MB and 20 per finding. Their type is sniffed from the bytes; the claimed type and a sanitized name are kept for display only; HTML, SVG, XML and PDF are flagged as active content. With OpenBao configured, each is encrypted with a fresh AES-256-GCM data key wrapped by the org's key, the row id as associated data; without it they are stored unencrypted and say so -- the same "off means off" posture as scan artifacts. They are never rendered: the UI only offers a download, through a five-minute link signed (HMAC) for one attachment and one org, served as application/octet-stream with Content-Disposition: attachment, nosniff, default-src 'none'; sandbox and no-store. The link needs no cookie or bearer token, so BULWARK_ATTACHMENTS_ORIGIN can point downloads at a separate origin that holds neither.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Recording is ingest:write, reading ingest:read, like any import.
  • Found while building it, and fixed: correlation rebuilds findings without their taint path, so a path is attached after it; and the issue page only looked in the latest native scan, so an issue only an import or a person reported could not be opened at all -- it now shows the issue's most recent occurrence from any source.
  • Not done: editing a recorded finding (record a corrected one and revert the old), retests (§43.3, Week 64), and per-org link secrets (the HMAC key is BULWARK_LINK_SECRET, else derived from the deployment's API token).

docs.title: ADR-0045: Connectors pull through the ingest path, and never close on a pull they cannot trust
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-05), Week 60 (plan §42.5, §55.7, threat T25). Builds on ADR-0040, ADR-0017 and ADR-0032.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The plan asks for pull-based ingestion on a schedule -- GitHub code scanning and Dependabot alerts through the GitHub App, GitLab vulnerability reports, DefectDojo in both directions -- with a health state per connector that alerts "not only when it fails, but when it authenticates successfully and sees no data, which is how silent misconfiguration shows up", and credentials "in OpenBao with the narrowest scopes the source allows". Threat T25: a connector URL pointed at an internal service.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A pull is an import. Each pull fetches the source's complete list of open items and applies it with apply_import into the connector's own Test (close_missing on): an alert fixed or dismissed at the source is no longer listed and is closed here. An unchanged pull has the same digest as the last one and is a no-op. Findings are read by the same code an upload uses wherever one exists: GitLab nodes are reshaped into security-report records and read by the GitLab report parser.

Two pulls are never applied. - A partial pull: any failed page, a page cap exceeded (100 pages), or pagination pointing at another host fails the run; nothing is applied, because reimport would read the missing pages as "fixed". - An empty pull after a non-empty one is held back: "everything was fixed at once" and "the token lost access" look the same from here. The run is recorded as empty and nothing is closed, unless the connector opts into close_on_empty. GitLab supplied a third case on a live request: a viewer without access gets a valid page with no vulnerabilities and hasNextPage: true. That is reported as a permissions error, not paged through.

Health is a state, not a log line. never_run, ok, empty (connected, fetched nothing -- worded differently when it fetched items before), failing (with the reason, and an auth failure called one), disabled. Failures back off exponentially (×2 up to ×16 the interval). Every run is kept (connector_runs), and emits a connector.run outbox event for the rules and notifications to come.

Credentials. GitHub kinds store none: each pull mints a one-hour installation token from the App, whose installation must belong to the connector's org; the App needs only "Code scanning alerts: read" / "Dependabot alerts: read". GitLab and DefectDojo credentials go to OpenBao's KV store when it is configured; otherwise into the row, and the API, the health warning and the screen all say "not encrypted". A credential is write-only: no response contains it. Creating, changing, running and deleting a connector is audit-logged and needs ingest:write.

SSRF. Base URLs are https, without embedded credentials, and must resolve only to public addresses -- checked on save and again on every request, with redirects not followed. A private instance needs BULWARK_CONNECTOR_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1, an explicit operator decision.

DefectDojo in reads findings/?test__engagement__product=<id>&active=true&duplicate=false. The filter is not trusted: DefectDojo silently ignores one it does not know (?product=<id> returned every product's findings on a real 3.3.300), so each finding comes with its related_fields and one from another product refuses the whole pull.

DefectDojo out posts the project's open Issues as SARIF (the report exporter) to import-scan, then reimport-scan into the same DefectDojo Test with close_old_findings. Issues that came from DefectDojo are excluded, so a pair of connectors cannot echo each other's findings. Creating the product needs a product type (product_type_name, default "Bulwark"); DefectDojo refuses otherwise.

Scheduling. Celery beat checks every five minutes, one organization at a time (scoped sessions, as every cross-org job does); each due connector is its own task. "Run now" uses the same task.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Dependabot does not report the installed version, only the vulnerable range; the range stands in for the version so a Dependabot Issue is stable, and it will not merge with an OSV-Scanner Issue for the same package at an exact version.
  • A DefectDojo dynamic finding has its URLs in separate Endpoint objects that are not fetched; it is imported without a route.
  • What was verified live, and what was not, is in the Weeks 59-60 verification record: the GitLab query against gitlab.com; the DefectDojo round trip against a real DefectDojo 3.3.300, in, out and back (tests/integration/test_defectdojo_live.py), which found the product filter and product type bugs above; the GitHub endpoints only against GitHub's documented response shapes, since no App is registered.

docs.title: ADR-0046: SLA deadlines are computed, never stored; accepting a risk takes a second person
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-05), Weeks 61-62 (plan §44.1, §44.2, §55.3; the plan calls this ADR-019). Builds on ADR-0019 (the hash-chained audit log) and ADR-0018 (scoped API tokens).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Governance starts here. A project needs remediation deadlines per severity, starting at first detection and not restartable by re-uploading a report, with "due soon" and "breached" announced. And a risk may be lived with for a while -- but only with a justification, compensating controls, proof, an expiry capped by policy, and an approver who is not the requester, enforced on the server, with every step evidence an auditor can verify.

Until now one person could mark an Issue "accepted" through triage, alone.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
SLA. A policy per project, versioned by insertion like dedup settings (migration 0033): per severity band, days to fix and a "due soon" window. Off until someone saves one; the starter values (7/30/90/180 days, Info none) are offered, not imposed. The deadline is computed from the policy, the Issue's severity and its clock -- first_seen_at, which reimport never resets, or sla_started_at once a risk acceptance restarted it -- and never stored, so a policy or severity change moves every deadline at once. The issues table filters by SLA state in SQL that a test checks against the rules at every band boundary. A sweep every five minutes announces each crossing into due soon or breached once (issues.sla_notified): an outbox event for the rules engine (Week 65) and one message per project to Slack, Discord and the outbound webhook. Priority bands, the plan's alternative basis, wait for the priority engine (Week 63).

Risk acceptance. A risk_acceptances row covers one or more Issues of one project (migration 0034): decision (accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid), justification and controls (required), proof (links, and files stored like manual-finding evidence: sniffed, encrypted, downloaded by signed link), an expiry no later than the policy maximum (90 days, BULWARK_RISK_ACCEPTANCE_MAX_DAYS, the same as the policy gate's rule), and whether the SLA restarts on expiry. core.acceptance.service enforces, whatever a screen does:

  • The Issues stay open until approved. The approver's actor differs from the requester's, and is a personal API token -- the shared deployment token is anyone, so it approves nothing. A named approver is the only one who can decide.
  • An Issue is under at most one live (requested or approved) acceptance.
  • Approval writes the existing triage fields (accepted until the expiry), so the active queue, the SLA pause and the policy gate read it unchanged. Expiry -- the job, or "expire now" -- reopens them, and restarts their SLA clock if asked.
  • "Reinstate" undoes "expire now" only within the approved dates; anything later is an extension, which is a new request needing its own approval. A request whose date passes unapproved lapses.
  • Every change is a hash-chained audit entry and an outbox event, and appears in each Issue's history.

Triage can no longer accept a risk (HTTP 409, pointing at the request); it still marks "not a risk" and reopens. Issues accepted alone before this become legacy acceptances, grouped by project, person, expiry and reason, approved if still in date and expired otherwise -- no expiry date lost, and marked as never approved by a second person.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• "Someone else" is a different API token, not a different human. Bulwark has no user accounts yet; one person holding two tokens can approve their own request. The screens say so, and SSO and SCIM (Week 75) are what close it. The approver list is the org's live personal tokens that can write, other than the asker's.
  • The SLA sweep and the expiry job each read every open Issue of every organization every five minutes. That is fine at today's scale; a large deployment would want the due-time index the computed deadline avoids storing.
  • Without OpenBao, proof files are stored unencrypted, as manual-finding evidence is (the API says which).
  • Found on the way: CORS allowed only GET and POST, so every PUT, PATCH and DELETE from the web app on another origin was refused (settings, threat model, connectors). It now allows every method a route uses.

docs.title: ADR-0047: Priority is v2's score made a policy; context only lowers it; recomputation holds a lock
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-05), Week 63 (plan §44.3, §55.7, change C17). Builds on ADR-0046 (SLA policies, versioned by insertion) and the v2 risk score (risk-score.md, core/risk/score.py).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: v2's risk score was one fixed formula. Plan C17: a payments service and an internal wiki should not rank the same issue the same way. §44.3 asks for weights per factor, the project's business context, a preview of how the top 50 would reorder before saving, a background recomputation that two edits cannot race, and every rank still explaining itself. Week 61 also left SLA deadlines by priority band waiting for this.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
One engine, weights as exponents. Every factor is a multiplier relative to "no effect", and a project's weight for it is an exponent: multiplier ** weight. 1 is the factor as designed, 0 ignores it, 2 doubles its pull either way. Known exploitation (CISA KEV) stays a floor, scaled: 90 × weight (80 when nothing imports the package). Factors: severity, EPSS, KEV, reachability, taint confirmation, runtime (DAST) confirmation, tool agreement, path context (test, example, docs, vendored code), the triage assistant's verdict, and the business context. The arithmetic, factor order and rounding are v2's, so with the new factors at 0 and no context the engine gives the v2 score exactly; a test holds that over more than a thousand findings.

No policy, no change. A project without a saved policy keeps the v2 score stored on each occurrence (priority version 0); migration 0035 copies it onto every existing Issue, organization by organization. The starter (every factor at 1) is offered on the Priority page, not imposed.

Business context only lowers. Internet-facing, data sensitivity and criticality default to the worst case when not set; saying a project is internal, handles public data or matters little lowers its scores. The first design boosted exposed projects instead. On a 2,500-Issue project in the browser it put 770 Issues in P1 and tied the whole top 50 at 100, which made bands meaningless and handed the order to the tie-breaker. Context scales every Issue of a project alike, so it moves scores, bands and SLA deadlines, not the order within the project. The KEV floor ignores it: known-exploited stays at least 90 unless the KEV weight is lowered.

Stored per Issue. issues.priority_score, priority_band (P1 ≥ 80, P2 ≥ 60, P3 ≥ 30, P4) and priority_factors (each with its weight and the multiplier it applied), so the issues table sorts and filters by priority in SQL and an SLA can key on the band. They are written at ingest (every scan, import, DAST campaign and manual finding goes through repo.add_findings), when an Issue is confirmed at runtime or gets an assistant verdict, when a hypothesis is promoted, and by recomputation.

Saving recomputes in the background, under a lock. A priority_policies row is versioned like SLA policies, and it records its own recomputation: pending, running, done, failed, or superseded. While the newest version's job is pending or running, another save gets HTTP 409. A job that has made no progress for ten minutes is taken over and stops at its next batch. Two saves that both pass the check still cannot both land, because (project, version) is unique. The job re-ranks every Issue of the project in batches of 500, a commit each, from the stored occurrence, with no scanner, feed or network. It runs on the worker; with no worker, the API runs it after responding.

Preview before saving. POST …/priority/preview ranks the open queue under the current rules and the proposed ones: the new top 50 with ranks and scores before and after, the Issues leaving it, and counts per band. The page only offers Save for weights it has just previewed.

SLA by priority band. An SLA policy's basis is severity or priority; with priority, bands are P1-P4 and the deadline follows the Issue's band, in Python and in the SQL filter alike.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The v2 score on each occurrence is unchanged and still drives exports, the CI gate and policy input; priority is what the issues table ranks by. The two agree until a project saves weights.
  • Recomputation uses the EPSS and KEV values stored at scan time, not today's feed. A rescan refreshes them.
  • Band thresholds are fixed for now. The SLA's priority bands key on them, so changing them later moves deadlines.
  • Measured on SQLite in one process, at 2,500 Issues: recompute 227 ms, preview 169 ms. Larger projects were not measured. The preview loads every open Issue's latest occurrence in one request.
  • The new factors' strengths (taint ×1.1, runtime ×1.25, non-production path ×0.6, context 0.65-0.9) are judgment calls, like v2's, kept in core/priority/engine.py. None is validated against outcomes.

docs.title: ADR-0048: Assessments, retests and collaboration
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-06), Week 64 (plan §43.1, §43.3, §49, §55.2, threat T24). Builds on ADR-0039 (engagements and tests), ADR-0040 (imports), ADR-0044 (manual findings and evidence) and ADR-0046.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Milestone M14 asks that "a pen test runs end to end inside the platform". Until now an engagement was only a container for tests, with a name, a type and dates. A tester could record findings and import a tool's report into one, but had nowhere to keep the scope, the people or a checklist, and had no retest, no notes and no report. Issues could not carry tags. Evidence downloads had a configurable origin, but nothing stopped them being served from the API's own host.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
An assessment is any engagement but the standing "ci" and "import" ones. It gains a scope (targets, routes, an out-of-scope note), a lead and testers, start and end dates, an optional OWASP checklist, and a lifecycle: planned → in progress → reporting → closed. Reporting can go back to in progress, and a closed one can be reopened. Older assessments map onto it (active → in progress, completed → closed). People are names, or API token names, until user accounts exist in Week 75. Every change is a hash-chained audit entry.

Checklists are OWASP's own data, pinned. - WSTG 4.2 has 114 tests. - ASVS 4.0.3 has 128 requirements at L1, 259 up to L2 and 278 up to L3. - Both ship as JSON taken from the projects' tagged releases, with ids and text unchanged. - Both are CC BY-SA 4.0, credited in the licence notices, on the checklist screen and in the report. - Only entries someone touched get a row; "done" means passed, failed or not applicable.

An engagement's findings are every Issue its uploads reported, not only each test's latest snapshot. Each manual finding is its own upload, so a snapshot holds just the last one. Findings fixed during the test therefore stay in its report. Where another source reports the same Issue, the engagement says so ("Also found by Opengrep taint", or another test's name), which is §55.2's cross-source correlation where the tester works.

Closing writes the report as a snapshot. It is stored as JSON on the engagement and rendered on download as Markdown or HTML. A later change to an Issue never rewrites a delivered report. Every outside value is escaped for its format: - HTML is fully escaped, and the page allows no script and no remote loads. - Markdown is HTML-escaped, because viewers render embedded HTML. The characters Markdown acts on are backslash-escaped. With brackets escaped, no link or image can form.

This is a fixed engagement template. The report builder with editable templates is Week 72.

Retest is a short workflow on the Issue. - Requested. A developer marks the Issue ready for retest. - Passed. A tester confirms it fixed, and the Issue becomes fixed. It reopens as "reintroduced" if anything reports it again. - Failed. A tester reproduces it and must write a note; the Issue stays open.

For a scanner's Issue, the next scan or upload is the retest. The shared Issue writer (repo.apply_reimport_plan) decides any requested retest: "still reported by…" or "no longer reported by…". These outcomes are outbox events in the same transaction, not audit entries, because they are a scan's results rather than a person's decision. Undoing the upload undoes the outcome.

A targeted retest re-runs one check at one location. - A rule. Check out the default branch afresh, copy only the Issue's file to an empty directory at the same path, and run only the tool that found it, in its usual sandbox with the whole repository's language context. The Issue is still present if a finding has its fingerprint, or if the same rule fires on the same file. - A DAST template. Run only that Nuclei template, or ZAP's passive baseline keeping only that alert, against that one URL. This happens only if ownership verification still passes, and goes through the campaign egress proxy.

A run has its own row (retest_runs), never a scan, so it cannot become "the latest scan" or close another Issue. It runs on the worker, or in the API process when there is no worker. It is not offered for an Issue only a person or an imported report found.

Notes are plain text, threaded one level deep. - @mentions resolve to the organisation's live personal tokens by handle (the name lowercased, punctuation trimmed). Each person mentioned gets an outbox event and finds the note under Mentions. An edit announces only people newly added. - Only the author edits or deletes. Deleting keeps the row, so replies stay in context, but removes the body and the files. - Files on notes use the evidence store: content-sniffed, encrypted with OpenBao, downloaded only through a short-lived signed link.

The attachments origin is enforced. With BULWARK_ATTACHMENTS_ORIGIN set, that host serves only signed downloads, and only those: everything else there is a 404. The API's own host refuses those downloads, and no response on the files host sets a cookie. Without the setting, downloads come from the API host, which sets no cookies either; the separate origin is defence in depth for a file someone opens anyway.

Tags inherit downward. A tag on a portfolio applies to its projects, and a project's tags apply to its Issues; an Issue's own tags are added on top. A project now belongs to at most one portfolio, through a new assets.portfolio_id. Inherited tags are shown with where they come from and are changed there. The issues table filters by a tag wherever it was set, in SQL.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• "Another person" is another API token until Week 75: a lead, a tester and a mention are names.
  • An Issue a person or a targeted retest confirmed fixed leaves the issues table and the fix-first queue, even though the last scan's rows still list it.
  • Mentions are found by reading the organisation's notes. That is fine at this size but is not indexed.
  • A targeted retest of a rule that depends on other files (cross-file analysis) sees only the one file. For the per-file rules Bulwark ships, that is the same answer as a full scan.
  • Notifications for mentions and retests are outbox events only. Delivering them to Slack, email and an in-app inbox is Weeks 65–66.

docs.title: ADR-0049: Rules run on the outbox, conditions are Rego, and bulk or chained actions stop for a person
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-06), Week 65 (plan §45, threat T26; the plan's ADR-020). Builds on the outbox (plan §41.1, every domain event written in the same transaction as its change), the OPA policy gate (policy.md, core/policy/opa.py) and ADR-0048 (people are personal tokens until Week 75).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Plan §45: "automation teams configure without writing code" -- WHEN an Issue is found, IF it is P1 in a payments project, THEN assign it, set its priority, file a ticket, notify a channel. Threat T26 names what goes wrong: loops, mass closure and runaway fix requests. Since Week 54 every change has written an outbox event, but nothing read the outbox.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Rules read the outbox. A dispatcher (core.dispatch, every ten seconds on the worker) hands each batch of new events to its subscribers -- the rules engine now, notifications next week -- and then marks the batch dispatched. Delivery is at least once; one organization at a time, under a Postgres advisory lock held on a connection of its own (a session's connection can change at each commit). Migration 0037 marks every event already waiting as dispatched, so the first rule does not fire on a month of history. A rule never fires on events from before it was created.

Triggers are Issue events (found, back, fixed, assigned, retest requested or decided), SLA due soon and breached, a risk acceptance expiring within seven days (announced once each by the expiry sweep) or expired, a scan or import completing, and two the sweep fires without an event: no completed scan or import for N days (once per quiet stretch) and schedules (hourly, daily or weekly, UTC, once per slot). "Advisory matched" arrives with the advisory engine (Week 68).

Conditions are Rego, evaluated by the OPA the policy gate already uses: one policy language. A condition is the body of one rule, written against input.issue, input.project and input.event; Bulwark wraps it in a fixed module and evaluates a whole batch in one opa eval (hits contains i if { some i, item in input.items; match with input as item }), so a scan's five hundred new Issues are one process, not five hundred. The condition is untrusted code even from an Admin: http.send, net.lookup_ip_addr and opa.runtime are removed from OPA's capabilities, the network allow-list is empty, opa runs with an empty environment and a ten-second limit, and a condition may not declare its own package or imports. A field with no value is absent from input, never filled with a guess.

Actions: assign (to a person's @handle), set a priority band, add tags, mark ready for retest, request a verified fix, and notify. A band set by hand or by a rule is stored apart from the computed one (issues.priority_override) and wins wherever a band is read -- the issues table, the SLA when it is by priority -- and no recomputation clears it. That is how a rule "applies a stricter SLA": named per-Issue SLA policies were not built. Ticket and group actions come with ticketing (Week 66). Each action reports per subject whether it changed something, changed nothing, was skipped or failed, with why; one failing does not stop the others. notify sends one message per run, not one per Issue.

Safety (T26). - Dry run. "Test this rule" replays the last seven days of the trigger's events (or the current state, for the sweep's triggers) through the condition, without acting: "would have matched 37 issues; 1 of its 4 runs would wait for an Admin". It reads each Issue as it is now, and says so. - Bulk confirmation. Matches are grouped by cause: the scan or import that caused them, else the event type, project and minute. A cause that would have a rule act on more Issues than its threshold (25 by default, 1 to 1,000) applies nothing: the run is held, and an Admin applies or dismisses it. Later matches from the same cause join the held run. - Depth limit. An event a rule caused carries the chain's depth; a rule set off at depth 3 does not run and a depth_limited run says so. An action that changes nothing announces nothing, so a rule cannot re-fire itself on its own no-op. - Idempotence. Each run records the (event, subject) pairs it handled; a redelivered batch is recognised and never acted on twice. - AI budget. A fix request is refused when the organization's monthly token budget is spent, or when the rule already requested max_per_day (default 3, at most 20) fixes in the last day. - Admins only. Writing, testing, enabling and deleting rules and deciding held runs need the new rules:write scope. Reading rules and runs is scans:read. - Audit. Every rule change is a hash-chained entry with the whole definition and a new version; every run is one too (rule.run.applied, .held, .confirmed, ...), and each change a rule makes to an Issue is its own entry by rule:<id>, which the Issue's history names.

Runs have their own table (rule_runs): rule and version, cause, depth, status, the subjects, the event keys and each action's result. A run is committed before it acts, so an action that fails rolls back only its own work, never the record that the run happened. Deleting a rule keeps it and its runs, and dismisses its held runs.

Amended 2026-10-12 (load test). A run whose actions only change Bulwark's own rows (assign, priority, tag, retest, group) applies them in one transaction with its audit entries and its result (repo.audit_in_one_commit), each action in a savepoint: a failing action still undoes only itself, and its audit entry goes with it. Before, every change and every audit entry was its own commit, which held one dispatcher to about 520 events a second; now about 880. A run with a ticket, a fix request or a notification still commits per action: those reach outside, or commit on their own.

OPA ships in the app image, pinned to the release CI uses and checked against its published SHA-256 for amd64 and arm64.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rules act seconds after the event (the dispatch interval), not inside the transaction that caused it. A crash between acting and marking the batch only means the batch is seen again.
  • "Admin" is a token scope until roles exist (Week 75).
  • The dry run's count is today's view of last week's events; an Issue fixed since still counts.
  • Grouping by minute is a heuristic: a burst of SLA crossings in one sweep is one cause, but two unrelated assignments in the same minute in one project share a cause too. That only affects when confirmation is asked for, not whether an action runs twice.
  • Rule evaluation latency at p95 under load (plan §60) was not measured this week.

docs.title: ADR-0050: Notifications by kind and channel; tickets with one owner per field; groups on one ticket
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-06), Week 66 (plan §49, §45, §55.7). Builds on ADR-0049 (the outbox dispatcher, rules), the Week 51 integrations (core/integrations, one-way filing and status metadata) and ADR-0048 (mentions as outbox events, people as tokens).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Plan §49 asks for watchers and "notification preferences per event and per channel (in-app, email, Slack, Teams, webhook), with a daily digest option so notifications don't become noise", and for "ticketing sync with Jira and GitHub Issues in both directions. Issue groups map to one ticket. Status mapping is configured per project. For each field, one side is the source of truth (status from the ticket, severity from the platform) instead of last-writer-wins." Week 64 left mentions and retests as outbox events nobody delivered. Week 51 could file a ticket per new Issue and record a ticket's open or closed state, but never acted on it. §55.7 asks for a rules editor with a Rego view, "Test this rule", and a template gallery.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Two audiences, two sets of channels. A person hears through the in-app inbox and email; the team through the organization's Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams and outbound webhook together. For each kind of event each channel is off, instant or in the daily digest, at the hour the person or team chose (UTC). A missing preference is the default -- in-app instant and email in the digest for people; instant for the team, which is what every organization already had -- so a new kind needs no migration. The existing team notifiers (scan summaries, SLA crossings, risk acceptances, a rule's notify) ask one gate first: instant sends as before and now to Teams too, digest stores the line, off drops it.

Who hears what is decided from the outbox, by a second subscriber to the dispatcher: mentions to the person mentioned; new notes, retests, SLA crossings and ticket status changes to the Issue's watchers (and its assignee); assignments to the assignee; risk acceptances to the named approver and then the requester; a held rule run to every person who can confirm it. Taking part makes you a watcher (assigned, mentioned, wrote a note, asked for a retest), and anyone can watch or stop. The person who caused something is not told about it. Each notification is written once per (person, event, kind), so a redelivered batch never notifies twice.

Text is plain everywhere. The inbox renders text; email is text/plain with header values stripped of line breaks; a notification's title is collapsed to one line, so an issue title cannot add an email header or fake a line in a digest. Slack text is escaped and Discord mentions are off (Week 65); Teams cards escape the Markdown characters that make links and emphasis.

Email goes through the operator's SMTP server, configured for the deployment (BULWARK_SMTP_*) because it is a server the operator runs or rents, not something an organization should point anywhere. No host: email is off and the settings page says so; digest items that cannot be sent are marked skipped, not retried forever. An address is stored per person, set by that person; the audit log records that it changed, not what it is.

Tickets: one source of truth per field. A project's ticket settings name Jira (project key) or GitHub Issues (repository), using the organization's stored credentials. - Summary, severity, description: Bulwark's. Severity is a bulwark-severity-* label; labels someone added by hand are kept (Jira by add/remove verbs, GitHub by merging). A sync writes only when what Bulwark owns changed (a digest of what it last pushed). - Status: the ticket's, by default. Each ticket status maps to nothing or to "ready for retest" (defaults: Jira's done category and GitHub's closed -> ready for retest; closed (not planned) -> nothing). Bulwark never marks an Issue fixed because a ticket closed: a scan, a targeted retest or a tester decides, as before. When the Issues on a ticket are all fixed or one comes back, Bulwark comments. A project may instead give the status to Bulwark: then it closes and reopens the ticket (Jira by status category, so no per-workflow transition ids) and ignores what the ticket says. - Assignee: the ticket's, shown on the Issue, never written. Mapping Jira or GitHub accounts to Bulwark people waits for real user accounts (Week 75). Changes arrive by the existing webhooks and by a poll every ten minutes of tickets not synced for ten minutes, so a Bulwark that Jira cannot reach still syncs. Every call to Jira passes the SSRF guard first (its address is an operator setting, now also checked when saved); GitHub is always api.github.com. A project with ticket settings is no longer filed issue by issue by the Week 51 path.

Groups. An Issue belongs to at most one group in its project. Filing a grouped Issue files the group: one ticket titled with the group's name and count, a link row for each member; an Issue that joins later is added to the same ticket with a comment. Rules gain "put in a group" and "file or update its ticket", and notify can name people.

The editor writes Rego. Trigger, condition and action builders produce the condition's Rego lines; the Rego view shows them inside the fixed module OPA runs, and editing there makes the condition hand-written -- the builder takes over again only if every line is one it can show. "Test this rule" runs the server's dry run on the unsaved draft, and OPA's own errors appear by the condition with the condition's own line numbers. The gallery ships nine whole drafts, each with what it still needs from you; a test saves every one.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Jira and GitHub were exercised only against responses in their documented formats, never a live site; that is recorded as unproven until a real site is used.
  • Teams' Workflows webhook format follows Microsoft's documentation; nothing was posted to Teams.
  • "A person" is still a token: one person with two tokens has two inboxes.
  • The digest is per person or team, once a day; there is no weekly digest and no per-project routing of team channels.
