  • The §49 calendar (engagements, SLA due dates, expiring risk acceptances) was added after this week as a read of existing data (core/calendar.py, GET /v2/calendar, the Calendar page): no table of its own, and SLA dates the same as the issues table's because both compute them from the policy in force.

docs.title: ADR-0051: The component inventory -- one row per library, SBOMs by source, versions in each ecosystem's order
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-06), Week 67 (plan §46.1). Builds on the Week 40 SBOM summary (core/sbom/syft.py, Scan.sbom_summary), the Week 52 import path (ADR-0040) and reachability v1 (core/reachability).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Plan §46.1: "Every package from every SBOM (Syft for native scans, uploaded CycloneDX or SPDX for imports), stored per asset per scan by package URL (purl) and version. That answers the question every team asks the morning a big CVE drops: 'where do we use this?' ... Index on purl so this answers in under a second across the whole organization." Until now each scan kept its SBOM as one JSON blob for the Dependencies screen, and an imported CycloneDX or SPDX file without a vulnerabilities section was read, counted and thrown away.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A library is one row per organization (libraries): its ecosystem plus its name as that ecosystem compares names -- PEP 503's normal form for PyPI, lower case for npm, exact for Go and Maven -- so Flask_Login and flask-login are one library. Names are kept the way OSV writes them (Maven as group:artifact), so Week 68's advisories find a library by the name an advisory gives.

A component is a library at a version in one project's SBOM from one scan or import (components), with the manifests it was found in, whether it is a direct dependency, its license, and -- for Bulwark's own scans -- whether the application's code imports it (reachability v1, the same verdict dependency findings already get: yes, no, or "can't tell", never a guessed no). Each row says which SBOM it came from: scan for Bulwark's scans, test:<id> for files imported into a Test. current marks each source's latest SBOM, decided from the database (the source's newest scan by time), so two scans finishing out of order, or an import being reverted, leave the right one current. Older rows stay with their scan as history and go when the scan goes.

What is recorded: the SBOM of a completed full scan of a project's real state (a pull-request scan describes code that may never merge -- the same rule as Issue history), and every CycloneDX or SPDX file imported, with or without vulnerabilities. Packages cross the parser sandbox as a bounded list the API re-checks, like findings. Projects scanned before this week are filled in from their latest SBOM by an hourly task; files imported before it cannot be, because their uploads were deleted once applied.

Versions are compared the way the library's ecosystem orders them (core/versions.py): PEP 440 through packaging; for Maven the algorithm of Maven's own ComparableVersion, read off Maven 3.9.16's bytecode; and for npm and Go, semver read as leniently as osv-scanner reads it (its osv-scalibr parser: 1.2 is 1.2.0, 19.03.0 is 19.3.0, 9.6.0b1 is a prerelease), because OSV's own npm and Go data hold such versions and Week 68's matching must agree with osv-scanner on them; for strict semver the order is semver 2.0.0's. Each is tested against the real implementation -- 2,518 pairs compared by maven-artifact 3.9.16 and 6,000 by npm's semver 7.8.5, out of 34,017 and 6,000 checked during development with no disagreement. A PyPI version that is not PEP 440 (latest), or a library of an ecosystem not yet supported, is reported as "could not be compared" and counted neither in nor out. Week 68's range matching uses the same keys, so the search and the advisory engine cannot disagree.

The search (GET /v2/components?purl=&version=<2.17.1) finds the library by its key, counts its current versions with one indexed aggregate (ix_components_library_current), checks each distinct version against the condition once, and only then reads the matching rows. It answers with the projects, their business units, how many are internet-facing (the project's priority context; "not set" said separately) and how many import the library from application code. Listing libraries (GET /v2/libraries, the search box) reads each library's project and version counts, kept as SBOMs are recorded and recounted hourly, so it never aggregates every component.

Amended in Week 68 (ADR-0052): a PyPI version that is not PEP 440 is no longer "could not be compared" but ordered as setuptools' legacy versions, before every PEP 440 version, as osv-scanner orders it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Speed, measured (scripts/bench-components.py): 1,000 projects, each with two SBOMs of 1,500 libraries (3,000,608 component rows, 1,500,305 current; 40,001 libraries), on Postgres 16 under forced RLS as an application role. Every search the screen makes answered in under 30 ms at the 95th percentile -- "log4j-core <2.17.1" across 211 projects in 5.9 ms at the median. Recording an SBOM of 1,500 libraries took about 0.3 s at first, growing to about 0.75 s by 3M rows.
  • "Imported by application code" is reachability v1: Python and JavaScript only, and an import is not a call to the vulnerable function. Go and Maven components say "can't tell". Imported files say nothing about it either.
  • The counts in the library list can lag behind a deleted project by up to an hour; the search is always exact.
  • Only PyPI, npm, Go and Maven versions are compared. Other ecosystems are stored and searchable by name, and every version condition on them is reported as not comparable.

docs.title: ADR-0052: The advisory engine -- OSV's data, osv-scanner's matching, impacts kept, Issues in one click
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-06), Week 68 (plan §46.2, §55.5). Builds on ADR-0051 (the inventory and core/versions.py), ADR-0040 (imports and reimport) and ADR-0050 (groups, tickets, notifications).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Plan §46.2: "Ingest OSV (every ecosystem), GitHub Security Advisories, CISA KEV additions, and NVD on a schedule. Match by purl and version ranges, using OSV's range semantics (SEMVER, ECOSYSTEM, GIT). Getting range matching right is the hard part; test it against osv-scanner on the same SBOMs. Each new advisory produces an impact view (§55.5): affected assets, reachability, owners, and one-click creation of Issues grouped by advisory. Global deduplication by library: one advisory affecting 30 repositories becomes one Issue group with 30 Occurrences, not 30 unrelated rows."

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Sources. OSV's per-ecosystem data for PyPI, npm, Go and Maven -- which carries GitHub's reviewed advisories, the PyPI and Go databases and the OpenSSF malicious-package reports, so GitHub needs no token -- CISA's KEV catalog, and CVEs NVD changed recently (its public API, no key, requests spaced for its 5-in-30-seconds limit). The first OSV run reads the ecosystem's all.zip; later runs read modified_id.csv newest first down to the last change seen and fetch only those records. Fetches go to three fixed HTTPS hosts, certificates verified against certifi's bundle, sizes bounded; a failing source is recorded on its feed state and the rest carry on. Every six hours on the worker. Advisory data is public and shared by all organizations (no org_id, no RLS); a KEV download with fewer than 100 entries never replaces the catalog.

One vulnerability, one key. OSV publishes the same vulnerability under several ids (GHSA-x, PYSEC-y, CVE-z as aliases). vuln_key is a record's lowest CVE alias, else its lowest id or alias; OSV aliases are symmetric, so the records of one vulnerability share it, as osv-scanner's groups do. Everything an organization sees is per vuln_key.

Matching follows osv-scanner, and where it does not, the ecosystem. OSV's evaluation: a range's events in version order, the last at or below the version decides. Versions in each ecosystem's order (ADR-0051). Where osv-scanner behaves in a particular way the data depends on, Bulwark does the same, each found by comparing the two: - npm and Go versions read leniently (osv-scalibr's semver parser), because OSV's data has 19.03.0, 2.62 and 9.6.0b1; - PyPI versions that are not PEP 440 in setuptools' legacy order, before every PEP 440 version; - an affected entry with a GIT range is matched by its explicit versions list alone. Where osv-scanner departs from the ecosystem's own definition, Bulwark keeps the ecosystem's: Maven versions as Maven 3.9.16 orders them (9.0.0-M1 is 9.0.0.M1), a PyPI version in the versions list when PEP 440 says it is equal (6.0.0 is 6.0), and Go module paths in their real case. Each of these means Bulwark reports a vulnerability osv-scanner misses, never the reverse; the cross-check (scripts/osv-crosscheck.py, docs/evaluation-advisory-matching.md) lists every one. A version or range that cannot be compared is kept as "may be affected" (certain = false), never dropped.

Impacts are kept, not searched. advisory_impacts holds each vulnerability at each library version in each project's current SBOM, with the fixed version that applies. Matching runs for what changed: after an SBOM is recorded (for that project only, in its own transaction after the inventory commits, so a failure never undoes the inventory), and after a feed update (for the changed vulnerabilities, every record sharing their key, in every organization; everything when more than 5,000 changed). Only rows whose answer changed are written. An impact no longer true is resolved, and reopens if it comes back.

"Each new advisory produces an impact view." The first time a vulnerability affects an organization, an advisory_states row and an advisory.matched outbox event: the team channels (a new team notification kind, advisory) and each affected project's owner hear of it once.

The impact view (§55.5) -- the vulnerability, KEV status, and for each project: version, fix, whether its code imports the library (reachability v1), owner, exposure, and its Issue. Projects whose code imports the library come first. "Not by application code" is as far as the words go: the screen never says code is unreachable.

Issues in one click. Creating Issues marks the vulnerability adopted. Each affected project then holds an "Advisories" Test whose content is, at every moment, a finding per adopted vulnerability per affected library version -- imported through the ordinary path, so the Issues deduplicate with osv-scanner's for the same package and CVE, and close when a later SBOM no longer has an affected version (a scan's evidence, never a ticket's), and reopen if it returns. In each project the Issues of one vulnerability form an issue group named after it, so a project with ticket settings gets one ticket; the project's owner is assigned. "One Issue group with 30 Occurrences" is, in Bulwark's model, one vulnerability with an Issue in each of 30 projects, grouped per project for tickets and gathered on one impact view.

Owners. A project has an owner: a person (until user accounts, Week 75, a personal token), set by @handle on the project page.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Only PyPI, npm, Go and Maven. The plan says every ecosystem; others are a matter of a version order each (Cargo, NuGet, RubyGems, Packagist are next).
  • Reachability is v1, import-level, Python and JavaScript only. Only Go's database names vulnerable functions; call-path evidence per advisory is not attempted.
  • Malicious-package records (222,000 of npm's 230,000) are stored and matched: a project that has one sees it as critical.
  • NVD is used only for the CVSS and description of CVEs whose OSV records carry none; its API without a key is slow by design (a page per 6.5 seconds).
  • "Draft VEX for the others" (§55.5) is Week 69.

docs.title: ADR-0053: VEX drafted from code evidence and confirmed by a person; compliance as cited data; evidence an auditor can check
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-06), Week 69 (plan §46.3, §47, §55.5). Builds on ADR-0052 (advisories and impacts), ADR-0019 (the audit log and its Rekor checkpoints) and ADR-0046 (SLAs and risk acceptance).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Plan §46.3: record why a dependency Issue is "not a risk" in OpenVEX's vocabulary, export OpenVEX and CycloneDX VEX, and propose vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path "with the call-graph evidence attached, and a person confirms it". §47: mappings as versioned data that cite their source, an ASVS benchmark per project, and an evidence pack whose audit-log extract an auditor "can check instead of trust". M15: "VEX exports carry call-graph evidence."

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
What the evidence can be. Only Go's vulnerability database names the vulnerable functions (931 of OSV's Go records; none of its PyPI, npm or Maven records). So there are two kinds of evidence, and they are labelled as different things:

  • symbols (Go): at scan time Bulwark parses the project's Go source (tree-sitter; never built or run) and keeps, per imported package, the names the code uses from it, and every method or field name it selects anywhere (code_usage). A Go vulnerability is proposed as not in the execute path when no vulnerable function of any affected package is referred to. Matching is by name and deliberately over-inclusive -- any .Next( counts as a call of Tokenizer.Next, a dot-import's bare names count, a local variable named like a package counts -- because a false "not executed" is the error that matters. An import whose bound name cannot be told from its path (Go rejects unused imports, so no candidate being used means the name is unknown) makes the answer "can't tell".
  • imports (Python, JavaScript, and Go records naming no functions): reachability v1 says the package is declared but not imported by application code, or only by tests.

"Call-graph evidence" in the plan is therefore, for Go, use of the vulnerable functions in the application's own code; neither kind follows calls into other dependencies, and both say so in the statement. No evidence, no proposal: Maven, uncertain versions, malicious packages (their code runs at install), projects never scanned by Bulwark.

A proposal is not a claim. "Draft VEX for the others" writes vex_statements in state proposed; nothing is exported until a person confirms it, with a personal token (the shared token could be anyone). Confirming marks the matching Issue not a risk with the justification; reopening that Issue withdraws the statement. A rejected proposal is not proposed again until a later scan changes the evidence. Every step is audit-logged.

Exports. One statement per vulnerability per library version in the project's current SBOM: a confirmed statement (not_affected, its justification, the evidence and its limits in impact_statement, who confirmed it), else an Issue dismissed with a justification (or with only a reason, exported as the impact statement), else affected with the fix, or under_investigation when the version could not be compared. A confirmed statement the latest scan contradicts is exported as under_investigation, never as still true. OpenVEX v0.2.0 and CycloneDX 1.6; the justification mapping is Bulwark's own (neither specification defines one), and CycloneDX statements keep the OpenVEX value and the evidence in properties.

Compliance as cited data. One file per framework in core/compliance/frameworks/, each with its source, version, terms and a mapping version; each control maps to kinds of evidence Bulwark holds. OWASP Top 10 and ASVS reuse OWASP's own data already shipped (CC BY-SA 4.0). PCI DSS, ISO 27001 and SOC 2 are copyrighted: requirement numbers and Bulwark's paraphrases only. Every surface says a mapping is not a certification.

ASVS: only a person says "met". Without a person's status a requirement shows what the evidence shows -- failed in an assessment, open Issues of its CWE, passed an assessment ("tested", not "met"), or not assessed. The absence of findings is never shown as a control working. A person's "met" that the evidence contradicts is flagged.

The audit log becomes per-organization without being split. It stays one chain (a split would need a re-hash of history). Version-2 entries (migration 0041 onwards) put the organization inside the hash through a body digest: entry_hash = SHA256("2"|seq|prev_hash|body_digest), body_digest = SHA256(canonical JSON of timestamp, org, actor, action, target, payload digest). An organization's extract shows its own entries in full and everyone else's as (seq, prev_hash, body_digest, entry_hash): every hash is recomputed, nothing of another organization is revealed but that an entry exists. Version-1 entries (no organization recorded) are shown as hashes and can only be checked by link.

Evidence packs. A zip: the PDF, evidence.json, the audit extract (reaching to the first Rekor checkpoint after the period, so the period is anchored when one exists), each checkpoint's Sigstore bundle, verify.py (standard library only: manifest hashes, the chain, the checkpoints' positions) and manifest.json, signed with the deployment's cosign key when BULWARK_EVIDENCE_SIGNING_KEY is set; marked unsigned otherwise, and never produced unsigned when signing was asked for and failed. Checkpoints can go to a private Rekor (--rekor-url) and be verified offline against its trusted root.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• VEX proposals are only as good as name-based evidence in the application's own code; their precision is measured by the blind review the plan asks for (scripts/vex-review-kit.py), which needs a person and real projects and has not been done.
  • Only vulnerabilities the advisory engine knows (PyPI, npm, Go, Maven) appear in exports.
  • The audit chain's version-1 entries can never be attributed to an organization; extracts over them are weaker, and say so.
  • Evidence packs are built in the request: 3 s for 100,000 Issues on a laptop; a deployment with millions of Issues needs them on the worker.
  • Downgrading migration 0041 leaves version-2 entries that a version-1 verifier cannot check.

docs.title: ADR-0054: Metrics from summary tables refreshed on ingest, every one defined, measured at one million Occurrences
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-06), Weeks 70–71 (plan §48.1, §48.2, §60). The plan calls this "ADR-021"; that number was already taken by ADR-0021. Builds on ADR-0013 (forced RLS), ADR-0046 (SLAs and risk acceptance) and ADR-0052 (advisory impacts).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Plan §48.1: dashboards read "materialized views refreshed on ingest", and every metric has "a written definition". §55.4: every number opens the Issues behind it, and a percentage always shows its counts. Week 70: a synthetic dataset with one million Occurrences, with widget latency measured. The budget, from §60 and the task, is 300 ms at the 95th percentile for every widget.

Computing a dashboard from Occurrences on page load fails twice. It is too slow at this size, and each widget would calculate "open" its own way.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Ordinary tables, not materialized views. Postgres materialized views cannot have row-level security, and REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW rebuilds every organization at once. Every v3 table is under forced RLS (ADR-0013), so the summaries are ordinary tables with the same tenant_isolation policy. They are refreshed one project at a time by the application, as bulwark_worker. Migration 0042 creates six:

Table One row per Holds metric_open_issues open Issue band, severity, priority score, first seen, SLA deadline metric_issue_days project × day × band opened, fixed, total time to fix, risk opened and fixed metric_sla_days project × deadline day × band met, missed, still open past deadline, exempt metric_asset_status project last full scan, scanners that ran of those that applied metric_components library × project vulnerabilities, known-exploited ones metric_dirty project (or "components") when it was marked

Their organization foreign key cascades. They are derived data, and deleting an organization must not need to know about them.

One meaning of "open". An Issue is open when a scan or import still reports it (new, open or reintroduced), nobody has marked it not a risk, and no risk acceptance is in force. A row's band is the band set by hand if there is one, else the computed one. core.metrics.rollup is the only code that applies these rules, and every metric reads its output.

Refreshed on ingest, and marked automatically. An after_flush listener marks a project dirty whenever anything it touches changes in a session: an Issue, an SLA policy, the project itself, or a scan. Advisory impact changes mark the organization's components. The mark is written in the same transaction, so code that changes Issues cannot forget to mark them. A mark records when it was made. A refresh clears only marks made before it read the project, so a change made during a refresh stays dirty. What is dirty is refreshed:

  • straight away, after a full scan completes (core.pipeline) and after an import is applied (core.imports.jobs). This is "refreshed on ingest";
  • every 120 s on the worker (bulwark.refresh_metrics) for everything else, such as triage, priority changes and SLA policy edits;
  • for every project of every organization once an hour (bulwark.refresh_metrics_all). An acceptance that expires changes what is open without changing any row;
  • on demand with bulwark metrics refresh [--org].

A project is rebuilt from all of its Issues in one pass. That takes 50 ms for a project of 1,250 Issues, and it is simpler to reason about than incremental deltas. Each response carries pending_refresh, the number of projects waiting, so a stale number is labelled as stale.

One source of definitions. core/metrics/definitions.py holds the twelve metrics, each with its name, written definition, unit, whether the date range applies, and the table it reads. The API serves the definitions to each widget's title, and docs/metrics.md is generated from the same file. A test fails if the two differ.

Every number is traceable. Each metric returns its value with the counts behind it ("195 of 214"), plus rows or a weekly series. Each row carries a drill-down: the filter that GET /v2/metrics/issues uses to list the Issues behind it, one page at a time.

Filters. Portfolios, projects, a tag, and a date range of up to 731 days (90 by default). A tag selects whatever carries it, following the same inheritance rule as tags themselves: tagged projects, projects in tagged portfolios, and tagged Issues. Metrics that read per Issue honour all three. Metrics that read per project and day honour project and portfolio tags only, and their notes say so.

docs.title: Measurement
docs.text:
scripts/bench-metrics.py seeds an organization inside Postgres using generate_series:

  • 200 projects in 10 portfolios, each with 1,250 Issues: 250,000 Issues;
  • 4 scans per project, each finding every Issue: 1,000,000 Occurrences;
  • a year of history, about half of it fixed, 5% marked not a risk;
  • SLA policies, tags on 2 portfolios and on 1% of Issues;
  • 2,000 libraries, 150,000 advisory impacts, 5,000 advisory states;
  • risk acceptances and engagements.

It then runs VACUUM ANALYZE, refreshes every project as the worker would, and times every metric 20 times (after a warm-up) under five filter variants, plus the first page of Issues behind a number. The results are in benchmarks/metrics/one-million-occurrences.json. They were measured on an Apple M5 with 16 GB, against Postgres 16.15 in Docker, connected as bulwark_worker under forced RLS.

Seeding took 32 s. Refreshing all 200 projects took 13.3 s, and one project 0.05 s.

Milliseconds, p50 / p95:

Metric No filter Portfolio Project Project tag Issue tag open_issues 13.9 / 15.4 3.6 / 4.5 2.0 / 3.1 5.6 / 6.0 18.6 / 29.4 sla_adherence 11.5 / 15.4 5.4 / 7.6 2.6 / 3.6 34.4 / 39.4 3.1 / 13.6 mttr 68.2 / 79.7 8.6 / 9.0 3.2 / 4.5 60.3 / 76.8 3.2 / 3.9 new_vs_fixed 10.3 / 11.8 4.5 / 5.5 4.1 / 4.6 40.6 / 44.4 3.1 / 5.3 open_risk 27.3 / 29.4 8.3 / 9.5 5.6 / 8.9 13.7 / 14.8 18.7 / 29.0 backlog_age 30.8 / 32.2 34.7 / 39.5 4.7 / 6.2 56.3 / 62.1 87.5 / 99.1 past_sla 8.3 / 9.1 5.0 / 5.7 3.9 / 5.1 7.0 / 9.4 27.5 / 39.4 scan_coverage 1.8 / 2.0 1.4 / 1.5 1.1 / 1.2 1.9 / 2.0 2.8 / 4.5 vulnerable_components 2.7 / 3.0 2.4 / 2.6 2.1 / 2.2 3.0 / 3.4 3.8 / 15.5 expiring_acceptances 14.6 / 16.2 3.3 / 3.6 1.0 / 1.0 6.0 / 6.2 2.7 / 4.7 engagement_status 1.7 / 2.1 1.1 / 1.2 1.0 / 1.2 1.6 / 1.8 2.7 / 13.4 advisory_impact 23.8 / 31.5 12.8 / 16.0 12.3 / 13.6 21.0 / 23.7 3.5 / 6.5 The Issues behind a number (first page, P1) p50 / p95 open 1.7 / 1.8 past_sla 1.8 / 3.8 fixed 116.7 / 123.6

Every widget is within the 300 ms budget. The slowest metric is 99 ms at p95 (backlog age with an Issue tag). The slowest request overall is 124 ms: the Issues fixed in a period, which reads the live issues table because no summary row holds individual fixed Issues.

These timings are for the query layer: query.compute and query.issues in the worker's session. HTTP and JSON add a few milliseconds for responses this small. The browser's own budget, a widget drawn within 300 ms of its data arriving (§60), is checked separately in the Weeks 70–71 verification.

What the benchmark changed. The first full run found three problems:

  1. Advisory impact took up to 634 ms with a project filter, even on a small dataset. It checked each impact against lists of 500 vulnerability keys at a time. It is now a single join with advisory_states, which Postgres hashes.
  2. The Issues behind a number took up to 294 ms. Under RLS, Postgres cannot estimate a join on assets (org_id = current_setting(...) is one row as far as it knows), so it walked every Issue of the organization to fetch 51. The drill-down now looks up Issues by id, gets project names separately, and passes the organization's projects as a list. The result is 2 ms for open Issues and 124 ms for fixed ones.
  3. That first run was taken while autovacuum was still working through the newly loaded tables. Its numbers ran up to 238 ms for metrics that take 62 ms on a table at rest. The benchmark now runs VACUUM ANALYZE first (without parallel workers, since Docker's default 64 MB /dev/shm is too small for them). A real database is mostly at rest, but a large import followed by an immediate dashboard load can see the slower numbers for a few minutes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A dashboard number can be up to two minutes behind a triage change (one beat interval), and up to an hour behind an acceptance expiring. pending_refresh shows when that is happening. Scans and imports are reflected as soon as they finish.
  • Twelve metrics share one meaning of "open". A new metric reads the summary tables, gains a definition and a section in docs/metrics.md, and gets a row in the benchmark.
  • Refreshing a project costs one pass over its Issues. A 20,000-Issue project would take about 1 s per refresh, still fine for the worker. If projects grow much larger than that, incremental updates become worth their complexity.
  • The summary tables are in the RLS test (tests/integration/test_metrics_rls_docker.py). Each one is seeded for one organization and must be invisible to another, and the test fails for each table when its policy is removed.
  • Reproduce the benchmark with: python scripts/bench-metrics.py --projects 200 --issues 1250 --out results.json, with BULWARK_BENCH_OWNER_URL and BULWARK_BENCH_APP_URL pointing at a Postgres database at the current migration.

docs.title: ADR-0055: Reports rendered by sandboxed Chromium in the worker, signed, shared by revocable links
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-07), Week 72 (plan §48.3). Builds on ADR-0054 (metrics), ADR-0053 (compliance mappings, cosign signing of evidence packs) and ADR-0013 (RLS).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Plan §48.3 asks for:

  • reports built from blocks (cover, executive summary, metric widget, issue table, issue detail, risk acceptances, compliance mapping, engagement scope, appendix), with templates and schedules;
  • PDFs rendered with headless Chromium, signed with cosign, and shared through links that expire and can be revoked;
  • an executive summary the model can draft, "labelled as AI-written and edited before sending".

The existing PDFs (scan reports, evidence packs) use ReportLab, whose built-in fonts are Latin-1 only.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Chromium, in a container, in the worker. - A report is one self-contained HTML document. Every value is escaped, and the page's own CSP allows only its inline styles and data: images. - Chromium's headless shell prints it to PDF in a container with: - no network; - a read-only root filesystem; - all capabilities dropped and no new privileges; - the image's non-root user; - limits of 1 GB memory and 256 processes. - Chromium's own sandbox is off because it needs privileges the container withholds, so the container is the sandbox. - Even if a scanned Issue title contained live HTML, it would print as text, and nothing could load or post anything. - The image is mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.63.0-jammy, pinned by digest: the version the web tests already pin, and already present wherever the Playwright tests run. - Only the worker may start containers (in Compose the API has no Docker access, by design). So the API queues a run (report_runs.status = queued) and the worker renders it. A failure is recorded on the run, never retried in a loop. Schedules run in the worker anyway.

Signed like evidence packs. - Each PDF is kept as generated, with its SHA-256. - When BULWARK_EVIDENCE_SIGNING_KEY is set, cosign signs the PDF itself, offline with no transparency log, the same as evidence packs. The bundle is downloadable next to the PDF and next to any link.

Links: a token, only its hash, no RLS on that one table. - A link is 256 random bits, shown once, with its SHA-256 stored in report_links along with its expiry (at most 90 days) and revocation. - report_links carries no RLS, for the reason api_tokens carries none (migration 0007): following a link is what tells Bulwark the organization, so the lookup cannot need it first. - The row holds no report content. Every other query filters by org_id in code, and the PDF is read from report_runs, under forced RLS, only after the link has set its organization. - Opening a link is counted and audit-logged. Responses are no-store, noindex and no-referrer.

The summary: drafted from numbers, reviewed by a named person. - The model is a new gateway task, report, routed and budgeted like the others. It sees each metric's value and counts, and at most five Issue titles per table, scrubbed of anything that looks like a secret and wrapped as untrusted data. - The draft is stored as source: ai with the model's name. The server owns those fields; a save from the browser cannot claim a review. - Generating, by hand or on a schedule, is refused until a person confirms the summary with a personal token. - The PDF prints "Drafted by AI (model) from this report's data; reviewed by (name) on (date)."

Schedules email a link, not a file. - Weekly or monthly, at an hour in UTC, to at most 20 recipients. The link lasts what the schedule says (default 14 days). - The beat task runs every five minutes. - Without SMTP or BULWARK_API_PUBLIC_URL, the report is still generated, and its run records why nothing was sent.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• PDFs render Unicode, and reports look like the screens (the same CSS shapes, inline SVG bars). Rendering a four-page report takes about half a second on a warm Docker daemon.
  • A deployment needs the renderer image (3.2 GB, mostly the browsers Playwright ships), pulled once by the worker. A slimmer image holding only the headless shell would be smaller. That is future work, and BULWARK_PDF_IMAGE already allows it.
  • The issue-table block takes the metric filters (portfolio, project, tag, period, priority). Saved views of the Issues table are kept in the browser (web/lib/saved-views.ts), so a report cannot use them yet. That needs server-side saved views (plan §56, Week 73).
  • A report shows the data as of when it is rendered, not as of the end of its period: "the last N days" is a moving window. The appendix says what each number counts.

docs.title: ADR-0056: One query language, parsed twice; pages by cursor; counts exact or a true lower bound
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-07), Week 73 (plan §56). Builds on ADR-0054 (the org's projects as a list, not a join) and ADR-0013 (RLS).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Plan §56: "v3 organizations have tens of thousands of issues. The filter experience decides whether the product is usable at that size." It asks for a grouped filter panel, chips, filters in the URL, saved views, and

  • a query language for experts, with autocomplete (priority:P1 sla:breached project:payments-* -status:accepted), where "the panel and the query stay in sync: changing either updates the other";
  • cursor-based pagination on the server;
  • "counts above 10,000 shown as estimates ('about 48,000') instead of slow exact counts".

Until now each project had its own Issues table, paged by offset (/assets/{id}/issues), and nothing listed Issues across projects.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A small, written-down language. Terms separated by spaces: key:value[,value...], -key:value to exclude, "quoted values", * in project, business unit and path, dates as an age (>30d) or a day (>=2026-01-01, or a range a..b), and free words matched against the title. Fifteen keys, a few aliases (sev, prio, bu, owner, state). No OR between keys and no parentheses: the panel cannot show them, and the panel and the query must say the same thing. Errors carry the span of text at fault, so the query bar underlines it.

Parsed twice, on purpose, held together by shared cases. core/search/language.py is the authority: the API parses q and runs it. web/lib/issue-query.ts is its twin, so the browser can keep the panel and the query in step as you type, underline mistakes and know which key autocomplete is in, without a request per keystroke. The two cannot drift silently: both run every case in tests/fixtures/issue_query_cases.json (31 queries with their filters, canonical text, or error span), in pytest and in vitest. A query is always written back in one canonical order (the panel's group order), so "panel to query to panel" is lossless.

With no status in the query, the list is the active queue (status:open: untouched, or accepted with the acceptance run out), as the per-project table always was.

Pages by keyset cursor. A page ends with an opaque cursor: the sort, the last row's key and its id. The next page starts strictly after it. Ties break on the id in the same direction as the key, so one index on (key, id) serves an order both ways. Migration 0045 adds those indexes (priority as coalesce(priority_score, -1), first seen, last seen). A cursor from another order, or one that does not decode, is a 422 that says to start again.

Counts: exact while quick, else "more than 10,000". This is where the build departs from the plan's letter. Postgres's row estimate (EXPLAIN) was tried first, and on these filters it was off by 2 to 7 times: "about 24,000" for 100,000 Issues, "about 30,000" for 60,000. An estimate that far off misleads more than no number. Exact counts, on the other hand, took 65-225 ms even at 500,000 Issues. So: exact up to 10,000 (a capped count); past that, the full count runs inside a savepoint with a 200 ms statement_timeout. Done in time, it is exact; not, the response says {"value": 10000, "exact": false, "at_least": true} and the list says "more than 10,000", which is always true. The time limit is set and restored inside the savepoint, so nothing else in the request is cut short.

The org's projects as a list. Project and business-unit filters are resolved to project ids in Python (globs match a label or its last part, so payments-* matches acme/payments-api), and the query filters issues.asset_id IN (...), as the metrics layer does: a join on assets under RLS cannot be estimated and walks every Issue.

SLA state across projects. Each project has its own policy. Projects that share a policy are grouped and get one SLA clause per group, so a hundred projects on the starter policy cost one clause, not a hundred.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• At 100,000 Issues (twice the plan's 50,000), every page with its count is under 115 ms and every count is exact (benchmarks/issues/search-100k.json). Page 25 costs what page 1 does.
  • At 500,000 Issues a page alone is 6-64 ms, but free text is slow (0.24 s a page, 0.52 s with the count). Under row-level security Postgres applies a non-leakproof predicate such as LIKE only after the policy, so no index can serve "the title contains": a trigram index was built and measured, and the planner did not use it. Free text therefore scans the organization's matching Issues. A search index outside the RLS boundary would fix it; not needed at the plan's scale.
  • Spans count code points in Python and UTF-16 code units in the browser. They differ only for characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji), and only the browser underlines.
  • assignee: takes a person's handle or name, me (a personal token only: the shared token is nobody) or none. A name nobody has matches nothing rather than failing, so a saved view keeps working after someone leaves.

docs.title: ADR-0057: Saved views as named queries; bulk changes previewed, count-checked and undoable
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-07), Week 73 (plan §56). Builds on ADR-0056 (the query language) and follows the dashboards' sharing model (Week 71).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Plan §56 asks for saved views "personal or shared with a role", a column chooser and density "remembered per person", and "bulk actions across pages ('Select all 1,204 matching'), with a preview of the effect first (principle 9) and Undo for 10 seconds on reversible actions. Irreversible actions, such as risk acceptance, go through their own flow."

Until now saved views lived in each browser's localStorage, one project's filters at a time (web/lib/saved-views.ts), so a report could not use one (ADR-0055), and bulk triage worked on the rows ticked on one page of one project.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A saved view is a name for a query. It stores the query (written back canonically, so panel and query-bar views look the same), the sort and, optionally, columns. A query that cannot be parsed is refused with its span, never stored. Sharing copies the dashboards' rules exactly: the owner edits; a role it is shared with sees it read-only and can copy it; the shared token, being nobody in particular, sees and edits all; a save names the version it started from and a stale one is refused. Six views are built in ("Assigned to me", "Past their SLA", ...), read-only and copyable. assignee:me means whoever is looking, so one shared view serves a whole team.

Browser-saved views are imported once, by the browser. Only the browser knows the old views and which project each belonged to, so it turns each into a query (project:<name> plus its filters) and sends them together. The import is all or nothing; a name already taken gets "(imported)"; a view identical to one the person has is skipped, so importing twice adds nothing.

Table settings are a small per-person record (person_prefs, keyed by table): which columns, in what order, and the density. Not audit-logged: it changes only how one person's table looks.

A report's issues block can show a saved view, as it is when the report is generated, with me meaning the report's owner. The editor must be able to see the view when they pick it; a block left as it was is not re-checked, so unsharing a view never locks a report. A deleted view makes the block say so, as a deleted Issue already does.

Bulk changes: preview, then apply with the count the person saw. A selection is a query, optionally narrowed to Issues picked by id (an id that does not match, or is another organization's, is simply not selected). The preview counts what would change, what already is as asked, and what is left alone and why, by project and severity, in one sentence. Applying sends expected_count, the preview's selected count; if the list changed since, nothing is changed and the new count comes back (409). At most 10,000 Issues a batch.

Reversible actions: assign or unassign, mark not a risk (with a reason each Issue keeps), reopen, add or remove a tag. One transaction writes every changed Issue, one audit entry per Issue (the same action names a single change writes, so each Issue's history shows it), one for the batch, and, for assignment, the same issue.assigned events rules listen to. The audit entries are chained in one commit (repo.stage_audit_entries); if another append takes the same sequence numbers meanwhile, the whole change is rolled back and run again.

Undo restores only what is still as the batch left it. The batch keeps each changed Issue's previous values (issue_batches). Undo, by the person who made the change, puts back those Issues that nobody has changed since and says how many it left alone. The screen offers it for 10 seconds; the server allows 5 more for a slow network.

Left alone, with the reason: Issues under a risk acceptance (that is decided in its own flow), fixed Issues for assign and not-a-risk, and dependency Issues carrying a VEX justification for reopen: reopening those withdraws their VEX statement, which Undo could not put back, so they are reopened one at a time.

Risk acceptance is never a bulk change. It needs a second person (principle 10) and is made per project, so "accept" is preview-only: it groups the selection by project (up to 500 Issues each, the acceptance limit) and the screen opens each project's request form with them. Applying it is refused.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• At 100,000 Issues, tagging one business unit's 6,000 open Issues took 122 ms to preview, 708 ms to apply and 977 ms to undo, on Postgres under forced RLS (benchmarks/issues/search-and-bulk-100k-2026-10-07b.json).
  • A bulk assignment of thousands raises thousands of issue.assigned events, as thousands of single assignments would; rules and notifications see each one.
  • An Undo that comes too late is refused with what to do instead: another bulk change.
  • Saved views and table settings are per organization (forced RLS, migrations 0046 and 0047).

docs.title: ADR-0058: Accounts with scoped roles; OIDC and SAML through checked libraries; SCIM; a guest database role
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-07), Week 75 (plan §51). This is the plan's "ADR-022". Builds on ADR-0013 (RLS between organizations) and ADR-0018 (scoped tokens).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Until now a person was an API token pasted into a browser tab, and each person picked their own role (lead, engineer, tester) for their home page. Plan §51 asks for OIDC sign-in with PKCE and strict issuer, audience and nonce checks; SAML 2.0 "through a maintained library only", tested against signature wrapping, NameID comment injection and unsigned assertions; SCIM provisioning and deprovisioning "so someone leaving the company loses access within minutes"; and organization roles with per-portfolio and per-project overrides that cascade, proved by a two-project variant of the two-tenant test.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accounts. A user belongs to one organization and has an organization role: admin, member, viewer, or none (only what is granted). Overrides give a higher role on a business unit (reaching its projects) or one project. They only raise access, as DefectDojo's product permissions do; to give a contractor one project, their organization role is none. Roles become the token scopes the API already checks, so each route keeps its one require_scope(...): for a person, the scopes are those of their role on the project the path names (project, scan, Issue, acceptance, engagement, import, ...), else of their organization role. Organization-wide changes need an organization role; someone limited to some projects can read only the project list, the cross-project Issues list, saved views and their own things. A token a person makes acts as them, within its scopes and their role when it is used. Users are user:<id> actors everywhere people were (assignment, mentions, approvers); tokens from before accounts keep working as before.

Sessions. A sign-in creates a session: an HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure cookie with a random secret, stored as its SHA-256; 12 hours at most, 2 hours idle. A change made with a session needs its CSRF token in X-Bulwark-CSRF, which only this site's pages can read (/auth/session, over CORS with an explicit origin list and credentials). Signing out, turning someone off and SCIM deprovisioning end sessions at once. Evidence files are served with a sandboxing CSP, so a file that runs script on the API's host cannot use the cookie.

OIDC is ours on PyJWT: the protocol is small and the checks are the point, so they are written out and tested one by one (asymmetric algorithms only; exact issuer; audience and azp; expiry and issue time with a minute's skew; the nonce; PKCE S256; one-time state; HTTPS to the provider except on this machine). The provider's own description is read when it is saved and must name the issuer configured.

SAML is pysaml2 with xmlsec1: assertions must be signed, unsolicited responses are refused, and audience, destination and validity are pysaml2's checks. Bulwark never reads a SAML response itself. The attack tests assert why each forgery is refused, so a test cannot pass on an unrelated error.

Who signs in is decided by the provider's stable subject (OIDC sub, SAML NameID), linked to the account on the first sign-in: a second account at the provider with the same email cannot take someone's place, and an email changed at the provider does not move them. The email must be in one of the provider's domains and verified (OIDC), unless the provider is trusted for emails (Entra ID sends no email_verified). A first sign-in creates the account only when the provider is set to.

SCIM (/scim/v2/Users) takes only a token with the scim scope, made for the provider and belonging to no one. New people are viewers unless the provider sends a role. active: false or DELETE turns the person off in the same request; DELETE also hides them from the provider while keeping them for the audit trail, and provisioning them again restores the same account.

Projects a person may not see are hidden by Postgres, not only by the app. Their requests run as the bulwark_guest role (SET LOCAL ROLE), whose restrictive RLS policies on assets and every table that names a project -- directly, or through an Issue, a scan, an engagement or an engagement test -- keep only the projects in app.project_scope. The service roles may switch to it but do not inherit it (WITH INHERIT FALSE, SET TRUE, Postgres 16), because a policy applies to every role whose privileges a session has.

docs.title: Alternatives tried
docs.text:
• The same restrictive policies for every session ("all projects, or this list"). Postgres estimated that such a policy let 2 of 200 projects through, and plans through assets collapsed: at a million Occurrences the organization-wide "past SLA" metric went from a 7 ms median to 224 ms (its list of the ten most overdue Issues took 666 ms under EXPLAIN ANALYZE). Limited to the guest role, the policies cost nothing for everyone else.
  • JIT compilation. Turned off per transaction: on large counts it took 116 of 153 ms, and it was costing every large count before this week too (counting 100,000 Issues: 93 ms with, 44 ms without).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Postgres 16 or later from migration 0048. xmlsec1 in the API image and in CI.
  • Google Workspace, Entra ID and Okta are covered by standard OIDC (and Entra's missing claim by the trust setting), but only Keycloak was signed in through here.
  • A person limited to some projects cannot make organization-wide changes, including bulk changes on the cross-project Issues list; on their own projects' pages they can.
  • The first admin is made with bulwark users add --role admin, or by the shared token.
  • The WebSocket for live scans authenticates with a pasted token only; signed-in browsers fall back to polling, which the scan page already does.

docs.title: ADR-0059: An MCP server that acts as the person, labels untrusted text, and is read-only by default; /fix on pull requests, previewed, capped and never for forks
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-08), Week 76 (plan §50, threat T29). Builds on ADR-0027 (the verified-fix agent), ADR-0017 (the GitHub App) and ADR-0058 (people and scoped roles).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Plan §50 asks for two ways for agents to use Bulwark:

  • an MCP server with list_issues, get_issue (with the taint path and evidence), get_verified_fix, search_components and run_scan: "read-only by default, token-scoped and tenant-scoped under the same RLS", with snippets "wrapped and labelled as untrusted data" (T29);
  • /fix, a pull request comment that runs the verified-fix agent on the issues the pull request introduced, for organization members with Member or higher, "never on pull requests from forks (the pull_request_target lesson)", with the estimated cost shown before anything is spent.

The v2 rules still hold: the model never originates an Issue outside the Hypotheses lane, never changes a status without a person, and never runs without a budget.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The MCP server is a client of the API, not a second door to the database. bulwark mcp (stdio, the official Python SDK) calls the API with the person's personal token, read from BULWARK_MCP_TOKEN and never from the command line. Every rule the API enforces -- scopes, the role on each project, the guest database role, RLS -- applies unchanged, and nothing about tenancy is reimplemented. The deployment's shared token is refused: an agent must be someone. Ids are checked before they become a path, redirects are not followed, and a non-local API must be https, so the token goes nowhere but the configured address.

Read-only by default. Four tools read. run_scan is offered only when the server is started with --allow-scans and the token may write scans. No tool triages, accepts, closes or approves.

Untrusted text is labelled, default-deny. Every value in a result is wrapped as {"untrusted_text": ...} unless its key is one Bulwark sets (ids, severities, dates, counts) and its value looks like one; a key that is not an identifier (a file path used as a key) becomes a {key, value} pair with the key wrapped. Inside a wrapper, characters that hide or reorder text are shown as <U+XXXX>, terminal escapes as <ESC ...>, and long text is cut with a note. Each result says in one sentence what the wrapper means. Tool descriptions describe; they never address the agent. This informs the agent; it cannot stop one, which docs/mcp.md says plainly.

/fix is a two-step conversation on the pull request. /fix (the whole first line of a new comment) gets a preview: up to five findings this pull request introduced (new in the pull request scan, code, secrets or configuration -- a dependency bump is not a patch), the token cap (BULWARK_FIX_TOKENS_PER_FINDING per finding), its price when one is configured, and the budget left. Nothing runs. /fix confirm <code> starts one verified-fix run per finding; /fix cancel <code> withdraws it. A code works once and for 24 hours, and a new preview replaces the old one.

Who may. GitHub says who wrote the comment and how they relate to the repository (author_association: owner, member or collaborator, not contributor). Bulwark says what they may do: an admin links a GitHub login to a person (only an admin, since a person naming their own login could name someone else's; unique per organization without case), and that person's role on the project must be Member or higher. Both are checked on the preview and again on the confirm, with the pull request itself (open, not from a fork, head still the previewed commit), the budget, and the concurrency limit. A fork is refused outright: the agent runs the pull request's code (scanners, and tests when enabled), which must not happen with the base repository's credentials. The organization comes from the App installation; a comment from an unknown installation never creates one (a pull_request event still does, as in ADR-0017).

A pull request run needs no approval and writes nothing to the repository. The workflow's pull request mode skips the approval wait and the "open a pull request" step, and posts the verified patch -- or why there is none -- as a comment. People apply it. The run has no Issue (a pull request scan mints none), so verified_fix_runs.issue_id becomes optional and a run names its request and finding instead; a CHECK keeps one of the two set, and the guest policy reaches such a run through its request.

Every model token is budgeted. Found while building this: the fix agent counted its tokens but never charged them to the organization's monthly budget. Each attempt now checks the budget first and charges what it spent, and the run stops at its cap, checked before each model call (the last call can pass the cap by its own size, never more). The worker's activities now act for the run's organization; under forced RLS they could not see their own run before, so on Postgres every write was silently dropped.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An agent sees exactly what its person sees, and gets labelled text it can choose to treat as data.
  • /fix costs a person two comments and gives them the price before any spend.
  • New schema (migration 0050): users.github_login, scans.github_head_sha, pr_fix_requests (forced RLS, guest project policy), and the verified_fix_runs changes above.
  • The GitHub App also subscribes to the "Issue comment" event; its existing pull requests (read and write) permission covers reading the pull request and commenting -- docs/fix-on-pull-requests.md.
  • Not proven: a real GitHub App delivering a comment, and a real model (none is configured here). The live check used the real worker, Temporal, Postgres and Bandit, with the model scripted and GitHub's API recorded (docs/v2-week76-verification.md).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
A scan is six steps, in order:

  1. Run. Each scanner (Bandit, Semgrep CE, Gitleaks, Trivy, OSV-Scanner, and any third-party plugin an organization has allowlisted) runs in its own container: --network=none --read-only --cap-drop=ALL --user=10001 --memory=2g --pids-limit=256, with the target repository mounted read-only. A scanner never sees the network or the host, and never sees another scanner's output.
  2. Normalize. Every tool's own output format is parsed into one canonical Finding -- core/models/finding.py -- with a location, a taxonomy, a native severity and a fingerprint. Adding a new built-in scanner is "one ToolAdapter subclass", not a new pipeline.
  3. Correlate. Findings that are really the same underlying issue, reported by more than one tool, are merged: the same dependency plus a shared advisory id (SCA), or the same file, weakness family and nearby lines (SAST). Every contributing tool's evidence is kept; the highest severity among them wins.
  4. Map. Each finding is mapped to its CWE(s) and OWASP Top 10:2021 category.
  5. Rank. A 0-100 risk score combines severity with EPSS (the probability of real-world exploitation in the next 30 days), CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and, for Python/JavaScript dependencies, whether the vulnerable package is actually imported.
  6. Show and export. Web UI, API, CLI, and downloadable SARIF, HTML and PDF reports -- all reading the same stored findings, none of them a separate code path that could disagree with the others.

docs.title: Why findings are redacted before they're ever stored
docs.text: A scanner's own output can itself leak a secret -- Bandit's hardcoded-credential rules (B105-B107) echo the offending source line in their message, for instance. Every adapter either redacts at the source or has its output passed through core/redact.py, which withholds the snippet and scrubs quoted literals for anything near a detected secret, before a Finding is ever written to storage.

docs.title: Tenancy
docs.text: Every persisted row that belongs to an organization is additionally protected by Postgres row-level security with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY -- not just an application-level WHERE org_id = ... that a future query could forget. This is the same pattern used for issues, retention settings, the plugin allowlist and integration credentials alike.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Risk scoring -- exactly how the 0-100 score and its EPSS/KEV/reachability inputs combine.
  • Taxonomy -- how a finding's CWE maps to an OWASP Top 10:2021 category.
  • Reachability -- what "reachable" means for a dependency finding, and its limits.
  • Writing a plugin -- adding a scanner outside this list, without forking Bulwark.
